T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Only 2 papers name agro-pastoral systems, and neither gives a size [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. The parkland fodder statement is a review citing earlier work, and the US silvopasture statement is from a rich country and names water infiltration, not a drought loss [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. No finding in this row measures the benefit in a severe or extreme drought, and none compares the same farm with and without trees.

justification.mechanism: In agro-pastoral systems the two papers that name this system both point to a small reduction in drought impact, the same small benefit given for mixed crop-livestock systems, while the overall agroforestry drought row is conflicting. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In the United States, silvopastures are credited with better water infiltration rates [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9].

justification.statement: agroforestry reduces the impact of drought (strength not quantified in the evidence) in BFA, MLI, NER, USA; no measured evidence at severe or extreme drought (limited evidence, high agreement → medium confidence; transfer: in_context).

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: The rating is conflicting because the types of agroforestry disagree: trees and shrubs regenerated on cropland show a strong reduction in drought losses, general findings not tied to one type show a small one, and planted tree-crop alleys, shaded tree crops and silvopasture each have studies on both sides. Few of the benefit findings say how large the effect is. The clearest harm finding is a direct field measurement in Ghana: during the extreme drought of 2015/16 all cocoa plants under Albizia ferruginea shade trees died and cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality, while cocoa in full sun kept higher sap flux and soil water content was higher in full sun, pointing to competition for water between shade trees and cocoa [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. What separates the sides is mainly system and severity: deep-rooted trees in dryland fields and fodder trees in pastures read as buffers, while in shaded tree crops under extreme drought the trees compete with the crop for scarce soil water. Trade-offs pull the other way, now with more direct field evidence: in a semi-arid Kenyan growing season that received only 317 mm of rain, maize under dispersed Grevillea robusta trees yielded 0.02 t/ha against 1.53 t/ha in unshaded sole maize, a near-total loss under the trees in a dry season [ev_crop_yield_lott09_4]. In semi-arid Brazil, in a low-rainfall year, maize yielded very little whether or not it was grown among alley-cropped trees, with no significant difference between the two systems — the drought year erased the tree benefit rather than reversing it [ev_crop_yield_martins13_2]. A Senegal review finds no clear consensus on windbreak hedges in drought, with some studies reporting higher yields in drier years and others harm to rainfed crops [ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17]. The understorey yield benefit holds in drought years only, since tree shade can lower understorey yields under normal rainfall, and the Kenyan household link to perceived drought held in Burat but not in Kinna [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5]. Several findings are stand-ins or ratings rather than measurements: the Canadian and US findings are high-income evidence, and the FMNR finding is a practitioner rating [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The German soil-water difference was not significant everywhere and is high-income evidence, and the Nyando timber-sales finding is farmer-reported [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. The parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. The Latin American silvopastoral findings are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees, and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The Ethiopian Faidherbia result is a drought-year comparison reported as an 'up to' figure; the same study reports its normal-season gain separately, so this hazard-year gain is not the usual yield effect [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In shaded cocoa and coffee the evidence is split: a review cites that under warmer, water-limited conditions competition between trees and cacao for scarce soil water can reduce soil moisture and cacao yields below those of open-sun farms [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8]; and in the Ghana experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced yield decline and only partly compensated for it [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the Ethiopian study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in the extreme climate shocks [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]; and across cabruca cocoa farms in southern Bahia, Brazil, drought yield loss was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2]. Apart from the Ghana field study, these harm findings are second-hand readings in reviews. The cocoa and coffee findings are crop-specific and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; the Ghana shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. The Argentine multi-site study is the clearest statement of why severity matters: it explicitly frames the switch from facilitation to competition as a function of drought intensity, and shows the sign of the effect also depends on site aridity and on whether the stocking system is native-forest or planted silvopastoral, so it cannot be read as a single transferable number [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_6, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1]. The French walnut-pea result is a cushioned loss, not an absolute gain: agroforestry pea yield remained below the full-sun yield in both rainfall regimes, and the smaller drought-specific loss is a relative measure against each system's own rainfed baseline, from a single season and site with the two conditions not randomised within the parcel [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3]. Both of these are upper-middle-income Argentina and high-income France, sitting at a different distance from the low- and lower-middle-income target than the Kenyan and Ethiopian evidence already in this row. A multi-species silvopasture trial on degraded rangeland in arid India adds a further measured harm result on the pastoral side: understorey herbage yield fell further under drought beneath every tree and shrub species than in the treeless control, which the authors attribute to shading and competition for soil moisture; the same trial measured the trees also supplying extra dry-season browse fodder, a trade-off kept separate here rather than netting off against the herbage loss [ev_drought_hazard_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_2]. This Indian evidence is lower-middle income, inside the low- and lower-middle-income target. In the Senegal shrub trial the soil next to the shrubs dried faster during the imposed drought than soil far from them in two of three subplots, even as the millet yield gain held; that trial is a single site and a single shrub species [ev_soil_moisture_bogie18_2, ev_crop_yield_bogie18_1].

justification.mechanism: The studies disagree. Most findings say agroforestry reduces drought losses, but the result splits by type of agroforestry, and several measured results show no benefit or harm, especially in severe or extreme drought. On the benefit side: in Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, farmers said deep-rooted trees reach water from deep down and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind; the study concludes that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought, citing deep root systems that use a greater soil volume for water [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10, ev_t3_drought_roots_quandt17_2, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. Trees also share deep water: hydraulic redistribution in Sahelian parklands lets crop roots use deep soil moisture reached only by tree roots [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3]. In a Senegal field trial, pearl millet grown among the native shrub Guiera senegalensis under an imposed in-season drought produced almost 10 times the biomass and over seven times more panicles than millet where the shrubs had been removed [ev_crop_yield_bogie18_1]. In an induced drought in eastern Canada only the monocrop lost yield, and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Nyando District, Kenya, households in an agroforestry project typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods, and many farmers reported selling fuel wood and timber from their trees to buy food during the drought [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25% [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. Live fences of species such as Gliricidia sepium and Leucaena leucocephala supply livestock fodder in the dry season, when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. For shaded coffee and cocoa: in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest, the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly raised coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; and reviews cite a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season and low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11]. In a 25-year-old walnut-based alley-cropping system in southern France, winter pea still yielded less under the trees than in the full-sun control under both rainfall regimes, but the yield drop caused specifically by an imposed spring drought was smaller under the trees: full-sun yield fell 22% under drought while the alley-cropped yield rose by 12 to 20% relative to its own rainfed baseline, which the authors attribute to drought shifting yield formation from the shade-sensitive pod-set stage to grain filling [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3]. In a multi-site Argentine study of tree-covered pasture (silvopastoral systems) against treeless grassland, the normal-year forage benefit reversed under severe drought at some sites: at the semi-arid Santiago del Estero site the relative response swung from +2% in normal years to -89% in a dry year, while at the humid Chaco site it swung the other way, from -15% to +26%, and in the semi-arid aridity category overall there was no significant difference between systems in either normal or dry years — a result the authors attribute to tree-forage competition for water overtaking facilitation once drought intensity passes about 35% rainfall reduction [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_6].

justification.statement: agroforestry drought: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE across sub-practices in ARG, BFA, BRA, CAN, COL, CRI, DEU, ETH, FRA, GHA, HND, IND, KEN, MEX, MLI, NER, NIC, SEN, USA; the measured evidence also includes no-benefit or reversal results under drought, which discount the class; at severe or extreme drought the measured results mostly show no benefit (3 gain vs 4 failures); only 6 of 33 units in this direction say how big the effect is, so the class is capped at moderate; measured HARM (maladaptation) in 7 sources — the practice worsened this outcome for some adopters (robust evidence, medium agreement → medium confidence; transfer: in_context). CLASS SET BY SUB-PRACTICE VOTE: the family rows disagree (cross_family=low, planted_silvoarable=conflicting_evidence, regeneration_farmland=very_high, shaded_perennial=conflicting_evidence, silvopastoral=conflicting_evidence), so the roll-up states conflicting evidence rather than the pooled low.

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.mitigation_mechanism: The studies disagree. Most findings say agroforestry reduces drought losses, but the result splits by type of agroforestry, and several measured results show no benefit or harm, especially in severe or extreme drought. On the benefit side: in Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, farmers said deep-rooted trees reach water from deep down and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind; the study concludes that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought, citing deep root systems that use a greater soil volume for water [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10, ev_t3_drought_roots_quandt17_2, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. Trees also share deep water: hydraulic redistribution in Sahelian parklands lets crop roots use deep soil moisture reached only by tree roots [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3]. In a Senegal field trial, pearl millet grown among the native shrub Guiera senegalensis under an imposed in-season drought produced almost 10 times the biomass and over seven times more panicles than millet where the shrubs had been removed [ev_crop_yield_bogie18_1]. In an induced drought in eastern Canada only the monocrop lost yield, and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Nyando District, Kenya, households in an agroforestry project typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods, and many farmers reported selling fuel wood and timber from their trees to buy food during the drought [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25% [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. Live fences of species such as Gliricidia sepium and Leucaena leucocephala supply livestock fodder in the dry season, when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. For shaded coffee and cocoa: in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest, the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly raised coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; and reviews cite a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season and low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11]. In a 25-year-old walnut-based alley-cropping system in southern France, winter pea still yielded less under the trees than in the full-sun control under both rainfall regimes, but the yield drop caused specifically by an imposed spring drought was smaller under the trees: full-sun yield fell 22% under drought while the alley-cropped yield rose by 12 to 20% relative to its own rainfed baseline, which the authors attribute to drought shifting yield formation from the shade-sensitive pod-set stage to grain filling [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3]. In a multi-site Argentine study of tree-covered pasture (silvopastoral systems) against treeless grassland, the normal-year forage benefit reversed under severe drought at some sites: at the semi-arid Santiago del Estero site the relative response swung from +2% in normal years to -89% in a dry year, while at the humid Chaco site it swung the other way, from -15% to +26%, and in the semi-arid aridity category overall there was no significant difference between systems in either normal or dry years — a result the authors attribute to tree-forage competition for water overtaking facilitation once drought intensity passes about 35% rainfall reduction [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_6].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: This is a high-income scope row: all units come from Canada, Germany, the USA or temperate settings, outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. The Canadian result is reported second-hand in an IPCC chapter, which also notes N-fixation declined in both systems, the German soil-water result is a component measure that was not significant at all positions, and the US unit is a background statement that does not mention drought [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. No unit says how large the effect is, and none measures it in a severe or extreme drought. The French result adds a fourth high-income unit to this scope row: a single season and site, drought imposed experimentally with rainout shelters, and the two conditions not randomised within the parcel; the benefit is a smaller drought-specific loss, not a yield advantage over full sun [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: The understorey benefit holds in drought years only; the same review says tree shade can lower understorey yields under normal rainfall [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. The Nyando units rest on income and coping strategies as proxies for drought impact, and the timber-sales finding is farmer-reported rather than measured [ev_household_income_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_2]. None of the three units puts a size on the drought benefit, which is why the strength is not quantified [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Set against this, a reversal is measured directly in Kenya: in a growing season that received only 317 mm of rain, maize under dispersed Grevillea robusta trees yielded 0.02 t/ha against 1.53 t/ha in unshaded sole maize, a near-total loss [ev_crop_yield_lott09_4]. In semi-arid Brazil, in a low-rainfall year, maize yielded very little whether or not it was grown among alley-cropped trees, with no significant difference between the two systems — the drought year erased the tree benefit rather than reversing it [ev_crop_yield_martins13_2]. The Kenyan household link to perceived drought held in Burat but not in Kinna, and one Kenyan unit only states that agroforestry has been proposed for resilience rather than measuring it [ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. The Lott and Martins findings state sizes in the harm or null direction; most of the gain-side units still describe mechanism, household perception or an induced-drought trial outcome without a size, which is why the class is capped at moderate. The Lott and Martins findings are measured field results from lower-middle-income Kenya and upper-middle-income Brazil, closer to the LIC/LMIC target than the Canadian and German evidence, which is high-income temperate evidence from a single season or trial each; the French result is a cushioned loss (alley-cropped yield stayed below full sun) rather than an absolute gain [ev_crop_yield_lott09_4, ev_crop_yield_martins13_2, ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_crop_yield_blan22_2].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Studies disagree, and what separates the sides, as far as the evidence says, is twofold. First, whether the shade trees draw on the same scarce soil water as the crop: the losses, including the Ghana die-off, are attributed to that competition [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1, ev_crop_yield_watts22_8], while the gains come with a named companion tree (Gliricidia) or a shade-management setting (canopy openness) [ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]. Shade-tree species, density and canopy management are therefore the design questions; in the Ghana study the outcome differed by shade-tree species, total loss under one and heavy loss under the other [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. Second, a higher yield under shade is not the same as protection from drought: the Ghana experiment found the better performance of cocoa under shade can only partly compensate for the reduced yield during drought episodes [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. The Ghana experiment's shade came from artificial shade nets, not shade trees, so it has no below-ground competition and its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. All units are crop-specific (cocoa or coffee) and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop. The Ghana die-off was measured in an extreme drought; most other units do not say how severe the drought was [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]. justification.mechanism: Under drought, shade over cocoa and coffee has been found to protect the crop, to compete with it for water, and to make no difference. On the protective side, in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly raised coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; a review cites a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season (Lin 2006) [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8]; and another cites low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia (Schwendenmann et al. 2010; Köhler et al. 2010) [ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11]. On the competing side, the strongest measurement is a Ghana field study of a cocoa plantation through the extreme 2015/16 El Niño drought: all cocoa plants under the shade tree Albizia ferruginea died, cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality with sap flux density cut to 115 g cm2 day1 against 170 in full sun, sap-flux recovery afterwards was 163 in full sun against 37 under Antiaris, and soil water was higher in full sun, which the authors link to strong competition for soil water [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. A review adds that under warmer, water-limited conditions tree-cacao competition can push soil moisture and cacao yields below open-sun farms (Blaser et al. 2018) [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8]. Between them sit no-effect findings: in a Ghana rainwater-suppression experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced yield decline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the Ethiopian study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in the extreme climate shock [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]; and across cabruca cocoa farms in southern Bahia, Brazil, drought yield loss was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: The evidence splits by drought severity and which forage layer is measured, rather than agreeing on one direction. On the benefit side, the Colombian and Argentine forage and milk gains above hold up to around the authors' dry-year threshold [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1]. On the harm side, the same Argentine study found the benefit reverses under severe drought at some sites: at semi-arid Santiago del Estero the relative forage response swung from +2% in normal years to -89% in a dry year, at the humid Chaco site it swung the other way (-15% to +26%), and in the semi-arid aridity category overall there was no significant difference between systems in either normal or dry years — the authors attribute the reversal to tree-forage competition for water overtaking facilitation above about 35% rainfall reduction [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_6]. A multi-species silvopasture trial on degraded rangeland in arid India adds a second harm result: understorey herbage yield fell further under drought beneath every tree and shrub species than in the treeless control, attributed by the authors to shading and competition for soil moisture, though the same trees supplied extra dry-season browse fodder not counted in that herbage comparison [ev_drought_hazard_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_2]. What separates both sides is drought intensity and which forage layer is counted: below a site-specific dry-year threshold, or when browse is counted alongside grass, silvopasture holds or gains; once drought crosses that threshold, or when only understorey herbage is counted, tree-grass competition for scarce water dominates and the system does worse than open pasture. The Latin American silvopastoral units are mostly earlier studies cited in a Spanish-language review and a CATIE edited volume rather than new primary measurements; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees, and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The clearest primary magnitudes (Argentina, Colombia, India) are upper-middle or lower-middle income, and the US unit is high income, so the row as a whole transfers only as adjacent [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_drought_hazard_singhrao08_1].

justification.mechanism: In silvopastoral systems, the benefit runs through fodder availability and herd condition during drought. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant through intense drought while grass monoculture biomass fell to a quarter [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in the lowest-rainfall year in several decades milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which is said to reduce seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. A US silvopasture study lists better water infiltration among silvopasture's services, used here as a soil-water component of drought [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. In a multi-site Argentine study, forage production under trees exceeded treeless grassland or pasture at drought intensities at or below the authors' dry-year threshold, and held up in very humid areas in both normal and dry years, a result corroborated by a companion reading of the same sites [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: None of this evidence can set the class. Every comparison is against the unmanaged state rather than the farming-system counterfactual this cell asks about. justification.mechanism: In Vietnam, a review citing Nguyen et al. 2013 reports that farms with trees were less affected by an extreme flood that caused heavy crop losses in the region [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_11]. In Isiolo County, Kenya, households said trees planted in a line stop soil being swept away by water, and the study concludes that agroforestry builds livelihood resilience to floods [ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6, ev_t3_flood_conclusion_quandt17_11]. In Nyando District, Kenya, farmers reported that tree roots prevented extensive soil erosion and soil fertility loss during the floods, and some had fruit from their trees as their only steady food when other crops were underwater or washed away [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_1]. The same review also reports, citing Eychène et al. 2014, that in Mesoamerica coffee-based agroforestry can help prevent flood occurrences, reducing the adverse impact of extreme rainfall events [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.mitigation_mechanism: In Vietnam, a review citing Nguyen et al. 2013 reports that farms with trees were less affected by an extreme flood that caused heavy crop losses in the region [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_11]. In Isiolo County, Kenya, households said trees planted in a line stop soil being swept away by water, and the study concludes that agroforestry builds livelihood resilience to floods [ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6, ev_t3_flood_conclusion_quandt17_11]. In Nyando District, Kenya, farmers reported that tree roots prevented extensive soil erosion and soil fertility loss during the floods, and some had fruit from their trees as their only steady food when other crops were underwater or washed away [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_1]. The same review also reports, citing Eychène et al. 2014, that in Mesoamerica coffee-based agroforestry can help prevent flood occurrences, reducing the adverse impact of extreme rainfall events [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: The Vietnamese unit is cited second-hand and gives no size for the protective effect; the 40% figure it carries is the regional crop loss rather than the effect of trees [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_11]. The Nyando flood units are farmer-reported, from interviews and focus groups, and enter through soil erosion and food supply as components of flood impact [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_1].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: The measured evidence is not uniformly positive. In Senegal, windbreak hedges were reported to generally cause a slight rise in temperature in protected plots rather than cooling, with effects varying by crop and growth stage [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. A modelled sensitivity analysis under Faidherbia albida in Ethiopia found that without applied nitrogen fertiliser, the cooling under tree shade produced no yield response at all, because yield was limited by nutrients rather than heat [ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. No finding in this row measures mitigation under a severe or extreme heat event; the quantified cooling and livestock-productivity figures come mostly from pastoral and tree-perennial systems across Latin America, West Africa and China, spanning low- to high-income countries, with only a minority of sources set in the low- and lower-middle-income countries this scoping tool targets. The parkland heat-hours figure is a review citing an earlier study of two named tree species [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_1]. The cocoa statement is second-hand and gives no size [ev_microclimate_buffering_arizasal23_1].

justification.mechanism: The evidence points to a small reduction in heat-stress impact. Trees and shrubs shade crops, pasture and livestock, which lowers air and soil temperature compared with open conditions. Under tree crowns, researchers recorded temperature reductions of 2 to 9 degrees Celsius relative to open pasture in a review covering Costa Rica, Colombia and Nicaragua [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1], up to 13 degrees Celsius on the hottest days in a systematic review of silvopastoral systems [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1], and up to 6 degrees Celsius at midday under Faidherbia albida parkland trees in Ethiopia, where open-field temperatures reached 36 degrees Celsius against 29 degrees Celsius under the canopy [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1]. In Sahelian parklands, a review cites a study in which crops under shea and néré trees were exposed to temperatures above 40 °C for 1–9 hours a week, against 27 hours a week in the open field [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_1]. Shade-tree cover in cocoa agroforestry buffers daily maximum and minimum temperatures compared with monoculture [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1], and shelterbelts in China significantly lowered summer air temperature by 4.01% and raised relative humidity by 13.45% [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. This cooling reduces heat stress in livestock and raised milk production by 29% and 15% in two Latin American reviews of silvopastoral systems [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2], and a reduction in heat load is linked to a 6.8% rise in wheat grain yield under an agroforestry system in India [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6]. A West African cocoa study notes, citing earlier work, that cocoa agroforestry with well-managed shade lowers air and soil temperature extremes [ev_microclimate_buffering_arizasal23_1].

justification.mechanism: For trees and shrubs kept or regenerated on cropland, the evidence points to a small reduction in heat-stress impact, without a stated size for the effect on losses. Parkland trees cool crops and livestock: midday air temperature under Faidherbia albida canopies on Ethiopian wheat farms was up to 6°C lower than in the open field, peaking at 29 °C under the canopy against 36 °C outside [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1]. In the same Ethiopian study, a crop model found that the lower temperature under F. albida shade raised simulated wheat yield when nitrogen was applied, but without applied N simulated yield was extremely small and did not respond to temperature [ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. In Senegal's Ferlo, air under Acacia tortilis ranged between 29 °C and 36 °C against 26 °C and 42 °C outside [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, maximum daily temperature fell by an average of 1–2.5 °C and minimum air humidity rose by up to 5%, with stronger differences on hotter and drier days [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2]. A review also cites a study in which crops under shea and néré parkland trees were exposed to temperatures above 40 °C for 1–9 hours a week, against 27 hours a week in the open field [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_1].

justification.mechanism: Silvopastoral systems cut heat stress in cattle: intensive shrub–tree–rotational pasture models in the dry Colombian Caribbean reduce it, and eucalyptus–brachiaria systems in Brazil reduced the area at critical animal thermal-comfort levels by 20 to 100% against monoculture pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. Tree shade in pastures is associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover, attributed to less heat stress and more foliage and fruit, and other studies found increases above 15% for cows grazing silvopasture compared with cows in full sun [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2]. An IPCC climate-impacts assessment reports more generally that increased shade from trees or cost-effective structures can substantially reduce the incidence of high heat-stress days for livestock, reduce animal stress and increase productivity [ev_livestock_productivity_porter14_1].

justification.mechanism: The evidence points to a moderate reduction in waterlogging losses: trees take excess water out of waterlogged soil. A review reports, second-hand, that under waterlogging in Punjab, India, agroforestry systems had higher evapotranspiration than sole crops, indicating greater removal of excess water from the soil and a better soil environment for plant growth [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9]. A biodrainage field study planted parallel strip plantations of Eucalyptus tereticornis along canal-irrigated, waterlogged fields in Haryana, India; over three years these strips lowered the groundwater table beneath them by an average of 0.85 m compared with control wells in adjacent unplanted fields, mainly through the trees' heavy water use [ev_waterlogging_hazard_ram11_1]. With that lower water table letting rainwater percolate and relieving oxygen deficiency in the wheat root zone, overall wheat grain yield in the research plot was 2.2 t/ha, 3.4 times the 0.6 t/ha measured in adjacent fields without the plantation [ev_crop_yield_ram11_2]. A review of biodrainage in coastal Odisha, India, reports second-hand that the faster drainage let farmers start winter cropping 15–20 days earlier and that rice yield improved in Casuarina plantations, while in Eucalyptus plantations crop yields fell after 2 years because of shading and competition [ev_crop_yield_singhlal18_4].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Against this, a Spanish-language climate-risk review lists an explicit maladaptation example: planting shade trees that increases storm vulnerability by damaging existing infrastructure when the trees come down in high winds [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5]. The Puerto Rico study makes the same point for coffee: when winds are very strong, large shade trees are toppled and their trunks and canopies do considerable damage to the coffee below [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_perfecto19_5]. The overall rating is conflicting because the types of agroforestry disagree: windbreak and boundary-planting evidence reads as a benefit, while shaded tree crops are themselves split, between shelter and falling-tree damage in Puerto Rico and a Mexican coffee study that found no relationship between management and harvest loss [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. Only the Chinese shelterbelt study states a size for the wind-speed reduction; the rest describe mechanism or role without a size. Apart from the Puerto Rico hurricane, the evidence covers routine wind and erosion control rather than storm damage, and the Puerto Rico observations are qualitative and from a high-income country [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_perfecto19_4, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_perfecto19_5]. The Chinese and Mexican findings are from upper-middle-income countries and the Senegalese and Indian ones from lower-middle-income countries.

justification.mechanism: Windbreaks and shelterbelts work mechanically, by slowing the wind reaching the sheltered crop. A review on windbreak airflow states that a major effect of a windbreak is to reduce the incidence of low-frequency, high-magnitude damage events such as sandblasting or lodging [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_cleugh98_3]. The zone of reduced wind speed behind a windbreak typically extends 10 to 20 tree heights downwind, so large fields often need multiple barriers [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15]. In China, farmland shelterbelts cut wind speed by 35.8% compared with unsheltered farmland [ev_windbreak_protection_hao26_1]. In Senegal, windbreak hedges are described as having a major impact on wind and playing an important role in protecting sandy, degraded soils from wind erosion [ev_windbreak_protection_faosen24_12]. In India, live fences are used as windbreaks and to raise soil-moisture retention through litter accumulation [ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4]. More generally, on-farm trees serving as windbreaks and shelterbelts are also used to supply material for rebuilding storm-damaged property [ev_windbreak_protection_lasco14_1]. In Mexican shaded coffee, vegetation management had a significant effect on landslide risk but not on coffee harvest lost [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. In Puerto Rico after Hurricane Maria, coffee patches under shade trees were on some farms not as severely damaged as patches in open sun [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_perfecto19_4].

justification.mechanism: Windbreaks and shelterbelts work mechanically, by slowing the wind reaching the sheltered crop. A review on windbreak airflow states that a major effect of a windbreak is to reduce the incidence of low-frequency, high-magnitude damage events such as sandblasting or lodging [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_cleugh98_3]. The zone of reduced wind speed behind a windbreak typically extends 10 to 20 tree heights downwind, so large fields often need multiple barriers [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15]. In China, farmland shelterbelts cut wind speed by 35.8% compared with unsheltered farmland [ev_windbreak_protection_hao26_1]. In Senegal, windbreak hedges are described as having a major impact on wind and playing an important role in protecting sandy, degraded soils from wind erosion [ev_windbreak_protection_faosen24_12]. In India, live fences are used as windbreaks and to raise soil-moisture retention through litter accumulation [ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: This is an establishment-phase risk first, which is the phase a project funds and is exposed to: the measured damage falls mostly on seedlings and newly planted trees [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_3, ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_5], though established cabruca cocoa and its shade trees also died in the El Niño drought [ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_1, ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_2]. Seedling and young-system losses dominate: the Colombian source notes established systems were more drought-resilient than traditional pastures while young ones are vulnerable in their initial years [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4], and one cited study found drought did not increase seedling mortality, though growth was impaired [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_4]. The Bahia cocoa losses carry no unshaded comparator, so they show the damage to the asset, not whether shade made it worse or better [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1]. The cocoa findings are about one crop and count because shaded tree-crop systems are judged on their host crop. Brazil and Colombia are upper-middle income, close to but outside the low- and lower-middle-income countries this tool targets [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1, ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4]. The stem-diameter finding is second-hand, names two tree species and shows that large trees can be hit far harder than small ones [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_7].

justification.mechanism: Drought severely damages agroforestry itself: it kills the trees of the system and cuts its output. Severe drought can raise tree seedling mortality by 35 to 40% because seedlings cannot match transpiration demands [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_3]. In Colombia, droughts provoked by El Niño between 2015 and 2016 caused significant losses of trees planted by the project, and the area under the most recently planted intensive silvopastoral systems fell by 45 percent in the severe 2019 drought in a survey of 285 farms [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_5, ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4]. In cabruca cocoa agroforests in southern Bahia, Brazil, cocoa tree mortality was 15% during the El Niño event against under 1% normally, 7% of the 317 woody shade trees died, and potential yield fell from 242 to 26 kg/ha, an 89% reduction, still 83% lower nine months after the drought ended [ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_1, ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1]. A tropics review also cites a study in which drought cut the stem diameter of one large tree species, Saurauia nudiflora, by 80% against a 5% decrease in the smaller Archidendron bubalinum [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_7].

justification.mechanism: Strong wind and storms moderately damage agroforestry itself, mainly its trees. On 28 coffee farms in Puerto Rico, Hurricane Maria stripped an average 37.5% of the shade canopy, from about 40% cover to about 25% [ev_climate_shock_perfecto19_1], and farms with denser shade before the storm lost no smaller share of their canopy [ev_climate_shock_perfecto19_2]. All the interviewed farmers who had shade trees reported significant damage to them, and projected harvest fell to 219 kg/ha against a normal of about 1272 kg/ha [ev_climate_shock_perfecto19_3]. A study cited by Philpott et al., comparing abandoned pastures, mixed plantations, abandoned cacao and forests, found that areas with more complex vegetation were least resistant to hurricane damage, losing larger and more trees [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_8]. In a shaded-coffee trial in Paraná, Brazil, the Mimosa scabrella shade trees showed poor resistance to wind, breaking under gusts above 15 m/s [ev_climate_shock_caramori96_3]. In the establishment phase, silvopastoral tree seedlings need protection from excess sun and wind, among other threats [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_diasf08_4]. The compiler of the Burkina Faso WOCAT sheet on assisted natural regeneration of degraded land judged the technology to cope well with local windstorm [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1358_2017_local_windstorm].

All the interviewed farmers who had shade trees reported significant damage to them, and projected harvest fell to 219 kg/ha against a normal of about 1272 kg/ha [ev_climate_shock_perfecto19_3]. A study cited by Philpott et al., comparing abandoned pastures, mixed plantations, abandoned cacao and forests, found that areas with more complex vegetation were least resistant to hurricane damage, losing larger and more trees [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_8]. In a shaded-coffee trial in Paraná, Brazil, the Mimosa scabrella shade trees showed poor resistance to wind, breaking under gusts above 15 m/s [ev_climate_shock_caramori96_3]. In the establishment phase, silvopastoral tree seedlings need protection from excess sun and wind, among other threats [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_diasf08_4]. The compiler of the Burkina Faso WOCAT sheet on assisted natural regeneration of degraded land judged the technology to cope well with local windstorm [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1358_2017_local_windstorm].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Neither finding is a measurement: the Burkina Faso finding is a practitioner rating and the Kerala finding a second-hand review statement about a single crop [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1358_2017_local_windstorm, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_kumar22_1]. Both suggest little damage, but neither says how strong the winds were. Missing: a measured finding of storm damage to agroforestry trees or crops in a low- or lower-middle-income country.

T4_suitability_mappings.justification: Authored hard-exclusion interface for planted silvoarable. Apply confirmed jurisdiction/site or adopted project restrictions through an assessed true/false/unknown mask. WDPA is a screening input, not a universal permission codebook. Retires the unsupported IUCN I–II prohibition claim and unlinked three-source count; no country rule or human evidence approval is inferred. Other systems require their own explicit applicability contract.

legal_mask_contract.candidate_dataset_role: WDPA supplies protected-area locations and attributes for assessment; it does not itself determine agroforestry permission.
legal_mask_contract.category_handling: No IUCN category, designation name or missing category is automatically permission or prohibition. Raw WDPA attributes must not be passed as the boolean mask.
legal_mask_contract.false: Named rules and coverage have been assessed; no applicable exclusion was identified within that assessment. This is not general legal clearance.
legal_mask_contract.geometry_handling: Unresolved point-only locations and boundaries remain unknown within their declared uncertainty/assessment extent; no invented universal buffer.
legal_mask_contract.legacy_rule: IUCN_Cat_I_II automatic exclusion retired: management category is not a universal intervention prohibition.
legal_mask_contract.outside_polygons: Absence from WDPA alone is not a false mask; record coverage and applicable national/site/project rules before assigning false.
legal_mask_contract.overlap_handling: Any confirmed applicable exclusion is true; otherwise any unresolved applicable assessment is unknown; false only when all relevant assessments are complete and non-excluding.
legal_mask_contract.true: Applicable legal or adopted project exclusion prohibits the proposed intervention at this location.
legal_mask_contract.unknown: Missing assessment, incomplete coverage, unresolved permission or absent usable geometry.

T4_suitability_mappings.justification: Evidence-backed categorical gate. Castle Table 2 (PDF p8) defines alley cropping on annual cropland or forage grown between tree rows without grazing, excluding existing tree crops. WorldCover 40 maps annual cropland. WorldCover 30 is conditional on a verified managed-forage/non-grazing mask; it is not treated as pasture proof. Built-up, permanent snow/ice and permanent water cannot satisfy this host definition. Tree/shrub cover remains unknown because those classes mix farms and non-farms.

managed_forage_without_grazing.note: Confirm managed forage without grazing from a documented local management source. Grassland classes or livestock density alone cannot establish this condition.

input_contract.code_handling: Exact categorical codes; no bilinear interpolation. Masked, unknown and unlisted codes remain unknown.
input_contract.grassland_input: managed_forage_without_grazing: 1 confirmed managed forage without grazing; 0 confirmed absent/incompatible; null not assessed or missing. Required only for class 30.
input_contract.non_conversion: Tree cover, shrubland, bare ground, wetlands, mangroves and moss/lichen are unresolved for this gate; do not infer permission to convert native vegetation.
input_contract.scope: Existing host-system screen for planted silvoarable; not conversion permission or biophysical suitability.
input_contract.spatial_handling: Evaluate classes and conditions at source support before area summaries. Retain eligible, ineligible and unknown fractions separately; do not turn any eligible subpixel into full-pixel planting area.
input_contract.time_handling: 2021 classification is historical context; record any newer/local replacement and its explicit class crosswalk.

relationship_params.interpretation: binary host-system compatibility; not graded biophysical suitability

T4_suitability_mappings.justification: Evidence-backed categorical gate. WOCAT 507 describes restoring degraded wasteland and improving depleted farmland (Kenya example, PDF p1). Within the regeneration-on-farmland family, WorldCover alone cannot identify degradation or farmland history. Positive classes require observed depleted/degraded farmland masks; bare soil alone is never evidence of restoration potential. This gate establishes land-use compatibility, not regeneration success or rootstock presence. Tree cover remains unresolved. Pete input review 2026-10-20: depletion/degradation are targeting context; non-cropland requires farmland identity.

relationship_params.condition_role: Depletion/degradation characterize restoration need, not universal suitability. No severity cutoff established.

farmland_context.note: Agricultural, fallow or former-farmland identity; degradation alone cannot establish this context.

relationship_params.interpretation: binary host-system compatibility; not graded biophysical suitability

T4_suitability_mappings.justification: Evidence-backed categorical gate. Castle Table 2 (PDF p8) defines trees integrated with forage and grazing animals on pasture/grassland. WorldCover grassland requires independent grazing-system confirmation. Other vegetation classes remain unresolved because they may mix wooded pasture, natural vegetation and other systems. Supporting evidence remains held by Pete; default execution returns pending_evidence_review until that review is resolved. Pete clarification 2026-10-20: GPW cultivated or natural/semi-natural grassland plus local grazing confirmation; no GLW substitute.

grazing_system_present.note: Local grazing confirmation required for both GPW grassland classes. GLW density cannot replace confirmation.

T4_suitability_mappings.justification: Candidate applicability gate for windbreaks/shelterbelts only. Castle Table 2 PDF p8 places windbreaks on delineated cropland/pasture field boundaries in the US Midwest. WorldCover cropland requires independently mapped field-boundary placement; grassland additionally requires managed pasture confirmation. No universal buffer width or contour-siting rule is inferred. Report applicability zones and candidate line length, never eligible pixel area as planting footprint. Source and cross-context mapping remain pending review. Pete Steward approved B1 on 2026-10-20: boundary geometry required; buffer width varies by publications and regions. Field delineation may be less available in African extensive systems; missing geometry remains unknown. Pete input review 2026-10-20: field boundaries required for both cropland and pasture; no separate pasture-management gate.

field_boundary_zone.note: Upload field-boundary geometry and locally justified buffered zone; no global buffer width.

The denominator is each household adopting at least one land restoration practice [ev_project_cost_crs23_1, ev_project_cost_crs23_3].

T6E_economic_profile.conditionality: Studies disagree, and what separates them is where the trees' labour falls. Where the trees grow in the field and suppress weeds, as the Rwandan Tephrosia did, weeding labour falls [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3]; where tree biomass must be pruned, cut and carried, the extra handling outweighs the weeding saved, and in Nigeria the mulch was grown on a separate plot and carried in [ev_project_cost_korm99_4, ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. Between them sit no-change findings: A cocoa meta-analysis found the higher total production of agroforestry systems is not reflected in the costs compared with monoculture [ev_project_cost_niether20_1]. A meta-analysis of field studies in low- and middle-income countries reports agroforestry production cost -1.39% against a control across 10 studies, not significant (0.952), with an interval spanning a cost fall and a cost rise (-29.06 to 68.32), pooling agroforestry applied alone or in bundles [ev_project_cost_steward23wp_1]. The Cameroon costs mix establishment and recurrent pruning labour, and its trees were pruned only from the second year [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. The Colombian figure is a modelled recurrent saving from an upper-middle-income country and does not pool with the relative changes [ev_project_cost_cmscr20_7]. The coffee and cocoa findings are crop-specific [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3, ev_project_cost_niether20_1]. The field evidence is otherwise from low-income Rwanda and lower-middle-income Cameroon and Nigeria, within the low- and lower-middle-income countries this tool targets [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1, ev_project_cost_korm99_4]. Both readings add to the cost-increase side of this row rather than the cost-saving side: like the Cameroon and Nigeria mulching evidence already here, the extra labour is pruning and handling tree biomass, not time saved on weeding. The 4 m figure is drawn from an earlier cited labour study rather than measured by the modelling authors themselves, and the 2 m figure is the modelling authors' own assumption (more hedgerows to prune at closer spacing), not a measurement. Both are lower-middle-income Nigerian evidence, within the low- and lower-middle-income countries this tool targets. The Bolivian fertiliser saving is partly a trial design choice, since the agroforestry plots were given half the dose on purpose [ev_recurrent_cost_armengot16_1]. The Brazilian figures come from case studies summarised in a review [ev_recurrent_cost_ferraz24_3]. The Mexican fencing comparison is a farmer statement cited second-hand, with no cost figure [ev_establishment_cost_moran18_9].
T6E_economic_profile.effect_mechanism: Trees change farm costs in both directions, mostly through labour. Some systems save cost: In Rwanda, Tephrosia vogelii intercropped in smallholder coffee and cut as mulch required 30 man-days ha−1 less than current farmer management, because it cut the labour needed for weeding [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3]. In Colombia, production costs were US$127/ha lower on average under silvopastoral systems than under traditional ranching, an estimate from a Bank-commissioned business case attributed to improved animal nutrition, productivity and fertility and lower animal death and disease [ev_project_cost_cmscr20_7]. Others add cost: in the forest zone of Cameroon, Leucaena alley cropping raised labour from 75 to 104 (38%) person-days per hectare per year and variable costs by 34% averaged over the trial, for hedgerow planting, pruning and mulching [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]; and at Ibadan, Nigeria, maize mulched with cut-and-carry tree leaves needed more labour than fertilised or untreated plots, with 96% of the labour going to collecting and managing the mulch and only 4% to weeding [ev_project_cost_korm99_4]. A Nigerian alley-cropping model adds two further labour-cost readings, both increases: annual labour for maize production under 4 m-spaced Leucaena alley cropping is reported increased by 53 percent against the traditional bush-fallow control, because of the added labour for hedgerow pruning, and under the closer 2 m spacing the model assumes total labour increases by 87 percent, since more hedgerows need pruning [ev_project_cost_ehui90_5, ev_project_cost_ehui90_6]. In a long-term cacao trial in Bolivia, total costs were lower in agroforestry than in full-sun monoculture, mainly because the agroforestry plots received half the fertiliser dose and needed less weeding [ev_recurrent_cost_armengot16_1]. A review of shaded coffee and cocoa found costs per hectare on average 13.2% lower than in conventional systems, but the difference was not significant [ev_recurrent_cost_jezeer17_1]. A Brazilian review reports integrated-production cases that cut input costs by 50% and 45% and labour from 400 to 50 and from 300 to 60 person-days per hectare [ev_recurrent_cost_ferraz24_3]. In Veracruz, Mexico, farmers say, in a study cited by a review, that building fences with concrete posts and barbed wire is the most costly option compared with planting live fences of native species [ev_establishment_cost_moran18_9].

justification.statement: agroforestry cost_reduction: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE — material weight on both the benefit and the harm side, so no direction is stated. This is not a null finding: studies found real effects, in opposite directions, and the agreement note lists both sides. Read the conditionality for what separates them (transfer: in_context). Cost class: large (percent, lic_lmic context).

T6E_economic_profile.conditionality: The studies disagree, so no direction is stated. What separates them is the labour the trees bring: the saving comes with a weed-suppressing intercrop in an established tree crop [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3], while the cost rises come with cut-and-carry mulching and hedgerow pruning in annual maize systems, where cutting, carrying and spreading prunings is the added work [ev_project_cost_korm99_4, ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. The Cameroon variable costs mix hedgerow establishment with recurrent pruning, and fell from the first to the third year [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. The pooled meta-analysis interval spans both a cost fall and a cost rise (-29.06 to 68.32), its table pools observations where agroforestry was applied alone or in bundles with other practices, and the costs are mostly variable rather than establishment costs [ev_project_cost_steward23wp_1]. The cocoa finding is crop-specific and draws mainly on lower-middle-income countries [ev_project_cost_niether20_1]. For a project, labour demand at planting and pruning, and whether it falls in seasonal peaks, is the cost question to check. The Nigerian 4 m figure is drawn from an earlier labour study and the 2 m figure is the modelling authors' own assumption, not a measurement [ev_project_cost_ehui90_5, ev_project_cost_ehui90_6]. The Bolivian fertiliser saving is partly a trial design choice, since the agroforestry plots were given half the dose on purpose [ev_recurrent_cost_armengot16_1]. Bolivia is lower-middle income.
T6E_economic_profile.effect_mechanism: In low- and lower-middle-income settings, the evidence finds agroforestry costs sometimes lower, sometimes higher and sometimes unchanged, depending on what the trees do to the farm's labour. Where the trees replace a task, labour falls: in Rwandan smallholder coffee, Tephrosia intercropping required 30 man-days per hectare less than current farmer management because less weeding was needed [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3]. Where the trees add a task, labour rises: in Nigerian maize, plots mulched with tree prunings needed more labour than the fertilizer and untreated controls, with 96% of the labour spent collecting and managing mulch and only 4% weeding [ev_project_cost_korm99_4]; and in Cameroon, Leucaena alley cropping raised labour from 75 to 104 person-days per hectare a year (38%) and, averaged over 3 years, raised variable costs by 34% against the traditional system [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. Pooled studies sit between: a meta-analysis of field studies reports agroforestry production cost -1.39% against a control across 10 studies, not significant (0.952) [ev_project_cost_steward23wp_1], and a cocoa meta-analysis found the higher total production of agroforestry systems is not reflected in the costs compared with monoculture [ev_project_cost_niether20_1]. A Nigerian alley-cropping model reports that annual labour for maize under 4 m-spaced Leucaena alley cropping is 53 percent higher than under the traditional bush fallow, because of hedgerow pruning, and assumes 87 percent more labour at the closer 2 m spacing [ev_project_cost_ehui90_5, ev_project_cost_ehui90_6]. In a long-term cacao trial in Bolivia, total costs were lower in agroforestry than in full-sun monoculture, mainly because the agroforestry plots received half the fertiliser dose and needed less weeding [ev_recurrent_cost_armengot16_1].

justification.mechanism: In low- and lower-middle-income settings, the evidence finds agroforestry costs sometimes lower, sometimes higher and sometimes unchanged, depending on what the trees do to the farm's labour. Where the trees replace a task, labour falls: in Rwandan smallholder coffee, Tephrosia intercropping required 30 man-days per hectare less than current farmer management because less weeding was needed [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3]. Where the trees add a task, labour rises: in Nigerian maize, plots mulched with tree prunings needed more labour than the fertilizer and untreated controls, with 96% of the labour spent collecting and managing mulch and only 4% weeding [ev_project_cost_korm99_4]; and in Cameroon, Leucaena alley cropping raised labour from 75 to 104 person-days per hectare a year (38%) and, averaged over 3 years, raised variable costs by 34% against the traditional system [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. Pooled studies sit between: a meta-analysis of field studies reports agroforestry production cost -1.39% against a control across 10 studies, not significant (0.952) [ev_project_cost_steward23wp_1], and a cocoa meta-analysis found the higher total production of agroforestry systems is not reflected in the costs compared with monoculture [ev_project_cost_niether20_1]. A Nigerian alley-cropping model reports that annual labour for maize under 4 m-spaced Leucaena alley cropping is 53 percent higher than under the traditional bush fallow, because of hedgerow pruning, and assumes 87 percent more labour at the closer 2 m spacing [ev_project_cost_ehui90_5, ev_project_cost_ehui90_6]. In a long-term cacao trial in Bolivia, total costs were lower in agroforestry than in full-sun monoculture, mainly because the agroforestry plots received half the fertiliser dose and needed less weeding [ev_recurrent_cost_armengot16_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The overall rating is a moderate gain because the types of agroforestry differ: shaded tree crops and planted tree-crop alleys show strong gains, silvopasture a moderate gain, and linear plantings, regenerated farmland trees and general findings only small gains. Set against the gains, when traditional shaded coffee/cacao agroforest is intensified to sparse-shade plantation, a global meta-analysis found total species richness fell 46% and forest-species richness fell 65%, and converting natural forest to agroforest itself cost 11% of total species richness and 35% of forest-species richness — measured harm from two independent sources, read against intensification and against standing forest rather than against open farmland [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_4]. In Cameroon, cocoa yields above 1 t/ha were not attainable with more than 10 associated tree species, a direct yield-biodiversity trade-off [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seghieri19_7]. The same silvopastoral meta-analysis that found a gain against open pasture also found native-tree silvopasture held 18.1% lower biodiversity than native forest — a conservation benchmark, not the pasture-to-silvopasture counterfactual, so it does not contradict the open-pasture gain [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1]. A windbreak study in Queensland found the plantings useful for some birds but insignificant habitat for mammals and rainforest specialists, with much lower wildlife value than riparian vegetation [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_3], and the same pest-control meta-analysis that found more natural enemies found no significant effect of agroforestry on natural-enemy diversity in most studies (7 of 11) [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_2]. Most findings describe direction without a size, and the meta-analyses behind the clearest numbers (cocoa intensification, silvopasture) do not enumerate their study countries, so the result applies only indirectly to the low- and lower-middle-income countries this tool targets [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1]. A review of the same kind of Mexican coffee intensification gradient found species richness of ants, butterflies and birds declining as shade is simplified from forest through traditional and commercial polyculture to shaded monoculture, echoing the intensification harm above [ev_biodiversity_outcome_perf05_1]. A nature-based-solutions policy review frames the biodiversity benefit as likely but conditional: it depends on the variety, abundance and ecological suitability of the tree species planted, not a guaranteed property of agroforestry as such [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_3]. The gain is also not guaranteed by the practice alone: a Sahelian synthesis notes this is not always the case, since in some regions farmers protect Faidherbia albida with priority over other species, producing something closer to a monoculture than a diverse parkland [ev_biodiversity_outcome_boton10_5]. The global statement gives no size and no place [ev_biodiversity_outcome_griscom17_7].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Agroforestry moderately increases biodiversity: across its types, trees and shrubs add habitat and species diversity relative to the land uses they replace. In India, a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea system had the largest earthworm Simpson diversity index (0.62) against the smallest in sole pigeon pea (0.41) [ev_biodiversity_outcome_biswas22_1]. A cocoa meta-analysis across ten countries found a significantly higher number of animal species in agroforestry than in monoculture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1], and a coffee meta-analysis found bird diversity 120 to 306% higher in three shaded coffee systems than conventional coffee [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2]. In Niger, FMNR adoption increased tree diversity by one to three tree species per farm [ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1], and a WOCAT compiler for Kenyan FMNR rates both animal diversity and habitat diversity increased, noting many animal species find safe habitats in new FMNR sites [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_habitat_diversity]. In Colombian silvopasture, a global meta-analysis found silvopastoral systems supported 28.4% higher biodiversity than open pastures, with the gain largest for invertebrates (53.7%) [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_8]; a Colombian World Bank project evaluation reports increased species richness and abundance, including forest-dependent and endangered species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8], bird monitoring there found four times more birds and 35% higher species richness than grass monocultures, and ant species richness was 62% higher than in treeless pastures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2]. Properties with silvopastoral intervention in the Colombian Amazon significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. For linear plantings, reviews state that windbreaks may help conserve a large number of plant and animal species by providing food, cover from predators, refuge and travel lanes [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_2], that live fences, windbreaks and isolated trees may contribute to biodiversity conservation across fragmented tropical farm landscapes [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_4], and that pastures with isolated trees generally show higher bird diversity than pastures without them [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_1]. A review of silvopastoral research in Central America adds that animals visiting windbreak trees carry and deposit tree seeds, letting woody species persist and potentially re-establish in the pasture landscape, and cites a Costa Rican study finding significantly greater seed-rain density and species richness in windbreaks than in open pasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_dagang03_4]. Farmers in Colombia and Costa Rica report that live fences increase landscape connectivity, creating local corridors for fauna and flora, which they see as positive for native biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_moran18_6]. A tropical agroforestry meta-analysis found natural enemies of pests significantly more abundant under agroforestry than in controls [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_1]. A global silvopastoral meta-analysis breaks the 28.4% biodiversity gain down further: native-tree silvopasture held 36.3% more biodiversity than open pasture and planted-tree silvopasture held 20.9% more, with invertebrate abundance specifically about 60% higher under native-tree silvopasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_10, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_12]. A further Colombian Andes study of dung beetles — an indicator of ecological-process recovery, not just species counts — found significantly more beetles caught per trap in intensive silvopasture than in the treeless improved pasture it replaced (275 individuals across five species against 143 across three species), with the same three species found in both land uses plus two additional species recorded only in the silvopastoral system [ev_biodiversity_outcome_giraldo10_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_giraldo10_2]. In Maradi's Dan Saga and Aguié villages in Niger, farmer-managed natural regeneration took local woody species richness from only a few types of tree in the 1980s to at least 30 tree species today, with farmers reintroducing species that had disappeared [ev_biodiversity_outcome_boton10_4]. A global study of natural climate solutions states, citing its appendix, that trees in croplands also provide habitat for biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_griscom17_7].
