Properties with silvopastoral intervention in the Colombian Amazon significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. For linear plantings, reviews state that windbreaks may help conserve a large number of plant and animal species by providing food, cover from predators, refuge and travel lanes [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_2], that live fences, windbreaks and isolated trees may contribute to biodiversity conservation across fragmented tropical farm landscapes [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_4], and that pastures with isolated trees generally show higher bird diversity than pastures without them [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_1]. A review of silvopastoral research in Central America adds that animals visiting windbreak trees carry and deposit tree seeds, letting woody species persist and potentially re-establish in the pasture landscape, and cites a Costa Rican study finding significantly greater seed-rain density and species richness in windbreaks than in open pasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_dagang03_4]. Farmers in Colombia and Costa Rica report that live fences increase landscape connectivity, creating local corridors for fauna and flora, which they see as positive for native biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_moran18_6]. A tropical agroforestry meta-analysis found natural enemies of pests significantly more abundant under agroforestry than in controls [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_1]. A global silvopastoral meta-analysis breaks the 28.4% biodiversity gain down further: native-tree silvopasture held 36.3% more biodiversity than open pasture and planted-tree silvopasture held 20.9% more, with invertebrate abundance specifically about 60% higher under native-tree silvopasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_10, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_12]. A further Colombian Andes study of dung beetles — an indicator of ecological-process recovery, not just species counts — found significantly more beetles caught per trap in intensive silvopasture than in the treeless improved pasture it replaced (275 individuals across five species against 143 across three species), with the same three species found in both land uses plus two additional species recorded only in the silvopastoral system [ev_biodiversity_outcome_giraldo10_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_giraldo10_2]. In Maradi's Dan Saga and Aguié villages in Niger, farmer-managed natural regeneration took local woody species richness from only a few types of tree in the 1980s to at least 30 tree species today, with farmers reintroducing species that had disappeared [ev_biodiversity_outcome_boton10_4]. A global study of natural climate solutions states, citing its appendix, that trees in croplands also provide habitat for biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_griscom17_7].

The review-level findings generalise across cited studies rather than measuring anything themselves, and the review qualifies that agroforestry elements 'are not substitutes for the original vegetation' and that almost all its cited studies were in landscapes with some remnant forest nearby, so element value and landscape context are confounded [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_4]. None of these findings names a country, income group or farming system, so although the pattern is consistent it applies only indirectly to the low- and lower-middle-income countries this tool targets [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_4, ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_griscom17_7].

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Linear plantings add woody habitat structure to farmland. A tropical-agroforestry review states that, depending on their floristic diversity, structural complexity and management, windbreaks may help conserve a large number of plant and animal species, including a limited number of forest-dependent species, by providing food, cover from predators, refuge and travel lanes [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_2]. In Colombia and Costa Rica, farmers report that planting live fences increases landscape connectivity, creating local corridors that both fauna and flora can use, which they see as positive for native biodiversity conservation [ev_biodiversity_outcome_moran18_6]. The same review also reports a mixed case: in Queensland, Australia, planted eucalyptus windbreaks were useful habitat for some bird species but insignificant habitat for mammals and rainforest specialists, and held much lower value as wildlife habitat than riparian vegetation, which the authors attribute to the windbreaks' lower structural complexity and single-species planting [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_3].

In Cameroon, cocoa yields above 1 t/ha were not attainable with more than 10 associated tree species, a direct trade-off between tree diversity and cocoa yield that growers face as they add species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seghieri19_7]. Most units describe a significant difference without naming every taxon or giving a consistent metric across studies, and the certification, intensification-gradient and cocoa meta-analysis evidence does not enumerate study countries in the cited text, so the row sits in_context with, but is not a close match for, the LIC/LMIC target as a whole [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_1].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In shaded coffee and cacao systems, more structurally complex agroforestry supports more species than simpler, intensified alternatives. A ten-country cocoa meta-analysis found cocoa agroforestry held a significantly higher number of animal species, pooled across taxa, than cocoa monoculture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1]. A review of shaded coffee systems found bird diversity 120 to 306% higher in three shaded coffee systems of varying complexity than in conventional coffee [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2]. Along a Mexican coffee-intensification gradient (forest, traditional polyculture, commercial polyculture, shaded monoculture), estimated ant, butterfly and bird richness was higher at the less-intensified, more complex-shade end of the gradient that agroforestry occupies [ev_biodiversity_outcome_perf05_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Silvopasture moderately increases biodiversity relative to open pasture, the land use it replaces. A global meta-analysis (47 publications, 279 comparisons) found silvopastoral systems supported 28.4% higher biodiversity than open pastures, with native-tree silvopasture raising biodiversity by 36.3% and planted-tree silvopasture by 20.9%, both against open pastures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_12]. Soil carbon gains are not guaranteed: a meta-analysis found no significant change in soil carbon when pasture or grassland was converted to agroforestry, and losses when forest or uncultivated land was converted [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_20, ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_2]; conversion from pasture also did not change soil carbon in another meta-analysis, and silvopasture showed the smallest or no soil carbon gain [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_4, ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_3]. Field trials in Ethiopia and in cocoa systems found no significant soil carbon or soil chemistry difference from the comparison land use [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sida18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_niether20_1]. Changes in methane and nitrous oxide after conversion to agroforestry were inconsistent, with no clear direction [ev_carbon_sequestration_kim16_2]. The parkland soil-carbon figure is second-hand and names one tree species [ev_soil_organic_carbon_bayala14_1]. That ranking is a global model and gives no figure for agroforestry in any one place [ev_carbon_sequestration_griscom17_6].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Agroforestry moderately increases carbon storage: trees on farmland add carbon in wood and roots, and litter and root turnover can raise soil carbon over time. A global model of natural climate solutions ranks trees in croplands as the second-largest cost-effective agricultural pathway for climate mitigation, after cropland nutrient management [ev_carbon_sequestration_griscom17_6].

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Pooled across sub-practices, modelled mitigation-potential and stock-comparison studies consistently find a carbon benefit, though almost none of them gives a measured net CO2e balance for the practice. A pan-tropical soil study (71 studies, 225 pairs) found agroforestry significantly increased soil organic carbon storage compared with crop monocultures (overall effect size 1.21) and reduced soil erosion by 50%, with soil organic carbon up 40%, nitrogen storage up 13%, available nitrogen up 46% and available phosphorus up 11% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_muchane20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muchane20_2]. The IPCC AR6 AFOLU chapter cites a global analysis estimating agroforestry's technical mitigation potential at 9.4 GtCO2eq/yr, and further estimates a technical potential of 4.1 (0.3–9.4) GtCO2eq/yr for 2020-2050, of which 0.8 (0.4–1.1) GtCO2eq/yr is available at USD100/tCO2 [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_5]. A regional modelling study finds agroforestry's mitigation density about 45 tCO2eq/ha, and across the Africa-Middle East region its cost-effective mitigation potential at 0.19 GtCO2eq/yr (8% of the regional total) [ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_2]. In Brazil, a review reports agroforestry carbon sequestration rates varying by climate from 954 to 3670 tCO2/km2/yr, with a technical potential of 0.1 to 5.7 GtCO2eq/yr, the largest among the land uses it compared [ev_carbon_sequestration_santos25_3]. One directly measured finding in the row combines biomass and soil carbon sequestration with changes in net CH4 and N2O emissions and estimates a shift to agroforestry can mitigate 27.2 t CO2eq/ha/yr, at least over the early growth stage up to an average age of 14 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_kim16_1]. The Regreening Africa endline survey found a relative 3% increase in soil organic carbon compared with baseline, with significant variation across countries and sites [ev_soil_organic_carbon_rgaf23_2]. A global model of natural climate solutions ranks trees in croplands as the second-largest cost-effective agricultural pathway for climate mitigation, after cropland nutrient management [ev_carbon_sequestration_griscom17_6].

justification.mechanism: Pooled across sub-practices, modelled mitigation-potential and stock-comparison studies consistently find a carbon benefit, though almost none of them gives a measured net CO2e balance for the practice. A pan-tropical soil study (71 studies, 225 pairs) found agroforestry significantly increased soil organic carbon storage compared with crop monocultures (overall effect size 1.21) and reduced soil erosion by 50%, with soil organic carbon up 40%, nitrogen storage up 13%, available nitrogen up 46% and available phosphorus up 11% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_muchane20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muchane20_2]. The IPCC AR6 AFOLU chapter cites a global analysis estimating agroforestry's technical mitigation potential at 9.4 GtCO2eq/yr, and further estimates a technical potential of 4.1 (0.3–9.4) GtCO2eq/yr for 2020-2050, of which 0.8 (0.4–1.1) GtCO2eq/yr is available at USD100/tCO2 [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_5]. A regional modelling study finds agroforestry's mitigation density about 45 tCO2eq/ha, and across the Africa-Middle East region its cost-effective mitigation potential at 0.19 GtCO2eq/yr (8% of the regional total) [ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_2]. In Brazil, a review reports agroforestry carbon sequestration rates varying by climate from 954 to 3670 tCO2/km2/yr, with a technical potential of 0.1 to 5.7 GtCO2eq/yr, the largest among the land uses it compared [ev_carbon_sequestration_santos25_3]. One directly measured finding in the row combines biomass and soil carbon sequestration with changes in net CH4 and N2O emissions and estimates a shift to agroforestry can mitigate 27.2 t CO2eq/ha/yr, at least over the early growth stage up to an average age of 14 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_kim16_1]. The Regreening Africa endline survey found a relative 3% increase in soil organic carbon compared with baseline, with significant variation across countries and sites [ev_soil_organic_carbon_rgaf23_2]. A global model of natural climate solutions ranks trees in croplands as the second-largest cost-effective agricultural pathway for climate mitigation, after cropland nutrient management [ev_carbon_sequestration_griscom17_6].

Measured directly on Ethiopian wheat farms, soil organic C did not differ significantly under and outside the Faidherbia albida canopy at the end of the 2013 cropping season, so the cited 46 per cent canopy gain was not reproduced at that site; this null lowers the agreement rather than the class [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sida18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1]. T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Trees and shrubs kept or regenerated on cropland moderately increase carbon storage. In Sudano-Sahelian cropland, shrubs and trees on agricultural fields had an overall positive but variable effect on soil total carbon (+ 20 to 75%), and a cited meta-analysis reports that soil under Faidherbia albida canopy holds on average 46 per cent more organic carbon than outside it [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1]. The externally audited Humbo FMNR project in Ethiopia reports CO2 sequestered since 2007 [ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT compiler adds that increasing tree cover through FMNR is one of the ways to sequester carbon in biomass [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_507_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. In Lempira, Honduras, soil organic matter under the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system, monitored for four years in three places, increased from 2.4% to 4.5% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3]. In Sahelian parklands, a review cites an isotope study that found tree-derived soil carbon 30% higher under néré (Parkia biglobosa) than in adjacent treeless areas [ev_soil_organic_carbon_bayala14_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Carbon sequestration potential needs a net greenhouse-gas balance: carbon dioxide removed in biomass and soil, minus any methane and nitrous oxide the system emits. Most of what this cell's evidence measures is only one part of that balance, a biomass or soil carbon stock. A pan-tropical cocoa meta-analysis found 2.5 times more total biomass carbon in agroforestry than in monoculture [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1], and East African perennial tree-crop systems held an average of 29.9 Mg of carbon per hectare aboveground [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_4]. But a synthesis of agroforestry methane and nitrous oxide data found that shifting to shaded perennial-crop systems can increase net soil methane emissions rather than reduce them, because nitrogen from nitrogen-fixing shade trees can inhibit the soil bacteria that oxidise methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_kim16_4]. Only one unit in this row states a net greenhouse-gas balance that combines carbon removals with methane and nitrous oxide: a modelled estimate for Ghanaian cocoa of a 127% greater GHG removal under moderate shade than under near-full-sun management [ev_carbon_sequestration_hawkins24_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Set against this, the same global meta-analysis found soil organic carbon fell 44% converting forest to silvopasture at a shallower sampled depth (against the 32% gain reported at the deepest profile) and fell 47% converting uncultivated or other land to silvopasture — a reversal the engine counts as measured harm, which the authors attribute to the heterogeneity of the uncultivated/other category (bare, degraded or control land) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_6, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_40]. Converting pasture or grassland to silvopasture showed no noticeable change in soil organic carbon in the same meta-analysis, and two further global meta-analyses likewise found no significant effect of converting pasture to agroforestry on soil carbon, attributing it to perennial grass roots already dominating belowground carbon inputs before trees are added [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_9, ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_4, ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_3]. The forest-to-silvopasture figures are measured against existing natural forest, a conservation benchmark, not the pasture-to-silvopasture adoption counterfactual that matters for the practice's climate-mitigation role. All of this is global meta-analysis evidence without a Colombia/Costa Rica-specific breakdown, so only the World Bank project and Costa Rican figures anchor the row to its stated countries; as pooled global findings the SOC units transfer only as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_27, ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1]. Two further readings from the same Colombian Amazon chronosequence measure silvopasture's shallow surface-layer soil carbon against standing native forest rather than against the pasture it replaced, with the traditional pasture on the same land showing a comparable or larger gain over forest in that layer; the engine holds these out of the class for the same reason as the earlier forest-benchmark comparisons in this row — they measure recovery toward a forest reference, not the pasture-to-silvopasture adoption counterfactual, and here the gain mostly reflects grass-root carbon inputs after conversion rather than the trees [ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_4]. The full-profile null and the unstated-size deeper-layer gain both count toward the same-direction pool without stating a size, which is why only a minority of the same-direction units in this row state how big the effect is, holding the class at moderate; the system is also bundled with tillage, lime and phosphate-rock application at establishment, so the gain cannot be credited to the trees alone. The Brazilian pasture finding is a narrative review citing an underlying primary study without giving its own carbon value or stating the study's duration, so it corroborates the direction of the SOC gain without adding a size [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dagang03_1].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In Colombia and Costa Rica, silvopastoral systems are reported to raise carbon stocks and sequestration. The World Bank's Colombian Conservation and Sustainable Development of the Coffee Growing Regions project reports net accumulated CO2 removals of 1,131,056 t CO2e from converting pasturelands to dispersed trees in pasture, live fences, intensive silvopastoral systems and secondary-forest conservation [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10]. In Costa Rica, silvopastoral systems had a carbon storage potential of 1.2 to 4.5 Mg C/ha/yr, against below 1 Mg C/ha/yr in treeless pasture [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1]. A global meta-analysis of land-use conversions found soil organic carbon stocks rose 66% and 31% at different depths converting agriculture to silvopasture, 17% converting forest plantation to silvopasture, and 32% converting forest to silvopasture at the deepest sampled profile, where the authors note silvopasture held more SOC than the forest it replaced at that depth [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_27, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_39, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_24, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_38]. A Colombian review states a preliminary GHG balance where lower nitrogen losses and greater carbon capture in intensive silvopastoral systems offset livestock methane emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2], and silvopastoral systems built from degraded natural woodland are reported to mitigate climate change by increasing above- and below-ground carbon stocks [ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_4]. Among pasture-improvement practices assessed in a Colombian climate-smart-agriculture matrix, only tree-improved pastures and live fences showed a positive effect on the mitigation pillar [ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_6]. Properties with silvopastoral intervention in the Colombian Amazon also significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties, retaining forest carbon [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. In the Colombian Amazon (Caquetá), a chronosequence comparing silvopasture against the traditional pasture it replaced found no significant change in total soil organic carbon stock over the full sampled soil profile, but did find a gain confined to the deepest sampled layer, read by the authors as a sign the practice could turn the soil into a carbon sink in deeper layers over time [ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_2]. A review of pastures in semi-arid north-eastern Brazil reports a similar pattern: retaining native tree species (Ziziphus joazeiro and Spondias tuberosa) in pasture significantly raised total soil carbon compared with open pasture away from the trees, attributed to litterfall and fine-root turnover adding soil organic matter and to nitrogen fixation, though the review gives no carbon value [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dagang03_1].

justification.mechanism: In Colombia and Costa Rica, silvopastoral systems are reported to raise carbon stocks and sequestration. The World Bank's Colombian Conservation and Sustainable Development of the Coffee Growing Regions project reports net accumulated CO2 removals of 1,131,056 t CO2e from converting pasturelands to dispersed trees in pasture, live fences, intensive silvopastoral systems and secondary-forest conservation [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10]. In Costa Rica, silvopastoral systems had a carbon storage potential of 1.2 to 4.5 Mg C/ha/yr, against below 1 Mg C/ha/yr in treeless pasture [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1]. A global meta-analysis of land-use conversions found soil organic carbon stocks rose 66% and 31% at different depths converting agriculture to silvopasture, 17% converting forest plantation to silvopasture, and 32% converting forest to silvopasture at the deepest sampled profile, where the authors note silvopasture held more SOC than the forest it replaced at that depth [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_27, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_39, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_24, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_38]. A Colombian review states a preliminary GHG balance where lower nitrogen losses and greater carbon capture in intensive silvopastoral systems offset livestock methane emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2], and silvopastoral systems built from degraded natural woodland are reported to mitigate climate change by increasing above- and below-ground carbon stocks [ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_4]. Among pasture-improvement practices assessed in a Colombian climate-smart-agriculture matrix, only tree-improved pastures and live fences showed a positive effect on the mitigation pillar [ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_6]. Properties with silvopastoral intervention in the Colombian Amazon also significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties, retaining forest carbon [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. In the Colombian Amazon (Caquetá), a chronosequence comparing silvopasture against the traditional pasture it replaced found no significant change in total soil organic carbon stock over the full sampled soil profile, but did find a gain confined to the deepest sampled layer, read by the authors as a sign the practice could turn the soil into a carbon sink in deeper layers over time [ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_2]. A review of pastures in semi-arid north-eastern Brazil reports a similar pattern: retaining native tree species (Ziziphus joazeiro and Spondias tuberosa) in pasture significantly raised total soil carbon compared with open pasture away from the trees, attributed to litterfall and fine-root turnover adding soil organic matter and to nitrogen fixation, though the review gives no carbon value [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dagang03_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Studies disagree, and what separates them is the balance between higher tree water use and better infiltration, which tree density sets. The recharge gains are qualified to moderate density and to an optimal intermediate density in dryland parklands, so the benefit does not keep rising with tree cover [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ipccar6_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_vannoordwijk21_6]; the loss rests on the general point that more trees transpire more water than crops alone [ev_water_yield_zhu19_1]. The recharge statements are about drylands, while the water-use statement is general, so the row cannot say which side wins in a given catchment. All units are second-hand readings in reviews or assessments, the recharge units rest on the same primary work by Ilstedt et al., none states a size or a country, and no unit measures water leaving a catchment or reaching downstream users [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ipccar6_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_vannoordwijk21_6, ev_water_yield_zhu19_1]. This measured New Zealand evidence strengthens the loss side of the row directly, rather than only the general point that more trees transpire more water: both readings are from the same single silvopasture experiment, high-income temperate evidence outside the LIC/LMIC target, so the row's low agreement and out-of-context transfer are unchanged [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_pollock08_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_pollock08_2].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Trees change how much rain reaches groundwater and streams in opposite ways. On the recharge side, the IPCC assessment states that agroforestry increases groundwater recharge in drylands when managed at moderate density (Ilstedt et al. 2016; Bargués-Tobella et al. 2020) [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ipccar6_1], and, combining canopy interception and transpiration data of trees with their effects on water infiltration, Ilstedt et al. derived an optimal intermediate tree density for parklands from a groundwater-recharge perspective [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_vannoordwijk21_6]. On the water-use side, a review cites Wallace et al. (2005): because agroforestry systems include a share of trees, they use more water than pure agricultural systems, though less than full-cover forest, leaving less water to feed groundwater and maintain dry-season streamflow [ev_water_yield_zhu19_1]. Groundwater recharge is used here as a component of catchment water yield. In a New Zealand silvopasture trial, winter moisture available to recharge the soil profile was lower under silvopasture than under open pasture (113 against 142 mm in a normal-rainfall winter), and after a wet winter, deep drainage below 2 m was detected only under open pasture, not under the silvopastures, which the authors read as the trees retaining and using most of the incoming rainfall [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_pollock08_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_pollock08_2].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The sources point in opposite directions, so the row states no direction. What separates them, as far as the evidence says, is tree density and the balance between tree water use and the water trees let into the soil: the recharge gain is qualified to moderate density in drylands [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ipccar6_1], while the loss is the general case of trees using more water than crops alone [ev_water_yield_zhu19_1]. (2005), that because agroforestry systems include a proportion of trees they use more water than pure agricultural systems (though less than a full-cover forest), leaving less water to feed groundwater bodies and maintain dry-season streamflow [ev_water_yield_zhu19_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: On the harm side, the trees made drought losses worse. During the extreme drought of 2015/16 in Ghana, a field study found that all cocoa plants under Albizia ferruginea shade trees died and cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality, while cocoa in full sun kept higher sap flux; soil water content was higher in full sun, which the authors link to competition for water in the shaded systems [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. A multi-species silvopasture trial on degraded rangeland in arid India found the same kind of reversal in a grazing system: understorey herbage yield fell further under drought beneath every tree and shrub species than in the treeless control pasture, attributed by the authors to shading and competition for soil moisture; the trees did supply extra dry-season browse fodder, a trade-off kept separate from the herbage finding [ev_drought_hazard_singhrao08_1]. Elsewhere, a review says tree shade could decrease understorey yields under normal rainfall, and the Senegal review reports no clear consensus on windbreaks in drought, some studies finding higher yields in drier years and others harm to rainfed crops [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17]. In Kenya the link between agroforestry and perceived drought held in Burat but not in Kinna, and one Kenyan finding states only that agroforestry has been proposed for resilience [ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. Most benefit findings are reviews repeating earlier studies or household perception, the Canadian trial is high-income evidence, and the Kenyan FMNR finding is a practitioner judgement on a technology sheet, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The household evidence comes largely from lower-middle-income Kenya [ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10]. The Indian silvopasture result is likewise lower-middle-income evidence [ev_drought_hazard_singhrao08_1]. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. The French result is a relative cushioning of the drought impact, not a stated yield advantage over full sun, from a single season and site, and it is high-income evidence [ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3]. What separates the two sides: the benefits come mostly from household reports, reviews and practitioner ratings, and one Canadian and one French trial, while both harm results are direct field measurements in which the trees competed with the crop or pasture for scarce soil water, one of them in an extreme drought [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1, ev_drought_hazard_singhrao08_1]. So the overall picture is mixed.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: The studies disagree on whether trees on farms reduce the damage drought does to farm households: most findings say they do, but two measured field studies found the trees made drought losses worse. On the benefit side: In Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, a farmer said deep-rooted mango trees get water from deep down, others said trees do not dry up fast and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind; the study concludes that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10]. Reviews report that under drought understorey crop yields could be higher than in an open system even in intense shade, and that live fences supply livestock fodder when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. In an eastern Canadian soybean intercrop, experimentally induced drought caused crop losses in the monocrop only (Nasielski et al. 2015) [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet rates drought impacts as reduced, its compiler judging that FMNR improves micro-climate and soil moisture and therefore mitigates the impact of droughts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. In a French walnut-based alley-cropping system, an imposed spring drought cut full-sun pea yield by 22% while the alley-cropped yield was relatively improved by 12 to 20% against its own rainfed baseline [ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3].

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Across contexts, agroforestry raises household food security mainly through tree products adding to diets and smoothing shortfalls. In Malawi, fertilizer-tree adopters had food crop value 35% higher than non-adopters, driving greater food security [ev_t6_foodsec_ferttree_castle21_8]. In Kenya, agrosilvopastoral extension advice raised the household dietary diversity score by 1.22 points and the number of food groups consumed by 2.291, out of 12 analysed [ev_food_security_castle21s_1]. In Zambia, improved fallows raised the number of months per year with enough grown food by 1.069 months [ev_food_security_castle21s_3]. Across the Regreening Africa endline survey (Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Mali, Niger, Rwanda, Senegal, Somalia), the share of respondents meeting the minimum-dietary-diversity cut-off rose from 16 to 21%, a 31% relative increase, and households that intensified tree-product use saw significant dietary-diversity gains in Ethiopia, Ghana, Niger, Rwanda and Senegal [ev_food_security_rgaf23_8, ev_food_security_rgaf23_10]. A World Vision multi-country meta-analysis found project participants' months of food shortage significantly lower, by 0.26 months, than non-participants [ev_food_security_wvfmnr19_9]. In Senegal, only 3% of FMNR adopters failed to meet annual food needs for more than 4 months against 14% of non-adopters in one zone, and 0% versus 4% in another [ev_food_security_seghieri19_13]. In Nepal, the share of households food-sufficient rose from 52% to 69% after a market-oriented agroforestry intervention, a highly significant change [ev_food_security_pandit19_1], and in Tanzania, improved agroforestry secured enough food year-round for 40% of households against 18% on traditional farms [ev_food_security_reyes05_1]. In Kenya, fruit from on-farm trees was some farmers' only steady food source during the floods, and agroforestry-project households used fewer detrimental coping strategies during the drought and flood hunger periods that followed [ev_food_security_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_2]. In Rwanda, a positive association between tree density and food security was found in two of six agroecologies [ev_food_security_ndoli21_1]. Reviews summarise the same mechanism: the IPCC AR6 chapter links increased food security and household income to diversification of production avoiding trade-offs between crop and tree products [ev_food_security_ipccar6ch5_7], and a review states agroforestry could help up to 1.3 billion people on degrading agricultural land in food-security terms [ev_food_security_ipccsrccl6_6]. A synthesis across East African studies names fodder, food, firewood and income as the main livelihood benefits, diversifying livelihoods and acting as safety nets in times of climate shocks [ev_food_security_muthuri23_1]. In Niger, during the 2005 food crisis, farmers practising farmer-managed natural regeneration were less severely affected than other farmers and recorded relatively lower infant mortality, through income from selling wood and other forest products [ev_food_security_boton10_2].

justification.mechanism: Across regeneration-based farmland (FMNR), several sources find fewer households going hungry. A World Vision meta-brief across seven African and one Timorese project catchments found project participants reported significantly fewer months of food shortage, by 0.26 months, than non-participants [ev_food_security_wvfmnr19_9]. In Senegal, only 3% of FMNR adopters failed to meet annual food needs for more than 4 months in one zone, against 14% of non-adopters, and 0% versus 4% in another zone [ev_food_security_seghieri19_13]. In the Sahel, moving from low-intensity to young-level FMNR raised the household food consumption score by about 12% [ev_food_security_bina15_7]. In Ghana's Talensi project, households with sufficient diet diversity rose from 44.5% at baseline to 55.8% at endline, and households with one or more hungry months in the previous year fell from 68.2% to 41%, though this project bundled FMNR with savings groups, post-harvest storage and value-chain and livestock work, so the gain is not attributable to FMNR alone [ev_food_security_talensi21_3, ev_food_security_talensi21_4]. A WOCAT compiler for Kenyan FMNR rates food security and self-sufficiency improved, reasoning that more diversified livelihoods reduce the risk of food insecurity [ev_food_security_wocat_507_2019_food_security_selfsufficiency]. In Niger, during the 2005 food crisis, farmers practising the regeneration were less severely affected than other farmers and recorded relatively lower infant mortality, through income from selling wood and other forest products [ev_food_security_boton10_2].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The same shade can also warm conditions or show no significant effect, depending on species, age and season. In the Malaysian oil-palm trial, alleys intercropped with bamboo or bactris palm were significantly hotter (up to 37.0 degrees Celsius air temperature) than the monocultures, and the authors judged these two species unsuitable intercrops because of the increased air temperature [ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_4]. A Mexican coffee shade-gradient study found no significant difference in mean air temperature between high- and low-shade sites in either the wet or dry season, even though the high-shade site fluctuated less around the optimum temperature [ev_microclimate_buffering_lin07_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_lin07_2]. In Senegal, windbreak hedges were reported to generally cause a slight rise in temperature in protected plots rather than cooling, with effects varying by crop and growth stage [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. In the systematic review of silvopastoral systems, four of the seven cattle studies using the temperature-humidity index found no significant difference between silvopastoral and treeless pasture, partly because that index does not capture solar radiation, the main pathway through which trees reduce heat load [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_2]. Most of the quantified cooling is measured in upper-middle- and high-income countries (Malaysia, Brazil, Germany, China); evidence from low-income parkland systems in Ethiopia and the Sahel is present but thinner. The parkland heat-hours figure is second-hand and names two tree species [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_1]. The cocoa statement is second-hand and gives no size [ev_microclimate_buffering_arizasal23_1].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Agroforestry slightly reduces heat stress: shade from trees and shelterbelts lowers air and soil temperature for crops and livestock across many systems. Oil-palm alley cropping with black pepper or cacao in Malaysia cooled air by 1.3 degrees Celsius and soil surface by 2.1 degrees Celsius compared with a 15-year oil-palm monoculture [ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_3]; silvopastoral arrangements in Colombia and Costa Rica cooled paddocks by 1.7 to 3.6 degrees Celsius relative to open pasture, with tree groups giving the largest effect [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]; shelterbelts in China significantly lowered summer air temperature by 4.01% and raised relative humidity by 13.45% [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]; and under Faidherbia albida parkland trees in Ethiopia, midday air temperature fell by up to 6 degrees Celsius, with the open field reaching 36 degrees Celsius against 29 degrees Celsius under the canopy [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1]. A systematic review of silvopastoral studies found silvopastoral systems were mostly (57%) measured as having lower air temperature, soil-surface temperature and radiant heat load than treeless pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_1]. In Sahelian parklands, a review cites a study in which crops under shea and néré parkland trees were exposed to temperatures above 40 °C for 1–9 hours a week, against 27 hours a week in the open field [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_1]. A West African cocoa study notes, citing earlier work, that cocoa agroforestry with well-managed shade lowers air and soil temperature extremes [ev_microclimate_buffering_arizasal23_1].

justification.mechanism: Agroforestry slightly reduces heat stress: shade from trees and shelterbelts lowers air and soil temperature for crops and livestock across many systems. Oil-palm alley cropping with black pepper or cacao in Malaysia cooled air by 1.3 degrees Celsius and soil surface by 2.1 degrees Celsius compared with a 15-year oil-palm monoculture [ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_3]; silvopastoral arrangements in Colombia and Costa Rica cooled paddocks by 1.7 to 3.6 degrees Celsius relative to open pasture, with tree groups giving the largest effect [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]; shelterbelts in China significantly lowered summer air temperature by 4.01% and raised relative humidity by 13.45% [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]; and under Faidherbia albida parkland trees in Ethiopia, midday air temperature fell by up to 6 degrees Celsius, with the open field reaching 36 degrees Celsius against 29 degrees Celsius under the canopy [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1]. A systematic review of silvopastoral studies found silvopastoral systems were mostly (57%) measured as having lower air temperature, soil-surface temperature and radiant heat load than treeless pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_1]. In Sahelian parklands, a review cites a study in which crops under shea and néré parkland trees were exposed to temperatures above 40 °C for 1–9 hours a week, against 27 hours a week in the open field [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_1]. A West African cocoa study notes, citing earlier work, that cocoa agroforestry with well-managed shade lowers air and soil temperature extremes [ev_microclimate_buffering_arizasal23_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: All units are from high-income settings (Germany, Costa Rica, Australia and the USA), outside the LIC/LMIC target, and they describe air temperature or shade cooling, components of heat-stress impact, rather than measured heat-stress losses [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1]. The cattle-shade statement gives no tree system or density and is an old citation in a review, so it supports the direction only [ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Tree cover lowers air temperature in the units from high-income settings. A review reports, second-hand, that on hot summer days a poplar alley-cropping system in Germany was 3.4°C cooler than a sole wheat system [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4]. In Cañas, Costa Rica, a review reports, second-hand, that temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. In Costa Rican coffee, shade reduced maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C against full-sun plots [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4]. A review of cattle heat stress drawing on Queensland and Californian work cites Kelly et al. (1950) that trees are the most effective shade for cattle, combining protection from sunlight with cooling as moisture evaporates from the leaves [ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Not every heat measure moved: in the same review, results for the temperature humidity index were unclear, with four of the seven studies that used it finding no significant difference from treeless pasture; the authors attribute this partly to that index leaving out solar radiation, the main pathway through which trees cut heat load [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_2]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint and the dairy review rest on measurements [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the Cuban and Neotropical shade units repeat Fudora et al. and Harvey et al., the latter a reading of livestock keepers' knowledge rather than a measurement [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. The units report air temperature, thermal indices or animal comfort, components of heat-stress impact rather than measured losses, and the evidence is mainly from upper-middle-income Latin America with a high-income Costa Rican unit [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the dry Colombian Caribbean, silvopastoral models most intensive in shrubs, trees and rotational pasture reduce heat stress in cattle [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1]. In Cuba live fences came to be used to shade cattle and avoid stress, and Neotropical livestock keepers value shade because it reduces heat stress and supports reproduction, weight gain and milk production [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. A systematic review of silvopastoral systems for dairy cows, mostly in Brazil, found the effect on the thermal environment was mostly (57%) favourable: silvopasture gave lower air temperature, black globe temperature, soil surface temperature, black globe humidity index and radiant thermal load than treeless pasture, and cows there showed fewer drinking events, lower surface temperature and lower respiratory rate [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_1].

In the dry Colombian Caribbean, silvopastoral models most intensive in shrubs, trees and rotational pasture reduce heat stress in cattle [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1]. In Cuba live fences came to be used to shade cattle and avoid stress, and Neotropical livestock keepers value shade because it reduces heat stress and supports reproduction, weight gain and milk production [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. A systematic review of silvopastoral systems for dairy cows, mostly in Brazil, found the effect on the thermal environment was mostly (57%) favourable: silvopasture gave lower air temperature, black globe temperature, soil surface temperature, black globe humidity index and radiant thermal load than treeless pasture, and cows there showed fewer drinking events, lower surface temperature and lower respiratory rate [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_1].

Not every index moves: in the same systematic review, results for the temperature humidity index, which uses only air temperature and humidity, were unclear, with most of the studies that used it finding no significant difference between silvopasture and treeless pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_2]. The cattle-shade statement from Australia and the USA is an old citation without a tree system [ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In the dry Colombian Caribbean, silvopastoral models most intensive in shrubs, trees and rotational pasture reduce heat stress in cattle, and a Brazilian study found agroforestry reduced the area at critical thermal-comfort levels for animals by 20 to 100% compared with monoculture pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. In tropical silvopasture, temperatures under tree crowns can average 2-5°C lower than outside them throughout the year, depending on the characteristics of the trees [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_1]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. A systematic review of silvopasture and dairy cattle, mostly from Brazil, found the effect on the thermal environment was mostly (57%) favourable: silvopasture gave lower air temperature, black globe temperature, soil surface temperature and radiant thermal load than treeless pasture, and cows drank less often and had lower surface temperature and respiratory rate [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_1]. An older review cites Kelly et al. (1950) that trees are the most effective shade for cattle, adding evaporative cooling from the leaves to protection from sunlight [ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The types of agroforestry disagree with one another, so no single direction is stated: trees regenerated on cropland and general findings not tied to one type point to strong gains, while linear plantings, planted tree-crop alleys, shaded tree crops and silvopasture each have studies on both sides, split by spacing, shade and tree species. Many sources measured lower production for some adopters. A livestock-yield check on linear agroforestry, drawn from only 12 publications covering 36 paddock-years, could not establish an effect in either direction [ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_13]. A Kenyan on-station alley-cropping trial in Embu adds a direct species contrast within one experiment: maize alley-cropped with leucaena yielded significantly more than both the unfertilised and fertilised maize-monoculture controls, while the same maize alley-cropped with calliandra yielded less than the unfertilised control — same site, same design, opposite signs by hedgerow species [ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_1, ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_2]. In Niger, millet yields on fields with regenerated trees (100 to 370 kg/ha) were higher than on control fields without trees (50 to 270 kg/ha), a gain of 50 to 100 kg/ha the authors attribute to tree presence, and the same protected trees supply dry-season fodder that eases the feed shortage common at that time of year [ev_crop_yield_boton10_1, ev_forage_productivity_boton10_7]. Shade level splits the result within one crop too: in southern Brazil coffee shaded by Mimosa scabrella accumulated more clean coffee over the harvests than unshaded coffee, a gain the authors tie to less frost damage, while the same paper reports from earlier trials that excessive, permanent shade caused coffee production losses comparable to those caused by frosts [ev_crop_yield_caramori96_1, ev_crop_yield_caramori96_2]. Hedgerow competition is measurable: in the same Kenyan trial, maize alley-cropped with calliandra yielded 11% to 51% less than maize given the same prunings from trees grown elsewhere, and with leucaena 2% to 17% less [ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_3, ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_4]. Tree species matters within one region: a West African synthesis found crops did best near Faidherbia albida and some shrubs, but yielded less near Sclerocarya birrea, Albizzia lebbeck and Balanites aegyptiaca than without them, and groundnut showed no significant difference with or without trees or shrubs in Senegal [ev_crop_yield_felix18_5, ev_crop_yield_felix18_4]. A review notes that a few trees of aggressive species such as Senna spectabilis worsened maize yield losses under reduced tillage in Rwanda and Ethiopia [ev_crop_yield_vannoordwijk21_5]. The Niger and Senegal yield gains are second-hand or from a single trial site, each tied to named tree or shrub species [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_2, ev_crop_yield_felix18_3, ev_crop_yield_bogie18_1]. On the loss side, the European windbreak land taken out of annual crops is the authors' judgement within a model for high-income Europe, and they say it can be made up by yield gains on the sheltered cropland [ev_crop_yield_englund21_2]. The Colombian milk figure is second-hand, cited from an earlier World Bank study [ev_climate_shock_cmscr20_3]. Both coffee-resilience statements are second-hand and give no size; one rests on a model for Ethiopian coffee, and the other adds that shade trees also raise the plantation's water use [ev_climate_shock_dsantos23_5, ev_climate_shock_taboada20_1]. The pest, disease and weed findings are indirect: they show less pressure on the crop or herd, not a measured change in output, and the meta-analysis notes that only two studies tested whether pest control translated into crop yield [ev_crop_yield_pumarino15_1]. The live-fence and coffee-weed findings are second-hand [ev_ecosystem_service_moran18_10, ev_ecosystem_service_villa20_5], the Costa Rica and Cameroon finding is a correlation tied to one tree crop [ev_ecosystem_service_seghieri19_10], and the horn-fly counts are from upper-middle-income Colombia [ev_ecosystem_service_giraldo10_4, ev_ecosystem_service_giraldo10_5].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: The studies disagree on whether agroforestry closes the gap between actual and attainable farm output; the result depends on the type of agroforestry, the tree species and how close the trees stand to the crop. In a global review of windbreak and alley systems, wider tree spacing lifted yield — modelling predicted an 8.04% yield gain over a 20 tree-height buffer for windbreaks, and a 13% gain at 15 tree-heights for alley systems [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_8]. The same review found the opposite at close spacing: alleys under 10 tree-heights had reduced yields, and those under 2.5 tree-heights lost more than 25% [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_7]. In dryland agriculture, a separate literature review reported agroforestry techniques raising cereal yields by 69% on average [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. With trees and shrubs kept on Sahelian cropland, reviews cite millet yields of 690 kg/ha under a Faidherbia albida park against 350 kg/ha on control plots in Niger, and grain yields of 773 kg/ha near Guiera senegalensis shrubs against 382 kg/ha in open fields [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_2, ev_crop_yield_felix18_3]; in a Senegal trial under imposed drought, millet with the shrubs produced almost 10 times the biomass of millet without them [ev_crop_yield_bogie18_1]. In Colombia, a World Bank project report cites a study finding that farms with well-established silvopasture lost only 0.4-5.5% of milk productivity during periods of climate variability from 2009 to 2019, against losses of up to 19% on extensive ranches [ev_climate_shock_cmscr20_3]. Two Latin American reviews describe shaded coffee as more resilient to climate change and to climatic extremes [ev_climate_shock_dsantos23_5, ev_climate_shock_taboada20_1]. Findings on pest, disease and weed control under trees are counted here as an indirect measure of lost farm output. A pan-tropical meta-analysis (Pumariño et al.) found weeds significantly less abundant under agroforestry than in controls, and lower pest abundance and less plant damage in perennial crops such as coffee, cocoa and plantain, but no significant effect in annual crops such as maize, rice and beans [ev_ecosystem_service_pumarino15_1, ev_ecosystem_service_pumarino15_2, ev_ecosystem_service_pumarino15_3]. In Colombian silvopasture, fewer horn flies and fewer horn-fly larvae were caught than in treeless improved pasture (Giraldo et al.) [ev_ecosystem_service_giraldo10_4, ev_ecosystem_service_giraldo10_5]. A review of live fences (Morantes-Toloza et al.) cites a study in which they reduced moth populations and fruit-fly infestation in mango orchards [ev_ecosystem_service_moran18_10]; a coffee review (Villarreyna et al.) cites shade and the leaf-litter barrier of shade trees cutting the incidence of weeds, especially aggressive grasses, by more than 40% and up to 95% under dense shade [ev_ecosystem_service_villa20_5]; and regular spatial arrangements in the plot were correlated with lower frosty-pod rot attack in Costa Rica and lower mirid attack in Cameroon (Seghieri et al.) [ev_ecosystem_service_seghieri19_10].

justification.conditionality: The types of agroforestry disagree with one another, so no single direction is stated: trees regenerated on cropland and general findings not tied to one type point to strong gains, while linear plantings, planted tree-crop alleys, shaded tree crops and silvopasture each have studies on both sides, split by spacing, shade and tree species. Many sources measured lower production for some adopters. A livestock-yield check on linear agroforestry, drawn from only 12 publications covering 36 paddock-years, could not establish an effect in either direction [ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_13]. A Kenyan on-station alley-cropping trial in Embu adds a direct species contrast within one experiment: maize alley-cropped with leucaena yielded significantly more than both the unfertilised and fertilised maize-monoculture controls, while the same maize alley-cropped with calliandra yielded less than the unfertilised control — same site, same design, opposite signs by hedgerow species [ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_1, ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_2]. In Niger, millet yields on fields with regenerated trees (100 to 370 kg/ha) were higher than on control fields without trees (50 to 270 kg/ha), a gain of 50 to 100 kg/ha the authors attribute to tree presence, and the same protected trees supply dry-season fodder that eases the feed shortage common at that time of year [ev_crop_yield_boton10_1, ev_forage_productivity_boton10_7]. Shade level splits the result within one crop too: in southern Brazil coffee shaded by Mimosa scabrella accumulated more clean coffee over the harvests than unshaded coffee, a gain the authors tie to less frost damage, while the same paper reports from earlier trials that excessive, permanent shade caused coffee production losses comparable to those caused by frosts [ev_crop_yield_caramori96_1, ev_crop_yield_caramori96_2]. Hedgerow competition is measurable: in the same Kenyan trial, maize alley-cropped with calliandra yielded 11% to 51% less than maize given the same prunings from trees grown elsewhere, and with leucaena 2% to 17% less [ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_3, ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_4]. Tree species matters within one region: a West African synthesis found crops did best near Faidherbia albida and some shrubs, but yielded less near Sclerocarya birrea, Albizzia lebbeck and Balanites aegyptiaca than without them, and groundnut showed no significant difference with or without trees or shrubs in Senegal [ev_crop_yield_felix18_5, ev_crop_yield_felix18_4]. A review notes that a few trees of aggressive species such as Senna spectabilis worsened maize yield losses under reduced tillage in Rwanda and Ethiopia [ev_crop_yield_vannoordwijk21_5]. The Niger and Senegal yield gains are second-hand or from a single trial site, each tied to named tree or shrub species [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_2, ev_crop_yield_felix18_3, ev_crop_yield_bogie18_1]. On the loss side, the European windbreak land taken out of annual crops is the authors' judgement within a model for high-income Europe, and they say it can be made up by yield gains on the sheltered cropland [ev_crop_yield_englund21_2]. The Colombian milk figure is second-hand, cited from an earlier World Bank study [ev_climate_shock_cmscr20_3]. Both coffee-resilience statements are second-hand and give no size; one rests on a model for Ethiopian coffee, and the other adds that shade trees also raise the plantation's water use [ev_climate_shock_dsantos23_5, ev_climate_shock_taboada20_1]. The pest, disease and weed findings are indirect: they show less pressure on the crop or herd, not a measured change in output, and the meta-analysis notes that only two studies tested whether pest control translated into crop yield [ev_crop_yield_pumarino15_1]. The live-fence and coffee-weed findings are second-hand [ev_ecosystem_service_moran18_10, ev_ecosystem_service_villa20_5], the Costa Rica and Cameroon finding is a correlation tied to one tree crop [ev_ecosystem_service_seghieri19_10], and the horn-fly counts are from upper-middle-income Colombia [ev_ecosystem_service_giraldo10_4, ev_ecosystem_service_giraldo10_5].

justification.mechanism: The studies disagree on whether agroforestry closes the gap between actual and attainable farm output; the result depends on the type of agroforestry, the tree species and how close the trees stand to the crop. In a global review of windbreak and alley systems, wider tree spacing lifted yield — modelling predicted an 8.04% yield gain over a 20 tree-height buffer for windbreaks, and a 13% gain at 15 tree-heights for alley systems [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_8]. The same review found the opposite at close spacing: alleys under 10 tree-heights had reduced yields, and those under 2.5 tree-heights lost more than 25% [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_7]. In dryland agriculture, a separate literature review reported agroforestry techniques raising cereal yields by 69% on average [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. With trees and shrubs kept on Sahelian cropland, reviews cite millet yields of 690 kg/ha under a Faidherbia albida park against 350 kg/ha on control plots in Niger, and grain yields of 773 kg/ha near Guiera senegalensis shrubs against 382 kg/ha in open fields [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_2, ev_crop_yield_felix18_3]; in a Senegal trial under imposed drought, millet with the shrubs produced almost 10 times the biomass of millet without them [ev_crop_yield_bogie18_1]. In Colombia, a World Bank project report cites a study finding that farms with well-established silvopasture lost only 0.4-5.5% of milk productivity during periods of climate variability from 2009 to 2019, against losses of up to 19% on extensive ranches [ev_climate_shock_cmscr20_3]. Two Latin American reviews describe shaded coffee as more resilient to climate change and to climatic extremes [ev_climate_shock_dsantos23_5, ev_climate_shock_taboada20_1]. Findings on pest, disease and weed control under trees are counted here as an indirect measure of lost farm output. A pan-tropical meta-analysis (Pumariño et al.) found weeds significantly less abundant under agroforestry than in controls, and lower pest abundance and less plant damage in perennial crops such as coffee, cocoa and plantain, but no significant effect in annual crops such as maize, rice and beans [ev_ecosystem_service_pumarino15_1, ev_ecosystem_service_pumarino15_2, ev_ecosystem_service_pumarino15_3]. In Colombian silvopasture, fewer horn flies and fewer horn-fly larvae were caught than in treeless improved pasture (Giraldo et al.) [ev_ecosystem_service_giraldo10_4, ev_ecosystem_service_giraldo10_5]. A review of live fences (Morantes-Toloza et al.) cites a study in which they reduced moth populations and fruit-fly infestation in mango orchards [ev_ecosystem_service_moran18_10]; a coffee review (Villarreyna et al.) cites shade and the leaf-litter barrier of shade trees cutting the incidence of weeds, especially aggressive grasses, by more than 40% and up to 95% under dense shade [ev_ecosystem_service_villa20_5]; and regular spatial arrangements in the plot were correlated with lower frosty-pod rot attack in Costa Rica and lower mirid attack in Cameroon (Seghieri et al.) [ev_ecosystem_service_seghieri19_10].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The direction is not the same everywhere. The Canadian and US studies also found a small net wheat gain across the field once the sheltered zone is counted, and no shelter benefit in a very wet year [ev_crop_yield_kort88_5, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_3]. Several Costa Rican shaded-coffee comparisons found no yield difference from full sun [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_2, ev_crop_yield_villa20_2, ev_crop_yield_villa20_3]. Some components gained under trees: at a subarctic Canadian site, bean and potato yields were higher beside windbreaks than in the open [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2], and in Costa Rica milk yield and dry-season weight gain were reported higher for cattle on pasture with many trees [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. The French pea loss was smaller under drought [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2]. The losses are clearest for grain and legume crops and pasture competing directly with trees. All of this evidence is from rich countries and may not carry over to low-income farming. The European windbreak land loss is the authors' judgement within a model for high-income Europe, and they say it can be made up by yield gains on the sheltered cropland [ev_crop_yield_englund21_2].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In high-income countries the evidence points to a moderate widening of the production gap: trees compete with the neighbouring crop for light, water and nutrients. Canadian and US shelterbelt studies found a zone of no crop right next to the belt, a 50% reduction from competition a little further out, and higher yields in the sheltered zone beyond [ev_crop_yield_kort88_3, ev_crop_yield_kort88_4]; one Canadian study estimated a net yield loss equal to the width of the shelterbelt, though the authors doubt the mid-field baseline used [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_4]. In a French walnut alley system, pea yield under the trees was 25% to 77% lower than in full sun under normal rainfall [ev_crop_yield_blan22_1]. A Costa Rican shaded-coffee experiment found a 30% yield reduction against coffee monoculture [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11]. In New Zealand, pasture under radiata pine had completely gone after 15 years as the trees came to dominate soil moisture [ev_forage_productivity_pollock08_1], and in Costa Rica multistrata live fences may shade out grasses along pasture edges [ev_forage_productivity_garbach12_1]. A European model of windbreaks on cropland notes that they take a large share of land out of annual crops — one third of the landscape for short-rotation coppice windbreaks and one ninth for short-rotation forestry at full implementation [ev_crop_yield_englund21_2].

justification.statement: agroforestry production_gap: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE — material weight on both the benefit and the harm side, so no direction is stated. This is not a null finding: studies found real effects, in opposite directions, and the agreement note lists both sides. Read the conditionality for what separates them (transfer: in_context).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: On the loss side, the same Chinese shelterbelt study that found a 16.57% gain within the sheltered field also found yield 20.47% lower in the edge zone immediately next to the shelterbelt, where trees compete directly with the crop [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2], and the northeast China maize study found yield falling once shelterbelt density rose above the optimum [ev_crop_yield_zheng16_4]. In China, juvenile plumcot rows cut intercropped soybean yield by 46.03% and alfalfa hay yield by 51.83% against sole cropping, partly because the intercrop had less cropped area and a lower seeding rate [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]. In China, apricot-wheat intercropping significantly reduced wheat grain yield and its components in both years measured [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3]. In Brazilian agroforestry, soybean yielded only 500 to 700 kg/ha against about 2700 to 3000 kg/ha in monoculture over two seasons [ev_crop_yield_santos25_5]. In Indonesia, agroforestry maize yield was significantly lower by the third harvest, though soybean yield in the same system was unaffected across all three harvests [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_4]. In Brazilian dairy, a review of silvopastoral studies found no significant difference in milk production in the studies that measured it, and under high-density Acacia decurrens silvopasture in Colombia, milk per cow per day was lower than in the open field, though lower-density silvopasture there still out-performed the open field [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. During El Niño events, silvopastoral systems in Colombia lost less milk production than conventional systems, but still recorded a loss, not a gain [ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1]. In Brazil, drought-induced cocoa yield loss showed no relationship with shade-tree ground cover (p = 0.64), and in Mexico coffee harvest loss was unrelated to vegetation management, with all farms losing 18 to 40% of the harvest regardless of shade complexity [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. In Argentina, the forage benefit itself is conditional and sometimes reverses: it held in very humid areas in both normal and dry years, showed no difference between systems in semi-arid areas, and at the semi-arid Santiago del Estero site swung from a slight gain in normal years to an 89% loss in a dry year, with denser tree canopy associated with lower relative forage production across sites [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_7]. The same Brazilian coffee paper reports from earlier trials that complete, permanent shade caused coffee production losses comparable to those caused by frosts [ev_crop_yield_caramori96_2]. What separates the sides is mainly how dense the trees are and how close they stand to the crop or pasture: moderate shelter or shade gains, while dense canopy and the strip next to the trees lose. This evidence comes from China, Iran, Brazil, Colombia, Argentina and Sri Lanka and may not carry over directly to low-income countries. The Brazilian alley-cropping figures are a single trial, and its higher total-productivity and stability figures only hold once the trees' own fuelwood and fodder biomass are counted alongside the food crop, not for the food crop alone [ev_crop_yield_martins13_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_martins13_1, ev_yield_stability_martins13_1]. The Bahia shade-removal finding is a second-hand citation in a review editorial and is confounded with a simultaneous fertiliser change, so the yield gain cannot be attributed to shade removal alone [ev_crop_yield_vaast14_3]. The Colombian milk figure is second-hand, cited from an earlier World Bank study [ev_climate_shock_cmscr20_3]. The horn-fly counts are indirect: they show less pest pressure on the herd, not a measured change in milk or meat output, and the difference was significant on two of the three farms in the fly-capture count [ev_ecosystem_service_giraldo10_4, ev_ecosystem_service_giraldo10_5].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In upper-middle-income countries the studies disagree, as they do for agroforestry overall. On the gain side, several studies show agroforestry or silvopasture raising production. In China, a national meta-analysis found crop yield 16.57% higher within sheltered farmland than unsheltered [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1], and a separate study of shelterbelt-protected maize in northeast China found yield gains of 4.28 to 9.45% at the optimal level of tree protection across climatic-productivity zones, highest in the semi-arid west [ev_crop_yield_zheng16_1, ev_crop_yield_zheng16_2, ev_crop_yield_zheng16_3]. In Iran, intercropped wheat and barley yielded 35% and 39% higher near trees than in their respective monocultures [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_2]. In Brazil, second-year coffee yield under the best-performing shade-tree species reached up to 101.99 kg/ha while the unshaded monoculture control yielded nothing in the same year [ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1]. For livestock, Colombian intensive silvopasture raised milk production 32.1% over the same pasture grasses without shrubs or trees, and milk production still rose 10% in the lowest-rainfall year in several decades after a switch to intensive silvopasture that also allowed irrigation to be dropped [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Leucaena-based silvopasture in Colombia raised stocking rate and milk output while eliminating chemical fertiliser, and a review reports silvopasture beef output 12-fold higher per unit of land than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. In mixed crop-livestock Brazil, cattle in silvopasture gained 512 g/animal/day against 452 g/day in monoculture, and tree leaves added about 40 kg/ha of nitrogen in a cactus-pear-and-buffel-grass system, with potential to cut fertiliser costs [ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]. In Argentina, forage production under trees exceeded treeless grassland or pasture at drought intensities at or below the authors' dry-year threshold [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1], and in Colombia forage production held steady through intense drought while grass monoculture biomass fell to a quarter [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. In a mixed pasture of leucaena (Leucaena leucocephala) and the grass Setaria sphacelata, reported from Sri Lanka in the same review, nitrogen transferred from the tree gave the grass a 16% higher nitrogen yield than in monoculture, with 21% of the grass's nitrogen traced to the leucaena [ev_forage_productivity_dagang03_2]. A review also reports that integrating a grazed fodder bank — fodder trees or shrubs established on part of the pasture and then grazed — repeatedly raises animal production, though the gain is delayed by the trees' establishment period and by taking part of the pasture out of use while they establish [ev_livestock_productivity_dagang03_5]. In Brazil's semi-arid Cariri Paraibano, alley cropping cut maize-plus-bean biomass by about 38% against crops grown without trees over the whole experiment, though counting the trees' own leaf, twig and fuelwood biomass, total productivity in the tree system was 260% higher than in the treeless system, with biomass productivity also varying far less year to year (a coefficient of variation of 18.2% against 89.5%) [ev_crop_yield_martins13_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_martins13_1, ev_yield_stability_martins13_1]. In southern Brazil, coffee shaded by Mimosa scabrella accumulated 6584 to 7229 kg/ha of clean coffee over seven harvests against 4340 kg/ha unshaded, a gain the authors tie to less frost damage [ev_crop_yield_caramori96_1]. On a set of monitored Bahia cocoa farms, removing shade trees entirely alongside fertiliser use nearly doubled cocoa bean yield [ev_crop_yield_vaast14_3]. In Colombia, a World Bank project report cites a study finding that farms with well-established silvopasture lost only 0.4-5.5% of milk productivity during periods of climate variability from 2009 to 2019, against losses of up to 19% on extensive ranches [ev_climate_shock_cmscr20_3]. Findings on pest, disease and weed control under trees are counted here as an indirect measure of lost farm output. In Colombian silvopasture, fewer horn flies and fewer horn-fly larvae were caught than in treeless improved pasture (Giraldo et al.) [ev_ecosystem_service_giraldo10_4, ev_ecosystem_service_giraldo10_5].
