justification.conditionality: On the loss side, the same Chinese shelterbelt study that found a 16.57% gain within the sheltered field also found yield 20.47% lower in the edge zone immediately next to the shelterbelt, where trees compete directly with the crop [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2], and the northeast China maize study found yield falling once shelterbelt density rose above the optimum [ev_crop_yield_zheng16_4]. In China, juvenile plumcot rows cut intercropped soybean yield by 46.03% and alfalfa hay yield by 51.83% against sole cropping, partly because the intercrop had less cropped area and a lower seeding rate [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]. In China, apricot-wheat intercropping significantly reduced wheat grain yield and its components in both years measured [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3]. In Brazilian agroforestry, soybean yielded only 500 to 700 kg/ha against about 2700 to 3000 kg/ha in monoculture over two seasons [ev_crop_yield_santos25_5]. In Indonesia, agroforestry maize yield was significantly lower by the third harvest, though soybean yield in the same system was unaffected across all three harvests [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_4]. In Brazilian dairy, a review of silvopastoral studies found no significant difference in milk production in the studies that measured it, and under high-density Acacia decurrens silvopasture in Colombia, milk per cow per day was lower than in the open field, though lower-density silvopasture there still out-performed the open field [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. During El Niño events, silvopastoral systems in Colombia lost less milk production than conventional systems, but still recorded a loss, not a gain [ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1]. In Brazil, drought-induced cocoa yield loss showed no relationship with shade-tree ground cover (p = 0.64), and in Mexico coffee harvest loss was unrelated to vegetation management, with all farms losing 18 to 40% of the harvest regardless of shade complexity [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. In Argentina, the forage benefit itself is conditional and sometimes reverses: it held in very humid areas in both normal and dry years, showed no difference between systems in semi-arid areas, and at the semi-arid Santiago del Estero site swung from a slight gain in normal years to an 89% loss in a dry year, with denser tree canopy associated with lower relative forage production across sites [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_7]. The same Brazilian coffee paper reports from earlier trials that complete, permanent shade caused coffee production losses comparable to those caused by frosts [ev_crop_yield_caramori96_2]. What separates the sides is mainly how dense the trees are and how close they stand to the crop or pasture: moderate shelter or shade gains, while dense canopy and the strip next to the trees lose. This evidence comes from China, Iran, Brazil, Colombia, Argentina and Sri Lanka and may not carry over directly to low-income countries. The Brazilian alley-cropping figures are a single trial, and its higher total-productivity and stability figures only hold once the trees' own fuelwood and fodder biomass are counted alongside the food crop, not for the food crop alone [ev_crop_yield_martins13_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_martins13_1, ev_yield_stability_martins13_1]. The Bahia shade-removal finding is a second-hand citation in a review editorial and is confounded with a simultaneous fertiliser change, so the yield gain cannot be attributed to shade removal alone [ev_crop_yield_vaast14_3]. The Colombian milk figure is second-hand, cited from an earlier World Bank study [ev_climate_shock_cmscr20_3]. The horn-fly counts are indirect: they show less pest pressure on the herd, not a measured change in milk or meat output, and the difference was significant on two of the three farms in the fly-capture count [ev_ecosystem_service_giraldo10_4, ev_ecosystem_service_giraldo10_5].

justification.mechanism: In upper-middle-income countries the studies disagree, as they do for agroforestry overall. On the gain side, several studies show agroforestry or silvopasture raising production. In China, a national meta-analysis found crop yield 16.57% higher within sheltered farmland than unsheltered [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1], and a separate study of shelterbelt-protected maize in northeast China found yield gains of 4.28 to 9.45% at the optimal level of tree protection across climatic-productivity zones, highest in the semi-arid west [ev_crop_yield_zheng16_1, ev_crop_yield_zheng16_2, ev_crop_yield_zheng16_3]. In Iran, intercropped wheat and barley yielded 35% and 39% higher near trees than in their respective monocultures [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_2]. In Brazil, second-year coffee yield under the best-performing shade-tree species reached up to 101.99 kg/ha while the unshaded monoculture control yielded nothing in the same year [ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1]. For livestock, Colombian intensive silvopasture raised milk production 32.1% over the same pasture grasses without shrubs or trees, and milk production still rose 10% in the lowest-rainfall year in several decades after a switch to intensive silvopasture that also allowed irrigation to be dropped [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Leucaena-based silvopasture in Colombia raised stocking rate and milk output while eliminating chemical fertiliser, and a review reports silvopasture beef output 12-fold higher per unit of land than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. In mixed crop-livestock Brazil, cattle in silvopasture gained 512 g/animal/day against 452 g/day in monoculture, and tree leaves added about 40 kg/ha of nitrogen in a cactus-pear-and-buffel-grass system, with potential to cut fertiliser costs [ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]. In Argentina, forage production under trees exceeded treeless grassland or pasture at drought intensities at or below the authors' dry-year threshold [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1], and in Colombia forage production held steady through intense drought while grass monoculture biomass fell to a quarter [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. In a mixed pasture of leucaena (Leucaena leucocephala) and the grass Setaria sphacelata, reported from Sri Lanka in the same review, nitrogen transferred from the tree gave the grass a 16% higher nitrogen yield than in monoculture, with 21% of the grass's nitrogen traced to the leucaena [ev_forage_productivity_dagang03_2]. A review also reports that integrating a grazed fodder bank — fodder trees or shrubs established on part of the pasture and then grazed — repeatedly raises animal production, though the gain is delayed by the trees' establishment period and by taking part of the pasture out of use while they establish [ev_livestock_productivity_dagang03_5]. In Brazil's semi-arid Cariri Paraibano, alley cropping cut maize-plus-bean biomass by about 38% against crops grown without trees over the whole experiment, though counting the trees' own leaf, twig and fuelwood biomass, total productivity in the tree system was 260% higher than in the treeless system, with biomass productivity also varying far less year to year (a coefficient of variation of 18.2% against 89.5%) [ev_crop_yield_martins13_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_martins13_1, ev_yield_stability_martins13_1]. In southern Brazil, coffee shaded by Mimosa scabrella accumulated 6584 to 7229 kg/ha of clean coffee over seven harvests against 4340 kg/ha unshaded, a gain the authors tie to less frost damage [ev_crop_yield_caramori96_1]. On a set of monitored Bahia cocoa farms, removing shade trees entirely alongside fertiliser use nearly doubled cocoa bean yield [ev_crop_yield_vaast14_3]. In Colombia, a World Bank project report cites a study finding that farms with well-established silvopasture lost only 0.4-5.5% of milk productivity during periods of climate variability from 2009 to 2019, against losses of up to 19% on extensive ranches [ev_climate_shock_cmscr20_3]. Findings on pest, disease and weed control under trees are counted here as an indirect measure of lost farm output. In Colombian silvopasture, fewer horn flies and fewer horn-fly larvae were caught than in treeless improved pasture (Giraldo et al.) [ev_ecosystem_service_giraldo10_4, ev_ecosystem_service_giraldo10_5].

justification.statement: agroforestry production_gap: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE — material weight on both the benefit and the harm side, so no direction is stated. This is not a null finding: studies found real effects, in opposite directions, and the agreement note lists both sides. Read the conditionality for what separates them (transfer: in_context).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The class rests on a single Chinese experiment with young trees, so confidence is low and the size may not hold as the trees mature or in other designs [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1]. Part of the Chinese loss reflects the smaller cropped area and the lower seeding rate and irrigation given to the intercropped soybean, and yields are per unit of total plot area, so the tree rows count against the crop [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]. The Senegal result runs the other way over the whole protected plot, which separates the two: hedges bordering a plot lose crop near the hedge but can raise the plot total, while trees planted through the plot at close spacing take crop area and water directly [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13]. The Senegal figure is a second-hand reading in grey literature with no comparator stated beyond the unprotected plots. China is upper-middle income, outside the LIC/LMIC target; Senegal is lower-middle income, within it [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13]. The Indian biodrainage yield gain is attributed to relief from waterlogging through a lowered water table, not to any general shade or nutrient mechanism, and comes from a single planting in one location [ev_crop_yield_ram11_2, ev_crop_yield_ram11_3]. India, like Senegal, is lower-middle income, within the LIC/LMIC target.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In irrigated cropping, trees compete with the crop for water, nutrients and light. Between rows of juvenile plumcot trees in drip-irrigated, semi-arid Xinjiang, China, intercropped soybean yielded 46.03% less and intercropped alfalfa 51.83% less than the same crops grown alone, over two years [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]. In village irrigated perimeters of the Senegal River valley, hedges cut yields up to 10 metres from the hedge in the rainy season, while total yields across the protected plots rose 23 per cent in the off-season, as an FAO review reports from earlier work (Tamba; Samba et al.) [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13]. In canal-irrigated Haryana, India, a Eucalyptus biodrainage planting along field boundaries lowered the water table and raised wheat grain yield 3.4 times over compared with adjacent waterlogged fields without the plantation, though near the tree lines shading and root competition cut wheat yield by an estimated 11.7% [ev_crop_yield_ram11_2, ev_crop_yield_ram11_3].

justification.statement: agroforestry production_gap: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE — material weight on both the benefit and the harm side, so no direction is stated. This is not a null finding: studies found real effects, in opposite directions, and the agreement note lists both sides. Read the conditionality for what separates them (transfer: in_context).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: A sizeable minority of measured results go the other way, so the rating stays at moderate. In semi-arid Kenya, maize under dispersed Grevillea robusta trees yielded far less than unshaded maize in each of four seasons [ev_crop_yield_lott09_1, ev_crop_yield_lott09_2, ev_crop_yield_lott09_3, ev_crop_yield_lott09_4]; in a Kenyan alley trial, calliandra hedges cut maize yield by 11% to 51% and leucaena hedges by 2% to 17% against maize given the same prunings [ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_3, ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_4]; and in Brazil alley cropping cut maize-plus-bean biomass by about 38% [ev_crop_yield_martins13_1]. Crop yield next to shelterbelts was 20.47% lower in the edge zone in China, and lower in the strip next to the belt in Canada [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1]. In Niger the Ziziphus gain reversed when NPK fertiliser was used, and cowpea yielded less under the trees without fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_bado21_3, ev_crop_yield_bado21_4]. Groundnut and millet yielded less under Cordyla pinnata in Senegal, and crops near Sclerocarya birrea, Albizzia lebbeck and Balanites aegyptiaca yielded less than without them [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_11, ev_crop_yield_felix18_5]. What separates the sides is mainly tree species, tree density and fertiliser use. Several gains are second-hand or tied to named species, the Honduran figure is farmer-reported in a project-written article and bundles the trees with mulching and no burning [ev_crop_yield_welc02_6], and the Chinese, Brazilian, Canadian and French findings come from richer countries.On the loss side, a European model of windbreaks on cropland notes that they take a large share of land out of annual crops — one third of the landscape for short-rotation coppice windbreaks and one ninth for short-rotation forestry at full implementation [ev_crop_yield_englund21_2]. The European windbreak land loss is the authors' judgement within a model for high-income Europe, and they say it can be made up by yield gains on the sheltered cropland [ev_crop_yield_englund21_2].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In rainfed cropping the evidence points to a moderate reduction in the gap between actual and attainable crop output, while agroforestry overall is conflicting; 25 papers name this farming system. The gains come mostly from trees and shrubs kept in Sahelian and East African fields and from nitrogen-fixing trees. Reviews cite millet yields doubling or even tripling under Faidherbia albida in Senegal, and average gains of 150% for maize and 73% for sorghum under its canopy [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_8, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_9]; in Ethiopia, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns yielded more than open-field wheat in normal seasons and up to 85% more in a dry El Niño year [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In Niger, Ziziphus trees raised millet yields by 41% without fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_bado21_1], and in Senegal millet yielded 886 kg/ha with Piliostigma reticulatum shrubs against 499 kg/ha without [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_15]. A meta-analysis found maize yields rose after improved fallows and relay intercrops of woody legumes compared with unfertilised maize [ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_1, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_2], and in Cameroon alley cropping without fertiliser kept maize and groundnut yields above the treeless control [ev_crop_yield_tonye95_1, ev_crop_yield_tonye95_2]. Across Chinese studies, crop yield within sheltered farmland was 16.57% higher than unsheltered [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1]. In Honduras, farmers report maize yield gains of at least 60% after switching to the Quesungual system [ev_crop_yield_welc02_6].

justification.conditionality: A sizeable minority of measured results go the other way, so the rating stays at moderate. In semi-arid Kenya, maize under dispersed Grevillea robusta trees yielded far less than unshaded maize in each of four seasons [ev_crop_yield_lott09_1, ev_crop_yield_lott09_2, ev_crop_yield_lott09_3, ev_crop_yield_lott09_4]; in a Kenyan alley trial, calliandra hedges cut maize yield by 11% to 51% and leucaena hedges by 2% to 17% against maize given the same prunings [ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_3, ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_4]; and in Brazil alley cropping cut maize-plus-bean biomass by about 38% [ev_crop_yield_martins13_1]. Crop yield next to shelterbelts was 20.47% lower in the edge zone in China, and lower in the strip next to the belt in Canada [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1]. In Niger the Ziziphus gain reversed when NPK fertiliser was used, and cowpea yielded less under the trees without fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_bado21_3, ev_crop_yield_bado21_4]. Groundnut and millet yielded less under Cordyla pinnata in Senegal, and crops near Sclerocarya birrea, Albizzia lebbeck and Balanites aegyptiaca yielded less than without them [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_11, ev_crop_yield_felix18_5]. What separates the sides is mainly tree species, tree density and fertiliser use. Several gains are second-hand or tied to named species, the Honduran figure is farmer-reported in a project-written article and bundles the trees with mulching and no burning [ev_crop_yield_welc02_6], and the Chinese, Brazilian, Canadian and French findings come from richer countries.On the loss side, a European model of windbreaks on cropland notes that they take a large share of land out of annual crops — one third of the landscape for short-rotation coppice windbreaks and one ninth for short-rotation forestry at full implementation [ev_crop_yield_englund21_2]. The European windbreak land loss is the authors' judgement within a model for high-income Europe, and they say it can be made up by yield gains on the sheltered cropland [ev_crop_yield_englund21_2].

justification.mechanism: In rainfed cropping the evidence points to a moderate reduction in the gap between actual and attainable crop output, while agroforestry overall is conflicting; 25 papers name this farming system. The gains come mostly from trees and shrubs kept in Sahelian and East African fields and from nitrogen-fixing trees. Reviews cite millet yields doubling or even tripling under Faidherbia albida in Senegal, and average gains of 150% for maize and 73% for sorghum under its canopy [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_8, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_9]; in Ethiopia, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns yielded more than open-field wheat in normal seasons and up to 85% more in a dry El Niño year [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In Niger, Ziziphus trees raised millet yields by 41% without fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_bado21_1], and in Senegal millet yielded 886 kg/ha with Piliostigma reticulatum shrubs against 499 kg/ha without [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_15]. A meta-analysis found maize yields rose after improved fallows and relay intercrops of woody legumes compared with unfertilised maize [ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_1, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_2], and in Cameroon alley cropping without fertiliser kept maize and groundnut yields above the treeless control [ev_crop_yield_tonye95_1, ev_crop_yield_tonye95_2]. Across Chinese studies, crop yield within sheltered farmland was 16.57% higher than unsheltered [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1]. In Honduras, farmers report maize yield gains of at least 60% after switching to the Quesungual system [ev_crop_yield_welc02_6].

justification.statement: agroforestry moderately reduces production_gap in BEN, BFA, BRA, CAN, CHN, CMR, ETH, FRA, GMB, HND, IDN, IND, IRN, KEN, MLI, MRT, MWI, NER, NGA, RWA, SEN, TZA, ZMB, ZWE; measured HARM (maladaptation) in 12 sources — the practice worsened this outcome for some adopters (robust evidence, medium agreement → high confidence; transfer: in_context).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Gains are not universal. Under high-density Acacia decurrens silvopasture in Colombia, milk per cow per day was lower than in the open field, though a lower-density silvopasture at the same site still out-performed the open field, showing tree density itself can flip the sign [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. A review of Brazilian silvopastoral thermal-comfort and production studies found no significant difference in milk production in the studies that measured it [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. During El Niño events, silvopastoral systems in Colombia still lost milk production, just less than conventional systems did [ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1]. The Argentine multi-site forage evidence is the clearest statement that the benefit is severity- and site-dependent: it held in humid areas in both normal and dry years, showed no difference in semi-arid areas, and reversed from a slight gain to an 89% loss in a dry year at one semi-arid site, with denser canopy generally associated with lower relative forage production across sites [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_7]. Most of the Latin American livestock units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume rather than new primary measurements, and the clearest primary magnitudes (Colombia, Nicaragua, Costa Rica) are upper-middle or high income, while the Senegalese fodder evidence is lower-middle income, which is why this row's evidence sits adjacent to, rather than squarely inside, the LIC/LMIC target. Against this, a review of a regional silvopastoral conservation project in Esparza, Costa Rica reports that unpruned multistrata live fences can reduce forage availability by shading out the grasses along pasture edges [ev_forage_productivity_garbach12_1]. The same arid-India trial that supplies the browse-fodder finding also measured lower understorey herbage yield under every tree and shrub species than in a treeless control during drought years, a trade-off between the forage layers that this row's gain does not net off [ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_2].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Across silvopastoral systems, tree cover consistently raises forage and livestock output relative to open pasture. In Senegal, herbaceous biomass under Acacia tortilis and Balanites aegyptiaca canopies reached 2 to 5 times that measured in treeless areas, and tree leaves, fruit and pods make up about 40% of cattle diet and 80% of small-ruminant diet in the dry-to-wet-season transition [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_20, ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21]. Reviews report tree shade in pastures associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain generally [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4], and in Nicaragua and Costa Rica, milk production was 29% and over 15% higher on high tree-density or silvopasture compared with low-cover or full-sun pasture, with dry-season liveweight gains 2 to 5% higher on high-tree-density pasture, attributed to lower heat stress and more available foliage and fruit [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. In Colombia, intensive silvopasture raised milk production 32.1% over the same pasture grasses without shrubs or trees, raised milk per hectare per year under Leucaena against an open-field system, and a review reports beef output 12-fold higher per unit of land than traditional grazing, also higher than improved treeless pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Intensive silvopasture is also reported to raise stocking rate several-fold over extensive grazing, with proportional gains in meat and milk output, and better cattle feeding in critical drought periods is said to reduce seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. During a severe drought, Colombian silvopastoral forage production held steady while grass-monoculture biomass fell to a quarter, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are described as more drought-tolerant, giving more stable dry-season forage volumes [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. A review also reports that integrating a grazed fodder bank — fodder trees or shrubs established on part of the pasture and then grazed — repeatedly raises animal production, though the gain is delayed by the trees' establishment period and by taking part of the pasture out of use while they establish [ev_livestock_productivity_dagang03_5]. In arid India, trees and shrubs lopped for green leaf fodder supply sheep, goats and camels with browse in drought years, when grass is scarce [ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_2].

justification.statement: agroforestry moderately reduces production_gap in ARG, BRA, COL, CRI, IND, KEN, LKA, MEX, NIC, PER, SEN; measured HARM (maladaptation) in 4 sources — the practice worsened this outcome for some adopters (robust evidence, medium agreement → high confidence; transfer: adjacent).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The same Bolivia cacao trial that found lower cacao yield under shade also found that selling the plantain and banana grown alongside the cacao more than made up for the lost cacao revenue [ev_agricultural_production_value_armengot16_1] — so a crop-yield loss does not always mean a production loss once the other products in the system are counted. The direction turns on the shade and nutrient balance and the crop studied, which is why no single direction is stated. The same Brazilian paper reports from earlier trials that complete, permanent shade caused coffee production losses comparable to those caused by frosts [ev_crop_yield_caramori96_2]. What separates the sides is mainly the amount of shade and whether only the main crop or the whole system's output is counted. Both coffee-resilience statements are second-hand and give no size; one rests on a model for Ethiopian coffee, and the other adds that shade trees also raise the plantation's water use [ev_climate_shock_dsantos23_5, ev_climate_shock_taboada20_1]. These two findings are indirect, showing less weed or disease pressure rather than a change in output; the weed figure is second-hand and the frosty-pod and mirid finding is a correlation [ev_ecosystem_service_villa20_5, ev_ecosystem_service_seghieri19_10].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In tree-crop farming (mainly coffee and cocoa) the studies disagree, as they do for agroforestry overall; 22 papers name this farming system. Shade trees compete with the crop for light while also buffering climate stress and adding nutrients, and both effects show up in the evidence. On the loss side, a pan-tropical review found shaded coffee and cocoa yielded 26% less per hectare than conventional, unshaded systems [ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1]; a pan-tropical cocoa meta-analysis found cocoa bean yield 25% lower in agroforestry than in monoculture, though total system yield (cocoa plus the other products) was about ten times higher [ev_crop_yield_niether20_1]; and in Bolivia, full-sun cacao monocultures were 41% more productive in cacao alone than agroforestry plots, attributed to greater light reaching the trees [ev_crop_yield_armengot16_1]. On the gain side, a global meta-analysis of coffee systems found the odds of climate-related yield loss were lower under agroforestry than under conventional coffee, an odds ratio of 0.69, for both arabica and robusta coffee [ev_crop_yield_patil25_1, ev_crop_yield_patil25_10]; in southern Brazil, coffee shaded by Mimosa scabrella accumulated 6584 to 7229 kg/ha of clean coffee over seven harvests against 4340 kg/ha unshaded, which the authors tie to less frost damage [ev_crop_yield_caramori96_1]; and in Rwanda, intercropping coffee with Tephrosia (a nitrogen-fixing shrub) mulch raised coffee yield by 23% to 36%, rising to 25% to 42% when fertiliser was added too [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_1]. Two Latin American reviews describe shaded coffee as more resilient to climate change and to climatic extremes [ev_climate_shock_dsantos23_5, ev_climate_shock_taboada20_1]. Findings on pest, disease and weed control under trees are counted here as an indirect measure of lost farm output. A coffee review (Villarreyna et al.) cites shade and the leaf-litter barrier of shade trees cutting the incidence of weeds, especially aggressive grasses, by more than 40% and up to 95% under dense shade [ev_ecosystem_service_villa20_5], and regular spatial arrangements in the plot were correlated with lower frosty-pod rot attack in Costa Rica and lower mirid attack in Cameroon (Seghieri et al.) [ev_ecosystem_service_seghieri19_10].

justification.conditionality: The same Bolivia cacao trial that found lower cacao yield under shade also found that selling the plantain and banana grown alongside the cacao more than made up for the lost cacao revenue [ev_agricultural_production_value_armengot16_1] — so a crop-yield loss does not always mean a production loss once the other products in the system are counted. The same Brazilian paper reports from earlier trials that complete, permanent shade caused coffee production losses comparable to those caused by frosts [ev_crop_yield_caramori96_2]. What separates the sides is mainly the amount of shade and whether only the main crop or the whole system's output is counted. Both coffee-resilience statements are second-hand and give no size; one rests on a model for Ethiopian coffee, and the other adds that shade trees also raise the plantation's water use [ev_climate_shock_dsantos23_5, ev_climate_shock_taboada20_1]. These two findings are indirect, showing less weed or disease pressure rather than a change in output; the weed figure is second-hand and the frosty-pod and mirid finding is a correlation [ev_ecosystem_service_villa20_5, ev_ecosystem_service_seghieri19_10].

justification.statement: agroforestry production_gap: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE — material weight on both the benefit and the harm side, so no direction is stated. This is not a null finding: studies found real effects, in opposite directions, and the agreement note lists both sides. Read the conditionality for what separates them (transfer: in_context).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: A systematic review's pooled crop-yield effect has a confidence interval spanning zero, the sub-Saharan adoption meta-analysis found that agroforestry overall is not associated with a statistically significant effect on yield (Cohen's d = 0.35, 95% CI: −0.07 to 0.78) [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_1], an integrative review counts 15 of 21 studies favouring agroforestry and 5 favouring monoculture, and another review notes trade-offs between crop intensification and ecosystem services in most agroforestry [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_1, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_1, ev_crop_yield_vannoordwijk21_7]. The strong class therefore holds for well-designed tree–crop systems and for the better-quality studies; pooled adoption effects across all study types are smaller and less certain [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_1, ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_2]. The pest-control yield link rests on very few studies cited in the meta-analysis (Ogol, Spence and Keddie 1999; Sileshi et al. 2005) [ev_crop_yield_pumarino15_1]. The cited 69% cereal-yield figure reaches this row second-hand through Arslan et al.: the citing text does not describe the agroforestry techniques further and reports no significance [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. The pooled magnitude combines a crop-yield and a soil-nitrogen response ratio [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1]. The Lower Nyando productivity gain had large standard errors and was not significant [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1]. Livestock yield under linear agroforestry (alleys and windbreaks pooled) in a global review did not differ from the control: a 0.3% reduction with an even split of gains and losses over 36 paddock years [ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_13]. The weed finding is indirect: it shows less weed pressure, not a measured change in yield [ev_ecosystem_service_pumarino15_1].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: A sub-Saharan meta-analysis reports crop yield under agroforestry about twice that of non-agroforestry controls in the humid zone, and a pantropical meta-analysis finds higher soil nitrogen stocks than in crop monocultures, used here as a component [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1]. A meta-analysis cited in Arslan et al. (Branca et al.) associates agroforestry techniques with a 69% increase in cereal yields across the studies it consulted [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. IPCC assessments attribute higher land-equivalent ratios and large food-production benefits to well-planned agroforestry, and a cited review reports agroforestry systems 36-100% more productive than monoculture [ev_crop_yield_ipccar6ch5_8, ev_crop_yield_ipccsrccl6_3, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_12]. In Lower Nyando, Kenya, farmers in an agroforestry project improved farm productivity on average against a control group [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1]. A systematic review and meta-analysis of agroforestry adoption by smallholders in sub-Saharan Africa found a significant yield gain for maize in the high-quality studies (Cohen's d = 0.27, 95% CI: 0.12 to 0.42), and a pan-tropical meta-analysis of pest control reports that the only studies testing whether agroforestry pest control translated into crop yield both found a gain [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_2, ev_crop_yield_pumarino15_1]. Counted as an indirect measure of lost farm output, the same pest-control meta-analysis (Pumariño et al.) found weeds significantly less abundant under agroforestry than in controls [ev_ecosystem_service_pumarino15_1].

justification.statement: agroforestry strongly reduces production_gap in ETH, KEN, MWI, ZMB (robust evidence, high agreement → very_high confidence; transfer: adjacent).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Whether the net balance comes out positive depends on where yield is measured, how much water or wind stress the system faces, and the farming system. A global review of windbreak paddocks found crop yield averaged 8.3% lower than treeless paddocks when measured across the whole protected paddock, including the competition zone next to the trees [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1], a crop-specific effect since pasture yield in the same dataset rose by 3.1% [ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_4]; modelled instead as a response curve across a transect of tree heights downwind, the same data gave a net gain of 8.04% [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5]. In Saskatchewan, the competition strip and the sheltered gain beyond it both showed in a dry growing season, but the sheltered gain disappeared in a wet year when water was not limiting [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_3]. In Senegal, yield fell within 10 metres of hedges during the rainy season but rose by 23% across protected plots in the dry season [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13], while at Bambey the same hedges were reported to have a neutral effect on groundnut yield [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_14]. Pooled across many agroforestry studies, hedgerow systems specifically showed a lower yield response than other agroforestry practices in the same analysis [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_5]. In pasture systems, shade from live fences can reduce forage availability along the pasture edge [ev_forage_productivity_garbach12_1] and, if excessive, the overall productive pasture area of the farm [ev_livestock_productivity_moran18_14]. Benefit is more likely where the windbreak tree roots sit deeper than the crop roots, reducing below-ground competition [ev_crop_yield_moran18_11]. Most of the quantified evidence is from temperate, high-income systems in Canada, the United States and China; a fodder-tree feeding trial in Cambodia found cattle fed leucaena from living-fence stock gained weight while cattle on the standard dry-season diet lost weight [ev_livestock_productivity_gill20_1], but the low- and lower-middle-income evidence base for crop yield itself is thinner. A European model of windbreaks on cropland notes that they take a large share of land out of annual crops — one third of the landscape for short-rotation coppice windbreaks and one ninth for short-rotation forestry at full implementation [ev_crop_yield_englund21_2]. This is the authors' judgement within a model for high-income Europe, and they say it can be made up by yield gains on the sheltered cropland [ev_crop_yield_englund21_2]. The live-fence pest finding is second-hand and indirect: it shows less pest pressure, not a measured change in mango output [ev_ecosystem_service_moran18_10].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: A line of trees or shrubs beside a field acts in two opposing ways on crop and forage production. Downwind of the belt, slower wind speed, trapped snow and a milder microclimate can raise yield: in a classic pooled dataset of US and Canadian shelterbelt trials, the weighted mean yield increase was 20.8% in regions with persistent winter snow and 12.5% without it [ev_crop_yield_kort88_6, ev_crop_yield_kort88_7], and in north-east China maize yield across a whole sheltered field rose by 16.57% [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1]. Close to the belt itself, the trees instead compete with the crop for light, water, nutrients and physical space: in the same pooled dataset the zone from half to one tree height out of the belt lost 50% of its yield to competition before the shelter effect took over further out, leaving a net field-level gain of about 3.5% [ev_crop_yield_kort88_3, ev_crop_yield_kort88_5], and in the China study the edge zone next to the shelterbelt lost 20.47% even as the wider field gained [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]. In Saskatchewan, yields were depressed out to about 10 m from the shelterbelt before an above-average zone began further downwind [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2]. Findings on pest, disease and weed control under trees are counted here as an indirect measure of lost farm output. A review of live fences (Morantes-Toloza et al.) cites a study in which they reduced moth populations and fruit-fly infestation in mango orchards [ev_ecosystem_service_moran18_10].

justification.conditionality: Whether the net balance comes out positive depends on where yield is measured, how much water or wind stress the system faces, and the farming system. A global review of windbreak paddocks found crop yield averaged 8.3% lower than treeless paddocks when measured across the whole protected paddock, including the competition zone next to the trees [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1], a crop-specific effect since pasture yield in the same dataset rose by 3.1% [ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_4]; modelled instead as a response curve across a transect of tree heights downwind, the same data gave a net gain of 8.04% [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5]. In Saskatchewan, the competition strip and the sheltered gain beyond it both showed in a dry growing season, but the sheltered gain disappeared in a wet year when water was not limiting [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_3]. In Senegal, yield fell within 10 metres of hedges during the rainy season but rose by 23% across protected plots in the dry season [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13], while at Bambey the same hedges were reported to have a neutral effect on groundnut yield [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_14]. Pooled across many agroforestry studies, hedgerow systems specifically showed a lower yield response than other agroforestry practices in the same analysis [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_5]. In pasture systems, shade from live fences can reduce forage availability along the pasture edge [ev_forage_productivity_garbach12_1] and, if excessive, the overall productive pasture area of the farm [ev_livestock_productivity_moran18_14]. Benefit is more likely where the windbreak tree roots sit deeper than the crop roots, reducing below-ground competition [ev_crop_yield_moran18_11]. Most of the quantified evidence is from temperate, high-income systems in Canada, the United States and China; a fodder-tree feeding trial in Cambodia found cattle fed leucaena from living-fence stock gained weight while cattle on the standard dry-season diet lost weight [ev_livestock_productivity_gill20_1], but the low- and lower-middle-income evidence base for crop yield itself is thinner. A European model of windbreaks on cropland notes that they take a large share of land out of annual crops — one third of the landscape for short-rotation coppice windbreaks and one ninth for short-rotation forestry at full implementation [ev_crop_yield_englund21_2]. This is the authors' judgement within a model for high-income Europe, and they say it can be made up by yield gains on the sheltered cropland [ev_crop_yield_englund21_2]. The live-fence pest finding is second-hand and indirect: it shows less pest pressure, not a measured change in mango output [ev_ecosystem_service_moran18_10].

justification.mechanism: A line of trees or shrubs beside a field acts in two opposing ways on crop and forage production. Downwind of the belt, slower wind speed, trapped snow and a milder microclimate can raise yield: in a classic pooled dataset of US and Canadian shelterbelt trials, the weighted mean yield increase was 20.8% in regions with persistent winter snow and 12.5% without it [ev_crop_yield_kort88_6, ev_crop_yield_kort88_7], and in north-east China maize yield across a whole sheltered field rose by 16.57% [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1]. Close to the belt itself, the trees instead compete with the crop for light, water, nutrients and physical space: in the same pooled dataset the zone from half to one tree height out of the belt lost 50% of its yield to competition before the shelter effect took over further out, leaving a net field-level gain of about 3.5% [ev_crop_yield_kort88_3, ev_crop_yield_kort88_5], and in the China study the edge zone next to the shelterbelt lost 20.47% even as the wider field gained [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]. In Saskatchewan, yields were depressed out to about 10 m from the shelterbelt before an above-average zone began further downwind [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2]. Findings on pest, disease and weed control under trees are counted here as an indirect measure of lost farm output. A review of live fences (Morantes-Toloza et al.) cites a study in which they reduced moth populations and fruit-fly infestation in mango orchards [ev_ecosystem_service_moran18_10].

justification.statement: agroforestry production_gap: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE — material weight on both the benefit and the harm side, so no direction is stated. This is not a null finding: studies found real effects, in opposite directions, and the agreement note lists both sides. Read the conditionality for what separates them (transfer: adjacent).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Both sides carry real weight: a Kenyan biomass-transfer trial found a yield effect so large the authors called it "extraordinarily high... beyond reasonable effects based on nutrient content of the biomass", while an improved-fallow trial in the same study was not statistically significant [ev_crop_yield_place05_6]. A Kenyan on-station alley-cropping trial in Embu adds a direct species contrast within one experiment: maize alley-cropped with leucaena yielded significantly more than both the unfertilised and fertilised maize-monoculture controls, while the same maize alley-cropped with calliandra yielded less than the unfertilised control — same site, same design, opposite signs by hedgerow species [ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_1, ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_2]. The same trial shows the hedgerows compete with the crop: maize yield was 11% to 51% lower with calliandra hedges and 2% to 17% lower with leucaena hedges than in maize given the same prunings from trees grown elsewhere [ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_3, ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_4]. A review notes that a few trees of aggressive species such as Senna spectabilis worsened maize yield losses under reduced tillage in Rwanda and Ethiopia [ev_crop_yield_vannoordwijk21_5]. A biodrainage review from India reports second-hand that rice yield improved in Casuarina plantations on waterlogged land but crop yields fell in Eucalyptus plantations after 2 years because of shading and competition [ev_crop_yield_singhlal18_4]. What separates the sides is mainly alley width, hedgerow species and whether prunings are returned to the soil. The pest finding is indirect and found no effect; it neither adds to nor subtracts from the yield findings above [ev_ecosystem_service_pumarino15_3].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Planted silvoarable systems — trees planted in rows with crops growing between them — show opposite results depending on spacing and tree species, so the studies disagree. In a global review, wide alley spacing raised yield (13% at 15 tree-heights) [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_8], while the same review's overall average across 333 individual paddock-years was a 17.63% yield loss, with only 69 of those 333 responses (21%) showing a gain [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_6]; narrower alleys under 2.5 tree-heights lost more than 25% [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_7]. Pulling the other way, a Malawi study of fertiliser-tree fallows rotated with maize raised crop value by 3.85 (Hedges' g) [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_3], and a sub-Saharan Africa review found alley cropping lifting the crop-yield response ratio to 2.1 against the non-agroforestry control [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_3]. Findings on pest, disease and weed control under trees are counted here as an indirect measure of lost farm output. A pan-tropical meta-analysis (Pumariño et al.) found that agroforestry's effects on pest abundance and plant damage were not significant in annual crops such as maize, rice and beans [ev_ecosystem_service_pumarino15_3].

justification.statement: agroforestry production_gap: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE — material weight on both the benefit and the harm side, so no direction is stated. This is not a null finding: studies found real effects, in opposite directions, and the agreement note lists both sides. Read the conditionality for what separates them (transfer: in_context).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The gain depends on which trees are kept. Cereal yields were mostly reduced near parkland trees in one review, from a loss under Balanites to a small gain under Faidherbia [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1]; groundnut and millet yielded less under Cordyla pinnata in Senegal [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_11]; and crops yielded less near Sclerocarya birrea, Albizzia lebbeck and Balanites aegyptiaca than without them [ev_crop_yield_felix18_5]. Yield changes under trees ranged from -100% to +200% across Sudano-Sahelian fields [ev_crop_yield_felix18_2], and groundnut showed no significant difference with or without trees in Senegal [ev_crop_yield_felix18_4, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_10]. In Niger, farmer-managed regeneration did not raise cereal grain production against matched non-adopters, with the income gain coming from crop diversification instead [ev_crop_yield_haglund11_1], and a modelled Ethiopian result found the shade's cooling gave no wheat yield response without added nitrogen [ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. Many of the largest figures are second-hand and tied to named species, the Ghana and Honduran gains are farmer-reported, and the Honduran system bundles the trees with mulching and no burning [ev_crop_yield_talensi21_1, ev_crop_yield_welc02_5].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Trees and shrubs kept or regenerated on cropland strongly narrow the gap between actual and attainable farm output, mainly through higher cereal yields near certain species, more soil nutrients and extra fodder. Reviews cite millet yields of 690 kg/ha under a Faidherbia albida park against 350 kg/ha on control plots in Niger, millet yields doubling or even tripling under Faidherbia albida in Senegal, and average gains of 150% for maize and 73% for sorghum under its canopy [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_2, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_8, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_9]. In Ethiopia, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns yielded more than open-field wheat in normal seasons and up to 85% more in a dry El Niño year [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. Near Guiera senegalensis shrubs in Niger grain yields averaged 773 kg/ha against 382 kg/ha in open fields, and in Senegal millet yielded 886 kg/ha with Piliostigma reticulatum against 499 kg/ha without [ev_crop_yield_felix18_3, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_15]; in a Senegal trial under imposed drought, millet with Guiera senegalensis produced almost 10 times the biomass of millet without it [ev_crop_yield_bogie18_1]. In Niger, millet yields on fields with regenerated trees (100 to 370 kg/ha) were higher than on control fields without trees (50 to 270 kg/ha) [ev_crop_yield_boton10_1], and older farmer-managed regeneration gave larger millet yield increases [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1]. Soil under Faidherbia albida had 50% more total nitrogen, and soil under scattered shrubs in Niger 38% more, than treeless areas [ev_soil_nitrogen_faosen24_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_felix18_1]. The trees also feed livestock: herbaceous biomass under Acacia tortilis and Balanites aegyptiaca was 2 to 5 times that in a treeless area, and tree leaves, fruit and pods make up about 40% of the cattle diet in the dry-to-wet-season transition in Senegal [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_20, ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21, ev_forage_productivity_boton10_7]. In Ghana, 60 percent of households practising farmer-managed regeneration reported higher farm yields [ev_crop_yield_talensi21_1], and in Honduras farmers report maize yield gains after switching to the Quesungual system [ev_crop_yield_welc02_5, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1].

justification.conditionality: The gain depends on which trees are kept. Cereal yields were mostly reduced near parkland trees in one review, from a loss under Balanites to a small gain under Faidherbia [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1]; groundnut and millet yielded less under Cordyla pinnata in Senegal [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_11]; and crops yielded less near Sclerocarya birrea, Albizzia lebbeck and Balanites aegyptiaca than without them [ev_crop_yield_felix18_5]. Yield changes under trees ranged from -100% to +200% across Sudano-Sahelian fields [ev_crop_yield_felix18_2], and groundnut showed no significant difference with or without trees in Senegal [ev_crop_yield_felix18_4, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_10]. In Niger, farmer-managed regeneration did not raise cereal grain production against matched non-adopters, with the income gain coming from crop diversification instead [ev_crop_yield_haglund11_1], and a modelled Ethiopian result found the shade's cooling gave no wheat yield response without added nitrogen [ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. Many of the largest figures are second-hand and tied to named species, the Ghana and Honduran gains are farmer-reported, and the Honduran system bundles the trees with mulching and no burning [ev_crop_yield_talensi21_1, ev_crop_yield_welc02_5].

justification.mechanism: Trees and shrubs kept or regenerated on cropland strongly narrow the gap between actual and attainable farm output, mainly through higher cereal yields near certain species, more soil nutrients and extra fodder. Reviews cite millet yields of 690 kg/ha under a Faidherbia albida park against 350 kg/ha on control plots in Niger, millet yields doubling or even tripling under Faidherbia albida in Senegal, and average gains of 150% for maize and 73% for sorghum under its canopy [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_2, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_8, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_9]. In Ethiopia, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns yielded more than open-field wheat in normal seasons and up to 85% more in a dry El Niño year [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. Near Guiera senegalensis shrubs in Niger grain yields averaged 773 kg/ha against 382 kg/ha in open fields, and in Senegal millet yielded 886 kg/ha with Piliostigma reticulatum against 499 kg/ha without [ev_crop_yield_felix18_3, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_15]; in a Senegal trial under imposed drought, millet with Guiera senegalensis produced almost 10 times the biomass of millet without it [ev_crop_yield_bogie18_1]. In Niger, millet yields on fields with regenerated trees (100 to 370 kg/ha) were higher than on control fields without trees (50 to 270 kg/ha) [ev_crop_yield_boton10_1], and older farmer-managed regeneration gave larger millet yield increases [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1]. Soil under Faidherbia albida had 50% more total nitrogen, and soil under scattered shrubs in Niger 38% more, than treeless areas [ev_soil_nitrogen_faosen24_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_felix18_1]. The trees also feed livestock: herbaceous biomass under Acacia tortilis and Balanites aegyptiaca was 2 to 5 times that in a treeless area, and tree leaves, fruit and pods make up about 40% of the cattle diet in the dry-to-wet-season transition in Senegal [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_20, ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21, ev_forage_productivity_boton10_7]. In Ghana, 60 percent of households practising farmer-managed regeneration reported higher farm yields [ev_crop_yield_talensi21_1], and in Honduras farmers report maize yield gains after switching to the Quesungual system [ev_crop_yield_welc02_5, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: As with the Bolivia cacao case, a crop-yield loss does not always mean a production loss: the same trial found that selling the plantain and banana grown alongside the cacao more than made up for the lower cacao revenue [ev_agricultural_production_value_armengot16_1]. A weak negative relationship between shade-tree diversity and coffee productivity was also reported in Nicaragua, though the authors describe it as only weakly significant [ev_crop_yield_hagg17_1]. The Brazilian shaded-coffee gain comes from a single experimental farm with one plot per treatment and no yield statistics, in an upper-middle-income subtropical setting where the benefit is frost protection, and shaded coffee was not higher in every year, so its transfer to shaded coffee in low-income countries is uncertain [ev_crop_yield_caramori96_1]; the excess-shade loss is second-hand, summarised from earlier cited studies [ev_crop_yield_caramori96_2]. What separates the sides is on shade density, the companion species used, and whether the other products of the system (fruit, pepper, timber, bananas) are counted alongside the main crop. Both coffee-resilience statements are second-hand and give no size; one rests on a model for Ethiopian coffee, and the other adds that shade trees also raise the plantation's water use [ev_climate_shock_dsantos23_5, ev_climate_shock_taboada20_1]. The pest, disease and weed findings are indirect: they show less pressure on the crop, not a measured change in output; the weed figure is second-hand and the frosty-pod and mirid finding is a correlation [ev_ecosystem_service_pumarino15_2, ev_ecosystem_service_villa20_5, ev_ecosystem_service_seghieri19_10].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In shaded tree-crop systems (coffee, cocoa, coconut) the studies disagree: the crop's yield response to the shade trees runs both ways depending on shade density and the companion species. Coffee under 40-60% Erythrina shade cover produced 41% fewer fruits per bush than coffee under a maximum of 20% shade cover [ev_crop_yield_villa20_1]; a pan-tropical cocoa meta-analysis found cocoa bean yield 25% lower in agroforestry than monoculture, though total system yield was about ten times higher once the other products are counted [ev_crop_yield_niether20_1]; and in Bolivia, full-sun cacao monocultures were 41% more productive in cacao alone than agroforestry, attributed to greater light reaching the trees [ev_crop_yield_armengot16_1]. Against this, intercropping coconut with pasture grasses, black pepper and coffee was reported to increase coconut nut yield in Sri Lanka [ev_crop_yield_kumar22_1], and in Rwanda, intercropping coffee with nitrogen-fixing Tephrosia mulch raised coffee yield by 23% to 36% [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_1]. A global coffee meta-analysis found agroforestry reduced adverse climate impacts on yield in both arabica and robusta coffee [ev_crop_yield_patil25_10]. In southern Brazil, coffee shaded by Mimosa scabrella trees accumulated 6584 kg/ha of clean coffee over the harvests at the lowest density of 50 trees/ha against 4340 kg/ha unshaded, a response the authors relate closely to frost damage to the productive branches and floral buds [ev_crop_yield_caramori96_1]; the same paper reports from earlier trials that excessive, permanent shade caused coffee production losses comparable to those caused by frosts, because too little light at the canopy shifts bud differentiation away from flower buds [ev_crop_yield_caramori96_2]. Two Latin American reviews describe shaded coffee as more resilient to climate change and to climatic extremes [ev_climate_shock_dsantos23_5, ev_climate_shock_taboada20_1]. Findings on pest, disease and weed control under trees are counted here as an indirect measure of lost farm output. A pan-tropical meta-analysis (Pumariño et al.) found that in perennial crops such as coffee, cocoa and plantain, agroforestry was associated with lower pest abundance and less plant damage [ev_ecosystem_service_pumarino15_2]. A coffee review (Villarreyna et al.) cites shade and the leaf-litter barrier of shade trees cutting the incidence of weeds, especially aggressive grasses, by more than 40% and up to 95% under dense shade [ev_ecosystem_service_villa20_5], and regular spatial arrangements in the plot were correlated with lower frosty-pod rot attack in Costa Rica and lower mirid attack in Cameroon (Seghieri et al.) [ev_ecosystem_service_seghieri19_10].

justification.statement: agroforestry production_gap: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE — material weight on both the benefit and the harm side, so no direction is stated. This is not a null finding: studies found real effects, in opposite directions, and the agreement note lists both sides. Read the conditionality for what separates them (transfer: in_context).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: What separates the sides is mainly tree density, tree age and drought severity. Pooled across Argentine sites, silvopastoral forage production exceeded treeless grassland in both normal and dry years where the dry year's rainfall shortfall stayed at or below 35% of the long-term mean, but reversed into a competition process once the shortfall exceeded 35% [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2]. At one site the silvopastoral relative response went from +2% in normal years to -89% in a dry year, while at another site with a smaller shortfall the response went the opposite way, from -15% in normal years to +26% in the dry year [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_6]. The same study found forage production fell further as tree cover (shade intensity) increased, in both normal and dry years [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_7]. In arid India, herbage yield under most tree and shrub species was lower than the treeless control during drought years, significantly so for Acacia tortilis and Dichrostachys nutans, but the trees also produced leaf fodder that households cut for livestock during the same droughts, a trade-off of less grass for more browse [ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_2]. In New Zealand radiata-pine silvopasture, early complementarity between trees and pasture reversed as the trees matured, and by 15 years after planting the pasture had disappeared entirely under the trees [ev_forage_productivity_pollock08_1]. At the high-intensity end, an intensive Colombian silvopastoral system raised stocking to 4.3 cows per hectare and milk production to 130% of the conventional baseline while eliminating chemical fertiliser, and kept forage production constant through intense drought when the biomass of a grass monoculture fell to 25% [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1]. Most of the quantified evidence is from upper-middle- and high-income countries (Argentina, Colombia, New Zealand); the arid-India and Sri Lanka findings are the main lower-middle-income evidence. The Colombian milk figure is second-hand, cited from an earlier World Bank study [ev_climate_shock_cmscr20_3]. The horn-fly counts are indirect, showing less pest pressure on the herd rather than a measured change in output, and come from upper-middle-income Colombia [ev_ecosystem_service_giraldo10_4, ev_ecosystem_service_giraldo10_5].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: The studies disagree on whether silvopasture closes the production gap. Trees in a pasture add shade, deep-rooted drought buffering and nitrogen transfer to the grass layer, but they also compete with pasture grasses for light, water and nutrients; which effect wins depends on tree density and age. A global meta-analysis of silvopastoral paddocks found pasture yield fell by an average of 20.8% across 345 paddock-years and by 30% once tree density exceeded 800 trees per hectare, while newly planted trees had no effect at all and the oldest trees reduced pasture yield to below 50% of the open-pasture control [ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_9, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_10, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_11, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_12]. Livestock yield across the same global dataset fell by 18.6% on average, but 33% of paddock-years still showed higher animal productivity under trees than in the open [ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14], and the decline levelled off once density passed about 300 trees per hectare [ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_15]. Nitrogen-fixing trees can also transfer nitrogen to companion grasses: Setaria grass grown with leucaena in Sri Lanka had a 16% higher nitrogen yield than a grass monoculture [ev_forage_productivity_dagang03_2]. In Colombia, a World Bank project report cites a study finding that farms with well-established silvopasture lost only 0.4-5.5% of milk productivity during periods of climate variability from 2009 to 2019, against losses of up to 19% on extensive ranches [ev_climate_shock_cmscr20_3]. Findings on pest, disease and weed control under trees are counted here as an indirect measure of lost farm output. In Colombian silvopasture, fewer horn flies and fewer horn-fly larvae were caught than in treeless improved pasture (Giraldo et al.) [ev_ecosystem_service_giraldo10_4, ev_ecosystem_service_giraldo10_5].

justification.conditionality: What separates the sides is mainly tree density, tree age and drought severity. Pooled across Argentine sites, silvopastoral forage production exceeded treeless grassland in both normal and dry years where the dry year's rainfall shortfall stayed at or below 35% of the long-term mean, but reversed into a competition process once the shortfall exceeded 35% [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2]. At one site the silvopastoral relative response went from +2% in normal years to -89% in a dry year, while at another site with a smaller shortfall the response went the opposite way, from -15% in normal years to +26% in the dry year [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_6]. The same study found forage production fell further as tree cover (shade intensity) increased, in both normal and dry years [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_7]. In arid India, herbage yield under most tree and shrub species was lower than the treeless control during drought years, significantly so for Acacia tortilis and Dichrostachys nutans, but the trees also produced leaf fodder that households cut for livestock during the same droughts, a trade-off of less grass for more browse [ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_2]. In New Zealand radiata-pine silvopasture, early complementarity between trees and pasture reversed as the trees matured, and by 15 years after planting the pasture had disappeared entirely under the trees [ev_forage_productivity_pollock08_1]. At the high-intensity end, an intensive Colombian silvopastoral system raised stocking to 4.3 cows per hectare and milk production to 130% of the conventional baseline while eliminating chemical fertiliser, and kept forage production constant through intense drought when the biomass of a grass monoculture fell to 25% [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1]. Most of the quantified evidence is from upper-middle- and high-income countries (Argentina, Colombia, New Zealand); the arid-India and Sri Lanka findings are the main lower-middle-income evidence. The Colombian milk figure is second-hand, cited from an earlier World Bank study [ev_climate_shock_cmscr20_3]. The horn-fly counts are indirect, showing less pest pressure on the herd rather than a measured change in output, and come from upper-middle-income Colombia [ev_ecosystem_service_giraldo10_4, ev_ecosystem_service_giraldo10_5].

justification.statement: agroforestry production_gap: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE — material weight on both the benefit and the harm side, so no direction is stated. This is not a null finding: studies found real effects, in opposite directions, and the agreement note lists both sides. Read the conditionality for what separates them (transfer: adjacent).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The gains are not universal. In China, fruit-tree/crop intercropping measured a −0.29 reduction in household income (95% CI −0.52 to −0.07) tied to lost off-farm income and tree-crop competition, against a +0.52 gain found elsewhere in the same review for a Kenyan climate-vulnerability agroforestry programme [ev_household_income_castle21s_2]. A pan-tropical review of cocoa agroforestry found that, although total system production was higher under shade trees, this was not reflected in higher revenues, net present values, or lower costs [ev_economic_return_niether20_1]. Several sources measured lower income for some adopters. The Kenyan fallow gains are for two named fallow species [ev_economic_return_place05_4, ev_economic_return_place05_5]. The fuelwood finding is second-hand and measures money no longer spent on firewood, not a rise in income [ev_t6_ecosvc_firewood_castle21_12].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Agroforestry moderately raises rural household income, mainly through diversified and higher-value production. Pooling adoption studies across 13 Sub-Saharan African countries, agroforestry adoption had a positive effect on income of 0.28 (Cohen's d, 95% confidence interval 0.13 to 0.44) [ev_household_income_jemaneh26_1]; a broader pooled estimate across contexts found a smaller effect of 0.12 standardized mean difference, with a 95% confidence interval of −0.06 to 0.30 [ev_household_income_castle21s_1]. In western Kenya, fallow systems returned $2.17 per labour-day, 33% higher than continuous maize cropping with no inputs [ev_economic_return_place05_3]. In farmer-managed trials in western Kenya, improved fallows gave a seasonal net gain of $22.33 per acre with tephrosia and $19.96 with crotalaria compared with using no inputs [ev_economic_return_place05_4, ev_economic_return_place05_5]. A separate Sahelian estimate puts a Nigerien farmer's wood-sales income from the regeneration at more than 100 000 FCFA of fuelwood and construction wood after 5 years, rising as the regeneration ages [ev_household_income_boton10_8]. Fuelwood is counted here as an indirect measure of poverty: a systematic review (Castle et al.) reports, citing a Kenyan agroforestry programme, that agroforestry led to significant reductions in fuelwood purchases, with 49 percentage points fewer households buying firewood in Lower Nyando and 4 points fewer in Middle Nyando [ev_t6_ecosvc_firewood_castle21_12].

justification.mechanism: Agroforestry moderately raises rural household income, mainly through diversified and higher-value production. Pooling adoption studies across 13 Sub-Saharan African countries, agroforestry adoption had a positive effect on income of 0.28 (Cohen's d, 95% confidence interval 0.13 to 0.44) [ev_household_income_jemaneh26_1]; a broader pooled estimate across contexts found a smaller effect of 0.12 standardized mean difference, with a 95% confidence interval of −0.06 to 0.30 [ev_household_income_castle21s_1]. In western Kenya, fallow systems returned $2.17 per labour-day, 33% higher than continuous maize cropping with no inputs [ev_economic_return_place05_3]. In farmer-managed trials in western Kenya, improved fallows gave a seasonal net gain of $22.33 per acre with tephrosia and $19.96 with crotalaria compared with using no inputs [ev_economic_return_place05_4, ev_economic_return_place05_5]. A separate Sahelian estimate puts a Nigerien farmer's wood-sales income from the regeneration at more than 100 000 FCFA of fuelwood and construction wood after 5 years, rising as the regeneration ages [ev_household_income_boton10_8]. Fuelwood is counted here as an indirect measure of poverty: a systematic review (Castle et al.) reports, citing a Kenyan agroforestry programme, that agroforestry led to significant reductions in fuelwood purchases, with 49 percentage points fewer households buying firewood in Lower Nyando and 4 points fewer in Middle Nyando [ev_t6_ecosvc_firewood_castle21_12].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: How big the poverty effect is cannot be stated: the units report returns on investment or cash flow, components of household income rather than measured poverty change. The Senegalese figure is an earlier study read second-hand in a review [ev_economic_return_faosen24_15]. The Indian figure now comes from the original Ram et al. study rather than a second-hand reading, but it is still a single planting's first-rotation harvest, not a repeated or ongoing return [ev_economic_return_ram11_4]. The Chinese trial covers only the establishment years, and in the same trial the intercropped soybean and alfalfa yielded much less than sole crops, so the cash-flow gain comes from the fruit trees rather than from the crop [ev_economic_return_wang23_1]. The evidence comes from lower-middle-income Senegal and India and upper-middle-income China.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In irrigated cropland, trees bring returns from wood, fodder or fruit on top of the crop. A Senegalese review cites Fall et al. (2002) estimating that in the Senegal River valley a windbreak hedge in irrigated rice had an internal rate of return of 36 per cent, or 58 per cent when the woody products of the hedge were counted (Satin, 1998) [ev_economic_return_faosen24_15]. In canal-irrigated waterlogged fields at Hisar, India, a biodrainage study by Ram et al. found a benefit-cost ratio of 3.5:1 for the first rotation of Eucalyptus boundary strips, well above the 1.3:1 the same authors report for ordinary agricultural crops in Haryana, with returns from selling the trees after only an initial planting and maintenance cost [ev_economic_return_ram11_4]. In a drip-irrigated trial in Xinjiang, China, juvenile plumcot trees intercropped with alfalfa or soybean gave a higher average cash flow than the corresponding sole crops [ev_economic_return_wang23_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Against this, in Brazil a review of barriers to silvopastoral adoption states that, for this reason, farm income in the first years after establishing a silvopastoral system would be comparatively lower than under traditional pasture [ev_economic_return_diasf08_1]. The Brazilian and Nicaraguan units are an expert review and a modelled single-farm case rather than measured trials, the Peru-Colombia benefit-cost ratio is cited within a systematic review, and the milk-income gain already carries the cattle-stocking change that drives it, so the finding is reported as an establishment-phase income dip followed by a payback once the system matures [ev_economic_return_diasf08_1, ev_economic_return_diasf08_2].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In pastoral rangeland systems, silvopastoral conversion mostly pays once established. In Peru and Colombia, an intensive silvopastoral system had an operating benefit-cost ratio of 2.8 against 1.34 for a traditional system [ev_economic_return_saucedo23_1]. In the Colombian Amazon, producer income from milk sales rose 42.12 percent under an intensive silvopastoral system owing to its higher carrying capacity of 2.71 against 1.84 animal units for the intensive system and grass monoculture respectively [ev_household_income_montagnini15_1]. In Nicaragua, a modelled 20-hectare beef and dairy farm found silvopastoral net income overtaking traditional pasture income only in the fifth year after establishment [ev_economic_return_diasf08_2].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The benefit depends on which intercrop combination and management regime is used, and is not universal. A meta-analysis found that crop-fruit tree intercropping in China had a negative effect on productivity [ev_household_income_castle21s_2], and the same Indian Gmelina trial's higher net returns were measured against a high-cost mango sole crop, so the size of the gain depends on the alternative crop chosen [ev_economic_return_biswas22_2]. In Nigeria, net present value for sweet orange monocropped or intercropped was negative for the monocrop and for one intercrop combination, and positive only with cassava and maize or with chilli pepper and amaranthus [ev_economic_return_aiyel01_1]. Alley cropping with nitrogen-fixing trees and mulch from multi-purpose trees was profitable in land- and labour-abundant conditions [ev_economic_return_korm99_5] but, as the same source separately records, not where land is a scarce resource [ev_economic_return_korm99_6]. An improved-fallow system in Malawi stayed profitable, with a value-cost ratio above 4.0, only while fertiliser prices were low; when fertiliser prices rose, the comparable rotation fell to a value-cost ratio at or below 2.5 [ev_economic_return_snapp10_1]. Adoption of improved fallows and biomass transfer in Kenya remained too small in area after six years to produce a significant household-level welfare impact [ev_household_income_place05_2]. Most of the quantified gains are from low- and lower-middle-income countries in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, with one upper-middle-income harm finding from China. The fuelwood finding is second-hand and measures money no longer spent on firewood, not a rise in income [ev_t6_ecosvc_firewood_castle21_12].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Trees planted in rows with arable crops moderately raise income, mainly through fertiliser-tree soil fertility effects, intercrop diversification, and eventual timber or fruit harvests on top of the annual crop. Net revenue from a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea intercrop in India was reported as up to 2.66 times higher than the pigeon pea sole crop [ev_economic_return_biswas22_1], and alley cropping with Acacia senegal in Sudan raised sorghum net revenue from 501 to 558 Sudanese pounds per hectare [ev_economic_return_fadl13_4]. Eucalyptus timber intercropped with field crops in India gave a benefit-cost ratio of 3.5 to 1, compared with 1.3 to 1 for agricultural crops alone [ev_economic_return_ram11_4], and alley cropping in Nigeria returned a net present value of 1755 Nigerian naira per hectare, more than the no-till and other alley-cropping comparators [ev_economic_return_ehui90_7]. In farmer-managed trials in western Kenya, improved fallows gave a seasonal net gain of $22.33 per acre with tephrosia and $19.96 with crotalaria compared with using no inputs [ev_economic_return_place05_4, ev_economic_return_place05_5]. Fertiliser trees also protect farmers against drought-year crop failure: in Zambia, a farmer who had planted fertiliser trees lost only 90 US dollars in sunk cost when a crop failed, against 164 US dollars for a farmer who had invested in inorganic fertiliser [ev_economic_return_chaudhury11_1]. Fuelwood is counted here as an indirect measure of poverty: a systematic review (Castle et al.) reports, citing a Kenyan agroforestry programme, that agroforestry led to significant reductions in fuelwood purchases, with 49 percentage points fewer households buying firewood in Lower Nyando and 4 points fewer in Middle Nyando [ev_t6_ecosvc_firewood_castle21_12].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Against this, the same World Vision multi-country meta-analysis finds Uganda a clear outlier: participant households there were significantly less likely to report income improvements, which the authors attribute partly to participants being poorer households with different income-generation opportunities — the practice worsening the outcome for some adopters, counted here as measured harm [ev_household_income_wvfmnr19_6]. Several Sahel income gains are not statistically significant under the authors' own 5% convention (the 10% and 13% gross-income figures, and the low-to-young tree-product-value gain), though the authors describe them as increases [ev_household_income_bina15_1, ev_household_income_bina15_2, ev_household_income_bina15_4]. The Honduran and Ghanaian/Nigerien World Vision figures are grey-literature project self-evaluations or practitioner articles by project-promoter staff, with a positive-bias discount, and the World Vision brief itself states the FMNR effect cannot be fully disentangled from other project activities [ev_household_income_welc02_7, ev_economic_return_wvfmnr19_7, ev_economic_return_wvfmnr19_8, ev_household_income_wvfmnr19_5]. In Honduras, farmers using the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system gained a new income stream from renting their land for livestock grazing, because the system produces more stover [ev_household_income_welc02_7]. T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The gains above come from counting the whole system's products (shade-tree fruit, timber, fuelwood) or from a resilience advantage (the high-shade coffee farms' positive long-run return); the losses come from comparisons against an intensively managed or input-heavy full-sun alternative, where the certification premium or extra yield does not fully offset agroforestry's lower yield of the main crop. Whether shaded perennial systems reduce poverty depends on market access for the secondary products and on what the comparison system assumes.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In shaded coffee and cocoa systems, farm profit depends on whether the extra products and resilience from the shade trees outweigh what is given up in crop yield. A pan-tropical review found shaded coffee and cocoa farms had net returns 23% higher than conventional, sun-grown systems [ev_economic_return_jezeer17_1]. In Ghana, moderate-shade cocoa plots had 65% higher value of production than near-full-sun cocoa plots once cocoa, intercrops, fruit, fuelwood and timber are all counted [ev_economic_return_hawkins24_3]. In Costa Rica and Guatemala, modelled long-run returns for low-investment coffee farms were positive under high shade but negative on average under low shade [ev_economic_return_lalani24_1]. Against this, in Nicaragua a multiple regression found coffee net revenue fell as shade-tree diversity rose [ev_economic_return_hagg17_1]; in Ghana, modelling found Rainforest-Alliance-certified shaded cocoa less profitable than an intensive full-sun monoculture assumed to yield 20% more [ev_economic_return_vaast14_4]; and in Ecuador, net margin per hectare was lower under organic cacao agroforestry (US$1,565) than under technified full-sun cacao (US$2,323) [ev_economic_return_perezneira16_1].
