T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The gain is not immediate everywhere: in Brazil, household income from silvopastoral systems was found comparatively lower than under traditional pasture in the first years after establishment, before the system matures [ev_economic_return_diasf08_1]. A World Bank project review in Colombia, where 47.2% of prospective beneficiaries were below the poverty line at baseline (3.6% in extreme poverty), could not yet separate the project's poverty impact from drought and other climatic shocks, since many systems were still in their establishment phase at project closing [ev_rural_poverty_cmscr20_9]. The income figures come from a few projects and reviews in Colombia and Peru, which are upper-middle-income countries, so the rating is a moderate rather than a strong gain.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Silvopastoral systems moderately raise rural income, chiefly through better animal nutrition and productivity. In Colombia, switching from traditional ranching to a silvopastoral system increased farmers' annual income by as much as $523 per hectare, with production costs $127 per hectare lower, attributed to improved animal nutrition, productivity and fertility and lower disease and death [ev_household_income_cmscr20_6]. In the Colombian Amazon, milk income rose 42.12% under an intensive silvopastoral system, linked to a higher stocking capacity of 2.71 animal units per hectare against 1.84 under pasture monoculture [ev_household_income_montagnini15_1]. A review across Peru and Colombia found an operating benefit-cost ratio of 2.8 for an intensive silvopastoral system against 1.34 for a traditional system [ev_economic_return_saucedo23_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The rating is moderate because the types of agroforestry differ: general findings, planted tree-crop alleys and silvopasture show strong reductions, linear boundary plantings a moderate one, and trees regenerated on farmland and shaded tree crops only small ones. The cross-practice syntheses agree on large reductions: the sub-Saharan and pantropical meta-analyses and the review of compiled field studies, whose averages hold across silvopastoral, silvoarable and linear plantings alike [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_3]. Single-practice field evidence is often weaker than those averages, so the size a project can expect depends on site and practice [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. The compiled-review percentages are simple averages of study reductions, not weighted meta-analytic effects, and they mix temperate and tropical studies [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1]. The shade-tree effect represents little at catchment scale on the andisols studied [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3]. Site matters within a practice: erosion fell 35.3 percent in Colombia's Coffee Ecoregion but only 5.4 percent in the Cesar River Valley [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. The sub-Saharan authors warn the very large effect sizes could reflect publication bias and expect more modest effects with more studies [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1]. Regreening Africa observed no large overall change in erosion prevalence and found no link between more trees on farm and lower erosion, the FMNR result is participants' reported erosion, and the Nicaraguan hurricane result bundles trees with terraces and contour planting [ev_erosion_hazard_rgaf23_3, ev_erosion_hazard_rgaf23_5, ev_erosion_hazard_wvfmnr19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_9]. The WOCAT finding is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet, not an erosion measurement, and the siltation rating enters as a component [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. The Lower Nyando erosion finding is farmer-reported, not measured [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1]. The landslide and runoff results are earlier studies cited in a working paper, a CATIE edited volume and a Spanish-language review; the runoff findings enter as components of erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1, ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1, ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1]. The Chiapas landslide results are crop-specific coffee evidence from a single hurricane, with the landslide-volume and landslide-size trends only marginal (P = 0.062) and no effect of nearby forest cover [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_5, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_4]. The Honduran erosion claim is a narrative from a promoter-written grey-literature article with no measured erosion rate, and the effect belongs to the whole bundle of trees, mulch cover, zero tillage and no burning [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4]. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt finding is high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the low- and lower-middle-income countries this tool targets; it infers past erosion from soil markers and states no erosion rate [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5]. In China, a field study of windbreak patches found windbreaks reduced average wind-erosion soil loss by 20% compared with open farmland [ev_erosion_hazard_chang21_1]. The Kenya/Nigeria/Zimbabwe meta-analysis breaks its result down by agro-ecological zone rather than giving one pooled number, and both erosion response ratios in it are large enough that, alongside the sub-Saharan meta-analysis already in this row, the same publication-bias caution applies [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_2, ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_3]. Most of these newer findings are review or assessment statements rather than site measurements: the IPCC and farmland-resilience statements give no size or site, and the Argentine, Costa Rican and Kenyan farmer statements are a review citation, a Spanish-language case description and a single farmer's perception, not a measured erosion rate [ev_erosion_hazard_ipccar6ch5_5, ev_runoff_reduction_dobhal24_2, ev_erosion_hazard_montagnini15_1, ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11, ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6]. The Chinese windbreak study and the Kenya/Nigeria/Zimbabwe meta-analysis add upper-middle-income and low- and lower-middle-income evidence respectively, broadly consistent with the row's existing transfer. The Nigerian erosion figures are modelled, not measured, running a simplified USLE-based erosion model calibrated to plot-level erosion rates from the same research station, and the model's own ranking shows erosion as time-dependent: initial erosion rates are lower under no-till than under the 4 m alley, with the alley only overtaking by the end of the 20-year horizon. The Philippines result is bundled: each successive treatment adds a co-practice (contour tillage, then mulch from the hedgerow trimmings and crop residues, then zero tillage) on top of the hedgerows, so the hedgerow-alone share of the reduction cannot be separated from the tillage and mulch changes that go with it, and even the hedgerow-plus-contour-tillage treatment is still called 'considerable' soil loss by the authors, not yet a tolerable rate. In Lower Nyando, Kenya, farmers reported that tree roots prevented extensive soil erosion and soil fertility loss during the floods [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1]. During Hurricane Mitch in October 1998, Honduran farmers practising the Quesungual system suffered less landslide damage than those using traditional slash-and-burn [ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1]. In shaded perennial systems, a study on a Costa Rican coffee farm found shade trees reduced sheet erosion by a factor of 2 against full-sun plots [ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1], and after Hurricane Stan in Chiapas, Mexico, coffee farms with more complex vegetation suffered less landslide damage [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_10]. In Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual system report that soil erosion has been nearly stopped, and estimate nutrient loss through erosion at more than 10 times lower than under slash-and-burn [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4]. In Argentina, soil erosion and soil exhaustion under yerba mate grown as a monoculture were much lower when the crop was grown with trees in an agroforestry system [ev_erosion_hazard_montagnini15_1]. In Costa Rica, shade trees are described as protecting soil from sheet erosion and conserving fertility through organic-matter inputs [ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11]. In Kenya, a farmer in Isiolo County explained that planting trees in a line prevents soil from being swept away by water [ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6]. justification.conditionality: The rating is moderate because the types of agroforestry differ: general findings, planted tree-crop alleys and silvopasture show strong reductions, linear boundary plantings a moderate one, and trees regenerated on farmland and shaded tree crops only small ones. The cross-practice syntheses agree on large reductions: the sub-Saharan and pantropical meta-analyses and the review of compiled field studies, whose averages hold across silvopastoral, silvoarable and linear plantings alike [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_3]. Single-practice field evidence is often weaker than those averages, so the size a project can expect depends on site and practice [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. The compiled-review percentages are simple averages of study reductions, not weighted meta-analytic effects, and they mix temperate and tropical studies [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1]. The shade-tree effect represents little at catchment scale on the andisols studied [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3]. Site matters within a practice: erosion fell 35.3 percent in Colombia's Coffee Ecoregion but only 5.4 percent in the Cesar River Valley [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. The sub-Saharan authors warn the very large effect sizes could reflect publication bias and expect more modest effects with more studies [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1]. Regreening Africa observed no large overall change in erosion prevalence and found no link between more trees on farm and lower erosion, the FMNR result is participants' reported erosion, and the Nicaraguan hurricane result bundles trees with terraces and contour planting [ev_erosion_hazard_rgaf23_3, ev_erosion_hazard_rgaf23_5, ev_erosion_hazard_wvfmnr19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_9]. The WOCAT finding is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet, not an erosion measurement, and the siltation rating enters as a component [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. The Lower Nyando erosion finding is farmer-reported, not measured [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1]. The landslide and runoff results are earlier studies cited in a working paper, a CATIE edited volume and a Spanish-language review; the runoff findings enter as components of erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1, ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1, ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1]. The Chiapas landslide results are crop-specific coffee evidence from a single hurricane, with the landslide-volume and landslide-size trends only marginal (P = 0.062) and no effect of nearby forest cover [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_5, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_4]. The Honduran erosion claim is a narrative from a promoter-written grey-literature article with no measured erosion rate, and the effect belongs to the whole bundle of trees, mulch cover, zero tillage and no burning [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4]. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt finding is high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the low- and lower-middle-income countries this tool targets; it infers past erosion from soil markers and states no erosion rate [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5]. In China, a field study of windbreak patches found windbreaks reduced average wind-erosion soil loss by 20% compared with open farmland [ev_erosion_hazard_chang21_1]. The Kenya/Nigeria/Zimbabwe meta-analysis breaks its result down by agro-ecological zone rather than giving one pooled number, and both erosion response ratios in it are large enough that, alongside the sub-Saharan meta-analysis already in this row, the same publication-bias caution applies [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_2, ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_3]. Most of these newer findings are review or assessment statements rather than site measurements: the IPCC and farmland-resilience statements give no size or site, and the Argentine, Costa Rican and Kenyan farmer statements are a review citation, a Spanish-language case description and a single farmer's perception, not a measured erosion rate [ev_erosion_hazard_ipccar6ch5_5, ev_runoff_reduction_dobhal24_2, ev_erosion_hazard_montagnini15_1, ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11, ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6]. The Chinese windbreak study and the Kenya/Nigeria/Zimbabwe meta-analysis add upper-middle-income and low- and lower-middle-income evidence respectively, broadly consistent with the row's existing transfer. The Nigerian erosion figures are modelled, not measured, running a simplified USLE-based erosion model calibrated to plot-level erosion rates from the same research station, and the model's own ranking shows erosion as time-dependent: initial erosion rates are lower under no-till than under the 4 m alley, with the alley only overtaking by the end of the 20-year horizon. The Philippines result is bundled: each successive treatment adds a co-practice (contour tillage, then mulch from the hedgerow trimmings and crop residues, then zero tillage) on top of the hedgerows, so the hedgerow-alone share of the reduction cannot be separated from the tillage and mulch changes that go with it, and even the hedgerow-plus-contour-tillage treatment is still called 'considerable' soil loss by the authors, not yet a tolerable rate. Both the Philippines and Nigeria results sit inside the low- and lower-middle-income countries this tool targets; the Chinese trial is upper-middle-income evidence. The same Chinese trial found a reversal on runoff: mean runoff per event was higher in both tree-intercropped treatments than in mono-cropped peanut, even though soil loss was lower — the authors attribute the higher runoff to surface seals and crusts forming on the untilled soil under and between the tree rows, while tillage of the peanut area itself raised infiltration there; this counts as measured harm for some adopters [ev_runoff_reduction_wei07_3]. Absolute losses were small in both the shaded and unshaded plots on this farm, so the shaded advantage sits on a very low base, and the comparison is a single-farm case study with no replication or significance test, upper-middle-income Brazilian evidence [ev_erosion_hazard_decarvalho21_1]. The cocoa erosion statement is second-hand and gives no size [ev_erosion_hazard_arizasal23_2]. The European wind-erosion figure is a model for high-income Europe [ev_erosion_hazard_englund21_9].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The review-based average rests on a single review whose percentages are averages of compiled study reductions, not weighted meta-analytic effects, and which gives no country or income-group breakdown [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2]. The newer field and modelled evidence now carries most of the weight in this row and points the same way: in Nigeria, a modelled 2 m alley-cropping system gives the lowest predicted 20-year cumulative soil loss of the systems compared, and in the Philippines, a hillside field trial found soil loss fall from 124 to 40 t/ha/yr once contour hedgerows and contour tillage were added to the farmer's practice, falling further to 3 and then 0.2 t/ha/yr as mulch and zero tillage were added on top [ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_1, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_1, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_2, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_3]. The Nigerian erosion figures are modelled, not measured, running a simplified USLE-based erosion model calibrated to plot-level erosion rates from the same research station, and the model's own ranking shows erosion as time-dependent: initial erosion rates are lower under no-till than under the 4 m alley, with the alley only overtaking by the end of the 20-year horizon. The Philippines result is bundled: each successive treatment adds a co-practice (contour tillage, then mulch from the hedgerow trimmings and crop residues, then zero tillage) on top of the hedgerows, so the hedgerow-alone share of the reduction cannot be separated from the tillage and mulch changes that go with it, and even the hedgerow-plus-contour-tillage treatment is still called 'considerable' soil loss by the authors, not yet a tolerable rate. Both the Philippines and Nigeria results sit inside the LIC/LMIC target; the Chinese trial is upper-middle-income evidence. The same Chinese trial found a reversal on runoff: mean runoff per event was higher in both tree-intercropped treatments than in mono-cropped peanut, even though soil loss was lower — the authors attribute the higher runoff to surface seals and crusts forming on the untilled soil under and between the tree rows, while tillage of the peanut area itself raised infiltration there; the engine counts this as measured harm for some adopters [ev_runoff_reduction_wei07_3]. In China, mean soil loss per rainfall event fell with both younger and older intercropped trees against mono-cropped peanut, but mean runoff per event was higher in both tree treatments than in the mono-crop — a reversal the authors attribute to surface seals forming on the untilled soil near the trees rather than to the trees raising runoff generally [ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_1, ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_2].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Trees combined with crops, as alley cropping or contour hedgerow intercropping, protect the soil surface with living plants, litter and mulch and bind it with extended fine roots. A review compiling plot and field studies against sole crops found silvoarable agroforestry cut soil loss by 66% on average and water loss by 43% [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_2]. The same Nigerian alley-cropping model also projects soil loss directly: over a 20-year horizon on a sloping field, 2 m-spaced Leucaena alley cropping gives the lowest predicted cumulative soil loss of the systems compared (2.5 t/ha), against 17.8 t/ha for the traditional short-cycle bush fallow it is compared with; 4 m spacing follows at 9.9 t/ha, still below the no-till (14 t/ha) and bush-fallow controls [ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_1, ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_2, ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_3]. On a steep hillslope in Laguna, the Philippines, a randomised trial of contour hedgerows (Desmanthus virgatus) on maize-mungbean alleys found annual soil loss fell step-wise with each added practice: from 124 t/ha/yr under the farmer's up-and-down-slope tillage, to 40 t/ha/yr once contour hedgerows and contour tillage were added, to 3 t/ha/yr once the hedgerow trimmings and crop residues were also spread as mulch, to 0.2 t/ha/yr once zero tillage was added on top of hedgerows and mulch; the hedgerow-plus-contour-tillage treatment alone also produced only about half as much annual runoff as the farmer's practice [ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_1, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_2, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_3, ev_runoff_reduction_paningbatan95_4]. In Jiangxi Province, China, a randomised trial intercropping peanut with Choerospondias axillaris trees on a sloping field found mean soil loss per rainfall event fell by 25.3% with younger trees and by 32.0% with older trees compared with mono-cropped peanut [ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_1, ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_2].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Slope sets how much there is to gain: the Colombian reduction was large in the hilly Coffee Ecoregion and small in the flatter Cesar River Valley, where the project notes less scope for improvement [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. The Colombian figures are project measurements against degraded pasture from upper-middle-income Colombia [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1]. The review percentages are simple averages of compiled study reductions, not weighted meta-analytic effects, they mix temperate and tropical studies, and the review found no significant difference in soil-loss reduction between silvopastoral and other agroforestry systems [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_1]. The runoff findings from Central America are earlier studies cited in a CATIE edited volume and a Spanish-language review, and describe runoff, a driver of erosion, rather than soil loss itself, and the Costa Rica and Nicaragua figures span high- and lower-middle-income settings [ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1, ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Silvopasture moderately reduces soil erosion: trees in pasture hold soil and water on the slope. In Colombia's Coffee Ecoregion, soils under silvopasture lost 12.3 t/ha a year against 19 t/ha for degraded pasture, a mean reduction in erosion of 35.3 percent; in the flatter Cesar River Valley the figures were 17.5 against 18.5 t/ha [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. A review compiling field studies of agroforestry against its controls found that silvopastoral systems reduced soil loss by 68% and water loss by 73% on average [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_1]. In Costa Rica and Nicaragua, runoff equalled 28-48% of rainfall on pastures without trees against less than 10% in silvopastoral systems [ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1]. Runoff was higher on grass pasture than in tree-dominated fodder banks, so tree cover attenuates runoff and the soil erosion it causes [ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Set against this, when the same Malawi trial measures the crop's own soil moisture rather than system water-use efficiency, the sign often reverses: available soil water at the start of the cropping season was generally lower in the tree-based systems, consistent with trees depleting moisture through the dry season, and the decline from March to August was most pronounced in the gliricidia-based treatments; volumetric moisture was significantly lower under the gliricidia+maize+pigeonpea system at depth in one season reading and slightly lower in another, though a later-season reading found it significantly greater at depth, and the authors' overall conclusion is that pruned gliricidia does not create undue water competition under Malawi's rainfall, several season-level contrasts showing no significant difference [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_1, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_6, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_7, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_9]. In Ghana and across a ten-country cocoa meta-analysis, shaded cocoa and cocoa agroforestry measured significantly lower soil water than full-sun or monoculture systems, attributed to combined shade-tree and crop transpiration raising water uptake [ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]. In Ethiopia, subsoil moisture was lowest for wheat grown with Faidherbia albida, intermediate for sole tree and highest in the open field, though topsoil moisture showed no difference [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_2]. On the Canadian prairies, soil water near an old shelterbelt dropped noticeably in one year, tentatively attributed to uptake by the trees and grasses in the preceding fallow year [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. In Mexican coffee, high-shade sites showed smaller day-to-day swings in soil water from evaporation than low-shade sites, a buffering benefit rather than a higher measured moisture level, since shaded sites also gained less water after rain through canopy interception [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]; a German alley-cropping trial in a drought year found soil water lower on the open field than under trees, though not significant at every position [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. The types of agroforestry themselves disagree: general findings not tied to one type read a benefit, planted tree-crop alleys are split, and trees regenerated on cropland, shaded tree crops, linear plantings and silvopasture each read a slight increase in water stress, so no single direction is stated. Much of the evidence comes from low- and lower-middle-income Niger, Malawi, Ethiopia and Ghana; the Canadian and German findings are from rich temperate countries [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. A French walnut-alley trial shows the same split between surface and deeper soil: soil water in the plough layer was drier under the walnut alleys than in the full-sun control through spring, while at depth (50 cm or more) soil water dynamics were very similar between the two systems, consistent with the trees competing for moisture near the surface while deeper water use is comparable [ev_soil_moisture_blan22_4, ev_soil_moisture_blan22_5]. This is French evidence from a single season and site. Set against this, the same Malaysian trial found alley-cropping with bamboo measured significantly drier topsoil than the monocultures, attributed to bamboo's sparse canopy and gaps leaving the ground exposed to radiation — the wrong alley crop can dry the soil rather than conserve it [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_2]. In Brazilian coffee, soil moisture under shade was measured lower than under the unshaded area at every depth and throughout the monitored period, with the drying most pronounced soon after rain in drier periods, which the authors attribute to canopy interception lowering the rainfall reaching the soil and tree root uptake depleting the deeper layers — a clear case of shade drying the soil rather than conserving its moisture, even though the authors separately argue tree-coffee water-use complementarity kept available water sufficient for the coffee through the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_5, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_6, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_7]. In a New Zealand silvopasture, summer water use and end-of-summer soil moisture were no different from open pasture once the trees were four growing seasons old, as the maturing tree roots came to dominate water use across every system; and after a drier-than-normal winter, deep soil moisture under silvopasture was measured lower than under open lucerne, because the trees' higher winter water use had drawn down deep soil water the low winter rain did not replace — a further measured instance of trees competing with the crop or pasture for water under reduced rainfall [ev_soil_moisture_pollock08_1, ev_soil_moisture_pollock08_2]. The Brazilian and New Zealand findings do not name a drought: the Brazilian site describes a below-average-rainfall month and the New Zealand site a below-normal-rainfall winter, not an extreme event. Malaysia and Brazil are upper-middle income and New Zealand high income. In a Senegal trial with the shrub Guiera senegalensis, soil next to the shrubs dried faster during an imposed drought than soil far from them or in crop-only plots in two of three subplots, while before the drought there was little difference in moisture between plots with and without shrubs [ev_soil_moisture_bogie18_2, ev_soil_moisture_bogie18_3]. That trial is one site and one shrub species.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: The studies disagree on whether trees add water the system can use or compete with crops for it, and the separator is usually which water measure is used — system water-use efficiency (biomass per unit of water used, which counts the tree's own biomass) versus the crop's own soil moisture. In Niger, Ziziphus mauritiana trees raised millet's rainwater-use efficiency by 17 to 47% depending on fertiliser treatment, and raised the millet/cowpea intercrop's water-use efficiency by 11 to 17% [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_2]. In Malawi, a long-running gliricidia agroforestry trial found system water-use efficiency (total above-ground biomass, including the tree, per unit of seasonal water use) strongly and significantly higher in every season for gliricidia-based systems than for sole maize or maize-pigeonpea, by a wide margin (for example 1.43-1.97 g/kg for gliricidia+maize against 0.15-0.54 g/kg for sole maize) [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_5]. In Honduras, the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system retained 15% more soil water in the driest month than slash-and-burn (23% against 8% humidity), equivalent to about 20 mm of extra rainfall and 20 more days a crop could survive without rain, attributed to better infiltration through soil cover and higher organic matter [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1]. A sub-Saharan meta-analysis found agroforestry improved both infiltration and soil moisture content compared with controls [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1]. A continental-scale model finds rainfall dependent on upwind tree cover by 10 to 20%, rising with more tree cover and falling with upwind deforestation [ev_water_regulation_vannoordwijk21_4]. A WOCAT compiler for Kenyan FMNR rates water availability increased, attributing it to greater water retention raising groundwater levels [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. A second Malawi reading confirms the recharge-season pattern: available soil water tended to be greater in the gliricidia+maize+pigeonpea system at the peak of the recharge phase across two further seasons, attributed to increased infiltration and reduced soil evaporation [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10], and further seasonal readings of system water-use efficiency confirm gliricidia-based systems using water more efficiently than sole maize or maize-pigeonpea [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_6]. In Jiangxi Province, China, a peanut-tree alley-cropping trial found the profile-mean (0-150 cm) soil water potential drier in both tree-intercropped treatments than in mono-cropped peanut or either tree monoculture, consistent with tree-crop competition for water, with the difference larger in the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_wei07_4]. In Malaysian oil palm, alley-cropping with black pepper or cacao measured significantly wetter topsoil than the monocultures, which the authors attribute to greater leaf area, lower light penetration and reduced wind cutting evaporation from exposed soil [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_1].

justification.conditionality: Set against this, when the same Malawi trial measures the crop's own soil moisture rather than system water-use efficiency, the sign often reverses: available soil water at the start of the cropping season was generally lower in the tree-based systems, consistent with trees depleting moisture through the dry season, and the decline from March to August was most pronounced in the gliricidia-based treatments; volumetric moisture was significantly lower under the gliricidia+maize+pigeonpea system at depth in one season reading and slightly lower in another, though a later-season reading found it significantly greater at depth, and the authors' overall conclusion is that pruned gliricidia does not create undue water competition under Malawi's rainfall, several season-level contrasts showing no significant difference [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_1, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_6, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_7, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_9]. In Ghana and across a ten-country cocoa meta-analysis, shaded cocoa and cocoa agroforestry measured significantly lower soil water than full-sun or monoculture systems, attributed to combined shade-tree and crop transpiration raising water uptake [ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]. In Ethiopia, subsoil moisture was lowest for wheat grown with Faidherbia albida, intermediate for sole tree and highest in the open field, though topsoil moisture showed no difference [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_2]. On the Canadian prairies, soil water near an old shelterbelt dropped noticeably in one year, tentatively attributed to uptake by the trees and grasses in the preceding fallow year [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. In Mexican coffee, high-shade sites showed smaller day-to-day swings in soil water from evaporation than low-shade sites, a buffering benefit rather than a higher measured moisture level, since shaded sites also gained less water after rain through canopy interception [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]; a German alley-cropping trial in a drought year found soil water lower on the open field than under trees, though not significant at every position [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. The types of agroforestry themselves disagree: general findings not tied to one type read a benefit, planted tree-crop alleys are split, and trees regenerated on cropland, shaded tree crops, linear plantings and silvopasture each read a slight increase in water stress, so no single direction is stated. Much of the evidence comes from low- and lower-middle-income Niger, Malawi, Ethiopia and Ghana; the Canadian and German findings are from rich temperate countries [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. A French walnut-alley trial shows the same split between surface and deeper soil: soil water in the plough layer was drier under the walnut alleys than in the full-sun control through spring, while at depth (50 cm or more) soil water dynamics were very similar between the two systems, consistent with the trees competing for moisture near the surface while deeper water use is comparable [ev_soil_moisture_blan22_4, ev_soil_moisture_blan22_5]. This is French evidence from a single season and site. Set against this, the same Malaysian trial found alley-cropping with bamboo measured significantly drier topsoil than the monocultures, attributed to bamboo's sparse canopy and gaps leaving the ground exposed to radiation — the wrong alley crop can dry the soil rather than conserve it [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_2]. In Brazilian coffee, soil moisture under shade was measured lower than under the unshaded area at every depth and throughout the monitored period, with the drying most pronounced soon after rain in drier periods, which the authors attribute to canopy interception lowering the rainfall reaching the soil and tree root uptake depleting the deeper layers — a clear case of shade drying the soil rather than conserving its moisture, even though the authors separately argue tree-coffee water-use complementarity kept available water sufficient for the coffee through the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_5, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_6, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_7]. In a New Zealand silvopasture, summer water use and end-of-summer soil moisture were no different from open pasture once the trees were four growing seasons old, as the maturing tree roots came to dominate water use across every system; and after a drier-than-normal winter, deep soil moisture under silvopasture was measured lower than under open lucerne, because the trees' higher winter water use had drawn down deep soil water the low winter rain did not replace — a further measured instance of trees competing with the crop or pasture for water under reduced rainfall [ev_soil_moisture_pollock08_1, ev_soil_moisture_pollock08_2]. The Brazilian and New Zealand findings do not name a drought: the Brazilian site describes a below-average-rainfall month and the New Zealand site a below-normal-rainfall winter, not an extreme event. Malaysia and Brazil are upper-middle income and New Zealand high income. In a Senegal trial with the shrub Guiera senegalensis, soil next to the shrubs dried faster during an imposed drought than soil far from them or in crop-only plots in two of three subplots, while before the drought there was little difference in moisture between plots with and without shrubs [ev_soil_moisture_bogie18_2, ev_soil_moisture_bogie18_3]. That trial is one site and one shrub species.

justification.statement: agroforestry water_stress: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE — material weight on both the benefit and the harm side, so no direction is stated. This is not a null finding: studies found real effects, in opposite directions, and the agreement note lists both sides. Read the conditionality for what separates them (transfer: in_context).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The two units differ in practice, year and position, so they do not contradict each other directly: the German comparison is alley cropping against an open field in a drought year, while the Canadian study compares soil close to a shelterbelt with soil further into the same field [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. Neither measures crop water stress itself; both measure soil water as a component of it. The German differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1], and the Canadian drop appeared in 1990, not in 1989, and its cause is hedged [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. Both are high-income temperate sites (Germany, Canada), outside the LIC/LMIC target. Missing: further studies of each practice, and any measure of crop water stress. The French result narrows to depth: the drier reading is specific to the plough layer near the surface, and does not extend to deeper soil water, unlike the all-depth German and Canadian comparisons already in this row. It is a single season and site, with the two conditions not randomised within the parcel, and is high-income temperate evidence (France), outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_soil_moisture_blan22_4, ev_soil_moisture_blan22_5]. After a drier-than-normal winter, deep soil moisture under silvopasture was measured lower than under open lucerne pasture, attributed to the trees' higher winter water use drawing down deep soil water that the low winter rain did not replace [ev_soil_moisture_pollock08_2]. Both readings are from the same single New Zealand silvopasture trial as the German and Canadian evidence already in this row, adding a further high-income temperate measurement rather than a new country or practice; neither names a drought, describing instead an ordinary below-normal-rainfall winter.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Only two temperate field studies sit in this high-income row, and they point in opposite directions. In a German alley-cropping trial in a drought year, soil water content remained lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though differences were not significant for all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. Beside Saskatchewan field shelterbelts, spring soil water content in 1990 dropped noticeably from 0.1 to 0.05 relative distance from the belt, which the authors put down, tentatively, to uptake by the trees and grasses in the previous fallow year; in 1989 the pattern differed, with a slight trend of decreasing available water from the field edge to the centre [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. The first reads as less water stress with trees, the second as more water stress next to them. A French walnut-alley trial adds a third pattern: soil water in the plough layer was drier under the trees than in the full-sun control through spring, while at depth (50 cm or more) soil water dynamics were very similar between the two systems [ev_soil_moisture_blan22_4, ev_soil_moisture_blan22_5]. In a New Zealand silvopasture, summer water use and end-of-summer soil moisture were no different from open pasture once the trees reached four growing seasons old, as the maturing tree roots came to dominate water use across every system [ev_soil_moisture_pollock08_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Within low- and lower-middle-income evidence the sides still disagree: the sub-Saharan meta-analysis, the Malawi Gliricidia trial and the Niger Ziziphus trial point to less water stress, while the Faidherbia subsoil depletion in Ethiopia and the cocoa soil-water deficits in the meta-analysis and in Ghana point to more [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]. The separator is timing and depth: trees deplete soil water through the dry season and below the topsoil, so less may be available when the crop is sown, while recharge-season water and system water productivity favour the tree plots [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10]. Management matters: the Malawi conclusion holds for gliricidia pruned before and during the cropping season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11], and the Ethiopian parkland trees were heavily pruned on farmers' fields [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]. The Makoka water use efficiency figures are total above-ground biomass of the whole system, trees and crops together, per unit of seasonal water use, not grain per unit of water [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1]; the tree biomass inflates the tree-system figures, and the authors caution that soil evaporation and water-table uptake were not measured, so the gap is probably overstated. The Niger figures are crop biomass per unit of rainfall, from a trial with the trees in a single block and the tree-free comparison in a separate block, so tree presence was not randomised and the contrast carries block effects [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_2]. The Makoka findings therefore count here, for water stress, and are held out of the production gap because they say nothing about crop yield. The WOCAT finding is a practitioner judgement on a documented technology sheet, not a soil-moisture measurement, and stays on water access rather than soil moisture [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. Infiltration and groundwater-recharge findings for catchments are carried in the agroforestry catchment water yield rows. The cocoa findings are about one crop and do not measure crop water stress directly; the Ghanaian study is a single farm with shade trees of Albizia ferruginea and Antiaris toxicaria [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]. The Honduran soil-humidity figures come from a grey-literature article by the project's own promoters, report no replication or significance, and compare a bundle (trees with mulch, zero tillage and no burning) against slash-and-burn, so the trees cannot be credited alone [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1]. The Senegal shrub trial is a single site and one shrub species [ev_soil_moisture_bogie18_2].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In low- and lower-middle-income countries the studies disagree, as they do for agroforestry overall; timing and soil depth separate the sides. On the side of more soil water, a sub-Saharan meta-analysis finds that agroforestry improved infiltration and soil moisture content compared to the control (RR 1.6 for soil moisture, with 70% of soil-moisture observations above RR 1) [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1]. In a Gliricidia + maize trial at Makoka, Malawi, available water content tended to be greater in the gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea system at the peak of the recharge phase, which the authors attribute to increased infiltration and reduced soil evaporation under greater ground cover [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10], and in the second season's May water content in that system was much greater than in all other treatments at depths below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8]. Water use efficiency was also higher in the tree systems in every season, for example 1.97 against 0.15 g of biomass per kg of water for gliricidia + maize against sole maize in 1998/99 [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_6]. In Niger, Ziziphus mauritiana trees in the cropped block increased the rainwater use efficiency of millet by 17 and 47 % with farmyard manure and in the unfertilised control, and that of the millet/cowpea intercrop by 11 to 17 % [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_2]. On the side of less soil water, under Faidherbia albida parkland in Ethiopia soil moisture in the sub-soil was the least for wheat with tree, intermediate for sole tree and the highest for open field [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]; in cocoa, a pan-tropical meta-analysis found soils under agroforestry significantly lower in volumetric water content than under full-sun monocultures [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]; in a Ghanaian cocoa field, the combined transpiration of shade trees and cocoa resulted in higher water uptake and less soil water than under full sun [ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]; at Makoka the lower available soil water at the beginning of the cropping season in the tree-based systems suggests that the trees continued to deplete moisture during the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2], the March-to-August decline was most pronounced in the tree-based systems [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3], water content was slightly lower under gliricidia + maize in the dry season when the trees were left unpruned [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5], and in the first season's May water content under gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea was lower than in all other treatments below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4]. In a Senegal trial with the shrub Guiera senegalensis, soil next to the shrubs dried faster during an imposed drought than soil far from them or in crop-only plots in two of three subplots, while before the drought there was little difference in moisture between plots with and without shrubs [ev_soil_moisture_bogie18_2, ev_soil_moisture_bogie18_3]. Trees therefore draw down dry-season and subsoil water, while recharge-season soil water and whole-system water productivity favour them. justification.statement: agroforestry water_stress: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE — material weight on both the benefit and the harm side, so no direction is stated. This is not a null finding: studies found real effects, in opposite directions, and the agreement note lists both sides. Read the conditionality for what separates them (transfer: in_context).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The two results are not directly comparable — one measures the day-to-day swing in soil water under shade-grown coffee, the other the profile-mean water potential under peanut-tree alley cropping — but they sit on opposite sides of the benefit/harm split, which is why this scope row states conflicting evidence rather than a direction. Neither unit states a size for its effect, both are upper-middle-income evidence (Mexico and China), and neither names a drought: both describe an ordinary dry season or dry-season months, not an extreme event. The same Malaysian trial found the opposite for bamboo alleys, which measured significantly drier topsoil than the monocultures, attributed to bamboo's sparse canopy and gaps leaving the ground exposed [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_2]. In Brazilian coffee, soil moisture under shade was measured lower than under the unshaded area at every depth throughout the monitoring period, with depletion after rain much more intense in drier periods, attributed to canopy interception and deeper tree root uptake [ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_5, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_6, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_7]. These five new units split in both directions within the same upper-middle-income tier as the existing Mexican and Chinese evidence, which is why this scope row states conflicting evidence rather than a direction; none names a drought.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: This upper-middle-income scope row rests on two measured results that point opposite ways. In Chiapas, Mexico, a study of shaded coffee farms found soil water in weighing lysimeters fluctuated far less day-to-day under high and medium shade than under low shade, which the author reads as shade buffering soil-moisture loss through evaporation — though the same shaded sites also gain less water after rain, through canopy interception, so the benefit is a steadier moisture level rather than a wetter one [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. In Jiangxi Province, China, a peanut-tree alley-cropping trial found the profile-mean soil water potential drier in the tree-intercropped treatments than in mono-cropped peanut, which the authors attribute to tree-crop competition for water, worse in the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_wei07_4]. In Malaysian oil palm, alley-cropping with black pepper or cacao measured significantly wetter topsoil than the monocultures, attributed to greater leaf area, lower light penetration and reduced wind cutting evaporation from exposed soil [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_1].

justification.mechanism: In rainfed cropping the studies disagree, the same as for agroforestry overall; 9 papers name this farming system. Trees draw down deeper and dry-season soil water: under Faidherbia albida parkland with wheat in Ethiopia, soil moisture in the sub-soil was the least for wheat with tree, intermediate for sole tree and the highest for open field [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]; in a Gliricidia + maize trial at Makoka, Malawi, the lower available soil water at the beginning of the cropping season in the tree-based systems suggests that the trees continued to deplete moisture during the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2], the March-to-August decline was most pronounced in the tree-based systems [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3], water content was slightly lower under gliricidia + maize in the dry season when the trees were left unpruned [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5], and in the first season's May water content under gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea was lower than in all other treatments below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4]. Beside Saskatchewan field shelterbelts, spring soil water content in 1990 dropped noticeably from 0.1 to 0.05 relative distance from the belt, which the authors put down, tentatively, to uptake by the trees and grasses in the previous fallow year; in 1989 the pattern differed, with a slight trend of decreasing available water from the field edge to the centre [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. In a Senegal trial with the shrub Guiera senegalensis, soil next to the shrubs dried faster during an imposed drought than soil far from them or in crop-only plots in two of three subplots [ev_soil_moisture_bogie18_2]. Against this, at Makoka available water content tended to be greater in the gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea system at the peak of the recharge phase, which the authors attribute to increased infiltration and reduced soil evaporation [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10]; in the second season's May that system held much more water than all other treatments below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8]; and water use efficiency was higher in the tree systems in every season, for example 1.43 against 0.52 g of biomass per kg of water for gliricidia + maize against sole maize in 1997/98 [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_6]. At Sadore in the Nigerien Sahel, Ziziphus mauritiana trees in millet fields raised the rainwater use efficiency of millet by 17 and 47 % with farmyard manure and without fertilizer, and that of a millet/cowpea intercrop by 11 to 17 % [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_2]. A German alley-cropping trial in a drought year found soil water content remained lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. Several measurements found no difference: topsoil moisture under Faidherbia [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_2]; soil moisture before the imposed drought in the Senegal shrub trial [ev_soil_moisture_bogie18_3]; and at Makoka the generally comparable distribution of water in the profile [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_1], and no significant treatment effects in the second season, the second season's October, or December and January of the third season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_6, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_7, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_9]. The Makoka authors conclude that gliricidia pruned before and during the cropping season does not provoke undue competition for water with associated crops [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11]. In Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual system report 23% soil humidity in the driest month (April) against 8% in a traditional slash-and-burn field, a difference equivalent to 20mm of rainfall, or 20 more days that crops can be sustained without rain; they explain it by better infiltration through the soil cover and more soil organic matter [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1]. In France, a walnut-alley trial found a similar depth split: soil water in the plough layer was drier under the trees than the full-sun control through spring, while deep soil-water dynamics were very similar between the two systems [ev_soil_moisture_blan22_4, ev_soil_moisture_blan22_5]. In Jiangxi Province, China, a peanut-tree alley-cropping trial found the profile-mean (0-150 cm) soil water potential drier in both tree-intercropped treatments than in mono-cropped peanut or either tree monoculture, consistent with tree-crop competition for water, with the difference larger in the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_wei07_4].

justification.statement: agroforestry water_stress: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE — material weight on both the benefit and the harm side, so no direction is stated. T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: This row rolls up all tree-perennial farming-system evidence regardless of sub-practice family; in practice all three units come from shaded perennial-crop systems (cocoa, coffee). Most of the units measure less soil water under shade — the multi-country cocoa meta-analysis and the Ghana study — so the class is a slight increase in water stress rather than a benefit, and the Mexican coffee buffering result is the one offsetting signal, which keeps agreement at high rather than a stronger reading [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. None of the three states a size for the difference, and none measures a drought or other named water-stress hazard — all describe ordinary dry-season soil moisture [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. The Mexican result is a slower rate of loss and smaller swings under shade, not a higher measured moisture level, and the same site gained less water after rain through canopy interception [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. The cocoa evidence sits in lower- and upper-middle-income countries across Latin America, West Africa and Southeast Asia, in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. Every other new unit adds to the drying side already dominant in this row: the same Malaysian trial found bamboo alleys measured significantly drier topsoil than the monocultures, attributed to bamboo's sparse canopy leaving the ground exposed [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_2]; and in Brazilian coffee, soil moisture under shade was measured lower than under the unshaded area at every depth throughout the monitoring period, with the drying most pronounced soon after rain in drier periods — shade drying the soil rather than conserving it, even though the authors separately argue tree-coffee water-use complementarity kept available water sufficient for the coffee through the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_5, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_6, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_7]. None of the new units states a size or names a drought, and all are upper-middle-income evidence (Malaysia, Brazil), consistent with this row's existing transfer.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In tree-crop systems, shade and tree water use change soil moisture in opposing ways. A multi-country meta-analysis of cocoa agroforestry across Ghana, Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire, Indonesia, Malaysia, Costa Rica, Panama, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia found soils under agroforestry have a significantly lower volumetric water content than under monocultures [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]. In Ghana, the combined transpiration of shade trees and cocoa plants raised water uptake, with a consequent reduction in soil water compared with full-sun cocoa [ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]. Against this, in a Mexican coffee lysimeter study, soil water losses and gains fluctuated far more at the low-shade site than at the medium- and high-shade sites, showing that shade can buffer soil moisture loss through evaporation [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. In Malaysian oil palm, alley-cropping with black pepper or cacao measured significantly wetter topsoil than the monocultures, attributed to greater leaf area, lower light penetration and reduced wind cutting evaporation from exposed soil — the one unit in this row's newer evidence that reads as a soil-moisture benefit [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_1].

In a long-running Gliricidia + maize trial at Makoka, Malawi, system water-use efficiency (above-ground biomass including the tree, per unit of seasonal water use) was strongly and significantly higher in every season for gliricidia-based systems than for sole maize or maize-pigeonpea [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_6]. At the same site, available soil water was also greater in the gliricidia+maize+pigeonpea system at the peak of the recharge phase in two seasons, attributed to increased infiltration and reduced soil evaporation, and higher below 60 cm in the second season's May reading [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8]. In a German alley-cropping trial in a drought year, soil water content remained lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In Jiangxi Province, China, a peanut-tree alley-cropping trial found the profile-mean (0-150 cm) soil water potential drier in both tree-intercropped treatments than in mono-cropped peanut or either tree monoculture, consistent with tree-crop competition for water, with the difference larger in the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_wei07_4].

justification.statement: agroforestry water_stress: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE — material weight on both the benefit and the harm side, so no direction is stated. This is not a null finding: studies found real effects, in opposite directions, and the agreement note lists both sides. Read the conditionality for what separates them (transfer: adjacent).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Two findings point the other way. In Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual system report 23% soil humidity in the driest month against 8% in a slash-and-burn field, which they credit to soil cover and more organic matter; this is a project-written grey-literature account with no replication, and it bundles the trees with mulch, zero tillage and no burning [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet rates water availability increased through higher groundwater, a practitioner judgement about groundwater rather than soil moisture at the crop's roots [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. The drying findings are measured, but each comes from a single site and one tree or shrub species, and neither says whether pruning or tree density changes the result [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_moisture_bogie18_2].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: For trees and shrubs kept or regenerated on cropland, the measured evidence points to a slight increase in water stress for the crop, without a stated size. Under Faidherbia albida parkland in Ethiopia, subsoil moisture was lowest for wheat with the tree, intermediate for the tree alone and highest in the open field, though topsoil moisture did not differ [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_2]. In a Senegal trial with the shrub Guiera senegalensis, soil next to the shrubs dried faster during an imposed drought than soil far from them or in crop-only plots in two of three subplots, while before the drought there was little difference [ev_soil_moisture_bogie18_2, ev_soil_moisture_bogie18_3].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: This is the shaded perennial-crop family's own row; cocoa and coffee are this family's crops, so the same three units apply directly. Most of the units measure less soil water under shade — the multi-country cocoa meta-analysis and the Ghana study — so the class is a slight increase in water stress rather than a benefit, and the Mexican coffee buffering result is the one offsetting signal, which keeps agreement at high rather than a stronger reading [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. None of the three states a size for the difference, and none measures a drought or other named water-stress hazard — all describe ordinary dry-season soil moisture [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. The Mexican result is a slower rate of loss and smaller swings under shade, not a higher measured moisture level, and the same site gained less water after rain through canopy interception [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. The cocoa evidence sits in lower- and upper-middle-income countries across Latin America, West Africa and Southeast Asia, in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. Every other new unit adds to the drying side already dominant in this row: the same Malaysian trial found bamboo alleys measured significantly drier topsoil than the monocultures, attributed to bamboo's sparse canopy leaving the ground exposed [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_2]; and in Brazilian coffee, soil moisture under shade was measured lower than under the unshaded area at every depth throughout the monitoring period, with the drying most pronounced soon after rain in drier periods — shade drying the soil rather than conserving it, even though the authors separately argue tree-coffee water-use complementarity kept available water sufficient for the coffee through the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_5, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_6, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_7]. None of the new units states a size or names a drought, and both sources are upper-middle-income evidence (Malaysia, Brazil), consistent with this row's existing transfer.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In tree-crop systems, shade and tree water use change soil moisture in opposing ways. A multi-country meta-analysis of cocoa agroforestry across Ghana, Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire, Indonesia, Malaysia, Costa Rica, Panama, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia found soils under agroforestry have a significantly lower volumetric water content than under monocultures [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]. In Ghana, the combined transpiration of shade trees and cocoa plants raised water uptake, with a consequent reduction in soil water compared with full-sun cocoa [ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]. Against this, in a Mexican coffee lysimeter study, soil water losses and gains fluctuated far more at the low-shade site than at the medium- and high-shade sites, showing that shade can buffer soil moisture loss through evaporation [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. In Malaysian oil palm, alley-cropping with black pepper or cacao measured significantly wetter topsoil than the monocultures, attributed to greater leaf area, lower light penetration and reduced wind cutting evaporation from exposed soil — the one unit in this row's newer evidence that reads as a soil-moisture benefit [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: After a drier-than-normal winter, the same trial measured deeper (1-2 m) soil moisture lower under a silvopasture than under open lucerne pasture, attributing it to the trees' higher winter water use drawing down deep soil water that the below-normal winter rain did not replace [ev_soil_moisture_pollock08_2]. Both readings come from the same single New Zealand silvopasture experiment, high-income temperate evidence well outside the LIC/LMIC target; neither names a drought, describing instead an ordinary below-normal-rainfall winter. With only one independent source behind two readings that point one to no difference and one to a measured drying, agreement here is read as low.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In a New Zealand silvopasture, summer water use and end-of-summer soil moisture were no different from open pasture once the trees reached four growing seasons old, as the maturing tree roots came to occupy the profile at depth and dominate water use across every system [ev_soil_moisture_pollock08_1].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: The effect is off-site for farmers: the Tigray yield advantage compares exclosures with open grazing, so it measures a downstream benefit to cropland rather than production on the restored land, and it was larger in the drier first year than in the following year [ev_crop_yield_mezgebo26_3]. The co-management benefit is confined to forest income: participation did not mitigate the effect of rainfall shocks on non-forestry income, which shocks are likely to erode by 36% among participating households too, and this no-benefit result is what discounts the class [ev_household_income_kimwanga26_5]. The per capita gain under shocks reached moderately poor households rather than the poorest, and the authors report it as shifting away from the poorest decile [ev_household_income_kimwanga26_7]. The India reading rests on a compiler rating rather than a measurement, and the cross-family evidence bundles exclosure and planting with bunds and terraces [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_5243_2019_drought_impacts, ev_soil_water_retention_meaza22_1]. The modelled benefit is landscape-scale only and does not speak to plot-scale restoration [ev_drought_hazard_teo22_1].

justification.mechanism: Every sub-practice row that votes here finds forest restoration eases drought only a little, apart from the protection and community forest management row, and the vote, not the pooled count of beneficial units, sets the low class. In the protection and community forest management row, the India compiler credits the watershed programme with improved surface and subsurface hydrological functioning in the upper watershed, which raised springshed groundwater stores and dry-season stream and spring flows [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_5243_2019_drought_impacts]. In Malawi, households taking part in forest co-management through village natural resource management committees had 57% higher annual forestry income after a rainfall shock than non-participants [ev_household_income_kimwanga26_4], and under shocks the per capita income gain from participation showed up among moderately poor households, at 31.4% [ev_household_income_kimwanga26_7]. In the passive regeneration row, households in Tigray, Ethiopia, downstream of exclosures harvested 188 to 222 kg/ha more than households beside open grazing areas in the drought-affected 2023 season [ev_crop_yield_mezgebo26_1]. The cross-family row rests on a meta-analysis of Ethiopian catchment restoration reporting that exclosures, tree planting, bunds and terraces reduce water losses and improve water in soils, rivers and aquifers [ev_soil_water_retention_meaza22_1]. The pool also holds a Niger rating that assisted natural regeneration, by improving vegetation cover and woody production, helps reduce the impacts of long droughts in the rainy season, and a regional model of large-scale reforestation that found fewer extremely dry months in 9 of 15 regions [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_2325_2017_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_teo22_1].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Most of this evidence is about keeping existing forest, not restoring it. The pooled estimate is for natural forest kept under legal protection, and a study among those it pools found the reduced fire inside the protected forest came alongside more fire in the densely populated buffer zone just outside it, a leakage effect the pooled estimate does not count [ev_fire_hazard_malh25_1]. The cited fire-risk rise describes what is lost when existing tropical forest is cleared for farming, comes second-hand from another study, and its source is a preprint [ev_fire_hazard_yang24_1]. The India unit is a single practitioner rating from a programme that bundles plantations, assisted regeneration and nurseries with protection, and the compiler adds that in pine forests needle build-up remains a major fuel source whose removal is a challenge for land users [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_5243_2019_fire_risk]. The World Bank evaluation reports the outcome as a narrative across projects, only where it was monitored, with no measure of how much fire incidence fell [ev_fire_hazard_ieg13_1]. A further unit found no effect: a GEF evaluation's own before-and-after satellite analysis around a Thai community fire-management project, which bundles fire management with catchment management on existing forest, found only a small difference in median fire frequency; fire severity rose on about 110 hectares near the project border but recovered on about 2,800 hectares in the northwest [ev_fire_hazard_gefieo22_1]. No unit describes how well protection holds up in a severe or extreme fire season.

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: What separates the benefit from the nulls is scale and storm size. The gains are local, modelled or small-storm results; the nulls are about large basins and floods on the plains. The FAO synthesis finds no evidence that reforesting watersheds reduces or prevents floods except at the very local scale of a few hundred hectares [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_5, ev_flood_hazard_ham08_6]. A Himalayan analysis concludes that reforestation will not likely have significant beneficial impact on local flooding, and certainly not on the hydrological character of the Ganges and Brahmaputra mainstreams [ev_flood_hazard_ives87_1], and a conference overview warns that reforestation in the mountains conceived as a palliative for the problems of the plains is likely to reap only disappointment [ev_flood_hazard_ivesmt87_1], and both come from the same lead author, so they count as a single line of argument. An FAO–CIFOR review concludes that massive programmes of forestation proclaimed as the answer to preventing floods simply will not do the job, although reforestation may have many other benefits [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_3], and a published comment argues that reforestation does not necessarily reduce flooding, for example if soil properties do not recover, river bed morphology does not change, and settlements, roads and drains remain unaltered [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_5]. A review of coastal tree belts adds a coastal null: the science on short-period wave damping should not be taken to show that vegetation can reduce the effects of storm surges [ev_flood_hazard_feagin10_1]; this is an expert argument about coastal plantings, not a measurement. These are expert positions and reviews rather than new measurements. The co-benefit listing is second-hand and states no size, place or scale [ev_flood_hazard_griscom17_3]. The UNESCO review's statement is local only, its supporting table cannot be read so no size is available, and the planting half of the sentence pools reforesting with terracing and contouring, so it cannot be credited to trees alone [ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_6, ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_7]. The flood-cover review adds that afforestation yields only gradual reductions, smaller than the rises in peak flow that follow deforestation and shaped by forest maturity, with peak flow in small catchments falling by up to 14% on limited data [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_2, ev_flood_hazard_herath25_4]; its pooled peak-flow points come from modelled scenarios in mostly temperate catchments, so it is a synthesis of other studies' models rather than new measurement. The modelled benefit itself shrinks as rain continues, from 29% for the shortest rain duration to 17% for the longest [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_3], and all catchment models are scenarios of large forest-cover gains in temperate high-income basins; the largest figure, a 42.3% peak reduction from converting all arable land to forest, is a secondary citation with no basin named [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_4]. The Oregon recovery comes from a clear-cut harvest study, measured against the freshly cut state rather than against unrestored land, and the paper does not say whether the regrowth was planted or natural [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5]. The low- and lower-middle-income evidence is a compiler rating and expert positions, not measured flows or flood damage. The forest-water review pools restoration with forestry and afforestation and reports vote counts rather than magnitudes [ev_flood_hazard_filoso17_1]. No unit measures a benefit at severe or extreme flood; the only reading at the 1% AEP event is that review's pooled modelled points [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_5]. Studies of what existing forest does, such as harvest experiments and the Himalayan essays on forest loss, sit in the protection family row and do not set this class. justification.conditionality: What separates the benefit from the nulls is scale and storm size. The gains are local, modelled or small-storm results; the nulls are about large basins and floods on the plains. The FAO synthesis finds no evidence that reforesting watersheds reduces or prevents floods except at the very local scale of a few hundred hectares [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_5, ev_flood_hazard_ham08_6]. A Himalayan analysis concludes that reforestation will not likely have significant beneficial impact on local flooding, and certainly not on the hydrological character of the Ganges and Brahmaputra mainstreams [ev_flood_hazard_ives87_1], and a conference overview warns that reforestation in the mountains conceived as a palliative for the problems of the plains is likely to reap only disappointment [ev_flood_hazard_ivesmt87_1], and both come from the same lead author, so they count as a single line of argument. An FAO–CIFOR review concludes that massive programmes of forestation proclaimed as the answer to preventing floods simply will not do the job, although reforestation may have many other benefits [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_3], and a published comment argues that reforestation does not necessarily reduce flooding, for example if soil properties do not recover, river bed morphology does not change, and settlements, roads and drains remain unaltered [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_5]. A review of coastal tree belts adds a coastal null: the science on short-period wave damping should not be taken to show that vegetation can reduce the effects of storm surges [ev_flood_hazard_feagin10_1]; this is an expert argument about coastal plantings, not a measurement. justification.mechanism: In this evidence restored forest cover lowers flood peaks moderately, and mainly at local scale and for smaller storms. Catchment models show it: in Slovakia's Hornad watershed a reforestation scenario cut a simulated flood peak from 84.8 to 74.9 m3/s and, for a 50% increase of forest, reduced peaks by about 24% on average in rain-duration tests, more for short storms than long ones [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_1, ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_3], and an afforestation simulation for Luxembourg's Alzette basin decreased the peak by 8% [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_5]. A systematic review of forest cover and catchment flooding finds peak flow changes by roughly half the change in forest cover, so a 20% increase in forest cover tends to reduce peak flow by 10% across small, medium and large catchments, with only minor differences in mean reductions across event intensities up to the 1% AEP event; the review attributes this to forests detaining floodwater through infiltration, canopy interception and evapotranspiration [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_1, ev_flood_hazard_herath25_5]. Another systematic review found that flooding or peak flows decreased with forest cover expansion in 82% of the studies reporting them [ev_flood_hazard_filoso17_1]. A UNESCO review of moist tropical forest hydrology states that the beneficial effects of reforesting, terracing and contouring degraded lands on stormflow and peakflow are evident at small-basin scale, as is the regenerative capacity of most ecosystems when left alone [ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_6, ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_7]. In a clear-cut Oregon basin, peak discharges recovered gradually as the basin revegetated, which the authors attribute to changes in evapotranspiration [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5]. An FAO synthesis expects flash flooding to be reduced locally for frequent short, low-intensity storm events where soils are deep [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_7], and a global review states that afforestation in energy-limited environments will help to reduce flood risks [ev_flood_hazard_zhang17_1]. An Ethiopian WOCAT compiler for a regeneration-based technology rates downstream flooding as strongly reduced, noting that runoff from the watershed is highly reduced [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1072_2011_downstream_flooding]. A global study of natural climate solutions also lists flood control among reforestation's well-demonstrated co-benefits, citing an earlier assessment, with no size given [ev_flood_hazard_griscom17_3].

justification.mechanism: Restored forest cover lowers flood peaks in this evidence by a moderate amount. A systematic review of forest cover and catchment flooding finds peak flow changes by roughly half the change in forest cover, so a 20% increase in forest cover tends to reduce peak flow by 10% across small, medium and large catchments, which the review attributes to forests detaining floodwater through infiltration, canopy interception and evapotranspiration [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_1]. A global systematic review of forest restoration and water found that flooding or peak flows decreased with forest cover expansion in 82% of the studies with data on them [ev_flood_hazard_filoso17_1]. A harvest experiment in Oregon adds a measured recovery: after clear-cutting, peak discharges recovered gradually over time as the basin revegetated, which the authors attribute to changes in evapotranspiration [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5]. A global study of natural climate solutions also lists flood control among reforestation's well-demonstrated co-benefits, citing an earlier assessment, with no size given [ev_flood_hazard_griscom17_3].
