T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: The harvest studies, the forest-loss analyses and the two classic reviews describe what existing forest does; they enter through the existing-forest comparator (the flood-cover review's deforestation reading among them [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_3]), which routes them to this protection family and keeps them out of the restoration families, so none of them is a restoration or protection-programme result. The Malaysian study also carries the harm finding in this row: where the forest converted was wetland (peat-swamp) forest, deforestation reduced flooding, a large effect (semi-elasticity = 38.0%), which the authors link to drainage installed at conversion lowering the water level; so keeping forest is not a flood defence in every forest type [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_3]. The same study found no significant effect of deforestation on the number of floods per month, which the authors put down to a problem in defining that variable rather than to forest having no effect [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_5]. Its inland-forest figures are semi-elasticities per 1% of basin area converted, not whole-catchment contrasts, and the oil palm and rubber results are from a single period of conversion, not restoration [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_1, ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_2], while the urban figure was not estimated very precisely (P = 0.094) [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_4]. The Oregon large-basin increase is bundled with forest road construction and is stated as an upper bound, as much as [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_1]. The service fades with storm size and basin size. Complete clear-cutting without roads produced significant increases in fall and winter events but not for large events as a group [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_4], and at Andrews 10 large events did not change after 100% clear-cutting [ev_flood_hazard_jon00_2]. In the same study other types of winter events did not change, so only rain-on-snow peaks rose in winter [ev_water_regulation_jon00_7], and in the fog-prone basins changes in cloud water interception apparently offset changes in evapotranspiration in two partially cut basins [ev_water_regulation_jon00_5]. The fall increases came in small events (0.22- or 0.28-year return periods), not in large events [ev_water_regulation_jon00_1]. For the rarer prolonged or high-intensity storms, once the soil layer becomes saturated water will run off even where there is full, undisturbed forest cover [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_4]; Hamilton's earlier essay makes the same point, that for major storms the effect of forest on or forest off is dwarfed by the rainfall itself, since soil can only store so much water [ev_flood_hazard_ham87_6]. He judges that the June 1985 floods that killed 237 persons in six Indian states were caused by too much rain in too short a time, with some areas receiving 414 mm in 24 hours on already saturated soils, and that even a fully forested basin would have flooded; this is his judgement, not data [ev_flood_hazard_ham87_12]. Forest soils reduce runoff only in small-scale rainfall events, which are not responsible for severe downstream flooding, and forests cannot stop catastrophic large-scale floods caused by severe meteorological events [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_1, ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_2]; and small to medium peak flows are affected most while the largest events do not change noticeably [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_3]. At basin scale the link is not shown. A worldwide review of watershed research found no cause and effect between forest cutting in the headwaters and floods in the lower basin; Hamilton cites it both in his earlier essay, where he adds that there are no valid reasons to suggest forests can prevent major floods on the large rivers of the subcontinent, and in his later FAO synthesis, so this is a single finding [ev_flood_hazard_ham87_4, ev_flood_hazard_ham08_2]. Long records from meso-scale basins of up to 14500 km2 in Taiwan and northern Thailand that had lost much forest showed no systematic trend in flood magnitude, climate dominating, although the review notes that much of that forest loss was probably followed by regeneration rather than cropping [ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_8]. A Himalayan analysis contends that on the Himalayan scale human influences, so far, are insignificant [ev_flood_hazard_ives87_2]. The cross-country analysis itself found little evidence that further forest loss changed flood deaths or damage [ev_flood_hazard_bradshaw07_3, ev_flood_hazard_bradshaw07_4], and a reanalysis found the correlation between forest cover or cover loss and flood frequency appears absent [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_1]. Read the slight class as a local, small-to-medium storm service, not a defence against severe or extreme floods. For farmers the effect is off-site, arriving downstream of the protected forest.

justification.mechanism: This row describes the flood regulation that standing forest provides and that protection keeps; nearly all of it is evidence about existing forest, read through what happens when it is cut. In paired experimental basins in Oregon, a high-income setting, discharges in small basins increased by 50% in the first 5 years after clear-cutting and were 25 to 40% higher than pretreatment up to 25 years later, and forest harvesting with roads has increased peak discharges by as much as 50% in small basins and 100% in large basins over the past 50 years [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_2, ev_flood_hazard_jg96_3, ev_flood_hazard_jg96_1]. A later analysis of the same basins found large events increased by 25% at Andrews 1, 16% at Andrews 6 and 26% at Coyote 3 after 100% clear-cutting [ev_flood_hazard_jon00_1]. The same Oregon study separates the event types. Forest canopy removal accounted for significant increases (31–116%) in peak discharges during the first postharvest decade in 8 of 10 treated basins, but the affected events were small and fell in the fall (September–November), when soils are in moisture deficit, rather than in spring [ev_water_regulation_jon00_1]. Changes in snowpack dynamics accounted for significant increases (25–31%) in winter rain-on-snow events in four of five basins at the H. J. Andrews Experimental Forest [ev_water_regulation_jon00_6]. Two reviews of forest hydrology state the general rule: after forest cutting or conversion there is usually, in response to each storm, an increase in peak flow, storm-flow volume and storm-flow duration [ev_flood_hazard_ham87_5], and a certain increase in stormflow volume and peakflow cannot be avoided after forest conversion, with the relative increase largest for small events (which may be doubled) and smallest for large ones (perhaps in the order of 10 per cent or less) [ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_5]. An FAO synthesis states that partial or complete removal of tree cover accelerates water discharge, increasing the risk of flood during the rainy season, and that for frequent rainfall events of short duration or low intensity forested soils may reduce or prevent flash floods locally [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_1, ev_flood_hazard_ham08_3]. At the local scale forests and forest soils reduce runoff through enhanced infiltration and storage, and peak flows rise after forest removal in small experimental catchments [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_1, ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_2]. A country-level analysis of developing countries predicted that a further hypothetical 10% loss of natural forest cover would raise flood frequency by 3.5% to 28.1% and flood duration by 3.8% to 7.9% [ev_flood_hazard_bradshaw07_1, ev_flood_hazard_bradshaw07_2]; in Peninsular Malaysia, a river-basin panel study by Tan-Soo and colleagues found that converting 1% of a basin from inland forest to oil palm increased the number of days flooded by 26.8%, and to rubber by 26.5%, with conversion to urban use also having a large effect (semi-elasticity = 35.9%) [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_1, ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_2, ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_4]; a systematic review of forest cover and catchment flooding finds that deforestation consistently increases peak flows [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_3]; and in Swiss valleys with more than 30% forest, snowmelt was more gradual and flooding risk lower [ev_flood_hazard_iufro18_2].

justification.mechanism: Drought moderately damages restoration plantings. Drought kills planted seedlings during establishment: a review attributes rising mortality of recently outplanted seedlings in dry regions to hotter and drier conditions, and links high rates of seedling mortality at restoration sites in western North America to limiting conditions in the energy and hydrologic cycles [ev_establishment_survival_gross26_1, ev_establishment_survival_gross26_3]. In northern Thailand, seeds sown to help a degraded forest regrow germinated far less when rain failed, and seedlings were easily scorched by direct sun [ev_establishment_survival_hardwick97_1]; in a nursery test, germination in full sun was significantly reduced by dry-season drought but stayed high when seeds were watered [ev_establishment_survival_hardwick97_2].

justification.mechanism: On a Mediterranean dryland reforestation project in Spain, the drought index correlated strongly with the course of plantation mortality (r = −0.72); about one quarter of the plantation was dead by the first year and more than half in the second, and the trend worsened in an exceptional, severe drought [ev_establishment_survival_delcampo21_1, ev_establishment_survival_delcampo21_2]. justification.mechanism: Wind damages planted stands once storms pass a threshold, and the damage grows quickly above it. A review of wind damage to planted and managed forests suggests damage starts when canopy-top hourly wind speeds exceed approximately 8.5 m s−1 and gusts outside the forest exceed 25–30 m s−1, with damage increasing almost exponentially as gust speed rises [ev_climate_shock_gardiner21_1]. The same review finds that in the same storm a taller, more mature stand is generally more likely to fail than a shorter younger one [ev_climate_shock_gardiner21_2], that new gaps or edges from thinning, harvesting, clear-cutting upwind stands or roads leave the remaining trees particularly vulnerable [ev_climate_shock_gardiner21_3], and that the effects last for years through further wind or insect damage to weakened trees or reduced growth [ev_climate_shock_gardiner21_4]. In central Vietnam typhoon damage is a continuing concern for smallholder plantations and leads planters to favour short rotations [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_ieg18_1]; on a Spanish dryland reforestation project, windstorms blew away tree shelters [ev_climate_shock_delcampo21_1]; and in the south-eastern United States, Hurricane Michael (October 2018) caused over $2 billion in losses to the timber industry in Florida, Alabama, and Georgia [ev_climate_shock_wiener20_1].

T6E_economic_profile.effect_mechanism: Cost per hectare depends mainly on method: modelled implementation cost has a median of US$140/ha for natural regeneration [ev_project_cost_busch24_1], and natural regeneration methods are cited at US$12-3,880/ha against US$105-25,830/ha for restoration projects in the tropics and subtropics [ev_project_cost_williams24_2]. A Brazilian cost survey reports the same gap: direct seeding and seedling planting cost approximately ten times more (about US$2000/ha) than natural and assisted regeneration and enrichment planting (about US$200/ha), mostly due to the higher input costs [ev_project_cost_branc19_1, ev_project_cost_branc19_2, ev_project_cost_branc19_3]. A World Bank irrigation and watershed project in Madagascar estimated US$1,500 per hectare for reforested area, against $300 per hectare for avoided deforestation [ev_project_cost_exact14_1]. The opportunity cost of land (median US$4,807/ha) is generally higher and more variable than implementation cost [ev_project_cost_busch24_5].

T6E_economic_profile.conditionality: No source gives a usable cost figure for this practice as a whole, so no cost class is given. The per-hectare ranges are a second-hand comparison spanning very different projects [ev_project_cost_williams24_1], the guideline statement is an expert view without a number [ev_project_cost_stanturf26_1], the Mexican figures are per plant at a single site and cannot be scaled to a per-hectare or programme cost [ev_project_cost_barajas13_1], and the high-cost statement has no figure [ev_project_cost_griscom17_5]. T6E_economic_profile.effect_mechanism: Most of the evidence says letting forest regrow is cheaper to establish than planting it. A global study of natural regeneration, citing earlier work, puts natural regeneration at US$12–3,880 per ha against US$105–25,830 for forest restoration projects in the tropics and subtropics [ev_project_cost_williams24_1], and reforestation guidelines list lower cost among the benefits of natural regeneration [ev_project_cost_stanturf26_1]. In a Mexican dry-forest planting trial, polyethylene mulch cut the cost per established plant, including the nursery, from US$18.00 on bare soil to US$2.45, because far more plants survived (92 of 180 against 10 of 180) [ev_project_cost_barajas13_1]. Pointing the other way, a global study of natural climate solutions, citing earlier work, says reforestation can incur high costs of establishment [ev_project_cost_griscom17_5].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The sub-practices do not all agree. One review names a harm: where forests can regenerate naturally, reforestation by tree planting can reduce biodiversity benefits if the species or management chosen do not provide suitable habitat [ev_biodiversity_outcome_williams24_1]. Some units found no gain: abundance in restored systems often does not differ from pasture and agricultural land [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jakovac24_3], there was no clear-cut evidence that a Vietnamese forest project helped biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_ieg18_1], and management transfers in Madagascar remained superficial while clearing continued [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_2]. The terrestrial restoration meta-analysis pools forest with non-forest ecosystems and natural with assisted restoration [ev_biodiversity_outcome_atkinson22_1]. Many supporting units are compiler ratings or forest-cover change standing in for biodiversity, and the Ethiopian result is a qualitative report from a bundled watershed programme [ev_biodiversity_outcome_woldearegay17_2]. The global co-benefit listing is second-hand and gives no size [ev_biodiversity_outcome_griscom17_2].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Restoring forest rebuilds the habitat that native species depend on, and the gain is moderate overall. A meta-analysis across 221 study landscapes found forest restoration enhances biodiversity by 15–84% and vegetation structure by 36–77% compared with degraded ecosystems [ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles16_1], and a meta-analysis of terrestrial restoration found restored sites had 20% higher mean biodiversity than unrestored sites [ev_biodiversity_outcome_atkinson22_1]. Natural regeneration outperforms active planting: restoration success for biodiversity was 34 to 56% higher [ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles17_1]. In Brazil restored areas, regardless of technique, show higher diversity than agricultural land and pasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jakovac24_2], and tree species richness rises with time since disturbance [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liebsch08_1]. Woody species richness in Senegal exclosures rose from 27 species at 1 year to 51 at 5 and 12 years [ev_biodiversity_outcome_badji13_1], and Ethiopian authors credit afforestation and area closures with improving biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_woldearegay17_2]. Compilers in Afghanistan, Bangladesh and India report animal, plant and habitat diversity rising under protection and regeneration [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_7460_2024_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_4372_2019_habitat_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_5243_2019_plant_diversity], and protection and community management retain forest cover [ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1]. A global study of natural climate solutions, citing an earlier assessment, lists biodiversity habitat among reforestation's well-demonstrated co-benefits [ev_biodiversity_outcome_griscom17_2].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Two units found no gain: management transfers in Madagascar remained superficial and did not stop clearing [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_2]. In the global community-forest review condition decreased in 32% of cases [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1], and in Bolivia two initiatives had intermediate and three weak protection effects [ev_biodiversity_outcome_robertson05_1]. The only measured species count is the Senegal study, which compares exclosures of different ages rather than closed with open land [ev_biodiversity_outcome_badji13_1]. The rest are compiler ratings, a qualitative report from a bundled watershed programme [ev_biodiversity_outcome_woldearegay17_2], a rapid qualitative rating of payment schemes, and forest-cover change standing in for biodiversity.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In low- and lower-middle-income settings, closing land to cutting and grazing and protecting forest strongly raises biodiversity. In Senegal, woody species richness in village exclosures rose from 27 species in a 1-year exclosure to 51 species in 5- and 12-year exclosures, more than 52% higher [ev_biodiversity_outcome_badji13_1]. In an Ethiopian watershed, the authors report improved biodiversity through afforestation and area closures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_woldearegay17_2]. Compilers report that migratory animals and birds returned to protected land in Afghanistan [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_7460_2024_animal_diversity], that habitat and animal diversity increased with canopy cover and tree density in Bangladesh [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_4372_2019_habitat_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_4372_2019_animal_diversity], and that Indian community forests provide more water and habitat for small animals and birds, with plant diversity up through better moisture, soil and microclimate [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_5243_2019_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_5243_2019_plant_diversity]. In Bolivia four of the payment-like initiatives showed marked environmental protection effects [ev_biodiversity_outcome_robertson05_1]. Community management retained forest cover in Nepal, India and Bolivia [ev_landscape_forest_cover_iufro20_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_3], and environmental condition improved in 56% of community-forest cases worldwide [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1].

justification.mechanism: In low- and lower-middle-income settings, closing land to cutting and grazing and protecting forest strongly raises biodiversity. In Senegal, woody species richness in village exclosures rose from 27 species in a 1-year exclosure to 51 species in 5- and 12-year exclosures, more than 52% higher [ev_biodiversity_outcome_badji13_1]. In an Ethiopian watershed, the authors report improved biodiversity through afforestation and area closures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_woldearegay17_2]. Compilers report that migratory animals and birds returned to protected land in Afghanistan [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_7460_2024_animal_diversity], that habitat and animal diversity increased with canopy cover and tree density in Bangladesh [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_4372_2019_habitat_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_4372_2019_animal_diversity], and that Indian community forests provide more water and habitat for small animals and birds, with plant diversity up through better moisture, soil and microclimate [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_5243_2019_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_5243_2019_plant_diversity]. In Bolivia four of the payment-like initiatives showed marked environmental protection effects [ev_biodiversity_outcome_robertson05_1]. Community management retained forest cover in Nepal, India and Bolivia [ev_landscape_forest_cover_iufro20_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_3], and environmental condition improved in 56% of community-forest cases worldwide [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: What separates the gain side from the loss side is what the land would do without planting. The cautions apply where forests can regenerate naturally and where the species or management chosen do not provide suitable habitat [ev_biodiversity_outcome_williams24_1]; the gains are on bare dunes and degraded tropical land with no unplanted control [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wydhayagarn09_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_1529_2012_habitat_diversity]. The actionable reading is a siting and design choice: planting looks favourable where nothing would regenerate otherwise, and risky where natural regeneration is possible unless the species and management provide habitat. Both sides remain thin. The loss side is a single review warning, not a measured comparison; the gain side is a compiler rating and a case study without a control. Plantation comparisons sit in the plantation family's biodiversity row, which is parked out of the forest-restoration roll-up.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Both directions are reported. On the gain side, planted stands create habitat and attract seed dispersers: beneath framework-species plantings in northern Thailand thirty-six tree seedling species recruited naturally, 25 of them animal-dispersed [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wydhayagarn09_1], and the WOCAT compiler for dune afforestation in Turkmenistan rates habitat diversity as raised, noting that the vegetation on the barkhan sands now provides habitat for 25-27 species of plants and animals [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_1529_2012_habitat_diversity]. On the loss side, a pantropical review warns that where forests can regenerate naturally or with some assistance, tree planting can reduce biodiversity conservation benefits if the species or management chosen do not provide suitable habitat [ev_biodiversity_outcome_williams24_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Richness gains do not always mean more wildlife: in the Brazilian dataset abundance in restored systems often did not differ from pasture and agricultural land [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jakovac24_3]. Restored sites also stay short of intact ecosystems: biodiversity was on average 13% lower than at reference sites [ev_biodiversity_outcome_atkinson22_2]; that comparison is with the target ecosystem, not the degraded starting point, so it is held out of the class as a recovery shortfall. The terrestrial meta-analysis pools forest with non-forest ecosystems [ev_biodiversity_outcome_atkinson22_1], and the Ethiopian result is a qualitative report from a bundled watershed programme [ev_biodiversity_outcome_woldearegay17_2]. The global co-benefit listing is second-hand and gives no size [ev_biodiversity_outcome_griscom17_2].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Across restoration approaches, restored land holds moderately more biodiversity than degraded land. A meta-analysis across 221 study landscapes found forest restoration enhances biodiversity by 15–84% and vegetation structure by 36–77% compared with degraded ecosystems [ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles16_1], and a meta-analysis of terrestrial restoration found restored sites had 20% higher mean biodiversity than unrestored sites [ev_biodiversity_outcome_atkinson22_1]. In Brazil, restored areas, regardless of technique, show higher diversity than agricultural land and pasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jakovac24_2], and in an Ethiopian watershed the authors report improved biodiversity through afforestation and area closures where the measures matched the landscape [ev_biodiversity_outcome_woldearegay17_2]. A global study of natural climate solutions, citing an earlier assessment, lists biodiversity habitat among reforestation's well-demonstrated co-benefits [ev_biodiversity_outcome_griscom17_2].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Recovery of composition and endemism is slow: composition after 20 years was only 33% of old-growth values [ev_biodiversity_outcome_poorter21_1], and in the Brazilian Atlantic Forest regaining mature-forest endemism was estimated to take 1987 years [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liebsch08_3]. A global meta-analysis found biodiversity in naturally regenerated forests lower than in reference forests for every class of socioeconomic, biogeographic and ecological factor it examined [ev_biodiversity_outcome_latawiec16_1]; that comparison is with old-growth or less-disturbed forest, not with the degraded land regeneration starts from, so it is held out of the class as a recovery shortfall, not a loss caused by regeneration. The pantropical meta-analysis compares regeneration with planting rather than with degraded land [ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles17_1], and the Senegal result compares exclosures of different ages at one site rather than exclosures with open grazed land [ev_biodiversity_outcome_badji13_1]. The gain accrues to the regenerating forest and the landscape, not to the adopting farmer's fields.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Natural regeneration rebuilds biodiversity strongly as secondary forest develops. Across tropical chronosequences species richness recovers fastest and composition slowest, with richness after 20 years at 78% of old-growth values [ev_biodiversity_outcome_poorter21_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_poorter21_2]; tree species richness in Brazil's Atlantic Forest rises with time since disturbance [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liebsch08_1]; and in the western Andes of Colombia restored bird and dung beetle communities closely resembled those of old growth forests after 15–30 yr [ev_biodiversity_outcome_chazdon16_1]. A pantropical meta-analysis finds natural regeneration outperforms active planting for plants, birds and invertebrates [ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles17_1], and in Senegal's southern Groundnut Basin woody species richness in exclosures rose from 27 species after 1 year to 51 species after 5 and 12 years, an increase of more than 52% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_badji13_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The loss is stated without a size: the loss-side units are review statements and a cited case, none of which measures the decline against the land a plantation replaced, so the row reports a direction only. What separates loss from gain is what the plantation replaces: intact native ecosystems, a nesting beach or a diverse cover replaced by monocultures on the loss side [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_badola05_12, ev_biodiversity_outcome_feagin10_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_4], a highly degraded landscape where the trees help native vegetation return on the gain side [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_2]. Both coastal reviews are second-hand for most of their harm statements, and the Vietnam review hedges its warning as something that may happen [ev_biodiversity_outcome_feagin10_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_veettil21_2]. The pooled comparison against regeneration is not significant [ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_1], and the Canadian results differ by tree species and by group of plants, and are second-hand [ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_4, ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_5]. Three further units point toward loss but are held out of the class because they compare plantations with reference native forest rather than with the starting point of a project: a global meta-analysis found tree plantations supported on average 29.3% lower species-specific abundance than reference native forests (95% interval 22.0 to 35.9%) [ev_biodiversity_outcome_hua22_1], INRAE states that plantations generally lead to decreases in biodiversity, or at least to changes in composition at the expense of native species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_6], and it cites a 40% loss of local species richness in forest plantations relative to uncut control forest [ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_2]. These describe a shortfall from a natural baseline, not a restoration effect. The INRAE evidence is temperate and boreal, and only the Indian cases come from the low- and lower-middle-income target. The plantation family is kept out of the forest-restoration roll-up, because plantation monocultures may not count as a nature-based solution, and this row is published on its own: read it as evidence about plantations, not about restoration toward a natural baseline.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: The findings that set the rating point toward a small biodiversity loss, but none states how large it is. A review of nature-based solutions states that if non-native tree plantations replace intact native ecosystems such as ancient grasslands, peatlands or woodlands, the outcomes for biodiversity will be poor [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_1]. On the Orissa coast of India, extensive Casuarina plantations established as a storm protection measure caused destruction to olive ridley sea turtle nesting beaches [ev_biodiversity_outcome_badola05_12]. A review of coastal tree belts reports, partly from earlier work, that in India sand dunes have been flattened to make way for Casuarina plantations, destroying sea turtle nesting habitat, that Casuarina roots can prevent turtles from nesting above the high tide line, and that Casuarina is known to harm tropical birds and invade mangroves [ev_biodiversity_outcome_feagin10_2]. A review of coastal tree belts in Vietnam argues that plantings of non-native species may damage native ecosystems, noting, second-hand, that Casuarina tends to invade mangrove forests in low-salinity settings [ev_biodiversity_outcome_veettil21_2]. The nature-based solutions review also reports research in north-west India showing that although afforestation activities can lead to an aggregate increase in forest cover, in most cases they result in loss of diversity and promote monocultures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_4]. Against this, the review allows a gain in a narrower case: establishing plantations of non-native trees in a highly degraded landscape might benefit biodiversity locally if the trees enable native vegetation to regenerate, or regionally if plantations take pressure off native biodiverse forest [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_2]. An INRAE expert synthesis's own small meta-analysis of species richness in plantations against natural regeneration of the stand after regeneration cutting finds no clear difference: -0.24, a very imprecise estimate from a very small number of cases, with an interval that spans zero [ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_1]. Cited Canadian studies compared plantations with forest left to regrow after clear-cutting: spruce plantations had less rich and less diverse moss communities [ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_5], while hybrid larch plantations had significantly richer plant communities and hybrid poplar plantations showed no clear difference [ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_4].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Most units measure forest cover, deforestation or threat reduction, a component proxy for biodiversity, and the Mexican figure is a before-after comparison with no counterfactual [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1]. In south-west Madagascar transfers of management to communities were found superficial and unable to stop forest clearing [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_2], and GEF project sites likely exposed to urban encroachment showed forest losses [ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_3]; the GEF evidence concerns existing forest under a bundle of protection and management rather than restoration. Governance effects are uneven: in the global community-forest analysis environmental condition decreased in 32% of community-forest cases [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1]; In the same Indian Himalayan village-council (Van Panchayat) forests, crown cover of broad-leaved forest did not differ significantly from neighbouring state-managed forest, a direct boundary comparison for pine forest likewise found no significant difference, but a propensity-score-matched comparison across the whole sample found council-managed pine forest had significantly higher crown cover than matched state forest [ev_landscape_forest_cover_somanathan09_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_somanathan09_2, ev_landscape_forest_cover_somanathan09_3]. This is a comparison of both management regimes for forest that already exists, not a restoration of cleared or degraded land. An evaluation of Vietnam's special-use forests found no clear-cut evidence that the project improved biodiversity, noting that its tracking tool was not a suitable proxy [ev_biodiversity_outcome_ieg18_1], and Bank-supported payment schemes were applied broadly rather than targeting high-value forest areas [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_1]. These governance units measure forest cover, deforestation or threat reduction rather than species, the Indian and Bolivian estimates are cited in a systematic review, and the World Bank statements report outcomes only where they were monitored. That is a biodiversity-component proxy (forest cover, not species counts) for existing protected forest rather than restoration, and the review itself notes it is less confident the pooled effect generalises across contexts given that heterogeneity [ev_landscape_forest_cover_malh25_2].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Protection and community forest management retain and expand forest habitat. GEF sustainable forest management projects show less deforestation than matched areas without projects [ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_2], community forest management in Nepal reduced deforestation [ev_landscape_forest_cover_iufro20_1], and forest cover increased by 8% under community management in Mexico's Sierra Norte de Puebla [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1]. A global analysis of community forests found environmental condition improved after community forest management in 56% of the 524 cases tracking it [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1]. WOCAT compilers rate diversity as increased under protection: in India plant species diversity rose with improved moisture availability, soil conditions and microclimate, and the area provides more water and habitat for small animals and birds [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_5243_2019_plant_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_5243_2019_animal_diversity]; in Afghanistan migratory animals and birds returned due to the protection measures and the prohibition of human activities [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_7460_2024_animal_diversity]. Forest governance instruments retain forest habitat: a meta-analysis of payments for environmental services found improved forest cover (SMD = 0.32, 95% CI [0.10, 0.55]) and reduced deforestation (SMD = −0.12) against comparison areas [ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_2]; in a systematic review of decentralised forest management, community-managed Van Panchayats in India improved the annual forest cover change rate by 0.40 percentage points and decentralised administration of protected forests in Bolivia by 0.80 percentage points [ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_3]. World Bank evaluations report reduced deforestation, regeneration of degraded forests and protection of biodiversity under participatory forest management, and less deforestation under Bank-supported payment schemes in some countries [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_ieg13_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_1], and in Bolivia most payment-like initiatives showed marked or intermediate environmental protection effects, and the rest weak ones [ev_biodiversity_outcome_robertson05_1]. The same systematic review's pooled estimate for forest cover under protected areas, across 14 estimates, finds more forest retained than on comparable unprotected land (Hedges' g of 0.17), though with high heterogeneity (I-squared 96 percent) across the pooled studies [ev_landscape_forest_cover_malh25_2].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The gain is moderate rather than large, and much of the size evidence is not a fresh measurement. The IPCC values are compiled default tables carried forward from earlier guidance with a stated uncertainty of plus or minus 90% and no sample size [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc19_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc19_4], the global regrowth rates are model outputs for above-ground carbon [ev_carbon_sequestration_cookpatton20_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_cookpatton20_2], the plot synthesis and IPCC tables report dry matter, not carbon, and the global reforestation figure is a model of total potential across the world, not a per-hectare rate, with a wide range that its authors call highly uncertain [ev_carbon_sequestration_griscom17_1]. One source names a harm: afforestation on peaty soils can lead to losses of soil carbon that outweigh that sequestered as the trees grow [ev_carbon_sequestration_seddon21_7], so organic and peat soils need separate treatment. Four units found no gain: soil carbon under forest did not increase significantly over cropland in the first 0–5 years [ev_soil_organic_carbon_yang23_5], a REDD+ pilot in Nepal had no significant effect on forest carbon in community forests [ev_carbon_sequestration_snilstveit19_1], and in Madagascar transfer of management to communities remained superficial while clearing continued [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_2]. Forest cover and soil carbon enter as parts of the carbon picture, not direct measures of it, and practitioner ratings make up several of the agreeing units.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Restoring forest cover rebuilds the carbon stored in trees and soil that cleared or degraded land lacks. A global meta-analysis puts natural regeneration removal rates at 9.1–18.8 t CO2 per hectare per year during the first 20 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_bernal18_3]. A pantropical synthesis of field plots gives above-ground biomass growth in naturally regrowing secondary forest, for example 7.6 tonnes of dry matter per hectare per year in younger African rainforest stands and 0.5 in older subtropical Asian mountain stands [ev_carbon_sequestration_requena19_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_requena19_22]. A global model puts the average rate of natural forest regrowth at 3.16 Mg C per hectare per year [ev_carbon_sequestration_cookpatton20_2]. Planting native trees on former pasture in Brazil built up 21.85, 25.78 and 38.29 Mg/ha of carbon in successively older plantings [ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_3]. Protection and community forest management keep carbon in standing forest by retaining cover, measured as forest-cover change in payment schemes, community forests and GEF sites [ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_1]. A global model of natural climate solutions finds reforestation is the largest natural pathway, with a maximum mitigation potential, under food, fibre and biodiversity safeguards, of 2.7–17.9 Pg CO2e per year (95% confidence interval) [ev_carbon_sequestration_griscom17_1].

justification.mechanism: Restoring forest cover rebuilds the carbon stored in trees and soil that cleared or degraded land lacks. A global meta-analysis puts natural regeneration removal rates at 9.1–18.8 t CO2 per hectare per year during the first 20 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_bernal18_3]. A pantropical synthesis of field plots gives above-ground biomass growth in naturally regrowing secondary forest, for example 7.6 tonnes of dry matter per hectare per year in younger African rainforest stands and 0.5 in older subtropical Asian mountain stands [ev_carbon_sequestration_requena19_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_requena19_22]. A global model puts the average rate of natural forest regrowth at 3.16 Mg C per hectare per year [ev_carbon_sequestration_cookpatton20_2]. Planting native trees on former pasture in Brazil built up 21.85, 25.78 and 38.29 Mg/ha of carbon in successively older plantings [ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_3]. Protection and community forest management keep carbon in standing forest by retaining cover, measured as forest-cover change in payment schemes, community forests and GEF sites [ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_1]. A global model of natural climate solutions finds reforestation is the largest natural pathway, with a maximum mitigation potential, under food, fibre and biodiversity safeguards, of 2.7–17.9 Pg CO2e per year (95% confidence interval) [ev_carbon_sequestration_griscom17_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The young Brazilian plantings held only 15.7 to 27.6% of reference-forest biomass [ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_4]; that comparison with mature forest is held out of the class as a reference shortfall, but it shows how far young plantings remain from the baseline they restore toward. The same review marks where planting reverses the sign: the soil disturbance associated with afforestation causes significant losses in carbon-rich soils, especially of the deep soil carbon that takes many decades to accumulate [ev_soil_organic_carbon_seddon21_5], and afforestation on peaty soils can lead to losses of soil carbon that outweigh that sequestered as the trees grow [ev_carbon_sequestration_seddon21_7]. These are review sentences carrying cited findings rather than new measurements. Apart from the Brazilian stock measurements the evidence is a compiler rating, and soil organic carbon enters this row as a component proxy. Site choice is the lever: avoid peaty and carbon-rich soils.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Planting native trees on former pasture in Brazil's Atlantic Forest built up carbon storage in biomass and litter of 21.85, 25.78 and 38.29 Mg/ha in successively older plantings, against 138.94 Mg/ha in mature forest [ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_3]. T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Soil storage takes time to show: in the erosion-zone meta-analysis there was no significant increase in soil organic carbon under forestland compared with cropland in the first 0–5 years, so the removal is not something a short project will see in its soils [ev_soil_organic_carbon_yang23_5]. Neither meta-analysis, nor the global model, separates planting from natural regeneration, so the gain cannot be credited to a particular restoration family [ev_carbon_sequestration_jakovac24_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_yang23_3]. The Brazilian result is a carbon stock compared with degraded references rather than a net balance of removals, the soil figure is a change in carbon content rather than a stock, and neither comes from a low- or lower-middle-income setting. The removals are a climate benefit, off-site for the farmer. The global figure is a modelled worldwide total, not a per-hectare rate, and its authors call it highly uncertain [ev_carbon_sequestration_griscom17_1].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Returning degraded or cropped land to forest stores carbon in biomass and soil as woody vegetation and litter build up. A meta-analysis of Brazilian restored biomes finds that restored areas, regardless of the restoration technique, hold more carbon than degraded agricultural lands and pastures [ev_carbon_sequestration_jakovac24_1]. A meta-analysis of vegetation restoration in erosion zones found that returning cropland or bare land to forest raised soil organic carbon content by 25.28% compared with cropland [ev_soil_organic_carbon_yang23_3]. A global model of natural climate solutions finds reforestation, which there includes both planting and assisted regeneration, is the largest natural pathway, with a maximum mitigation potential under safeguards of 2.7–17.9 Pg CO2e per year (95% confidence interval) [ev_carbon_sequestration_griscom17_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Above-ground biomass recovers slowly, taking 12 decades by one pantropical estimate [ev_carbon_sequestration_poorter21_1], so a project cycle captures only the early part of the gain. Much of the size evidence is modelled: the global regrowth rates are model outputs for above-ground carbon, assume steady growth over 30 years, and the soil rate of 0.42 Mg C per hectare per year is a default its authors say needs further research [ev_carbon_sequestration_cookpatton20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_cookpatton20_3]; the global potential holds only if regrowing forests can establish and persist [ev_carbon_sequestration_williams24_1]. The IPCC dryland figures are compiled default tables carried forward from earlier guidance with a stated uncertainty of plus or minus 90% [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc19_1], and the plot synthesis and IPCC values are dry matter, not carbon. The field chronosequences are from upper-middle-income Brazil and Colombia. Young regrowth holding less than old-growth is incomplete recovery, not a loss.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Secondary forest regrowing on cleared or abandoned land adds carbon in biomass and soil. A global meta-analysis gives natural regeneration removal rates of 9.1–18.8 t CO2 per hectare per year during the first 20 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_bernal18_3]. A pantropical synthesis of field plots gives above-ground biomass growth of up to 7.6 tonnes of dry matter per hectare per year in younger African rainforest stands, falling to 0.5 in older subtropical Asian mountain stands [ev_carbon_sequestration_requena19_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_requena19_22]. Global models estimate an average regrowth rate of 3.16 Mg C per hectare per year, with mapped rates from 0.058 to 6 [ev_carbon_sequestration_cookpatton20_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_cookpatton20_1], a median 30-year accumulation of 60.2 tC per hectare in biomass and soil [ev_carbon_sequestration_busch24_1], 51 t of above-ground carbon per hectare in a 20-year-old moist tropical forest [ev_carbon_sequestration_busch19_1], and 23.4 Gt of C over 215 Mha in 30 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_williams24_1]. Field chronosequences agree: Amazon secondary forests held 50% (229 t/ha) of mature forest biomass after 25 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_gehring05_1], Colombian Andean regrowth reached about half of old-growth carbon within 15–30 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_chazdon16_1], and an Atlantic Forest fragment regrown for 60 years reached 297 Mg/ha against 313 Mg/ha in preserved forest nearby [ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_5]. Soil carbon recovers fastest, reaching 90% of old-growth values in about 5 years [ev_soil_organic_carbon_poorter21_1], with average gains of 0.447% of pre-transition soil carbon per year [ev_soil_organic_carbon_busch19_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The class is held at moderate because few of the units that agree on direction state a size. The IPCC values are compiled defaults carried forward from earlier guidance, in dry matter rather than carbon, and the Uzbekistan figure is a compiler's statement. The soil gain is not universal: afforestation in the boreal zone caused an average soil-carbon loss of about 1.5% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_lagan09_4], soil carbon did not change on low-clay soils [ev_soil_organic_carbon_lagan09_7], plantation density made no measurable difference [ev_soil_organic_carbon_lagan09_10], and other conifers had little effect on soil carbon (2%) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_lagan09_13]. A global meta-analysis found plantations held 32.8% less above-ground biomass than reference native forests (95% interval 16.5 to 45.9%) [ev_carbon_sequestration_hua22_1]; that is a comparison with natural forest, not with the land a plantation replaced, so it is held out of the class, but it shows plantations store less than the forest they might stand in for. The plantation family is kept out of the forest-restoration roll-up. A Mexican planting trial that reports high seedling survival (95% to 100%) is counted here, but it measures survival, not carbon [ev_establishment_survival_keyes97_1].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Plantations moderately increase carbon storage. Planted forests and woodlots accumulate carbon quickly in their early decades: compiled measurements give planted-forest removal rates of 4.5 to 40.7 t CO2 per hectare per year in the first 20 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_bernal18_1], and IPCC default tables give above-ground growth of tropical plantations from about 5 to 20 tonnes of dry matter per hectare per year depending on zone and continent [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc19_8, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc19_7]. Soil organic carbon rose by 26% on average under afforested former cropland in a global review [ev_soil_organic_carbon_lagan09_1]; the same review found soil carbon up approximately 12% under eucalyptus and pine and more than 25% under other broadleaf trees [ev_soil_organic_carbon_lagan09_11, ev_soil_organic_carbon_lagan09_12], and the Uzbekistan compiler reports surface biomass growth of 20 t per hectare per year [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_1533_2011_biomass_above_ground_C].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The class is held at moderate because the only size estimates for carbon come from models: the forest-keeping comparison is a model of above-ground carbon in existing secondary forest, not measured removals [ev_carbon_sequestration_robinson25_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_robinson25_3], the GEF carbon estimate is also derived from a model over existing forest [ev_carbon_sequestration_gefieo19_1], and the global avoided-conversion pathway is a model that states its size only in a figure, adding that costs may matter less than public policy challenges where land tenure is unclear [ev_carbon_sequestration_griscom17_10]. Much of the rest is forest-cover change standing in for carbon, and the India figure is a compiler's citation of earlier work [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_5243_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. Several units found no effect: community management transfers in Madagascar did not halt clearing [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_2], the REDD+ pilot in Nepal had an insignificant effect on forest carbon in community forests (SMD = 0.09) [ev_carbon_sequestration_snilstveit19_1], and a boundary comparison of crown cover under Van Panchayats found no significant difference from neighbouring state forest [ev_landscape_forest_cover_somanathan09_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_somanathan09_2], though a matched whole-sample comparison found pine crown cover higher under council management [ev_landscape_forest_cover_somanathan09_3]. Some GEF sites showed harmful outcomes [ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_3], condition decreased in 32% of community-forest cases in the global analysis [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1], the Mexican result has no counterfactual [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1], and the protected-area pool varies widely across contexts (I-squared of 96 percent) [ev_landscape_forest_cover_malh25_2]. T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Protecting and managing forest keeps carbon stored in standing biomass and lets more build up. GEF sustainable forest management sites sequester more carbon each year than their counterfactual and avoid deforestation [ev_carbon_sequestration_gefieo19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_2], community forest management reduced deforestation in Nepal and increased forest cover in Puebla, Mexico [ev_landscape_forest_cover_iufro20_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1], environmental condition improved after community forest management in 56% of the 524 cases tracking it in a global analysis [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1], and the India compiler states that carbon storage is increased by the plantation, citing an average sequestration rate of 3.5 t ha -1 yr-1 for Van Panchayat forests [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_5243_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. A meta-analysis of payments for environmental services found improved forest cover (SMD = 0.32, 95% CI [0.10, 0.55]) and reduced deforestation against comparison areas [ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_2]; Van Panchayats in India improved the annual forest cover change rate by 0.40 percentage points and municipal management in Bolivia by 0.80 [ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_3]; protected areas retained more forest than comparable unprotected land (Hedges' g of 0.17) [ev_landscape_forest_cover_malh25_2]; and World Bank evaluations report reduced deforestation under participatory forest management [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_2, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_1]. A global model finds existing secondary forests kept standing could remove 20.7 MgC per hectare on average over their best 25-year window, against 18.8 for new regeneration [ev_carbon_sequestration_robinson25_2], and that 8-year-old forest in the Brazilian Amazon would remove 36% more carbon by 2030 than newly growing stands (10.5 versus 7.7 MgC per hectare) [ev_carbon_sequestration_robinson25_3]. T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: What separates the two sides is the forest planted and the place. The losses come mostly from fast-growing exotic plantations on former grassland or cropland, and Filoso's cases are dominated by temperate and Oceania studies that pool restoration with forestry and afforestation [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_1, ev_water_yield_bruij90_3]. Trees use more water than the grass or crops they replace, through rain caught and evaporated from the canopy in wet spells and higher transpiration in dry periods [ev_water_yield_bruij90_3]; in water-limited places large-scale afforestation will worsen water scarcity, a management statement (Zhang et al.) citing an earlier source [ev_water_yield_zhang17_7]. The gains come from exclosures on degraded Ethiopian land compared with cropland [ev_water_regulation_meaza22_1], from model runs of large-scale reforestation in China and Myanmar (Teo et al.) that raised water yield in some regions by 11.4% to 84.9% while others saw small, non-significant falls [ev_water_regulation_teo22_1, ev_water_regulation_teo22_4, ev_water_regulation_teo22_5], from a modelled spruce reforestation in China retold by a review [ev_water_yield_zhang17_6], and from long-term records at two logged temperate US forests where the authors say succession may explain higher summer streamflow [ev_water_yield_jon12_3]. Zhang et al. found no significant link between forest gain and annual runoff in small watersheds, a significant fall only in large ones, and some watersheds where runoff rose [ev_water_yield_zhang17_2, ev_water_yield_zhang17_3, ev_water_yield_zhang17_5]. Natural regrowth after logging also reduces stream yield back toward pre-cutting levels as the forest regrows [ev_water_yield_ham87_3, ev_water_yield_bruij90_4], so regrowth is not always a gain. Much of the evidence is second-hand, modelled or from high-income or unspecified settings; the one measured gain in a low-income country is the Ethiopian exclosure synthesis. For an investment, the type of forest and the dryness of the site decide which side applies.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: The evidence on whether forest restoration gives a catchment more or less water is conflicting, because it splits by the kind of forest. Planted forest (plantations and afforestation) reduces the water leaving a catchment: a global systematic review (Filoso et al.) found that in about 80% of study cases annual water yield fell as forest cover expanded, with baseflow falling in 63% and groundwater in 67% of cases that measured them [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_1, ev_water_regulation_filoso17_2, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_filoso17_1]; a review of trees and water (Ellison et al.) restates the catchment syntheses, including Farley et al. 2005, as showing substantial losses in streamflow after afforestation and reforestation [ev_water_yield_ellison17_1]; and older tropical reviews (Bruijnzeel; Hamilton) report declines after planting pines or eucalypts on degraded grass- or cropland, with low flows usually diminished as well, especially where fast-growing, heavy water-using species are used [ev_water_yield_bruij90_3, ev_water_yield_ham08_6]. Fenced-off natural regrowth in a poorer country points the other way: a meta-analysis from Ethiopia (Meaza et al.) found the baseflow from catchments with exclosures was 1.5 to 4 times greater than from cropland [ev_water_regulation_meaza22_1]. The plantation family's own row, built on Farley et al. 2005, adds that dry-season flows fall proportionally more than annual flows after planting, especially in dry regions.

justification.agreement_note: Planted-forest syntheses and reviews point to less water [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_1, ev_water_yield_ellison17_1, ev_water_yield_bruij90_3, ev_water_yield_ham08_6, ev_water_yield_zhang17_3]; the Ethiopian exclosure synthesis, the reforestation model runs and some watersheds in the global review point to more [ev_water_regulation_meaza22_1, ev_water_regulation_teo22_4, ev_water_yield_zhang17_5].

Planted forest (plantations and afforestation) reduces the water leaving a catchment: a global systematic review (Filoso et al.) found that in about 80% of study cases annual water yield fell as forest cover expanded, with baseflow falling in 63% and groundwater in 67% of cases that measured them [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_1, ev_water_regulation_filoso17_2, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_filoso17_1]; a review of trees and water (Ellison et al.) restates the catchment syntheses, including Farley et al. 2005, as showing substantial losses in streamflow after afforestation and reforestation [ev_water_yield_ellison17_1]; and older tropical reviews (Bruijnzeel; Hamilton) report declines after planting pines or eucalypts on degraded grass- or cropland, with low flows usually diminished as well, especially where fast-growing, heavy water-using species are used [ev_water_yield_bruij90_3, ev_water_yield_ham08_6]. Fenced-off natural regrowth in a poorer country points the other way: a meta-analysis from Ethiopia (Meaza et al.) found the baseflow from catchments with exclosures was 1.5 to 4 times greater than from cropland [ev_water_regulation_meaza22_1]. The plantation family's own row, built on Farley et al. 2005, adds that dry-season flows fall proportionally more than annual flows after planting, especially in dry regions.

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks how much water leaves the catchment, not whether the restored land itself holds more. Neither gain measures restored forest against the land it replaced: the Ethiopian figure compares exclosure catchments with cropland, and the Irrawaddy figure is a mid-century model scenario at landscape scale, not a project observation. The opposing unit describes regrowth of a logged forest, following an example from a logged stream in Queensland, so it is recovery from a recent cut, not restoration of degraded land, and its setting is not clearly lower-income [ev_water_yield_ham87_3]. Read it alongside the unscoped catchment water yield row, which pools the wider measured evidence, before treating restoration in a lower-income catchment as a source of extra downstream water.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In the lower-income contexts in this scope, the gain-side evidence reads the other way from the pooled syntheses: baseflow from Ethiopian catchments with exclosures was 1.5 to 4 times greater than baseflow from cropland [ev_water_regulation_meaza22_1], and a regional land-climate model projects a significant 84.9% increase in water yield for the Irrawaddy under full reforestation potential by mid-century [ev_water_regulation_teo22_4]. One unit runs against them: an essay on Himalayan deforestation states that as forest regrows after cutting, its evapotranspiration rises and stream water yield decreases to approach pre-cutting levels in 6-12 years [ev_water_yield_ham87_3].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: What separates the sides is method and species. The losses are review statements about reforestation and afforestation in general and about planting with pines, eucalypts or other fast-growing, heavy water-using species [ev_water_yield_bruij90_3, ev_water_yield_ham08_6]; the gains are model projections for large regional reforestation scenarios rather than project-scale planting, and the same model shows nonsignificant declines in other regions where heightened evapotranspiration outstrips increases in precipitation [ev_water_regulation_teo22_5]. The lowered water table under new forest is also described as improving drainage, so on waterlogged land it is not purely a loss [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ham08_2]. The pine and eucalypt decline is the review's reading of other studies, and its source table is not readable, so it gives a direction without a size [ev_water_yield_bruij90_3]. Measured paired-catchment losses after afforestation, and the review report that China's Grain-for-Green programme reduced water supply, sit in the plantation family row, which is parked out of the roll-up; check that row before assuming that restoration planting avoids them. This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks how much water leaves the catchment, not whether the restored land itself holds more.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Reviews of reforestation and afforestation find water yield falling. A UNESCO review of moist tropical forest hydrology reads catchment studies, including work in sub-humid Fiji and South Africa, as showing a decline in water yield after forestation of degraded grass- or cropland with pines or eucalypts, caused by higher evaporative loss from tall vegetation in rainy spells and higher transpiration in dry periods [ev_water_yield_bruij90_3]. An FAO synthesis states that the effects of reforestation or afforestation on water yields are usually the reverse of those for forest removal, and that low flows are usually diminished as well, especially where fast-growing, heavy water-using species are employed [ev_water_yield_ham08_5, ev_water_yield_ham08_6]; planting forests on open land where the water table is close to the surface will lower groundwater levels [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ham08_2]. A global review warns that large-scale afforestation in water-limited environments will inevitably exacerbate water scarcity [ev_water_yield_zhang17_7]. The gain side is modelling: under full reforestation potential, water yield increased in 7 of 15 Asia-Pacific regions, significantly in four, by 11.4%, 16.9%, 17.6% and 84.9% [ev_water_regulation_teo22_1, ev_water_regulation_teo22_2, ev_water_regulation_teo22_3, ev_water_regulation_teo22_4], and spruce reforestation of a Heihe River headwater was predicted to increase annual runoff by 8.6% [ev_water_yield_zhang17_6].

The syntheses read scale differently: in the systematic review the decrease shrinks at larger time and space scales [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_3], while the global review found no significant relationship in small watersheds and a significant reduction only in large ones [ev_water_yield_zhang17_2, ev_water_yield_zhang17_3]. T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: What separates the sides is the starting point and the time scale. The two review units are about regrowth on freshly cut land, measured against the cut state; they are harvest-recovery evidence, not a comparison with long-degraded land, and the UNESCO review says more work is needed on how long the return takes [ev_water_yield_bruij90_4, ev_water_yield_ham87_3]. The gains compare exclosures with cropland rather than with unrestored land, so that size is a contrast with farmed land, not a measured restoration gain [ev_water_regulation_meaza22_1], and the US result is a tentative attribution at sites logged long ago, with no intervention described [ev_water_yield_jon12_3]. The positive class runs against the measured syntheses on forest cover expansion in the other catchment water yield rows; whether regeneration behaves differently from planting in this respect is suggested here, not shown. This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks how much water leaves the catchment, not whether the restored land itself holds more.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In Ethiopia, catchments under exclosure pass more baseflow downstream than cropland does: baseflow from catchments with exclosures was 1.5 to 4 times greater than the baseflow from cropland [ev_water_regulation_meaza22_1]. Against these, two reviews describe regrowth after cutting using up the extra streamflow that cutting released: a UNESCO review of moist tropical forest hydrology reports a rather irregular decline in streamflow gain as the new cover establishes, with a return to pre-cut totals under natural regrowth unquantified and perhaps taking more than eight years [ev_water_yield_bruij90_4], and an essay on Himalayan deforestation states that as the forest regrows its evapotranspiration rises and stream water yield decreases to approach pre-cutting levels in 6-12 years [ev_water_yield_ham87_3].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: These are afforestation and production-plantation results, mostly paired catchments where grassland or shrubland was replaced by fast-growing pine or eucalypt. In proportional terms low flow kept falling as plantations aged to about 25 years and then began to recover somewhat [ev_water_yield_farley05_7]; in South Africa the largest decreases come early in fast-growing stands and then diminish [ev_water_yield_ham08_10]. The New Zealand figure is modelled, the Fiji and South Africa cases and the Grain-for-Green result are retold by reviews, and the settings are high-income or upper-middle-income; none is in a low-income country. Two units compare plantations with natural forest rather than with the land planted, so they are held out of the class: native-species plantations aged 25 to 45 years give dry-season streamflow deficits exceeding 50% relative to old-growth forest, a US finding cited second-hand [ev_water_regulation_iufro18_3], and a global meta-analysis (Hua et al.) found 13.4% lower water yield in tree plantations than in reference native forests [ev_water_yield_hua22_1]. Read this row as evidence about plantations, not about restoring natural forest.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Plantations strongly cut the water leaving a catchment, and they cut dry-season flow proportionally more than annual flow. A global synthesis of afforestation (Farley et al.) found annual runoff fell on average by 44% when grasslands and 31% when shrublands were planted [ev_water_yield_farley05_1, ev_water_yield_farley05_2]; low flow fell in the same way but by an even larger proportion, and the authors predict low-flow losses even more severe than annual losses, possibly turning streams in dry regions from flowing all year to flowing only part of the year [ev_water_yield_farley05_3, ev_water_yield_farley05_7]. Losses were far greater at the driest grassland site, 62%, which the authors read as afforestation hitting water yield harder in drier regions [ev_water_yield_farley05_4]; on former grassland, eucalypts cut runoff by 75% and pines by 40% [ev_water_yield_farley05_5, ev_water_yield_farley05_6]. In Fiji, planting Caribbean pine in dry-zone grasslands cut dry-season streamflow by 65 percent [ev_water_yield_ham08_7], and in South Africa, where nearly all plantations are on former native grassland, water reductions are in some cases felt as soon as two years after planting [ev_water_yield_ham08_10]. A national model for New Zealand (Dymond et al.) finds new pine forests reduce water yield by between 30% and 50% [ev_water_yield_dymond12_2], and a review (Seddon et al.) reports that China's Grain-for-Green programme used mainly fast-growing non-native species that have reduced water supply, and that intensively managed plantations may reduce water availability in arid regions [ev_water_yield_seddon21_10, ev_water_yield_seddon21_9].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks how much water leaves the catchment, not whether the protected land itself holds more, and it can coexist with the local gains recorded in the protection water stress row. Every unit compares existing forest with its harvest, clearance or loss, which is why the row sits in the protection family and not in the forest restoration roll-up; none measures the outcome of a protection or community forest management project. Two results run the other way. Where infiltration after forest removal is degraded so far that extra stormflow exceeds the baseflow gain, diminished dry-season flow is the result [ev_water_yield_bruij90_16]; the dry-season gains above come from controlled experiments where infiltration was kept, so this is the case they leave out. Very small summer events also decreased by more than 40% in the first 2 years after canopy removal in the fog-prone Fox Creek basins [ev_water_yield_jon00_1]. Nulls stay named: 12 (of 61) large and 33 (of 252) small watersheds showed no significant change in annual runoff despite forest cover loss [ev_water_yield_zhang17_4], and basins of 7 to 727 km2 on Hainan and the 14500 km2 Pasak basin in northern Thailand showed no systematic streamflow change despite extensive forest loss; the review expects detectable change mainly where forest is replaced by annual cropping rather than left to regenerate [ev_water_yield_bruij90_9]. The groundwater statement also cuts both ways: removal can move soil salts into the rooting zone [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ham08_1].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Forests use more water than the land cover that replaces them, so standing forest passes less water downstream. As both natural and human-established forests use more water than most replacement land cover, even partial forest removal increases downstream water yields [ev_water_yield_ham08_1], and replacing forest cover with other land uses almost always results in increased runoff and streamflow [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_2]; a UNESCO review of moist tropical forest hydrology calls it beyond doubt that both natural and mature man-made forests use more water than most agricultural crops or grassland [ev_water_yield_bruij90_1]. A worldwide review of paired catchments found that forest cutting consistently gave more total water yield, in proportion to cutting intensity, because tall forests evaporate and transpire more; Hamilton retells it in both his earlier essay and his later FAO synthesis, so it counts once [ev_water_yield_ham87_1, ev_water_yield_ham08_4]. Reported first-year increases after forest clearance range between 110 and 825 mm, depending on local rainfall, and converting lowland rain forest to well managed grassland or annual cropping may produce permanent increases of 200 - 300 mm a year [ev_water_yield_bruij90_1, ev_water_yield_bruij90_2]. The extra flow arrives through the year: in most tropical small-basin experiments the bulk of the increase came in the dry season or baseflow [ev_water_yield_bruij90_15], the FAO synthesis puts the greatest percentage increase in the dry season, citing that review among others [ev_water_yield_ham08_2], and Hamilton's essay reports increased flows throughout the year, including the dry season [ev_water_yield_ham87_2]. Daily late-summer flows rose by up to 300% after experimental harvest, though most daily changes were 50% or less [ev_water_yield_jon12_2]. Global syntheses agree: more forest cover loss tends to increase annual runoff in both large and small watersheds [ev_water_yield_zhang17_1], an increase in forest coverage reduces the share of rainfall leaving as runoff [ev_water_yield_zhou15_1], and changes to forests in water-limited watersheds can lead to larger water-yield responses [ev_water_yield_zhou15_2]. Harvesting or removing forest also raises groundwater levels [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ham08_1].

The model unit is a landscape-scale scenario, and the drop in extremely dry months was concentrated in regions where total annual precipitation also increased [ev_drought_hazard_teo22_1]. No unit says how the effect holds in severe or extreme drought, and the Indian benefit arrives off-site, as dry-season flow from a restored upper catchment.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: WOCAT compilers report that assisted natural regeneration in Niger helps to reduce the impacts of long droughts during the rainy season by improving vegetation cover and increasing the production of woody vegetation [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_2325_2017_drought_impacts], and that broadleaf plantations with assisted regeneration in India decreased drought impacts through improved surface and subsurface hydrological functioning in the upper watershed, which increased springshed groundwater stores and enhanced stream and spring flows in the dry season [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_5243_2019_drought_impacts]. A regional climate model found reforestation broadly reduced the probability of extremely dry months, with a decline in extreme dry events in 9 of 15 regions [ev_drought_hazard_teo22_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: What separates the benefit from the nulls is scale and storm size. The gains are local, modelled or small-storm results; the nulls are about large basins and floods on the plains. The FAO synthesis finds no evidence that reforesting watersheds reduces or prevents floods except at the very local scale of a few hundred hectares [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_5, ev_flood_hazard_ham08_6]. A Himalayan analysis concludes that reforestation will not likely have significant beneficial impact on local flooding, and certainly not on the hydrological character of the Ganges and Brahmaputra mainstreams [ev_flood_hazard_ives87_1], and a conference overview warns that reforestation in the mountains conceived as a palliative for the problems of the plains is likely to reap only disappointment [ev_flood_hazard_ivesmt87_1], and both come from the same lead author, so they count as a single line of argument. An FAO–CIFOR review concludes that massive programmes of forestation proclaimed as the answer to preventing floods simply will not do the job, although reforestation may have many other benefits [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_3], and a published comment argues that reforestation does not necessarily reduce flooding, for example if soil properties do not recover, river bed morphology does not change, and settlements, roads and drains remain unaltered [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_5]. A review of coastal tree belts adds a coastal null: the science on short-period wave damping should not be taken to show that vegetation can reduce the effects of storm surges [ev_flood_hazard_feagin10_1]; this is an expert argument about coastal plantings, not a measurement. These are expert positions and reviews rather than new measurements. The co-benefit listing is second-hand and states no size, place or scale [ev_flood_hazard_griscom17_3]. The UNESCO review's statement is local only, its supporting table cannot be read so no size is available, and the planting half of the sentence pools reforesting with terracing and contouring, so it cannot be credited to trees alone [ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_6, ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_7]. The flood-cover review adds that afforestation yields only gradual reductions, smaller than the rises in peak flow that follow deforestation and shaped by forest maturity, with peak flow in small catchments falling by up to 14% on limited data [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_2, ev_flood_hazard_herath25_4]; its pooled peak-flow points come from modelled scenarios in mostly temperate catchments, so it is a synthesis of other studies' models rather than new measurement. The modelled benefit itself shrinks as rain continues, from 29% for the shortest rain duration to 17% for the longest [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_3], and all catchment models are scenarios of large forest-cover gains in temperate high-income basins; the largest figure, a 42.3% peak reduction from converting all arable land to forest, is a secondary citation with no basin named [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_4]. The Oregon recovery comes from a clear-cut harvest study, measured against the freshly cut state rather than against unrestored land, and the paper does not say whether the regrowth was planted or natural [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5]. The low- and lower-middle-income evidence is a compiler rating and expert positions, not measured flows or flood damage. The forest-water review pools restoration with forestry and afforestation and reports vote counts rather than magnitudes [ev_flood_hazard_filoso17_1].
