T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The class is moderate because the evidence agrees only in part. The harvest studies, the forest-loss analyses and the two classic reviews describe what existing forest does; they enter through the existing-forest comparator (the flood-cover review's deforestation reading among them [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_3]), which routes them to this protection family and keeps them out of the restoration families, so none of them is a restoration or protection-programme result. The Malaysian study also carries the harm finding in this row: where the forest converted was wetland (peat-swamp) forest, deforestation reduced flooding, a large effect (semi-elasticity = 38.0%), which the authors link to drainage installed at conversion lowering the water level; so keeping forest is not a flood defence in every forest type [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_3]. The same study found no significant effect of deforestation on the number of floods per month, which the authors put down to a problem in defining that variable rather than to forest having no effect [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_5]. Its inland-forest figures are semi-elasticities per 1% of basin area converted, not whole-catchment contrasts, and the oil palm and rubber results are from a single period of conversion, not restoration [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_1, ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_2], while the urban figure was not estimated very precisely (P = 0.094) [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_4]. The Oregon large-basin increase is bundled with forest road construction and is stated as an upper bound, as much as [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_1]. The service fades with storm size and basin size. Complete clear-cutting without roads produced significant increases in fall and winter events but not for large events as a group [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_4], and at Andrews 10 large events did not change after 100% clear-cutting [ev_flood_hazard_jon00_2]. In the same study other types of winter events did not change, so only rain-on-snow peaks rose in winter [ev_water_regulation_jon00_7], and in the fog-prone basins changes in cloud water interception apparently offset changes in evapotranspiration in two partially cut basins [ev_water_regulation_jon00_5]. The fall increases came in small events (0.22- or 0.28-year return periods), not in large events [ev_water_regulation_jon00_1]. For the rarer prolonged or high-intensity storms, once the soil layer becomes saturated water will run off even where there is full, undisturbed forest cover [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_4]; Hamilton's earlier essay makes the same point, that for major storms the effect of forest on or forest off is dwarfed by the rainfall itself, since soil can only store so much water [ev_flood_hazard_ham87_6]. He judges that the June 1985 floods that killed 237 persons in six Indian states were caused by too much rain in too short a time, with some areas receiving 414 mm in 24 hours on already saturated soils, and that even a fully forested basin would have flooded; this is his judgement, not data [ev_flood_hazard_ham87_12]. Forest soils reduce runoff only in small-scale rainfall events, which are not responsible for severe downstream flooding, and forests cannot stop catastrophic large-scale floods caused by severe meteorological events [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_1, ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_2]; and small to medium peak flows are affected most while the largest events do not change noticeably [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_3]. At basin scale the link is not shown. A worldwide review of watershed research found no cause and effect between forest cutting in the headwaters and floods in the lower basin; Hamilton cites it both in his earlier essay, where he adds that there are no valid reasons to suggest forests can prevent major floods on the large rivers of the subcontinent, and in his later FAO synthesis, so this is a single finding [ev_flood_hazard_ham87_4, ev_flood_hazard_ham08_2]. Long records from meso-scale basins of up to 14500 km2 in Taiwan and northern Thailand that had lost much forest showed no systematic trend in flood magnitude, climate dominating, although the review notes that much of that forest loss was probably followed by regeneration rather than cropping [ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_8]. A Himalayan analysis contends that on the Himalayan scale human influences, so far, are insignificant [ev_flood_hazard_ives87_2]. The cross-country analysis itself found little evidence that further forest loss changed flood deaths or damage [ev_flood_hazard_bradshaw07_3, ev_flood_hazard_bradshaw07_4], and a reanalysis found the correlation between forest cover or cover loss and flood frequency appears absent [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_1]. Every unit compares forest with cleared or less-forested land, so the row shows what losing forest costs rather than the outcome of a protection or community forestry programme. Benefits fall downstream, off-site for farmers.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: This row describes the flood regulation that standing forest provides and that protection keeps; nearly all of it is evidence about existing forest, read through what happens when it is cut. In paired experimental basins in Oregon, a high-income setting, discharges in small basins increased by 50% in the first 5 years after clear-cutting and were 25 to 40% higher than pretreatment up to 25 years later, and forest harvesting with roads has increased peak discharges by as much as 50% in small basins and 100% in large basins over the past 50 years [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_2, ev_flood_hazard_jg96_3, ev_flood_hazard_jg96_1]. A later analysis of the same basins found large events increased by 25% at Andrews 1, 16% at Andrews 6 and 26% at Coyote 3 after 100% clear-cutting [ev_flood_hazard_jon00_1]. The same Oregon study separates the event types. Forest canopy removal accounted for significant increases (31–116%) in peak discharges during the first postharvest decade in 8 of 10 treated basins, but the affected events were small and fell in the fall (September–November), when soils are in moisture deficit, rather than in spring [ev_water_regulation_jon00_1]. Changes in snowpack dynamics accounted for significant increases (25–31%) in winter rain-on-snow events in four of five basins at the H. J. Andrews Experimental Forest [ev_water_regulation_jon00_6]. Two reviews of forest hydrology state the general rule: after forest cutting or conversion there is usually, in response to each storm, an increase in peak flow, storm-flow volume and storm-flow duration [ev_flood_hazard_ham87_5], and a certain increase in stormflow volume and peakflow cannot be avoided after forest conversion, with the relative increase largest for small events (which may be doubled) and smallest for large ones (perhaps in the order of 10 per cent or less) [ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_5]. An FAO synthesis states that partial or complete removal of tree cover accelerates water discharge, increasing the risk of flood during the rainy season, and that for frequent rainfall events of short duration or low intensity forested soils may reduce or prevent flash floods locally [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_1, ev_flood_hazard_ham08_3]. At the local scale forests and forest soils reduce runoff through enhanced infiltration and storage, and peak flows rise after forest removal in small experimental catchments [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_1, ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_2]. A country-level analysis of developing countries predicted that a further hypothetical 10% loss of natural forest cover would raise flood frequency by 3.5% to 28.1% and flood duration by 3.8% to 7.9% [ev_flood_hazard_bradshaw07_1, ev_flood_hazard_bradshaw07_2]; in Peninsular Malaysia, a river-basin panel study by Tan-Soo and colleagues found that converting 1% of a basin from inland forest to oil palm increased the number of days flooded by 26.8%, and to rubber by 26.5%, with conversion to urban use also having a large effect (semi-elasticity = 35.9%) [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_1, ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_2, ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_4]; a systematic review of forest cover and catchment flooding finds that deforestation consistently increases peak flows [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_3]; and in Swiss valleys with more than 30% forest, snowmelt was more gradual and flooding risk lower [ev_flood_hazard_iufro18_2].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The slight class is set by the measured Malawi survey: the food consumption gain from co-management is small, and it pulls the row down from the strong Niger and India compiler ratings, which are judgements rather than measured changes in hunger or food consumption [ev_food_security_kimwanga26_3, ev_food_security_wocat_2325_2017_food_security_selfsufficiency, ev_food_security_wocat_5243_2019_food_security_selfsufficiency]. Food security does not always rise. The Cabo Verde afforestation compiler rates food self-sufficiency unchanged because the practice reduces the options of land use [ev_food_security_wocat_1523_2011_food_security_selfsufficiency], and under Mexico's payments for environmental services, as cited in a systematic review, households in common-property areas showed a statistically insignificant food-index effect of 0.09 SMD [ev_food_security_snilstveit19_1]; that unit concerns a payment scheme rather than a restoration practice. The Malawi result is a cross-sectional comparison of committee members with non-members, not a before-and-after measure. Studies of what existing forest and protected areas provide for diets are kept to the protection and community forest management row and do not count here.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Restoration and co-managed forest improve food security mainly through more fodder, water and forest foods around regenerating sites, though the measured gain is small. In Niger the compiler for assisted natural regeneration on agro-pastoral, sylvo-pastoral and pastoral land reports that it contributes to food security and food self-sufficiency in the southern regions, estimates the impact at 20% at least, and notes that in the northern pastoral zone it reduces forage deficits so that livestock keepers are not forced to sell their animals in the lean season [ev_food_security_wocat_2325_2017_food_security_selfsufficiency]. In India the compiler for broadleaf plantations, assisted tree regeneration and fodder nurseries reports better village self-sufficiency because animal productivity rose with more and better fodder and water availability increased [ev_food_security_wocat_5243_2019_food_security_selfsufficiency]. T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Standing forest keeps the land surface cooler than cleared land, and protection keeps that cooling; the benefit is small and its size for heat stress is not stated. Satellite and flux tower data show tropical forest surfaces significantly cooler than nearby cleared areas, by 0.2–2.4 degrees C a year (mean 0.96) [ev_microclimate_buffering_lawrence22_1], and temperate forest cover cools by 0.02–1.0 degrees C (mean 0.4) [ev_microclimate_buffering_lawrence22_2]. A worldwide satellite comparison finds tropical forests 2.41 degrees C cooler than nearby open land over the day, and mid-latitude forests 0.27 degrees C cooler in the northern hemisphere and 0.97 in the southern [ev_microclimate_buffering_li15_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_li15_2]. T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: No source measures a change in poverty itself: the evidence is rates of return, profitability and income shares. The Vietnamese gains depended on subsidised loans [ev_household_income_ieg18_1], the Costa Rican income comes from the payments rather than the timber, and the 63.9% figure is a perception score [ev_household_income_padilla17_1, ev_household_income_padilla17_3]. The global profitability figure is a model and says nothing about who benefits [ev_economic_return_busch24_1]. The Indian figure is second-hand from the project's own reporting, and the review notes that cutting trees for fuelwood works against the plantations' protective purpose [ev_household_income_feagin10_3]. Only the Indian case is from a lower-middle-income country; Costa Rica and Vietnam are upper-middle-income.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Timber and protective plantations moderately raise household income in this evidence. In Vietnam a World Bank evaluation found the economic rate of return for smallholder plantations was 13.2% at completion, against 17.0% expected at appraisal [ev_economic_return_ieg18_1], and the financial gains for participating smallholders were substantial, mainly because low-interest loans from the project reduced up-front costs to near zero [ev_household_income_ieg18_1]. In Costa Rica, payments for environmental services on reforested land made up 18.66% of participants' income during the contract [ev_household_income_padilla17_1], other Latin American studies cited there found payments reach around 10% of family income [ev_household_income_padilla17_2], and participants' perceived economic benefit scored 63.9% of the maximum, mainly from covering planting and upkeep costs, family employment and secure land title [ev_household_income_padilla17_3]. A global cost analysis finds plantations would be profitable even without carbon payments across 28.3% of the area where they are feasible [ev_economic_return_busch24_1]. In Andhra Pradesh, India, a review reports, from the project's own material, returns from Casuarina coastal plantations of Rs. 25,000/ha (USD 600/ha) after 4 years, shared half with the community and half reinvested in more planting, plus access to fuelwood and small timber [ev_household_income_feagin10_3].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The pool is divided. The global community-forest review that reports income gains in 68% of cases also records 26% with no change and 6.3% with decreases [ev_household_income_hajjar21_1]. In south-west Madagascar community management contracts were not profitable and did not raise incomes [ev_economic_return_ramamo12_1, ev_household_income_ramamo12_1]; the GEF forest-management portfolio has a benefit-cost ratio of 0.69 [ev_economic_return_gefieo19_1]; REDD+ contributions in Nepal were nominal, from 3.2% of the poorest households' income to 0.3% for the less poor, local studies found no effect of REDD+ on material well-being, and an analysis in Indonesia found potentially harmful effects [ev_household_income_iufro20_4, ev_household_income_iufro20_5, ev_household_income_iufro20_6]; payment programmes have a small beneficial or neutral effect on poverty [ev_rural_poverty_iufro20_3]; and Mexico's payment scheme was less cost-effective than a protected area [ev_economic_return_snilstveit19_2]. Benefits skew to the better-off: in Nepal poor and low-caste households receive much less while bearing more costs [ev_household_income_iufro20_3]; near Uganda's District Forestry Service forests forest income rose by an insignificant 2 per cent and lowest-quartile households lost 6 per cent and 10 per cent [ev_household_income_samii14_4, ev_household_income_samii14_5]; at Bach Ma benefits were shared unevenly and products over-harvested [ev_household_income_ieg18_3]. After rainfall shocks, Malawi participants held fewer durable assets than non-participants around Mua-Livulezi, a 2.846 unit decrease, and Vwaza Marsh, a 1.677 decrease [ev_farm_asset_index_kimwanga26_11, ev_farm_asset_index_kimwanga26_14], participation did not stop shocks eroding non-forestry income by 36% [ev_household_income_kimwanga26_5], and the study compares members with non-members at a single point in time rather than before and after. Just two out of 37 closed World Bank protected-area projects achieved their livelihood aims, and benefit-sharing around Vietnam's special-use forests, averaging US$1,053 per community, was too small to have any discernible impact [ev_household_income_ieg13_1, ev_household_income_ieg18_2]. A large household survey adds that forests are a weak safety net: only 7.8% of households turned to forests as their main response to an income shock, 10.4% to any wild resource [ev_household_income_wunder14_1]; that unit is carried but does not set the class. The protected-area studies measure what living near standing forest provides, not a restoration outcome; the Colombian benefit of $411–1,236 per hectare a year is a carbon valuation, not cash income [ev_economic_return_wri17_3]; and many figures are review citations or World Bank estimates without a comparison group.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Protection and community forest management moderately reduce poverty through forest income and employment. Community forest management in Nepal reduced both poverty and deforestation across 18,000 community forests [ev_rural_poverty_iufro20_2], 68% of community forestry cases reporting livelihood outcomes showed income increases [ev_household_income_hajjar21_1], and community forestry in Madagascar had a small but beneficial impact on living standards [ev_household_income_iufro20_2]. Protected areas contributed to poverty alleviation in Costa Rica and Thailand [ev_rural_poverty_puri16_1, ev_rural_poverty_iufro20_1]; a meta-analysis of counterfactual studies finds small gains in local monetary outcomes (g = 0.028) and poverty outcomes (g = 0.117) [ev_household_income_kandel22_1, ev_rural_poverty_kandel22_1]; households in the Chitwan National Park buffer zone of Nepal have 19 percent higher per capita income [ev_household_income_kandel22_2]; and living within 10 km of protected areas with tourism lowers the likelihood of poverty by 16.1%, with poverty 8.8% lower near multiple-use protected areas [ev_rural_poverty_naidoo19_1, ev_rural_poverty_naidoo19_2]. Co-management raised regular forest income in Malawi by 26 per cent and by 66% for low-income households, consumption in Ethiopian participatory forest management communities by 35 per cent, and forest income near Uganda's National Forestry Authority forests by 16 per cent [ev_household_income_samii14_1, ev_household_income_samii14_2, ev_household_income_samii14_3, ev_household_income_samii14_6]. Around Malawi's forest reserves, taking part in co-management is associated with 17.48% more forestry income and 21.07% more non-forest income [ev_household_income_kimwanga26_1, ev_household_income_kimwanga26_2], 26.6% higher per capita income among the poorest households without rainfall shocks [ev_household_income_kimwanga26_6], and, after shocks, 57% higher forestry income [ev_household_income_kimwanga26_4] and a 31.4% per capita income gain for moderately poor households [ev_household_income_kimwanga26_7]; participants also owned more durable goods [ev_farm_asset_index_kimwanga26_9, ev_farm_asset_index_kimwanga26_10, ev_farm_asset_index_kimwanga26_8, ev_farm_asset_index_kimwanga26_12, ev_farm_asset_index_kimwanga26_13]. World Bank support raised participating household incomes in Albania by an estimated 30 percent and in Honduras by 62 percent, and in Andhra Pradesh poorer households compensated for lost land access gained 40 percent [ev_household_income_ieg13_2, ev_household_income_ieg13_3, ev_household_income_ieg13_4]. Community forestry in Mexico's Sierra Norte de Puebla provides year-round wage labour and a profit share of 10 to 20 thousand pesos per member [ev_household_income_ceballos21_1], households near GEF sites in Uganda show income gains [ev_household_income_gefieo19_1], groups selling environmental services in Bolivia improved economically [ev_household_income_robertson05_1], and non-timber income rose after benefit-sharing at Bach Ma, Vietnam [ev_household_income_ieg18_3].

justification.mechanism: Protection and community forest management moderately reduce poverty through forest income and employment. Community forest management in Nepal reduced both poverty and deforestation across 18,000 community forests [ev_rural_poverty_iufro20_2], 68% of community forestry cases reporting livelihood outcomes showed income increases [ev_household_income_hajjar21_1], and community forestry in Madagascar had a small but beneficial impact on living standards [ev_household_income_iufro20_2]. Protected areas contributed to poverty alleviation in Costa Rica and Thailand [ev_rural_poverty_puri16_1, ev_rural_poverty_iufro20_1]; a meta-analysis of counterfactual studies finds small gains in local monetary outcomes (g = 0.028) and poverty outcomes (g = 0.117) [ev_household_income_kandel22_1, ev_rural_poverty_kandel22_1]; households in the Chitwan National Park buffer zone of Nepal have 19 percent higher per capita income [ev_household_income_kandel22_2]; and living within 10 km of protected areas with tourism lowers the likelihood of poverty by 16.1%, with poverty 8.8% lower near multiple-use protected areas [ev_rural_poverty_naidoo19_1, ev_rural_poverty_naidoo19_2]. Co-management raised regular forest income in Malawi by 26 per cent and by 66% for low-income households, consumption in Ethiopian participatory forest management communities by 35 per cent, and forest income near Uganda's National Forestry Authority forests by 16 per cent [ev_household_income_samii14_1, ev_household_income_samii14_2, ev_household_income_samii14_3, ev_household_income_samii14_6]. Around Malawi's forest reserves, taking part in co-management is associated with 17.48% more forestry income and 21.07% more non-forest income [ev_household_income_kimwanga26_1, ev_household_income_kimwanga26_2], 26.6% higher per capita income among the poorest households without rainfall shocks [ev_household_income_kimwanga26_6], and, after shocks, 57% higher forestry income [ev_household_income_kimwanga26_4] and a 31.4% per capita income gain for moderately poor households [ev_household_income_kimwanga26_7]; participants also owned more durable goods [ev_farm_asset_index_kimwanga26_9, ev_farm_asset_index_kimwanga26_10, ev_farm_asset_index_kimwanga26_8, ev_farm_asset_index_kimwanga26_12, ev_farm_asset_index_kimwanga26_13]. World Bank support raised participating household incomes in Albania by an estimated 30 percent and in Honduras by 62 percent, and in Andhra Pradesh poorer households compensated for lost land access gained 40 percent [ev_household_income_ieg13_2, ev_household_income_ieg13_3, ev_household_income_ieg13_4]. Community forestry in Mexico's Sierra Norte de Puebla provides year-round wage labour and a profit share of 10 to 20 thousand pesos per member [ev_household_income_ceballos21_1], households near GEF sites in Uganda show income gains [ev_household_income_gefieo19_1], groups selling environmental services in Bolivia improved economically [ev_household_income_robertson05_1], and non-timber income rose after benefit-sharing at Bach Ma, Vietnam [ev_household_income_ieg18_3].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The benefit is largely off-site for farmers: much of it is reduced runoff and sediment reaching downstream land and channels rather than better soil on their own plots [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_5243_2019_downstream_siltation]. Scale and time limit the downstream effect. The UNESCO review warns that, because of storage effects, it may take several decades for basins larger than several hundred square kilometres before stream sediment loads downstream become noticeably smaller [ev_sediment_retention_bruij90_14]. Nulls and dissent stay named. In China the soil conservation measures, including vegetation and engineering, contributed 12.1–13.9% sediment reduction in the Three-Gorge Reservoir Area, so the vegetation share should be less than 10% in most instances [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_2]; decreased Pearl River sediment loads had little to do with soil conservation measures [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_3]; and on the Loess Plateau an inversely decreasing trend of erosion reduction with vegetation cover was attributed to the immaturity of the planted species [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_4]. A Himalayan position paper judges that reforestation will not likely have significant beneficial impact on soil loss [ev_erosion_hazard_ives87_1], young second-growth timber falls far short of providing the root support of its older predecessors [ev_erosion_hazard_bishop64_5], abandoned land in previously terraced landscapes can be particularly prone to gully erosion and landslides [ev_erosion_hazard_iufro18_4], and the REDD+ pilot in Nepal had an insignificant effect on signs of soil erosion in community forests (SMD = −0.15, 95% CI [−0.31, 0.02]) [ev_erosion_hazard_snilstveit19_1]. The largest measured reductions are bundles: the Pakistan results combine planting with grazing control and, in the watershed study, erosion control structures, and the Taiwan programme combines reforestation with soil conservation on cultivated land, fire control and check dams, so none can be credited to tree cover alone [ev_erosion_hazard_hanif90_1, ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2]. The Tigray results are bundles of afforestation and area closures with trenches, percolation pits and check-dams, from showcase sites, and the dam figure is an upper bound carried from an earlier report [ev_erosion_hazard_woldearegay17_3, ev_erosion_hazard_woldearegay17_1]. The UNESCO sediment statement also offers tree planting as one option among soil conservation measures, not as a measured tree effect [ev_sediment_retention_bruij90_13]. The erosion-zone meta-analysis reports its forest-only effect sizes only in a figure, so it sets the direction but not a size [ev_erosion_hazard_yang23_1]. The runoff results measure a component of erosion risk rather than soil loss [ev_runoff_reduction_meaza22_1]. Studies of what existing forest does, including logging and harvest landslide studies, sit in the protection family row and do not count here, and plantation results are kept in their own family row, out of this roll-up.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Tree cover reduces erosion by protecting the soil surface, slowing runoff and holding slopes, and the sub-practice rows agree on that direction. A UNESCO review of moist tropical forest hydrology locates the surface protection in the litter and herb layer: erosion is minimal where the soil surface is protected by a well-developed litter and herb layer, rises only slightly when the understorey is removed, and rises dramatically when the litter layer is destroyed or removed [ev_erosion_hazard_bruij90_10]. The same review states that tree planting, like soil conservation measures, may well reduce the sediment from surface erosion and shallow land slips entering the drainage system [ev_sediment_retention_bruij90_13]. In the passive regeneration evidence, an Ethiopian meta-analysis finds areas closed for grazing and agriculture had runoff coefficients of 4% against 19% on control sites [ev_runoff_reduction_meaza22_1], the Tanzanian enclosure compiler rates surface runoff as decreased as a result of vegetation cover and downstream siltation as decreased through improved vegetation cover and controlled erosion [ev_runoff_reduction_wocat_1607_2014_surface_runoff, ev_sediment_retention_wocat_1607_2014_downstream_siltation], and the higher probability of landslides after timber removal diminishes substantially 15–25 yr after harvesting as replacement trees mature [ev_erosion_hazard_sidle06_2]. The planting evidence carries the measured magnitudes: in Pakistan a watershed restoration reduced storm runoff and sediment yields by 55 and 78% [ev_runoff_reduction_hanif90_1, ev_erosion_hazard_hanif90_1], Chir pine planting with elimination of grazing at Balakot reduced surface runoff by 57% and sediment production by 69% against adjacent grazed land [ev_runoff_reduction_hanif90_2], tree planting on degraded Ethiopian catchments cut annual runoff from 242 to 148 mm/year [ev_runoff_reduction_meaza22_2], and vegetation restoration in China could reduce soil erosion by at least 80% once cover exceeds 60% [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_1]. A Slovak catchment model shows reforestation decreasing surface runoff [ev_runoff_reduction_bahremand06_1]. A meta-analysis of vegetation restoration in erosion zones finds that both forestland and grassland restoration of cropland or bare land were effective methods for controlling erosion, cutting sediment and runoff, with canopies, root systems and the organic surface layer not differing in their impact [ev_erosion_hazard_yang23_1, ev_runoff_reduction_yang23_2]. In Tigray, Ethiopia, upstream treatment with deep trenches, percolation pits and afforestation reduced siltation of May Demu dam by up to 60%, a figure the chapter takes from Woldearegay's earlier 2011 report, and in the Abreha Weatsbeha watershed the authors observed significant improvements in reducing soil erosion after afforestation, area closures and water-harvesting works [ev_erosion_hazard_woldearegay17_3, ev_erosion_hazard_woldearegay17_1]. FAO syntheses call forest restoration one of the best ways of reducing sedimentation in degraded cleared land, list reducing soil loss among the very good reasons for rehabilitating watersheds, and cite Taiwan, where a rehabilitation programme reduced reservoir sedimentation by 55 percent of the base rate [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_1, ev_erosion_hazard_ham08_1, ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2]. An FAO review of forests and landslides in Asia asserts that tree planting on susceptible slopes can reduce risk [ev_erosion_hazard_forbes11_1], and land abandonment with an increase in forest and grassland led to less soil erosion in one cited case [ev_erosion_hazard_iufro18_5]. At community-managed sites the India compiler credits trees and other vegetation with mitigating displacement of soil from upstream areas to the lowlands and with slowing sediment and runoff [ev_erosion_hazard_wocat_5243_2019_soil_loss, ev_sediment_retention_wocat_5243_2019_downstream_siltation], and a World Bank evaluation lists reduced soil erosion among the outcomes participatory forest management projects reported where they were monitored [ev_erosion_hazard_ieg13_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The evidence is thin. The Hornad result is a model scenario and covers runoff, a component of erosion risk, not soil loss [ev_runoff_reduction_bahremand06_1]. The Taiwan reduction is credited to a bundled programme of reforestation with soil conservation on cultivated land, fire control and check dams, cited in an FAO review, so it cannot be credited to tree cover alone [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2]. The US root-support point is cited second-hand from an earlier study, and it is about how slowly regrowth restores protection, not a measured erosion change [ev_erosion_hazard_bishop64_5]. Missing here: a measured soil-loss or sediment comparison between restored and unrestored land in a high-income setting. The row applies only to high-income contexts and does not transfer directly to low-income settings. Plantation results are kept in their own family rows, out of forest restoration.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In high-income settings the row rests on three units, and none is a measured plot-level soil-loss study. A catchment model of Slovakia's Hornad watershed finds that reforestation results in decreasing surface runoff and flood volume, though it raises interflow, baseflow and evapotranspiration [ev_runoff_reduction_bahremand06_1]. In Taiwan, reservoir sedimentation from 1965 until 1985 was reduced by 55 percent of the base rate set from 1957 data, attributed to a rehabilitation programme [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2]. A US report cites the conclusion that young second-growth timber falls far short of providing the root support that its much larger and older predecessors did, so slope protection returns only as the forest matures [ev_erosion_hazard_bishop64_5].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The class is capped at moderate because few of the units that point the same way say how big the effect is, and the Chinese review itself bounds the gain. In the Three-Gorge Reservoir Area, soil conservation measures including vegetation and engineering contributed 12.1–13.9% sediment reduction, so the contribution from vegetation restoration should be less than 10% in most instances [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_2]. On the Pearl River the decreased sediment loads had little to do with soil conservation measures over 20 years [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_3], and in 12 small Loess Plateau watersheds the erosion-reduction benefit fell as cover rose, attributed to the immaturity of the planted species [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_4]. The benefit therefore depends on cover reaching a high threshold and on plantings maturing, and young or sparse restoration may do little. The erosion-zone meta-analysis reports its forest-only effect sizes only in a figure, so it sets the direction but not a size [ev_erosion_hazard_yang23_1]. The Philippine and landslide results are cited secondary findings, the landslide one tracking regrowth after timber harvest without separating replanting from natural regeneration [ev_erosion_hazard_sidle06_2]. Benefits fall largely off-site for farmers, as less sediment downstream.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In upper-middle-income settings the evidence is a critical review of China's vegetation restoration programmes, which plant trees, shrubs and grass on hillslopes, a review of erosion in steep tropical terrain, and a meta-analysis of vegetation restoration in erosion zones. Restored cover protects soil once it is dense enough: once vegetation cover exceeds 60%, the restoration strategy could reduce soil erosion by at least 80%, while below that threshold the erosion-reduction benefit rises sharply with cover [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_1]. In Leyte, Philippines, recovering forest on former slash-and-burn land generated the smallest share of overland flow among the land uses compared, behind fallow pasture, hedgerow systems and mulched cornfields [ev_runoff_reduction_sidle06_1], and on harvested slopes the higher probability of landslides diminishes substantially 15–25 yr after harvesting as replacement trees mature [ev_erosion_hazard_sidle06_2]. A meta-analysis of vegetation restoration in erosion zones finds that both forestland and grassland restoration of cropland or bare land were effective methods for controlling erosion, cutting sediment and runoff, with canopies, root systems and the organic surface layer not differing in their impact [ev_erosion_hazard_yang23_1, ev_runoff_reduction_yang23_2].

In Leyte, Philippines, recovering forest on former slash-and-burn land generated the smallest share of overland flow among the land uses compared, behind fallow pasture, hedgerow systems and mulched cornfields [ev_runoff_reduction_sidle06_1], and on harvested slopes the higher probability of landslides diminishes substantially 15–25 yr after harvesting as replacement trees mature [ev_erosion_hazard_sidle06_2]. A meta-analysis of vegetation restoration in erosion zones finds that both forestland and grassland restoration of cropland or bare land were effective methods for controlling erosion, cutting sediment and runoff, with canopies, root systems and the organic surface layer not differing in their impact [ev_erosion_hazard_yang23_1, ev_runoff_reduction_yang23_2].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The Pakistan results are bundles - planting with grazing control and, in the watershed study, check dams and spillways - so the reduction cannot be credited to planting alone [ev_erosion_hazard_hanif90_1, ev_runoff_reduction_hanif90_2]. The downstream effect is slow in large basins: the UNESCO review warns that, because of storage effects, it may take several decades for basins larger than several hundred square kilometres before stream sediment loads downstream become noticeably smaller, and its sediment statement is a review judgement, not a measurement [ev_sediment_retention_bruij90_14, ev_sediment_retention_bruij90_13]. The Chinese evidence carries its own nulls: in the Three-Gorge Reservoir Area vegetation and engineering measures together contributed 12.1–13.9% sediment reduction, so the vegetation share should be less than 10% in most instances [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_2]; decreased Pearl River sediment loads had little to do with soil conservation measures in the past 20 years [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_3]; and a four-year measurement in 12 small Loess Plateau watersheds found an inversely decreasing trend of erosion reduction with vegetation cover and attributed it to the immaturity of the planted species [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_4]. A Himalayan position paper judges that reforestation will not likely have significant beneficial impact on soil loss [ev_erosion_hazard_ives87_1]. The Slovak result is modelled, runoff and sediment enter as components of erosion risk, and the Ethiopian runoff measurements are the only evidence from a low-income setting [ev_runoff_reduction_meaza22_2]. Plantation results, including the warnings that dense planted monocultures without understorey or litter can raise erosion, sit in the plantation family's erosion row, out of this row and the roll-up.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Planted cover reduces runoff and soil loss on the restored slope and catchment, so the benefit reaches farmers off-site, through less sediment and runoff arriving downslope and downstream rather than on the plot itself. In Pakistan a watershed restoration of tree planting, control of grazing and erosion control structures reduced storm runoff and sediment yields by 55 and 78% [ev_runoff_reduction_hanif90_1, ev_erosion_hazard_hanif90_1], and Chir pine planting with elimination of grazing at Balakot reduced surface runoff by 57% and sediment production by 69% against adjacent grazed areas with natural vegetation [ev_runoff_reduction_hanif90_2]. A review of Chinese vegetation restoration finds it could reduce soil erosion by at least 80% once vegetation cover exceeds 60% [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_1]. A Slovak catchment model shows reforestation decreasing surface runoff [ev_runoff_reduction_bahremand06_1], and in Ethiopia tree planting on degraded catchments reduced annual runoff depth from 242 to 148 mm/year [ev_runoff_reduction_meaza22_2]. A UNESCO review of moist tropical forest hydrology states that tree planting, like soil conservation measures, may well reduce the sediment from surface erosion and shallow land slips entering the drainage system [ev_sediment_retention_bruij90_13].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The class is capped at moderate because few units say how large the effect is: the Taiwan reduction and the Tigray dam figure carry sizes, while the FAO and UNESCO statements are review judgements without a measured value and the erosion-zone meta-analysis reports its forest-only effect sizes only in a figure [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2, ev_erosion_hazard_woldearegay17_3, ev_erosion_hazard_bruij90_10, ev_erosion_hazard_yang23_1]. The UNESCO litter finding pools natural forests, fallows, plantations and tree gardens; it says the soil is protected only while litter and understorey are kept, which is a condition on any restoration, not a guaranteed benefit [ev_erosion_hazard_bruij90_10]. The Tigray results are bundles of afforestation and area closures with trenches, percolation pits and check-dams, from showcase sites, and the dam figure is an upper bound carried from an earlier report, so neither can be credited to tree cover alone [ev_erosion_hazard_woldearegay17_3, ev_erosion_hazard_woldearegay17_1]. The Taiwan reduction is credited to a bundled programme of reforestation with soil conservation on cultivated land, fire control, check dams and gully control, fruit trees and agroforestry, and conservation farming, so it cannot be attributed to forest restoration alone [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2]. The same synthesis is explicit that achieving substantial flood reduction is not among the reasons to rehabilitate watersheds [ev_erosion_hazard_ham08_1]. The Tigray units are the only evidence here from a low-income setting. Landslide risk is recorded under erosion here for lack of a landslide category.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Review statements that name restoration generically, not a single family, sit here. An FAO regional review of forests and landslides in Asia asserts that tree planting on susceptible slopes can reduce risk, and that natural regeneration and tree planting on failed slopes can help control after-effects such as sediment release into rivers [ev_erosion_hazard_forbes11_1]. A UNESCO review of moist tropical forest hydrology finds erosion minimal where the soil surface is protected by a well-developed litter and herb layer, only slightly higher without the understorey, and dramatically higher once the litter layer is destroyed or removed, so the protection comes from what lies on the ground [ev_erosion_hazard_bruij90_10]. An FAO forests-and-water synthesis calls forest restoration one of the best ways of restoring productivity and reducing sedimentation in degraded areas of cleared land experiencing accelerated erosion [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_1], and lists reducing soil loss and keeping sediment out of streams among the very good reasons for rehabilitating watersheds [ev_erosion_hazard_ham08_1]. It cites Taiwan, where reservoir sedimentation from 1965 until 1985 was reduced by 55 percent of the base rate, attributed to a rehabilitation programme [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2]. A meta-analysis of vegetation restoration in erosion zones finds that both forestland and grassland restoration of cropland or bare land were effective methods for controlling erosion, cutting sediment and runoff, with canopies, root systems and the organic surface layer not differing in their impact [ev_erosion_hazard_yang23_1, ev_runoff_reduction_yang23_2]. In Tigray, Ethiopia, upstream treatment with deep trenches, percolation pits and afforestation reduced siltation of May Demu dam by up to 60%, a figure the chapter takes from Woldearegay's earlier 2011 report, and in the Abreha Weatsbeha watershed the authors observed significant improvements in reducing soil erosion after afforestation, area closures and water-harvesting works [ev_erosion_hazard_woldearegay17_3, ev_erosion_hazard_woldearegay17_1]. The effect is off-site for farmers: stabilised slopes and less sediment reaching rivers and reservoirs, at slope and catchment scale rather than on the farm plot.

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The same global assessment reports that abandoned land in previously terraced landscapes is particularly prone to gully erosion and landslides [ev_erosion_hazard_iufro18_4]. Regrowth is slow to restore slope protection: young second-growth timber falls far short of providing the root support that its much larger and older predecessors did [ev_erosion_hazard_bishop64_5], and the landslide recovery result tracks regrowth after timber harvest, not a restoration project, without separating replanting from natural regeneration [ev_erosion_hazard_sidle06_2]. Apart from these reviews and the Ethiopian meta-analysis, which measures runoff as a component of erosion, the remaining units are Tanzanian compiler ratings rather than measurements, and the Ethiopian closures are compared with open control sites rather than isolating regrowth from other changes in use [ev_runoff_reduction_meaza22_1]. Benefits fall largely off-site for farmers, as less runoff and sediment downstream.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Recovering vegetation cover slows runoff and holds soil: the compiler for area enclosure in Tanzania rates surface runoff and downstream siltation as decreased, as a result of improved vegetation cover and controlled erosion [ev_runoff_reduction_wocat_1607_2014_surface_runoff, ev_sediment_retention_wocat_1607_2014_downstream_siltation]. A meta-analysis from Ethiopia finds areas closed for grazing and agriculture had runoff coefficients of 4% against 19% on control sites [ev_runoff_reduction_meaza22_1], and in Leyte, Philippines, recovering forest on former slash-and-burn land generated the smallest share of overland flow among the land uses compared [ev_runoff_reduction_sidle06_1]. On harvested slopes, the higher probability of landslides following timber removal diminishes substantially 15–25 yr after harvesting as replacement trees mature [ev_erosion_hazard_sidle06_2], and a global forest-water assessment adds that land abandonment with expanding forest and grassland has in some cases decreased soil erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_iufro18_5].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: What separates the sides is the erosion process and the ground layer under the trees. The gains are on mass movement and on erosion where canopy and cover are good: mature stands reinforce slopes against landslides, and sediment falls under good tree cover [ev_erosion_hazard_dymond12_1, ev_erosion_hazard_reidpage03_1, ev_erosion_hazard_porto09_1]. The losses are surface erosion where understorey, vegetation and litter are absent, cleared or collected [ev_erosion_hazard_faocifor05_3, ev_erosion_hazard_ham08_4]. The actionable reading is a management condition, keeping understorey and litter, rather than a property of plantations as such. Both loss statements come from syntheses rather than measurements and state no comparator, and the gain side is a high-income Italian catchment study and New Zealand models: the Waipaoa calculation assumes a lower landslide frequency under forest, its targeting result is a scenario, and the national model's benefit applies once forests are mature and pauses after harvest while roots decay [ev_erosion_hazard_reidpage03_1, ev_erosion_hazard_reidpage03_4, ev_erosion_hazard_dymond12_1]. The plantation family is parked out of the forest-restoration roll-up and this row is published on its own: read it as evidence about plantations, not about restoration toward a natural baseline. A global meta-analysis found plantations gave 60.6% less erosion control than reference native forests [ev_erosion_hazard_hua22_1]; that compares plantations with natural forest, not with the land planted, so it is held out of the rating.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: The plantation evidence points both ways, so no direction is stated. Under good tree cover erosion falls: in eucalyptus afforestation in Calabria, Italy, sediment concentrations were substantially greater on a plot with little or no tree cover, confirming the importance of the forest canopy in reducing erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_porto09_1]. In New Zealand, converting pasture to production forest cuts landslide erosion: in the Waipaoa catchment, calculated landsliding for 1990 and 1995 conditions suggests reforestation over that period produced a 10% decrease in sediment from landslides, equivalent to a 2% decrease in suspended load, and a scenario reforesting the 66 km2 of pasture in the most susceptible areas would cut landslide sediment inputs by 20% [ev_erosion_hazard_reidpage03_1, ev_erosion_hazard_reidpage03_4]; a national model finds new radiata pine forests, once mature, generally reduce mass-movement erosion by an order of magnitude [ev_erosion_hazard_dymond12_1]. Erosion can also worsen under plantations: particularly serious erosion problems arise in plantations where the soil has been cleared of vegetation and litter to reduce fire hazard or where litter is collected for livestock bedding or fuel [ev_erosion_hazard_faocifor05_3], and an FAO synthesis names dense, planted monocultures with little or no understorey and ground cover as experiencing increased surface erosion rates [ev_erosion_hazard_ham08_4].

justification.statement: forest_restoration soil_erosion_risk: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE — material weight on both the benefit and the harm side, so no direction is stated. This is not a null finding: studies found real effects, in opposite directions, and the agreement note lists both sides. Read the conditionality for what separates them (transfer: out_of_context).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The row carries one harm finding, on how the protection works: experimental evidence cited in Hamilton's essay shows raindrop impact on bare soil under tree canopies greater than 10 m in height is greater than on bare soil in the open; what protects the soil from splash and sheet erosion is the organic matter, the surface litter and the low vegetation, not the canopy [ev_erosion_hazard_ham87_7]. Where litter or understorey is removed, tall forest does not by itself protect the soil. The same essay holds that it is not the cutting of trees as such that causes large increases in on-site erosion, but the way the products are removed [ev_erosion_hazard_ham87_8]. Root protection has a depth limit. T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: The rating is low because most of the coastal-protection evidence describes existing, mature mangrove forest, not replanting. By rule, studies of what existing forest does count only in their own coastal group, the tidal-coastal flood row, which is rated much higher, and are not credited to replanting. Replanted mangroves take years to give that protection: the restoration results here are models that assume the new stands protect like mature or historic forest (the Bangladesh model represents trees at maturity), so the benefit only arrives once the belts have grown [ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1, ev_avoided_damage_value_wbphl17_2]. The Philippine authors caution that many places that lost mangroves may have been built on in ways that prevent restoration [ev_avoided_damage_value_wbphl17_2], the Bangladesh authors say mangroves alone will not protect against large surges without embankments [ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1], and the global model assumes working dikes behind the restored areas [ev_flood_hazard_tiggeloven26_1]. The project share is what projects report about themselves, and the Viet Nam result is second-hand [ev_frmg_nara16_5, ev_frmg_erw09_2]. The money values are avoided damage to property and public assets, a benefit to society more than to farm households [ev_avoided_damage_value_beck22_2]. Nothing here is measured at severe or extreme floods. Settings are lower-middle-income Bangladesh and Haiti, upper-middle-income Philippines and Viet Nam, and global models.

justification.mechanism: Replanting mangroves gives a low reduction in flood impacts on the land behind them, judged on the evidence that is about restoration itself. A global model of restoring all restorable mangroves in front of dikes (Tiggeloven et al.) finds about 140,000 fewer people (3%) affected by flooding each year and expected damage to buildings cut by 2.3% [ev_flood_hazard_tiggeloven26_1]. A Bangladesh model of planted belts on embankment foreshores (Dasgupta et al.) finds a large cut in water flow speed (29–92%) but only a modest drop in surge height (4–16.5 cm) [ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1]. In the Philippines, a World Bank model (Losada et al.) finds that restoring the mangroves lost since 1950 would bring more than US $450 million a year in flood protection [ev_avoided_damage_value_wbphl17_2], and a Caribbean model (Beck et al.) finds mangrove restoration near Port au Prince, Haiti, costing less than $168,000 per hectare would still pay back in avoided flood damage [ev_avoided_damage_value_beck22_2]. A Viet Nam restoration model, cited by Erwin, gives higher benefit-cost ratios once the avoided upkeep of sea dikes protected from storm surge is counted [ev_frmg_erw09_2], and 50% of mangrove restoration projects reviewed by Narayan et al. state that they improve protection from storm events [ev_frmg_nara16_5]. Storm-surge findings are now filed under flooding.

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: No study here measures a planted stand lowering flood water; both results are models, which is why the rating is held at moderate and confidence is medium. The Bangladesh model treats the planted belts as fully grown forest, so the benefit only comes once plantings mature, and its authors say mangroves alone will not fully protect against large surges and must be combined with embankments [ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1]. The Haiti figure is a break-even value of avoided damage to property, which goes to the public rather than to the households who plant or tend the mangroves [ev_avoided_damage_value_beck22_2]. Neither source covers severe or extreme floods as measured events. Part of the effect is off-site, on the coast and land behind the belt rather than on the adopting farm.

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Almost all the sized evidence describes existing mangrove forest, not planted stands: the wave meta-analysis, the Florida surge measurements, the surge models, the global and Philippine models and the Indian and Bangladesh village comparisons all compare having standing mangroves with losing them [ev_frmg_nara16_1, ev_flood_hazard_krauss09_1, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_marois15_3, ev_flood_hazard_menendez20_1, ev_flood_hazard_wbphl17_1, ev_flood_hazard_badola05_7, ev_flood_hazard_akber18_7]. That a planted belt will do the same once grown is assumed, not measured. Lowering of surge and tidal water is much weaker than wave reduction [ev_flood_hazard_gijsman21_3, ev_flood_hazard_mcivor12_2], the World Bank Bangladesh model finds mangroves change total design water level by less than 4% because the surge dominates [ev_flood_hazard_wbmang25_1], and in Orissa mangroves gave less protection against larger surges [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_dasvincent09_3]. The village studies are small surveys after a single cyclone that their authors call only indicative, and in the Sidr survey the unsheltered site was closer to the cyclone path [ev_flood_hazard_badola05_7, ev_flood_hazard_akber18_7, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_akber18_5]. The restoration-specific evidence is weak: the project share is self-reported, and the Viet Nam, Bangladesh and Philippine restoration results are models that assume mature trees [ev_frmg_nara16_5, ev_frmg_erw09_2, ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1, ev_avoided_damage_value_wbphl17_2]. A no-effect result lowers the rating: in a similar New Zealand forest cut by drainage channels there was no measurable drop in water level, because the water ran along the channels [ev_flood_hazard_montgomery18_2]; this matters for planting on low, channelled mudflats. The global restoration model assumes working dikes behind every restored area [ev_flood_hazard_tiggeloven26_1], and the Caribbean figure is a break-even value of avoided property damage for the public rather than a measured drop in flooding [ev_avoided_damage_value_beck22_2]. Benefits fall on the coast and the public at large, partly away from the farm.

justification.mechanism: Mangrove belts strongly reduce flood impacts on the land behind them. They slow and break waves and, far more weakly, lower storm-surge water as it passes through the forest [ev_flood_hazard_gijsman21_1, ev_flood_hazard_gijsman21_3]. A meta-analysis of field measurements finds existing mangroves cut wave heights by 31% [ev_frmg_nara16_1], and measured surge peaks fall by 5 to 50 centimetres per kilometre of mangrove width [ev_flood_hazard_mcivor12_1, ev_flood_hazard_krauss09_1]. Storm-surge findings are now filed under flooding: a review (Marois et al.) finds models and laboratory experiments support mangroves reducing the height and speed of cyclone storm surges [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_marois15_1], and a US model it cites finds a 7–8 km wide mangrove forest could cut a Category 3 hurricane's surge by about 80% [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_marois15_3]. A global model (Menéndez et al.) estimates that current mangroves reduce expected flood damage from tropical cyclones by US$ 60 billion a year and protect 14 million people [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_menendez20_1], and that 28% more people would be flooded each year if they were lost [ev_flood_hazard_menendez20_1]; a Philippine model gives 24% more [ev_flood_hazard_wbphl17_1]. After super cyclones in India and Bangladesh, villages sheltered by existing mangrove forest had less salt water in houses and crop fields, and in Bangladesh flood water stood in crop fields for fewer days [ev_flood_hazard_badola05_7, ev_flood_hazard_akber18_7]; standing-crop damage after cyclone Sidr was highest at the site without mangrove shelter [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_akber18_5]. A World Bank model for Bangladesh finds mangrove belts protect embankments from erosion and strong currents [ev_erosion_hazard_wbmang25_1, ev_erosion_hazard_wbmang25_2, ev_flood_hazard_wbmang25_2], and a second Bangladesh model finds planted belts cut surge water speed sharply but surge height only modestly [ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1]. Of restoration projects reviewed, 50% report better storm protection [ev_frmg_nara16_5], and a Philippine model values restoring mangroves lost since 1950 at more than US $450 million a year in avoided flood damage [ev_avoided_damage_value_wbphl17_2]. In New Zealand, an existing mangrove forest about 1 km wide with no drainage channels lowered peak water by about 24 cm per km [ev_flood_hazard_montgomery18_1], and a global model of restoring all restorable mangroves in front of dikes finds about 140,000 fewer people (3%) affected by flooding each year [ev_flood_hazard_tiggeloven26_1]. A Caribbean model finds restoration near Port au Prince, Haiti, costing less than $168,000 per hectare would still pay back in avoided flood damage [ev_avoided_damage_value_beck22_2].

justification.mechanism: Cyclones can cause moderate damage to mangrove stands. After Category 5 Typhoon Odette in the Philippines, 85.71% of trees in planted stands were damaged against 77.14% in natural stands [ev_climate_shock_baring24_1], and most of the Rhizophora stylosa deaths, 14 trees, were in planted plots [ev_climate_shock_baring24_2]. Red mangrove (Rhizophora mangle) was significantly less resistant to hurricane damage than black mangrove (Avicennia germinans) in the French Caribbean [ev_climate_shock_imbert18_3], and a review reports higher death rates for Rhizophora trees in strong winds [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_gijsman21_2]. In the French Caribbean, Hurricane Hugo stripped 19% to 71% of the trunk area from the worst-hit stands [ev_climate_shock_imbert18_1], and recovery took about as long as the usual gap between hurricanes, so stands may never fully recover [ev_climate_shock_imbert18_2]. In Florida, 62% of mangroves suffered canopy damage from Hurricane Irma, worst in tall forests [ev_climate_shock_lagomasino21_1], and in Australia Cyclone Debbie damaged 18.1% of mangrove trees in the affected area [ev_climate_shock_rowl26mg_1]. Newly planted stands in Vietnam and Bangladesh were also lost or badly damaged by storms before they established [ev_frmg_vnppar_6, ev_frmg_vnppar_7, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_ahammad13_4]. In Australia, Category 5 Cyclone Yasi caused severe windthrow on 16% of 13,795 ha of mangroves, worst in Rhizophora stands as winds passed 280 km/hr [ev_climate_shock_asbridge18_1], and many damaged areas showed no or very limited recovery, with canopy cover falling from above 90% to below 20% [ev_climate_shock_asbridge18_2]. In the Florida Keys, tree mortality after Hurricane Irma rose to 36.6% after 9 months, and to 19.8% at a less hard-hit site [ev_climate_shock_radabaugh19_1, ev_climate_shock_radabaugh19_2]. A review puts full recovery of a hurricane-damaged forest at 20–30 years, given enough time between hurricanes [ev_climate_shock_krauss23_2]. For planted stands, hurricanes on St Croix were partly to blame for losses the year after a restoration planting [ev_climate_shock_krauss23_1], and after Typhoon Haiyan in the Philippines mangroves younger than 8 years fully recovered within 2 years while those older than 32 years had 95% mortality [ev_climate_shock_asbridge18_3]. In Florida and Honduras, trees killed by hurricane wind and surge left the forest floor sinking as the dead roots rotted [ev_climate_shock_cah06_1].

justification.mechanism: Sediment burial can harm mangroves, but how much depends on how much sediment arrives and how fast. Heavy or sudden burial caused dieback: in Sarawak, Malaysia, the decline of Sonneratia alba in the inner part of a natural stand was attributed to burial of its breathing roots, and no new roots had formed on the dead trees [ev_climate_shock_muro99_1]; on the Mekong coast of Vietnam, forest density fell moving inland as root burial deepened, citing the authors' own earlier measurements [ev_climate_shock_fagh17_1]; and large, sudden sedimentation events can bury many trees in a short time and cause large-scale dieback, as also reported, second-hand, along a river in Indonesia loaded with volcanic sediment [ev_climate_shock_fagh17_2]. Reviews citing earlier work add that rapid sedimentation can cause delayed death of trees by smothering their aerial roots [ev_establishment_survival_gijsman21_1, ev_climate_shock_ellis04_3], and that the effect depends on the sediment's texture and on how much arrives and how fast [ev_climate_shock_woodroffe16_1]. In Florida after Hurricane Irma, trees under a thicker layer of storm-deposited mud were more likely to die in the following months, though the mud did not affect how many died at first [ev_climate_shock_radabaugh19_3]. Mild burial and slow build-up did little harm. In a New Zealand estuary with sedimentation as high as 23 mm a year, mangroves at the muddiest sites were taller, had more breathing roots and new seedlings and were less stressed [ev_climate_shock_ellis04_1], though the site with the most sediment showed more deaths of breathing roots and seedlings, which the authors call a potential negative effect [ev_climate_shock_ellis04_2]. In a seedling experiment in China, every species survived a modest burial treatment except the small pioneer Sonneratia apetala, of which 2 of 12 seedlings died [ev_climate_shock_vhes22_1, ev_climate_shock_vhes22_2].

justification.mechanism: Planted mangroves fail where the shore is exposed to waves and erosion. A global review of planted-mangrove survival names wind and wave erosion, along with flooding and drying out, as a common reason restoration projects fail [ev_climate_shock_gorman22_4]. A review of eroding mud coasts, including Indonesia, finds that the loss of sediment behind the erosion also stops mangroves from coming back [ev_climate_shock_winterwerp20_8]. On an eroding shoreline in Singapore, the project team judged simple planting insufficient to rebuild the forest [ev_climate_shock_ellison20_5]. Young seedlings are the weak point. On the Mekong coast of Vietnam, waves and currents eroding the soft muddy bottom of one fringe prevented seedlings establishing, with erosion pins showing 17 cm of erosion there against less than 1 cm on a stable sandy fringe where saplings spread [ev_climate_shock_fagh17_3]; the same paper cites work showing as little as 1–3 cm of vertical erosion can make seedlings fail, and that storm currents dislodge them [ev_climate_shock_fagh17_4]. In a seedling experiment in China, significantly more seedlings died when the bed was eroded than when it was buried, for every species [ev_climate_shock_vhes22_3]. Losses differed by species: all Sonneratia apetala seedlings died [ev_climate_shock_vhes22_6]; Avicennia marina and Laguncularia racemosa each lost 33% dead, with 17% and 42% toppled [ev_climate_shock_vhes22_4, ev_climate_shock_vhes22_5]; Rhizophora stylosa and Kandelia obovata had low survival [ev_climate_shock_vhes22_7, ev_climate_shock_vhes22_8]; and Aegiceras corniculatum seedlings were eroded before growing anchoring roots [ev_climate_shock_vhes22_9]. Bruguiera sexangula survived all erosion treatments, and Bruguiera gymnorhiza fared about as well as Avicennia marina [ev_climate_shock_vhes22_10, ev_climate_shock_vhes22_11].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The same meta-analysis found no major difference in crab or fish production and diversity between restored mangroves and unvegetated tidal flats, and its metric merges production with diversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_su21_2], so the gain depends on the comparison: it holds against degraded mangrove, not against the open tidal flat. The Bangladesh entries are compiler ratings, not measurements. The Vietnam cover figure is before-and-after project data with no counterfactual, which stakeholders described as only partly attributable to the project; it includes casuarina windbreak planting and protection of existing forest, and it is cover rather than a count of species [ev_frmg_vnppar_3]. The return of crabs and shellfish is an anecdotal observation, and it came with protection contracts given to smallholders as well as the replanting [ev_frmg_vnppar_4].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In a global meta-analysis of mostly planted mangrove restoration, restored mangroves exhibit higher levels of crab production and diversity than degraded mangroves (RR′ = 0.80, 95% CIs = 0.64 to 0.97) [ev_biodiversity_outcome_su21_1]. A WOCAT mangrove afforestation sheet from Bangladesh reports that the plantation site supports habitats for birds and crabs and develops suitable habitats for wildlife and fish [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_4300_2019_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_4300_2019_habitat_diversity]. In Vietnam's southern Mekong Delta an independent evaluation relays that forest cover in the protection zones increased from around 50 percent in 2000 to 96 percent in 2007 as a result of the project, and that the zones around mangrove roots protected from the violence of the sea created breeding grounds for fish and shellfish, with sea crabs and shellfish re-appearing in some places and increasing in others [ev_frmg_vnppar_3, ev_frmg_vnppar_4].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Song et al. describe the sediment figure as carbon storage 'or preservation' and assume the site's water flow is good enough for the mangroves to develop; the yearly rate is derived from a predicted stock that includes carbon already in the sediment before restoration, so it overstates what restoration adds [ev_carbon_sequestration_song23_2]. Shrub-type stands remove much less than tree stands [ev_carbon_sequestration_bernal18_5]. The gain depends entirely on the plantings surviving, and several sources record failure: in the Philippines about 440 million propagules planted over 20 years averaged only 5 – 10% survival [ev_establishment_survival_winterwerp20_4], an earlier World Bank-funded project had 17-19% survival 10 years after planting [ev_establishment_survival_baring24_3], a Singapore planting lost about 94% of its propagules [ev_establishment_survival_ellison20_1], juvenile mangroves behind sediment dams in Indonesia disappeared after one or two years as the ground sank [ev_establishment_survival_winterwerp20_2], and in Mexico all planting contracts were cancelled for non-compliance [ev_establishment_survival_hernmel17_1]. In Bangladesh, survival of two planted species was less than 50% after five years, and the authors advise planning replacement planting [ev_establishment_survival_dasgupta19_3]; this is the authors' judgement rather than a reported measurement. Other projects report 70–90 percent survival in Viet Nam and averages near 74.3% in Aceh, but these are self-reported by implementers [ev_establishment_survival_wbicr6719_1, ev_establishment_survival_wibsua08_1]. Few units give a size that can be compared, which holds the rating at moderate. The Viet Nam and Indonesia project figures are modelled, the Indonesia total includes avoided pond emissions, and a Senegal model simply assumes a rate for young mangroves [ev_carbon_sequestration_gcffp013_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_wbidn22_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_iisd26_6]. The Thai and review findings are cited second-hand and give no rate, and the Philippine figure is a projection its authors call preliminary [ev_soil_organic_carbon_prayunita26_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_uddin24_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_duncan16_1].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Restored mangroves moderately increase carbon storage, in their trees and in waterlogged soils. A global review of measurements (Bernal et al.) found planted tree mangroves removing up to 23.1 t of CO2 per hectare per year in the first 20 years and 10.5 t in the following 40 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_bernal18_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_bernal18_4], while planted shrub-type mangroves removed far less, 6.7 t per hectare per year in the first two decades and 1.7 t after [ev_carbon_sequestration_bernal18_5]. A global meta-analysis of reforested mangrove (Song et al.) predicts 127.7 Mg C ha−1 in above-ground trees at 40 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_song23_1] and sediment carbon of 139.2 Mg C ha−1, which works out at about 3.5 Mg C per hectare per year of sediment carbon accumulation [ev_carbon_sequestration_song23_2]. Another meta-analysis found restored mangroves store more carbon than bare tidal flats [ev_carbon_sequestration_su21_1], and over longer periods successful rehabilitation can raise soil carbon by 83 to 96 Mg C/ha [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ellison20_4]. Project estimates point the same way: a Viet Nam project reports 1.12 million tons of CO2 equivalent absorbed by 4,028 hectares of regenerated mangrove [ev_carbon_sequestration_gcffp013_2], and a World Bank model for Indonesia gives 38.5 tCO2e per hectare per year for restoring mangrove on old fish ponds [ev_carbon_sequestration_wbidn22_2]. A project in Thailand found higher soil carbon down to two meters in planted areas than in unplanted controls over 18 years, as reported in a review [ev_soil_organic_carbon_prayunita26_1], another review concludes that restoration raises organic carbon in sediments compared with mud flats [ev_soil_organic_carbon_uddin24_1], and a Philippine model estimates that letting 377.25 ha of abandoned fishponds revert to mangrove would add 4691.73 Mg of carbon in vegetation over 6.5 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_duncan16_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: No study here measures a planted stand lowering flood water. The dyke-cost figure is second-hand and does not say whether the mangroves were planted or existing [ev_avoided_damage_value_badola05_10], the project share is self-reported [ev_frmg_nara16_5], and the other results are models [ev_frmg_erw09_2, ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1, ev_avoided_damage_value_wbphl17_2]; the Bangladesh and Philippine models assume the restored trees are fully grown, so the benefit comes only once plantings mature. The savings fall to the public and to dyke owners, not as income to the households who work the coast. The global model points to a small overall reduction: it assumes working dikes behind every restored area, leaves out cyclone damage to the mangroves, and its share is small because many coastlines have no mangroves to restore [ev_flood_hazard_tiggeloven26_1]. The Caribbean figure is a model of avoided direct damage to property, so it is a break-even value for the public rather than a measured drop in flooding [ev_avoided_damage_value_beck22_2].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Mangroves in front of sea dykes reduce the damage and upkeep the dykes need: a review cited by an Indian study reports a 20–30% reduction in dyke repair and maintenance costs depending on the width of mangrove in front [ev_avoided_damage_value_badola05_10]. Of mangrove restoration projects reviewed worldwide, 50% report better storm protection [ev_frmg_nara16_5], and a model for northern Vietnam, cited second-hand, finds restoration pays off even more once the saved dike upkeep is counted [ev_frmg_erw09_2]. In Bangladesh, a model of mangrove planting belts finds they cut cyclone surge water speed by 29–92% and surge height by 4–16.5 cm [ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1], and in the Philippines a model values restoring mangroves lost between 1950 and 2010 at more than US $450 million a year in flood protection [ev_avoided_damage_value_wbphl17_2]. A global model of restoring all restorable mangroves in front of dikes finds expected flood damage to buildings could fall by US$800 million a year, only 2.3% of damage on mangrove coastlines, with about 140,000 fewer people (3%) affected [ev_flood_hazard_tiggeloven26_1]. A Caribbean model of flood protection finds many coastlines where mangroves give long-term flood protection worth hundreds of thousands of dollars per hectare, so that restoration near Port au Prince, Haiti, costing less than $168,000 per hectare would still pay back [ev_avoided_damage_value_beck22_2].

In Bangladesh, a model of mangrove planting belts finds they cut cyclone surge water speed by 29–92% and surge height by 4–16.5 cm [ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1], and in the Philippines a model values restoring mangroves lost between 1950 and 2010 at more than US $450 million a year in flood protection [ev_avoided_damage_value_wbphl17_2]. A global model of restoring all restorable mangroves in front of dikes finds expected flood damage to buildings could fall by US$800 million a year, only 2.3% of damage on mangrove coastlines, with about 140,000 fewer people (3%) affected [ev_flood_hazard_tiggeloven26_1]. A Caribbean model of flood protection finds many coastlines where mangroves give long-term flood protection worth hundreds of thousands of dollars per hectare, so that restoration near Port au Prince, Haiti, costing less than $168,000 per hectare would still pay back [ev_avoided_damage_value_beck22_2].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Most of this evidence describes existing forest, so it shows what keeping mangroves protects; that a planted belt will do the same once grown is assumed [ev_frmg_nara16_1, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_marois15_3, ev_flood_hazard_menendez20_1, ev_flood_hazard_wbphl17_1, ev_flood_hazard_badola05_7]. Surge and tidal water is lowered much less than waves [ev_flood_hazard_gijsman21_3], a World Bank Bangladesh model finds mangroves change total design water level by less than 4% [ev_flood_hazard_wbmang25_1], and in Orissa protection was smaller against larger surges [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_dasvincent09_3]. The village surveys are small and their authors call them only indicative [ev_flood_hazard_badola05_7, ev_flood_hazard_akber18_7], and the money values are avoided damage to society, not income to the households working the coast [ev_economic_return_das11_1, ev_economic_return_marois15_1]. One source runs against the practice: in Orissa, coastal land was worth more in other uses than the house protection mangroves gave, so on that basis alone rehabilitation could not be justified [ev_economic_return_das11_2]. The restoration-specific results are self-reported or modelled with fully grown trees assumed [ev_frmg_nara16_5, ev_frmg_erw09_2, ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1, ev_avoided_damage_value_wbphl17_2]. In a similar New Zealand forest cut by drainage channels there was no measurable drop in water level [ev_flood_hazard_montgomery18_2]. The global restoration model assumes working dikes behind every restored area [ev_flood_hazard_tiggeloven26_1], and the Caribbean figure is a break-even value of avoided property damage for the public rather than a measured drop in flooding [ev_avoided_damage_value_beck22_2].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Mangrove belts strongly reduce coastal flooding by breaking waves and, more weakly, lowering surge water as it passes through the forest [ev_flood_hazard_gijsman21_1, ev_flood_hazard_gijsman21_3]. Existing mangroves cut wave heights by 31% in a meta-analysis of field measurements [ev_frmg_nara16_1], and measured surge peaks fall by 5 to 50 centimetres per kilometre of mangrove [ev_flood_hazard_mcivor12_1]. Storm-surge findings are now filed under flooding: a review (Marois et al.) finds models and experiments support mangroves reducing the height and speed of cyclone surges [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_marois15_1], and a US model it cites finds a 7–8 km wide forest could cut a Category 3 hurricane's surge by about 80% [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_marois15_3]. A global model (Menéndez et al.) finds current mangroves reduce expected flood damage from tropical cyclones by US$ 60 billion a year and protect 14 million people [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_menendez20_1], and that losing them would flood 28% more people each year [ev_flood_hazard_menendez20_1]; a Philippine model gives 24% more [ev_flood_hazard_wbphl17_1]. In India and Bangladesh, villages sheltered by existing mangrove forest took less salt water and flood water after super cyclones [ev_flood_hazard_badola05_7, ev_flood_hazard_akber18_7], and standing-crop damage after cyclone Sidr was highest at the site without mangrove shelter [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_akber18_5]. The avoided damage has been put in money terms: in Orissa mangroves protected houses worth USD 1218 per hectare of forest in a single cyclone [ev_economic_return_das11_1], and mangroves in front of sea dykes cut repair costs by 20–30% [ev_avoided_damage_value_badola05_10]. Of restoration projects reviewed, 50% report better storm protection [ev_frmg_nara16_5]. In New Zealand, an existing mangrove forest about 1 km wide with no drainage channels lowered peak water by about 24 cm per km [ev_flood_hazard_montgomery18_1], and a global model of restoring all restorable mangroves in front of dikes finds about 140,000 fewer people (3%) affected by flooding each year [ev_flood_hazard_tiggeloven26_1]. A Caribbean model finds restoration near Port au Prince, Haiti, costing less than $168,000 per hectare would still pay back in avoided flood damage [ev_avoided_damage_value_beck22_2].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: These are catch and harvest gains used as a stand-in for food security; no study measures diets or hunger. The Viet Nam shellfish figure is an uncontrolled report by the implementing organisation, and it was moved here from the income row because it measures harvest, not income [ev_household_income_ifrc11_1]. The Java fishery has no comparison site, and the authors name other possible causes and a risk of overfishing young fish [ev_fish_catch_debrot22_1]; the Aceh account is anecdotal and written by the implementer [ev_fish_catch_wibsua08_3]; the Sri Lankan link is only weakly significant [ev_fish_catch_sathi24_2]; and the Senegal figure is a model assumption with no source cited [ev_fish_catch_iisd26_3]. Evidence comes from very few sites per country, mostly upper-middle-income.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Restored mangroves slightly improve food supply by giving fish, crabs and shellfish places to breed and shelter. In northern Viet Nam, a Red Cross (IFRC) evaluation of mangrove planting found per-hectare yields of shellfish and oysters rose by 209-789 per cent [ev_household_income_ifrc11_1]. In a rehabilitated mangrove basin in Java, Indonesia, fishing for finfish grew from practically zero to a profitable livelihood within a few years [ev_fish_catch_debrot22_1]. In Aceh, crabs and oysters increased after planting, and women who used to travel up to 3 km for oysters could gather them near the village [ev_fish_catch_wibsua08_3]. In Sri Lankan lagoon villages, more community participation in mangrove restoration was linked to higher fish production per boat [ev_fish_catch_sathi24_2]. A Senegal model assumes restoration raises artisanal fishery output by 3.0%, after a long lag [ev_fish_catch_iisd26_3].
