justification.statement: riparian_buffer strongly reduces water_quality_risk in CAN, USA; measured HARM (maladaptation) in 3 sources — the practice worsened this outcome for some adopters (robust evidence, high agreement → very_high confidence; transfer: out_of_context).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The sink becomes a source under identifiable conditions, and not only at the snowmelt or dormant-season extremes below: riparian vegetation improves water quality through nitrogen uptake and denitrification, but in wet, oxygen-poor riparian soils the same vegetation-mediated processes can desorb phosphate from iron complexes and pass dissolved phosphorus into the stream [ev_nutrient_removal_dosskey10_2]. During most snowmelt runoff events the Guishui strips had little or no effect on nitrogen and runoff losses of total nitrogen, nitrate and ammonium increased at the outlet [ev_nutrient_removal_kumw24_9]; during the dormant season both the grass and the forested Illinois strips released dissolved and total phosphorus to the groundwater [ev_nutrient_removal_osbo93_2]; and nutrient-saturated strips act as a source rather than a sink, with the highest risk during high flow, ice thaw and bank erosion [ev_nutrient_removal_cole20_6]. Phosphorus behaves worst in the subsurface: no clear pattern of effect was evident across the reviewed studies and one found concentrations increased [ev_nutrient_removal_osbo93_14]. Width does not reliably buy performance — a meta-analysis found no impact of width on nitrogen removal efficiency, and increasing width from 4 to 8 m did not reduce soluble herbicide loadings [ev_nutrient_removal_cole20_3, ev_nutrient_removal_cole20_1] — and over the long run retention can decline: in one restored stream woody vegetation established only 13-17 years on, then shaded out the algal assimilation and ultimately contributed to increasing nutrient concentrations [ev_nutrient_removal_mcmi14_3]. Where fields are tile drained the drains bypass the strip and it is not as effective [ev_nutrient_removal_osbo93_6]. The largest percentages here are modelled rather than measured, and the same study's own low retention-efficiency assumption cuts the nitrogen and phosphorus gains to 35.1 and 37.1% [ev_nutrient_removal_lang22_1, ev_nutrient_removal_lang22_2, ev_sediment_retention_lang22_1]; the Guishui paper reports both 58% and 92.8% for phosphorus in the same treatment [ev_nutrient_removal_kumw24_4, ev_nutrient_removal_kumw24_7]; the Brazilian values are correlations whose authors stress that watershed-scale land cover explained water quality better than the riparian zone [ev_nutrient_removal_mello18_8]; and a run of the remaining claims is cited background or uncited assertion, including one about forest buffers between urban areas and streams [ev_nutrient_removal_zhao13_1, ev_nutrient_removal_zhao13_5, ev_sediment_retention_zhao13_1, ev_sediment_retention_schultz95_1]. In the fenced pasture buffer, the nutrient decline reversed after twelve years, once debris blockages became less common and aquatic macrophytes were shaded out by the now-established woody vegetation — a long-term waning of the benefit, not a measured harm [ev_nutrient_removal_dosskey10_7]. The catchment-scale sediment finding and the general nitrogen-removal and phosphorus-release findings above are citations within a review, not new measurement [ev_sediment_retention_dosskey10_6, ev_nutrient_removal_dosskey10_1, ev_nutrient_removal_dosskey10_2, ev_nutrient_removal_dosskey10_7], and the Brazilian trench study has no without-forest control: retention there is inferred from where buried sediment layers stop inside an existing forest [ev_sediment_retention_oliv10_1]. The temperature evidence is framed on vegetation loss, not planting [ev_stream_temperature_osbo93_16]. Illinois, China, Brazil, Mexico, Costa Rica and a UK review: no low-income measurement anywhere in the row.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Established or regrowing riparian vegetation removes load on three fronts. Dissolved nutrients are taken out as water passes through: shallow-groundwater nitrate fell by up to 90% behind the Illinois strips [ev_nutrient_removal_osbo93_1], with reviewed reductions of 79-98% in surface runoff, 68-100% and 40-100% in groundwater and subsurface waters for forested strips, and phosphorus reductions of 50-85% [ev_nutrient_removal_osbo93_10, ev_nutrient_removal_osbo93_7, ev_nutrient_removal_osbo93_8, ev_nutrient_removal_osbo93_12]; along the Guishui River an 18 m woody strip removed 89.8% of total nitrogen and retained 92.8% of total phosphorus, against 72.3% for grass and 43.9% for shrub cover and 17.62% with no buffer [ev_nutrient_removal_kumw24_4, ev_nutrient_removal_kumw24_5, ev_nutrient_removal_kumw24_6, ev_nutrient_removal_kumw24_7, ev_nutrient_removal_kumw24_8]; and the reviewed ranges for grass strips are markedly lower and more variable than for forested ones [ev_nutrient_removal_osbo93_8]; more broadly, riparian vegetation removes nitrogen through plant uptake and denitrification [ev_nutrient_removal_dosskey10_1], and in a long-term study of a trampled, overgrazed pasture riparian zone fenced off from livestock, rapid herbaceous and then woody regrowth was followed by declining stream nutrient levels over the first twelve years [ev_nutrient_removal_dosskey10_7]. Particles settle out: outflow sediment fell by 92%, 72% and 50% under woody, grass and shrub cover against a bare control trapping 22% [ev_sediment_retention_kumw24_1, ev_sediment_retention_kumw24_2, ev_sediment_retention_kumw24_3], trapping efficiency rises sharply over the first 10 m of buffer [ev_sediment_retention_cole20_1], fairly narrow strips of riparian vegetation reduce sediment input to surface water [ev_sediment_retention_osbo93_15, ev_sediment_retention_schultz95_1, ev_sediment_retention_zhao13_1]; at catchment scale, restoring vegetation to denuded, livestock-trampled riparian zones reduced sediment export from over 100 to less than 10 kilograms per hectare per year within one year, mainly through less bank erosion and a stabilised channel [ev_sediment_retention_dosskey10_6], and in a Brazilian cotton field bordered by an existing native riparian forest, sediment eroded from the cropped slope formed layers up to 14 cm thick in trenches a few metres inside the forest, with no buried sediment layer found further in [ev_sediment_retention_oliv10_1]; and in Brazilian watersheds nitrogen, phosphorus, solids and faecal coliforms fall while dissolved oxygen rises as riparian forest cover increases [ev_nutrient_removal_mello18_3, ev_nutrient_removal_mello18_4, ev_nutrient_removal_mello18_5, ev_nutrient_removal_mello18_6, ev_nutrient_removal_mello18_7, ev_nutrient_removal_mello18_8, ev_nutrient_removal_mello18_9, ev_nutrient_removal_mello18_12, ev_nutrient_removal_zhao13_1, ev_nutrient_removal_zhao13_2, ev_nutrient_removal_zhao13_3, ev_nutrient_removal_zhao13_4, ev_nutrient_removal_zhao13_5, ev_sediment_retention_mello18_1, ev_sediment_retention_mello18_2]. Modelled at national scale, meeting Costa Rica's legal minimum raises nitrogen retention by 81.4% and phosphorus retention by 85.9%, with sediment retention up 3.9% [ev_nutrient_removal_lang22_1, ev_sediment_retention_lang22_1]. Shade is the third front: removing riparian vegetation dramatically increases temperature in small shaded streams [ev_stream_temperature_osbo93_16].

Dissolved nutrients are taken out as water passes through: shallow-groundwater nitrate fell by up to 90% behind the Illinois strips [ev_nutrient_removal_osbo93_1], with reviewed reductions of 79-98% in surface runoff, 68-100% and 40-100% in groundwater and subsurface waters for forested strips, and phosphorus reductions of 50-85% [ev_nutrient_removal_osbo93_10, ev_nutrient_removal_osbo93_7, ev_nutrient_removal_osbo93_8, ev_nutrient_removal_osbo93_12]; along the Guishui River an 18 m woody strip removed 89.8% of total nitrogen and retained 92.8% of total phosphorus, against 72.3% for grass and 43.9% for shrub cover and 17.62% with no buffer [ev_nutrient_removal_kumw24_4, ev_nutrient_removal_kumw24_5, ev_nutrient_removal_kumw24_6, ev_nutrient_removal_kumw24_7, ev_nutrient_removal_kumw24_8]; and the reviewed ranges for grass strips are markedly lower and more variable than for forested ones [ev_nutrient_removal_osbo93_8]; more broadly, riparian vegetation removes nitrogen through plant uptake and denitrification [ev_nutrient_removal_dosskey10_1], and in a long-term study of a trampled, overgrazed pasture riparian zone fenced off from livestock, rapid herbaceous and then woody regrowth was followed by declining stream nutrient levels over the first twelve years [ev_nutrient_removal_dosskey10_7]. Particles settle out: outflow sediment fell by 92%, 72% and 50% under woody, grass and shrub cover against a bare control trapping 22% [ev_sediment_retention_kumw24_1, ev_sediment_retention_kumw24_2, ev_sediment_retention_kumw24_3], trapping efficiency rises sharply over the first 10 m of buffer [ev_sediment_retention_cole20_1], fairly narrow strips of riparian vegetation reduce sediment input to surface water [ev_sediment_retention_osbo93_15, ev_sediment_retention_schultz95_1, ev_sediment_retention_zhao13_1]; at catchment scale, restoring vegetation to denuded, livestock-trampled riparian zones reduced sediment export from over 100 to less than 10 kilograms per hectare per year within one year, mainly through less bank erosion and a stabilised channel [ev_sediment_retention_dosskey10_6], and in a Brazilian cotton field bordered by an existing native riparian forest, sediment eroded from the cropped slope formed layers up to 14 cm thick in trenches a few metres inside the forest, with no buried sediment layer found further in [ev_sediment_retention_oliv10_1]; and in Brazilian watersheds nitrogen, phosphorus, solids and faecal coliforms fall while dissolved oxygen rises as riparian forest cover increases [ev_nutrient_removal_mello18_3, ev_nutrient_removal_mello18_4, ev_nutrient_removal_mello18_5, ev_nutrient_removal_mello18_6, ev_nutrient_removal_mello18_7, ev_nutrient_removal_mello18_8, ev_nutrient_removal_mello18_9, ev_nutrient_removal_mello18_12, ev_nutrient_removal_zhao13_1, ev_nutrient_removal_zhao13_2, ev_nutrient_removal_zhao13_3, ev_nutrient_removal_zhao13_4, ev_nutrient_removal_zhao13_5, ev_sediment_retention_mello18_1, ev_sediment_retention_mello18_2]. Modelled at national scale, meeting Costa Rica's legal minimum raises nitrogen retention by 81.4% and phosphorus retention by 85.9%, with sediment retention up 3.9% [ev_nutrient_removal_lang22_1, ev_sediment_retention_lang22_1]. Shade is the third front: removing riparian vegetation dramatically increases temperature in small shaded streams [ev_stream_temperature_osbo93_16].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Planting does not guarantee a sink. Narrow buffers under 15 m actually contributed nitrogen to the riparian zone in six of the pooled studies [ev_nutrient_removal_maye07_3], buffer outflow in the early stages of a natural runoff event can contribute pollutants to surface waters [ev_nutrient_removal_mank07_5], and in the Connecticut restoration total Kjeldahl nitrogen and total phosphorus increased significantly as groundwater passed through the restored strip while the other groundwater nitrogen species did not respond [ev_nutrient_removal_clau00_3, ev_nutrient_removal_clau00_4]; part of that site's groundwater nitrate decline was due to the cessation of fertilisation rather than the planting [ev_nutrient_removal_clau00_2], and its authors warn that early-stage restoration may deliver much less than established buffers [ev_nutrient_removal_clau00_5]. What you plant decides the result: a 20 m oat buffer had no significant effect on total phosphorus where a 10 m rye grass strip did [ev_nutrient_removal_osbo93_4, ev_nutrient_removal_osbo93_5], the grass strip did little to reduce phosphorus in shallow groundwater [ev_nutrient_removal_osbo93_3], and at the least fertile Quebec site the planted poplars accumulated no more nitrogen than the unmanaged herbaceous buffer beside them [ev_nutrient_removal_fort10_2]. Mass is not concentration — 91.8 and 92.1% mass reductions against 42.9 and 44.4% in concentration, dissolved phosphorus down only 16%, nitrate 10-19% against 48-72% for ammonium [ev_nutrient_removal_mank07_1, ev_nutrient_removal_mank07_3, ev_nutrient_removal_mank07_4] — and intensity removes the soluble benefit: at 69 mm per hour removal fell to 50 and 28% and to 35% for phosphate behind the wider buffer, phosphate mass was not significantly reduced at that intensity, and soluble removal held above 60% in every storm but the most intense [ev_nutrient_removal_lee00_6, ev_nutrient_removal_lee00_7, ev_nutrient_removal_lee00_8, ev_nutrient_removal_lee03_8]. Performance also decays: the effectiveness of wooded buffers typically diminishes over time as the nutrient requirements of trees decrease with age [ev_nutrient_removal_cole20_7]. The thermal benefit can invert — newly restored streams whose canopy was removed during construction had higher temperatures [ev_stream_temperature_mcmi14_1] — and that urban study, bundled with channel regrading, rests on a sample of three for its nitrate result, with its phosphate comparison not significant [ev_nutrient_removal_mcmi14_1, ev_nutrient_removal_mcmi14_2]. Texture limits the sediment pathway, at 52% retention of clay against 93% of sand and silt and 35% on silty clay loam where sandy loam was almost 100% [ev_sediment_retention_lee00_3, ev_sediment_retention_cole20_2]; extra width adds little, with only 4.6 and 4.0% gained in modelling from 50 m to 100 m, and 30 m buffers failed to prevent increased stream sedimentation after partial clearcutting [ev_sediment_retention_sira20_2, ev_sediment_retention_lee04_2]. Whether that grass restoration was planted or left to regrow naturally is not stated in the review it comes from [ev_nutrient_removal_dosskey10_3]. Nearly all of it is plot-scale or modelled temperate high-income work — Iowa, Kansas, Missouri, Connecticut, Prince Edward Island, a UK review and a pooled analysis that states no study country — with the Bear Creek reach measured repeatedly across related studies; none of it is a planted buffer measured in a low-income farming system. The European figures are model results and the Quebec figures are cited second-hand; both come from rich countries [ev_nutrient_removal_englund21_4, ev_nutrient_removal_simard09_5, ev_stream_temperature_simard09_7].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: A planted strip works by settling, infiltration and uptake. Sediment-bound load is trapped: 70% and more than 92% of incoming sediment under simulated rainfall [ev_sediment_retention_lee00_1, ev_sediment_retention_lee00_2], 95% and 97% over natural events with a floor of 71% and 86% [ev_sediment_retention_lee03_1, ev_sediment_retention_lee03_3, ev_sediment_retention_lee03_7], 99.7% of suspended-solids mass in the Kansas plots [ev_sediment_retention_mank07_1], 97% behind an 8 m fescue strip and 91% within the first 4 m [ev_sediment_retention_blanco04_1, ev_sediment_retention_blanco04_2, ev_sediment_retention_blanco04_3, ev_sediment_retention_blanco04_4], and 92% of overland-flow suspended solids after a cropped strip was seeded to fescue [ev_sediment_retention_clau00_1, ev_sediment_retention_lee04_1, ev_sediment_retention_lee04_3, ev_sediment_retention_sira20_1]. Dissolved load is removed as water passes through: across 88 buffers, mean nitrogen removal effectiveness was 67.5%, at 0.394 mg per litre per metre [ev_nutrient_removal_maye07_1, ev_nutrient_removal_maye07_2]; the Bear Creek plantings removed 80% and 94% of total nitrogen over natural events and 64 to 93% under a 25 mm per hour simulation [ev_nutrient_removal_lee03_2, ev_nutrient_removal_lee03_4, ev_nutrient_removal_lee00_4, ev_nutrient_removal_lee00_5, ev_nutrient_removal_lee03_9, ev_nutrient_removal_schultz95_1]; a seeded Connecticut strip cut overland-flow total Kjeldahl nitrogen by 70%, nitrate by 83% and total phosphorus by 73% [ev_nutrient_removal_clau00_1, ev_nutrient_removal_clau00_5]; grass strips reduced nitrate in surface runoff by 54-84%, phosphorus by 61-83% and subsurface nitrogen by 10-60%, and 80 to 90% nitrate reduction was found in subsurface water after passage through grass and forest strips [ev_nutrient_removal_osbo93_11, ev_nutrient_removal_osbo93_13, ev_nutrient_removal_osbo93_9, ev_nutrient_removal_osbo93_5, ev_nutrient_removal_schultz95_2, ev_nutrient_removal_blanco04_1, ev_nutrient_removal_blanco04_2, ev_nutrient_removal_blanco04_3, ev_nutrient_removal_mank07_1]; a separately reviewed US riparian zone that had been cleared and cropped for a long time and was then restored to grass cover (planting vs natural regrowth not stated) showed a 35% reduction in groundwater nitrate [ev_nutrient_removal_dosskey10_3]; and nutrients are locked into the planted biomass, 770 and 90 kg of nitrogen per hectare in the Quebec poplar buffers [ev_nutrient_removal_fort10_1]. justification.statement: riparian_buffer strongly reduces water_quality_risk in CAN, GBR, USA; measured HARM (maladaptation) in 4 sources — the practice worsened this outcome for some adopters (robust evidence, high agreement → very_high confidence; transfer: out_of_context).

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: This buffer is not universal: in Zimbabwe, conservation-agriculture plots (predominantly planting basins) showed no specific impact in mitigating losses from either rainfall shortfalls or surpluses for millet and groundnut [ev_crop_yield_mich19_6]. Measured harm (maladaptation) — the practice worsening this outcome for some adopters — appears in 3 sources, and part of the benefit happens off-site (downstream or landscape scale) rather than on the adopting farm. The Africa-wide figure is a model, not a field measurement, and the Zimbabwe result is a single trial season with no yield figure [ev_crop_yield_lebel15_1, ev_soil_moisture_mand21_1]. At the extreme end the practice did not prevent total crop failure: at Lamego, the driest of Thierfelder and colleagues' on-farm sites in central Mozambique, the 2010/2011 season was so heavily affected by drought that no cowpea yield was obtained in any treatment, planting basins with mulch included [ev_crop_yield_thierf15_5].

justification.mechanism: Terracing's drought buffer strengthens as dry days increase. In a nationally representative survey of Ethiopian cereal plots, terraced fields saw yields 14% lower than matched unterraced plots when dry days were few, but 17% higher when dry days were most frequent [ev_crop_yield_kosm18_5]; looking at consecutive dry spells instead, yields were 9% lower with few dry spells but 33% higher with the most dry spells [ev_crop_yield_kosm18_7]. In Ethiopia's Sustainable Land Management Project — which combined water harvesting with small-scale irrigation, reduced grazing, afforestation and gully rehabilitation — vegetation and productivity gains were three times larger in watersheds that experienced severe drought than the average across all treated areas, with increases of 16.71% in vegetation greenness and 13.48% in gross primary productivity [ev_drought_hazard_cons22_1]. A continental model of in situ rainwater harvesting for rainfed maize across Africa finds that, where it steadies yields, the mean potential yield gain is 9 to 39% under the climate of the 1990s, rising to 14–50% by the 2050s depending on the climate model [ev_crop_yield_lebel15_1]. In a Zimbabwean cotton trial in the 2018–2019 drought season, tied contour ridges held significantly more moisture in the top 0–5 and 6–10 cm of soil than conventional tillage, though not at 11–15 cm [ev_soil_moisture_mand21_1].

justification.mechanism: Runoff-harvesting earthworks can store substantial water even in extreme drought: in the Canary Islands, the traditional 'gavias' system — collecting runoff from a hillslope catchment into walled fields — was found to store nearly 350 mm of water in the top metre of soil even in the driest years, when rainfall was below 100 mm, equivalent to about 150 mm available to the crop [ev_soil_moisture_roose17_3]. In a commercial potato-growing watershed in New Brunswick, Canada, terraced fields averaged 32.76 tonnes per hectare under dry conditions against 32.39 tonnes per hectare on non-terraced fields over the same years [ev_crop_yield_lian19_1].

justification.mechanism: A meta-analysis of water-harvesting technologies across semi-arid Africa and Asia found yield improvements significantly higher in years when rainfall fell below 330 mm than in wetter years [ev_crop_yield_boum16_4]. In Algeria, deep ploughing and contour ridging reduced erosion and improved fodder production even in a season with deficient rainfall (250 mm), although fodder shrubs planted at the same time failed [ev_forage_productivity_roose17_1]. In the Peruvian Andes, terraced maize plots fared better than sloped fields during a 2002 dry spell [ev_drought_hazard_post05_1].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.mitigation_mechanism: A meta-analysis of water-harvesting technologies across semi-arid Africa and Asia found yield improvements significantly higher in years when rainfall fell below 330 mm than in wetter years [ev_crop_yield_boum16_4]. In Algeria, deep ploughing and contour ridging reduced erosion and improved fodder production even in a season with deficient rainfall (250 mm), although fodder shrubs planted at the same time failed [ev_forage_productivity_roose17_1]. In the Peruvian Andes, terraced maize plots fared better than sloped fields during a 2002 dry spell [ev_drought_hazard_post05_1].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: At severe or extreme drought the measured results mostly show no benefit rather than a gain. In Niger, soil and water conservation works could not compensate when 2004 rainfall fell to only 200 to 250 millimetres, and villagers harvested nothing despite the works [ev_crop_yield_botreij09_17]; in Tunisia, four consecutive years of drought from 1998 to 2002 reduced agricultural and pastoral productivity gains and limited soil-conservation benefits [ev_drought_hazard_iegtun13_1]; and a general assessment states that crop yields cannot be sustained during a meteorological drought even where dry spells can be bridged by water-management investment [ev_crop_yield_rock10_2]. Soil and water conservation in Niger raised households' estimated surplus to 70% in good years but still left an estimated 28% deficit in low-rainfall years [ev_food_security_kabo04_1]. Only one of the studies reporting a benefit under drought gives a quantified size of effect [ev_drought_hazard_cons22_1]; the rest are qualitative statements of improved resilience. Most of the evidence is from low-income Sahelian and East African countries (Burkina Faso, Niger, Ethiopia), with programme-level evidence also from Tunisia, Brazil and China. The Africa-wide maize figure is a model, not a field measurement [ev_crop_yield_lebel15_1].

justification.mechanism: Pooled across water-harvesting structures, the benefit under drought is small. At a watershed scale, soil and water conservation works (zaï and half-moon pits, stone bunds, terraces, cisterns) raise water availability and buffer crop and rangeland productivity against drought. In Ethiopia, a large study of a national land-restoration programme found that in areas that experienced severe drought, programme effects on vegetation greenness and productivity were three times larger than the average programme effect, with increases of 16.71% in a vegetation index and 13.48% in gross primary productivity [ev_drought_hazard_cons22_1]; buffering effects were also significant under moderate drought [ev_drought_hazard_cons22_2] and, more weakly, under mild drought [ev_drought_hazard_cons22_3]. Zaï and half-moon pits in Burkina Faso retained soil moisture for 2 to 3 weeks longer, mitigating the impact of dry spells [ev_soil_water_retention_zour25h1_7]. A review of soil and water conservation technologies across multiple countries found they are particularly useful in regions with low rainfall or high climatic variability [ev_crop_yield_mala24_3], and a water-harvesting meta-analysis found significantly higher yield gains in seasons with rainfall below 330 millimetres [ev_crop_yield_boum16_4]. A continental model of in situ rainwater harvesting for rainfed maize across Africa finds that, where it steadies yields, the mean potential yield gain is 9 to 39% under the climate of the 1990s, rising to 14–50% by the 2050s depending on the climate model [ev_crop_yield_lebel15_1].

At a watershed scale, soil and water conservation works (zaï and half-moon pits, stone bunds, terraces, cisterns) raise water availability and buffer crop and rangeland productivity against drought. In Ethiopia, a large study of a national land-restoration programme found that in areas that experienced severe drought, programme effects on vegetation greenness and productivity were three times larger than the average programme effect, with increases of 16.71% in a vegetation index and 13.48% in gross primary productivity [ev_drought_hazard_cons22_1]; buffering effects were also significant under moderate drought [ev_drought_hazard_cons22_2] and, more weakly, under mild drought [ev_drought_hazard_cons22_3]. Zaï and half-moon pits in Burkina Faso retained soil moisture for 2 to 3 weeks longer, mitigating the impact of dry spells [ev_soil_water_retention_zour25h1_7]. A review of soil and water conservation technologies across multiple countries found they are particularly useful in regions with low rainfall or high climatic variability [ev_crop_yield_mala24_3], and a water-harvesting meta-analysis found significantly higher yield gains in seasons with rainfall below 330 millimetres [ev_crop_yield_boum16_4]. A continental model of in situ rainwater harvesting for rainfed maize across Africa finds that, where it steadies yields, the mean potential yield gain is 9 to 39% under the climate of the 1990s, rising to 14–50% by the 2050s depending on the climate model [ev_crop_yield_lebel15_1].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: In southern Malawi during the 2015/16 El Nino drought, 'banking' (ridge reinforcement while crops are growing) cut yields from 245 kg per hectare to 153 kg per hectare, a 37.6% reduction, and lowered the odds of a farm meeting the maize-yield threshold for food security from 0.12 to 0.054 [ev_crop_yield_boil19_5, ev_food_security_boil19_3]. In Zimbabwe, conservation agriculture overall showed no specific impact in mitigating losses from either rainfall shortfalls or surpluses for millet and groundnut [ev_crop_yield_mich19_6]. Measured harm (maladaptation) — the practice worsening this outcome for some adopters — appears in 1 source. The Zimbabwe tied-ridge result is a single trial season, measures soil moisture only and gives no yield figure [ev_soil_moisture_mand21_1]. At the extreme end the practice did not prevent total crop failure: at Lamego, the driest of Thierfelder and colleagues' on-farm sites in central Mozambique, the 2010/2011 season was so heavily affected by drought that no cowpea yield was obtained in any treatment, planting basins with mulch included [ev_crop_yield_thierf15_5].

justification.mechanism: In-situ water harvesting such as planting basins and ridge reinforcement raises soil infiltration so crops can draw on stored moisture when rains fail. In Zimbabwe, conservation-agriculture plots using planting basins improved maize yields both in above-average rainfall and during drought [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3], and improved sorghum and cowpea yields during times of drought [ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. In semi-arid and dry sub-humid East Africa, conservation-farming systems using ripping or pitting with fertiliser showed their largest yield advantage in rainy seasons with low and poorly distributed rainfall, by maximising infiltration so crops could bridge short periods of dry spell [ev_crop_yield_rock09_15]. In a Zimbabwean cotton trial in the 2018–2019 drought season, tied contour ridges held significantly more moisture in the top 0–5 and 6–10 cm of soil than conventional tillage, though not at 11–15 cm [ev_soil_moisture_mand21_1].

justification.mechanism: Farm ponds that capture and store runoff let farmers irrigate through dry spells. In northern Burkina Faso, a cement-lined pond supplying supplemental irrigation raised sorghum grain yield from 443 to 680 kg per hectare in 1999 and from 634 to 1138 kg per hectare in 2000 [ev_crop_yield_foxr03_4, ev_crop_yield_foxr03_5]. In eastern Kenya, sand dams across seasonal riverbeds store rainy-season runoff as groundwater in the sand: households without a dam saw their income fall by 38,056 Kenyan shillings a year, while households with a dam maintained or grew their income by 27,241 shillings — a difference of 65,297 shillings in a dry year, against an investment of about $35 per capita [ev_household_income_pauw08_1].

justification.mechanism: Terracing's drought buffer strengthens as dry days increase. In a nationally representative survey of Ethiopian cereal plots, terraced fields saw yields 14% lower than matched unterraced plots when dry days were few, but 17% higher when dry days were most frequent [ev_crop_yield_kosm18_5]; by consecutive dry spells instead, yields were 9% lower with few dry spells but 33% higher with the most [ev_crop_yield_kosm18_7]. In Burkina Faso, contour stone bunds with manure raised millet grain yields by 13% and sorghum grain yields by 34% over untreated control plots [ev_crop_yield_botreij09_12].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Much of the remaining support is authors' statements rather than measurements: Roose and co-authors' book chapters on contour barriers with pits in Burkina Faso, treated ravines in Haiti and wadi terraces in Morocco [ev_flood_hazard_roose17_1, ev_flood_hazard_roose17_2, ev_flood_hazard_roose17_3]; Roose's Moroccan manual on small dams during the serious floods of 2002-2003 [ev_flood_hazard_roos10_1]; World Bank completion reports on spate and diversion structures in Yemen and on hill terraces in Uttarakhand, India [ev_flood_hazard_yem12_4, ev_flood_hazard_utk22_7]; Embrapa's self-assessment of its barraginhas in Brazil [ev_flood_hazard_mira19_7]; Zougmoré and colleagues on stone bunds in heavy rain [ev_erosion_hazard_zoug14_2]; and Venot and colleagues' survey in northern Ghana, where users named limiting floods as a perceived benefit of small reservoirs [ev_flood_hazard_veno12_1]. WOCAT practitioner ratings from Burkina Faso, Kenya, Tunisia, Ethiopia, Uzbekistan and Somalia also report less flooding [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1528_2012_flood_impacts, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1537_2012_flood_impacts, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_6610_2022_downstream_flooding, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_6715_2023_downstream_flooding, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_6716_2023_flood_impacts, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_7553_2025_flood_impacts, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_7778_2026_flood_impacts]. Some structures make flooding worse: in Niger, diversion banquettes visibly increased peak discharges (Heusch) [ev_flood_hazard_heusch95_1], and Ritchie and colleagues pass on a warning that larger sand dams raise the risk of flooding, erosion and seepage [ev_flood_hazard_ritc21_1]. The benefit fades in big floods: check dams had minimal effect against extreme floods, especially if ill-designed or not maintained [ev_flood_hazard_luca21_3]; in the Tunisian catchment the volume of large floods and of the mean flood did not change significantly, only their peak and timing [ev_runoff_reduction_bergaoui00_4, ev_runoff_reduction_bergaoui00_7]; and in Morocco flood peaks fell only where floods were not too strong [ev_flood_hazard_roose17_3]. Much of the benefit falls downstream rather than on the farm that builds the works.

justification.mechanism: Water-harvesting and soil-conservation works slow runoff and spread it on the slope, giving a small reduction in flood impact. The main measured result is from a semi-arid Tunisian catchment treated with dry-stone contour walls, gully check structures and some bench terraces, alongside a grazing closure of the whole catchment (Bergaoui and Albergel, a before-and-after comparison with no control catchment): flood peaks were strongly clipped and flood rise and base times nearly doubled [ev_flood_hazard_bergaoui00_2], peak discharge of large floods fell to 60% or 87% of its pre-treatment level depending on the reference period [ev_flood_hazard_bergaoui00_3], and the paper's conclusion reports flood volume and peaks falling by about 50% [ev_flood_hazard_bergaoui00_1]. A meta-analysis of plot studies by Locatelli and colleagues found that infiltration trenches cut runoff by 46.4% on average [ev_runoff_reduction_locat20_1]. Reviews pass on further results second-hand: terraces on small mountain plots cut mean runoff and flood peaks (Roose) [ev_flood_hazard_roose06_1], stone bunds lower peak runoff at the foot of the slope in Burkina Faso (Roose) [ev_flood_hazard_roose94_1], check dams cut flooding and peak flow in Iran and withstood strong floods in Italian mountain torrents (Lucas-Borja and colleagues) [ev_flood_hazard_luca21_1, ev_flood_hazard_luca21_2], and the few catchment studies reviewed by Willems and colleagues found terraces reduce peak flow [ev_flood_hazard_willem21_1].

justification.mechanism: Infiltration trenches hold rain on the slope: among eleven studies that measured runoff on 52 plots, all showed a reduction, and on average trenches significantly reduced runoff by 46.4%, equal to 5.7% of rainfall [ev_runoff_reduction_locat20_1]. A global review of terracing finds catchment-level evidence scarce but notes that two studies using hydrological modelling and field measurements indicate terraces reduce peak flow [ev_flood_hazard_willem21_1]. A check-dam review cites check dams as effective in mitigating flooding and significantly reducing peak flow in Iran [ev_flood_hazard_luca21_1], and Embrapa credits its barraginhas, small runoff-retention basins dug along runoff paths in Brazilian mixed crop-livestock systems, with easing floods as well [ev_flood_hazard_mira19_7].

The main measured result is from a semi-arid Tunisian catchment treated with dry-stone contour walls, gully check structures and some bench terraces, alongside a grazing closure of the whole catchment (Bergaoui and Albergel, a before-and-after comparison with no control catchment): flood peaks were strongly clipped and flood rise and base times nearly doubled [ev_flood_hazard_bergaoui00_2], peak discharge of large floods fell to 60% or 87% of its pre-treatment level depending on the reference period [ev_flood_hazard_bergaoui00_3], and the paper's conclusion reports flood volume and peaks falling by about 50% [ev_flood_hazard_bergaoui00_1]. Reviews pass on plot and hillslope results: terraces on small mountain plots cut mean runoff and flood peaks, and stone bunds lower peak runoff at the foot of the slope in Burkina Faso and make flows last longer after rain (Roose) [ev_flood_hazard_roose06_1, ev_flood_hazard_roose94_1]; Zougmoré and colleagues state that stone bunds protect land from rapid flow in heavy rain [ev_erosion_hazard_zoug14_2]. A World Bank completion report credits compacted hill terraces with limiting damage from a major flood and landslides in Uttarakhand, India [ev_flood_hazard_utk22_7], and WOCAT compilers in Tunisia and Uzbekistan rate flooding as reduced [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_6610_2022_downstream_flooding, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_7553_2025_flood_impacts].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: The review groups temperature shocks with low rainfall and names no specific practice or size of effect, so it does not isolate heat-stress losses [ev_crop_yield_mala24_5]. The second paper is the authors' judgement, not a measurement or model result [ev_crop_yield_lebel15_2]. What is missing is a measured heat-stress comparison with and without the practice.

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Every unit in the row points the same way, so the practice is rated as worsening waterlogging, but none states how large the loss is or what share of a field is affected, so the strength is not quantified. The harm is tied to wet years, high-rainfall zones or sub-humid sites: it comes from using in-field water-holding practices (pits, basins, mulch, ridges, stone bunds) outside their rainfall window, and says nothing about storage or diversion structures, which have no waterlogging evidence left in this row. The Cameroon observation is unpublished work cited by the authors, and the Burkina Faso statements and the Tanzanian tied-ridge result are cited from earlier studies [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4, ev_crop_yield_roose94_3, ev_waterlogging_hazard_zoug14_1, ev_waterlogging_hazard_biaz12_15]. The Ethiopian finding is a field observation with no measured yield loss, and the source names a tillage treatment as the one particularly affected, so only part of the harm can be put on mulch and basins [ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_1, ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_2]. The southern African basin finding rests on a theoretical water balance plus extension reports and farmer testimony, and the sub-humid conclusion covers conservation agriculture bundled with reduced tillage [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_8, ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_7]. The Kenyan ridging loss is the authors' probable explanation rather than a measured waterlogging contrast, and the ridging is bundled with fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6]. The Cameroon, Burkina Faso and Kenyan losses are held out of the production classes as performance caveats and counted here as waterlogging evidence.

justification.mechanism: Practices that hold water on the cropped field backfire in wet conditions: in wet years stone bunds in Burkina Faso may cause waterlogging in some parts of the field, millet behind stone bunds can suffer waterlogging when monthly rainfall exceeds 200 mm, and in the Sudanian zone of Cameroon, where rainfall exceeds 1 200 mm per year, sorghum in zaï pits yielded less than on flat-cultivated fields [ev_waterlogging_hazard_zoug14_1, ev_crop_yield_roose94_3, ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]. In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial waterlogging lasting 3–5 days during early maize growth also affected the mulching and basin treatments [ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_1, ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_2]. In southern Africa an FAO study shows by a water-balance calculation that planting basins can depress yields when too much water concentrates in them under high rainfall or in seasons with abnormally high rainfall, and concludes that in sub-humid environments yields could be affected by water-logging in years with adequate rainfall [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_8, ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_7]. In a Kenyan on-farm trial, ridged plots with fertiliser at the relatively wetter sub-humid Rachuonyo site gave the lowest yields, slightly below conventional practice, which the authors say can probably be explained by waterlogging caused by ridging [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6]. Biazin et al. cite Jensen et al. (2003) from Tanzania: tied ridges helped maize in years of near-normal (500–600 mm) rainfall, but in wet years (700–900 mm) the maize showed waterlogging effects [ev_waterlogging_hazard_biaz12_15].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: The Cameroon result is an unpublished observation cited by the authors, with no magnitude [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]. The Ethiopian waterlogging finding is a field observation with no measured yield loss, and the source names a tillage treatment as the one particularly affected, so only part of the harm can be put on mulch and basins [ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_1, ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_2]. The southern African basin finding rests on a theoretical water balance plus extension reports and farmer testimony, and the author notes there are currently few published data to substantiate it [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_8]; the sub-humid conclusion goes beyond what the crop model simulates and covers conservation agriculture as basins or ripping with residue retention, so it is bundled with reduced tillage; neither gives a magnitude [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_7]. The Kenyan ridging loss is the authors' probable explanation rather than a measured waterlogging contrast, and the ridging is bundled with fertiliser; because it comes from using the practice at a wetter site than it suits, it is held out of the production classes as an envelope misfit (a suitability caveat) and counted here as waterlogging evidence [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6]. The Tanzanian finding is cited second-hand and gives no yield loss [ev_waterlogging_hazard_biaz12_15].

justification.mechanism: In the humid Sudanian zone of Cameroon, where daily rains exceed 80 mm, zaï pits concentrate infiltration and sorghum in the pits yielded less than on flat-cultivated fields [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]. In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, waterlogging lasting 3–5 days during early maize growth also affected the mulching and basin treatments, whose waterlogged plants had yellow leaves and stunted growth [ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_1, ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_2]. Primary sources from southern Africa make the same point: an FAO study shows by a water-balance calculation that planting basins can depress yields when too much water concentrates in them under high rainfall or in seasons with abnormally high rainfall, citing extension reports and farmer testimony of farmers scooping water from the basins [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_8], and concludes that in sub-humid environments yields could be affected by water-logging in years with adequate rainfall [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_7]. In a Kenyan on-farm trial, ridged plots with fertiliser at the relatively wetter sub-humid Rachuonyo site gave the lowest yields, slightly below conventional practice, which the authors say can probably be explained by waterlogging caused by ridging [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6]. In Tanzania, tied ridges that helped maize in years of near-normal rainfall (500–600 mm) caused waterlogging in wet years (700–900 mm) (Jensen et al. 2003, cited in a review) [ev_waterlogging_hazard_biaz12_15].

justification.mechanism: Sediment trapped behind water-harvesting structures slowly fills them, so they lose storage and soak up less water; the damage is real but builds up slowly, so it is rated slight. Sedimentation is described as perhaps the main reason sand dams fail [ev_asset_failure_ritc21_3]. In Tigray, Ethiopia, dams designed to last 30 years were set to fill in 4.4 to 5.7 years [ev_asset_siltation_saru19_1], and 50% of Ethiopian reservoirs studied were on course to lose their useful life before half their design period [ev_asset_siltation_saru19_2]. In Zambia, 8 of 10 reservoirs lost storage to silt and 3 lost over half their capacity [ev_asset_siltation_saru19_4]; 61% of Tigray micro-dams had benefits threatened by silt [ev_climate_shock_gebr18_5]; and in India 31% of earthen dams silted up within five years [ev_erosion_hazard_iegind11_12]. Check dams filled to more than 80% of their capacity within four years in Arizona [ev_sediment_retention_poly14_1_av] and fill quickly under heavy sediment loads in China [ev_climate_shock_shi19_4]; small Moroccan hill dams lose 0.5 to 1% of their capacity each year [ev_sediment_retention_roos10_1_av]. Silt on the floor of check dams and percolation tanks in India lowers how much water soaks into the ground [ev_climate_shock_dash17_4, ev_climate_shock_mass14_4, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_glen12_11_av]. In the field, stone bunds in Tigray trap less sediment once the space behind them fills [ev_climate_shock_gebr05_3_av], and in Burkina Faso larger half-moons of 2 and 3 m clog with a crust that cuts infiltration [ev_soil_permeability_zour25h1_8].

justification.mechanism: Sediment trapped behind water-harvesting structures slowly fills them, so they lose storage and soak up less water; the damage is real but builds up slowly, so it is rated slight. Sedimentation is described as perhaps the main reason sand dams fail [ev_asset_failure_ritc21_3]. In Tigray, Ethiopia, dams designed to last 30 years were set to fill in 4.4 to 5.7 years [ev_asset_siltation_saru19_1], and 50% of Ethiopian reservoirs studied were on course to lose their useful life before half their design period [ev_asset_siltation_saru19_2]. In Zambia, 8 of 10 reservoirs lost storage to silt and 3 lost over half their capacity [ev_asset_siltation_saru19_4]; 61% of Tigray micro-dams had benefits threatened by silt [ev_climate_shock_gebr18_5]; and in India 31% of earthen dams silted up within five years [ev_erosion_hazard_iegind11_12]. Check dams filled to more than 80% of their capacity within four years in Arizona [ev_sediment_retention_poly14_1_av] and fill quickly under heavy sediment loads in China [ev_climate_shock_shi19_4]; small Moroccan hill dams lose 0.5 to 1% of their capacity each year [ev_sediment_retention_roos10_1_av]. Silt on the floor of check dams and percolation tanks in India lowers how much water soaks into the ground [ev_climate_shock_dash17_4, ev_climate_shock_mass14_4, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_glen12_11_av].

The study links the decline to lack of regular maintenance and raising of the bunds, so the threat applies to unmaintained bunds [ev_climate_shock_gebr05_3_av]. justification.mechanism: Stone bunds trap the sediment that runoff carries, and that sediment wears down their function: on Tigray cropland, Gebremichael and colleagues found that when the depression behind a bund fills with sediment its trapping efficiency strongly decreases, and considerable soil is still lost, on average 18 t per hectare a year [ev_climate_shock_gebr05_3_av]. The threat is a decline in the service the bund gives, not damage to the bund itself [ev_climate_shock_gebr05_3_av].

justification.mechanism: Heavy rain moderately damages water-harvesting and conservation works. In China, storms caused widespread damage to terraces, with few local funds for repair [ev_climate_shock_iegchn07_7]; in Algeria, terraces and other traditional works were badly damaged or destroyed by extreme rain in recent years and are rebuilt after each event [ev_climate_shock_roose17_2_av], stone lines are overtopped by storms above 50 mm [ev_climate_shock_roose17_1_av], and unmaintained banquette networks breached in chains under long torrential rain [ev_climate_shock_arab04_1_av]. In a Kenyan trial, tied ridges collapsed in heavy rain and had to be rebuilt within the season [ev_climate_shock_ndun23_1_av]; in Morocco, earth bunds are overtopped in the biggest storms [ev_climate_shock_roos10_1_av]. A review of terraces worldwide reports riser collapse and landslides that can turn into debris flows in very heavy storms [ev_climate_shock_arna15_8_av, ev_climate_shock_arna15_9_av], poorly built vineyard terraces in Spain slid after a single storm [ev_climate_shock_wei16_2_av], and check dams often fail in extreme rain [ev_climate_shock_luca21_1_av]. Practitioner ratings agree: pits and bunds in Niger, terraces in Rwanda and Cape Verde and check dams in Nepal are rated as not coping well with local rainstorms [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1219_2014_local_rainstorm, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1613_2014_local_rainstorm, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1614_2014_local_rainstorm, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1616_2014_local_rainstorm, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1652_2014_local_rainstorm, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1553_2012_local_rainstorm, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1573_2013_local_rainstorm, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1493_2011_local_rainstorm].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: WOCAT compilers judge stone lines in Tunisia and a continuous bench terrace for tea in a high sloping area of Thailand to cope well with landslides, and vetiver-hedge bench terraces with trees in Haiti and bench terraces on hilly slopes in Bangladesh to cope very well [ev_asset_landslide_wocat_6610_2022_landslide, ev_asset_landslide_wocat_4281_2018_landslide, ev_asset_landslide_wocat_3223_2017_landslide, ev_asset_landslide_wocat_4284_2018_landslide]. The damage figures are secondary citations tied to marl and clay substrates and to abandonment rather than to maintained terraces, and the ratings are practitioner judgements [ev_climate_shock_arab04_2_av, ev_climate_shock_wei16_1_av].

retained_source_profiles.source_quote: Cultivated strips: On gentle slopes alternating cropping strips along the contour are built: the upper one is used as a catchment and the lower one is cropped. The width of the cropped strip ranges from 1 – 3 m. The C:A ratio is usually 1:1 but can reach 1:5 depending on rainfall and the crop. Often on the sides and the lower end of the cropped area soil bunds are constructed to impede runoff from the cropped area. source_purpose.quote:
Abstract Identifying potential sites for water harvesting
(WH) is a crucial task for efﬁcient water resources man-
agement in arid regions. In response, this paper proposes a
geographical information system-based model that combines
fuzzy logic and analytic hierarchy process (AHP) to delineate
suitable areas for constructing WH structures in arid south-
ern Iraq. Based on a literature review and available data, ﬁve
inﬂuential factors were selected to develop the model: hydro-
logical soil group, land cover, surface runoff depth, slope,
and distance to an intermittent river. A fuzzy logic-based
approach was used to standardize the factors, and AHP was
used to derive weights.

source_purpose.quote:
The main aim of this study is to present a technically robust and pragmatic methodology for evaluating
rainwater harvesting potential and identifying suitable sites for RWH and artiﬁcial recharge structures
using Geographic Information System (GIS)-based multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA). Unlike past
studies, this study proposes an approach to prioritize zones/sites for RWH and recharge structures, which
is of great importance for the effective implementation of RWH strategies. The derived themes ‘runoff
coefﬁcient’ and the basic themes of ‘slope’ and ‘drainage density’ were used for mapping rainwater
harvesting potential. Thereafter, suitable zones and sites for feasible RWH and recharge structures were
identiﬁed using suitability criteria and GIS-based Boolean logic.

T6E_economic_profile.conditionality: This is a single estimate from a single study, with no stated currency year, expressed per person gaining water access rather than per farmer or household, so it covers the water-access benefit only [ev_project_cost_lasage08_1]. The Kitui figure is the implementing NGO's own programme cost, reported by the organisation rather than independently audited, and the community's own labour and the local stone, sand and water it contributes are not costed [ev_project_cost_pauw08_1]. The two sand-dam cost estimates, from different Kenyan districts and different sources, agree closely on the per-capita order of magnitude.

T6E_economic_profile.effect_mechanism: In a Kenyan catchment, low-cost water measures built around sand dams are estimated to have given more than 100,000 people better access to water within 10 years at an investment of about 35 USD per capita [ev_project_cost_lasage08_1]. A separate account of sand dams in Kenya's Kitui District gives a similar material cost: about US$8,000 per dam on average, an investment of US$35 to 50 per person served [ev_project_cost_pauw08_1].

T6E_economic_profile.conditionality: The small cost class reflects the lower figures from Ethiopia, India, Yemen and Somalia; the Peru and China costs come from upper-middle-income settings, and the Jordan, Uzbekistan, Peru and China figures sit well above the rest [ev_project_cost_wocat_5770_2020_establishment, ev_project_cost_wocat_7553_2025_establishment, ev_project_cost_fao13c_1, ev_project_cost_wei16_1]. These are establishment costs, not costs per hectare restored, and the spread is wide because the technologies differ from hand-built terraces to engineered spate systems; the Ethiopian terracing figure is for terraces built with unpaid community labour decades ago [ev_project_cost_adgo13_8]. WOCAT figures are the compiler's own cost tables converted to USD with the sheet's exchange rate, not market prices. The India costs are described by the evaluator as high by national norms, the Peru figure is a 1994 assessment cited secondhand, and the Chinese terracing costs are a secondary table showing that steeper land costs more to terrace [ev_project_cost_iegind11_10, ev_project_cost_fao13c_1, ev_project_cost_wei16_1]. The Jordanian figure is cited second-hand from two other studies and covers only the mechanised bund construction, not the seedlings, planting or fencing established alongside it [ev_project_cost_tats21_3].

T6E_economic_profile.effect_mechanism: The pooled costs are up-front establishment or treatment costs per hectare. In Ethiopia, the initial investment in terracing was equivalent to US$ 46.51 per hectare in the first year of construction, with about US$ 48.8 per hectare needed to maintain it over the first three years [ev_project_cost_adgo13_8]. Indian watershed projects treated sub-watersheds at US$261 and US$217 per hectare [ev_project_cost_iegind11_10, ev_project_cost_iegind11_11], and spate systems in Yemen averaged USD 800-1200 per hectare to build, of which farmers paid 15-20% [ev_project_cost_yem12_8]. WOCAT compilers report establishment costs per hectare of 147.30 USD for gully works in Somalia, 345 and 1293 USD for technologies in Jordan and 2000 USD in Uzbekistan [ev_project_cost_wocat_7778_2026_establishment, ev_project_cost_wocat_5860_2021_establishment, ev_project_cost_wocat_5770_2020_establishment, ev_project_cost_wocat_7553_2025_establishment]. At the high end, rehabilitating pre-Columbian andenes in Peru cost USD 2,200 per hectare, and a review tabulates terracing costs in China of 1918 to 4045 USD per hectare, rising with the original slope from 5 to 25 degrees [ev_project_cost_fao13c_1, ev_project_cost_wei16_1]. At the low end, mechanised Vallerani micro-catchment bunds in Jordan's Badia cost an average of 20-30 US dollars per hectare to build, about 3 hectares per hour [ev_project_cost_tats21_3].

T6E_economic_profile.conditionality: Studies disagree because they cost different practices. The savings come where the practice removes a step, such as tillage or hand weeding, or where planning avoids building structures; the increase comes where the practice adds ridging [ev_project_cost_kida19_5, ev_project_cost_sime15h2_1, ev_project_cost_kar20_5, ev_project_cost_dalt14_2]. The Karnataka saving is against another conservation programme, not against doing nothing, and comes from a World Bank completion report [ev_project_cost_kar20_5]; the Ghana dam figures describe a spread of rehabilitation costs between implementers rather than a saving or an overrun [ev_project_cost_veno12_1]; the Mozambique basins also carry residue retention and herbicide weed control, and the Ethiopian statement gives no figure [ev_project_cost_kida19_5, ev_project_cost_sime15h2_1]. Cost evidence is ordinal here: read the row as which practices tend to cut or add costs, not as a price.
T6E_economic_profile.effect_mechanism: Water harvesting changes farm and programme costs in both directions. Practices that remove a step save money: in Mozambique labour costs were $153 per hectare for basins against $173 for conventional tillage, and in Ethiopia mulching reduced weed density and labour costs for weeding [ev_project_cost_kida19_5, ev_project_cost_sime15h2_1]. Better siting saves on construction: in Karnataka, land-resource-inventory planning avoided unnecessary structures, so works cost INR 14,228 per hectare against INR 18,739 under the conventional programme, a drop of 30 percent [ev_project_cost_kar20_5]. Practices that add earthworks raise costs: switching from flat-land production to tied ridges, with or without grass strips, increased the cost of production in Ghana's Nandom area [ev_project_cost_dalt14_2]. In Ghana, the share of small dams rehabilitated for less than USD 5,000 per irrigated hectare was 25% under government and 12% under development partners [ev_project_cost_veno12_1].

T6E_economic_profile.conditionality: What separates the sides is whether the practice removes work or adds a structure. The savings come from basins that replace conventional tillage, mulch that suppresses weeds and better siting of structures, which save labour or construction cost [ev_project_cost_kida19_5, ev_project_cost_sime15h2_1, ev_project_cost_kar20_5]; the cost increases come from building ridges or rehabilitating dams [ev_project_cost_dalt14_2, ev_project_cost_veno12_1]. The Mozambique saving is bundled with reduced tillage, residue retention and herbicide weed control, so it is not a pure capture effect [ev_project_cost_kida19_5]. The Karnataka saving is a planning-efficiency comparison between programmes rather than a with-and-without contrast, and the Ghana dam costs are thresholds from a review rather than a comparison with an alternative [ev_project_cost_kar20_5, ev_project_cost_veno12_1]. For scoping, expect labour savings from in-field moisture practices and added establishment costs for built structures.
T6E_economic_profile.effect_mechanism: Studies disagree on whether the practices lower or raise what farmers and projects pay. On the saving side: in Karnataka, planning structures from a land-resource inventory cut construction cost to INR 14,228 per hectare against INR 18,739 under the comparison programme, a drop of 30 percent [ev_project_cost_kar20_5]; in Mozambique, labour for the basin practice averaged $153 against $173 per hectare under conventional tillage [ev_project_cost_kida19_5]; and in Ethiopia mulching reduced labour costs for weeding [ev_project_cost_sime15h2_1]. On the cost side: in Ghanaian trials, switching from flat-land production to tied ridges with or without grass strips increased the cost of production [ev_project_cost_dalt14_2]; and in Ghana most rehabilitated small dams cost USD 5,000 or more per irrigated hectare, with only 25% of government and 12% of donor-rehabilitated dams below that [ev_project_cost_veno12_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Studies disagree, and what separates them is how the terrace is built and what is counted: hand-built stone bunds on cropland are credited with more crop diversity, while bulldozed earthen terraces on rangeland are linked to fewer wild herbaceous species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_6891_2023_plant_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_stav20_9]. Neither side is a measured species or habitat comparison: the Bhutan unit is a compiler rating and the Israeli unit a cited suggestion in a review, and neither comes from the target low-income contexts. A measured biodiversity outcome on terraced land, with the construction method stated, is needed before a direction can be given.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: The sources point in opposite directions for different kinds of terrace and different kinds of diversity. The WOCAT compiler for contour stone bunds in Bhutan rates plant diversity as greatly increased, linking it to the soil becoming suitable for more diverse crops [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_6891_2023_plant_diversity]. A rangeland-restoration review cites Stavi et al. (2015) from Israel suggesting that earthen contour bench terraces built by heavy machinery, which strip the soil's A-horizon from the hillslope, reduce the species richness of herbaceous vegetation, with Stavi and Argaman (2016) adding that the topsoil removal degrades soil quality [ev_biodiversity_outcome_stav20_9].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The gain is not universal: in Mexico, infiltration trenches were found to have actually decreased nitrogen and carbon content while increasing bulk density [ev_soil_organic_carbon_locat20_2], and in Burkina Faso, zai pits showed no significant change in soil fertility properties in the short term, even though biomass production had increased [ev_soil_organic_carbon_roose93_1]. Measured harm (maladaptation) — the practice worsening this outcome for some adopters — appears in 1 source. Within this family, micro-catchment systems score strongest and runoff-catchment weakest, so the roll-up states moderate rather than the pooled strong.

Soil organic matter and trapped sediment stand in for a measured carbon stock change, and carbon in check-dam sediment partly moves carbon eroded from upslope rather than removing new carbon from the air.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In semi-arid settings the practices add carbon removals mainly through soil storage: organic matter concentrated in zaï pits raised soil organic matter content from 1 to 1.4 percent on soils treated 3 and 5 years earlier in Burkina Faso, and farms using zaï and/or rock bunds there had more soil carbon than a control farm [ev_soil_organic_carbon_kabo04_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_sawa11h1_3]. T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: This benefit does not guarantee tree establishment. In an Ethiopian on-farm trial, micro-basins and trenches around newly planted tree seedlings showed no significant difference in survival compared with untreated control seedlings across three tree species; the authors attributed this null result to dry-season moisture scarcity too severe for the structures to bridge, together with insect and termite attack and browsing by free-grazing livestock [ev_establishment_survival_kinuthia20_1]. The evidence base is thin, three sources across Burkina Faso, China and Ethiopia, so this picture rests on a small, specific set of measurements rather than a broad literature.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Micro-catchment structures (fish-scale pits, micro-basins, trenches) concentrate scarce rainfall around planted trees or vegetation, building up soil carbon and biomass. A Burkina Faso practitioner rating found biomass production on treated sites increased 5 to 30 times compared with nearby unploughed soil, averaging 1000 to 1200 kilograms of dry matter per hectare against 70 to 110 on control plots [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_1528_2012_biomass_above_ground_C]. A meta-analysis of Chinese studies found fish-scale pits raised soil organic carbon storage on the Loess Plateau by 79.86% over 11 to 30 years, with terracing raising it by 14.11% to 60.96% over the same period [ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_12].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Both sides are real findings in semi-arid land, and what separates them is the outcome measured, the place and the scale of the works. The gain is groundwater and well levels on and around treated Sahelian fields and watersheds [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_zoug14_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_kabo04_1]; the loss is streamflow below a campaign of check dams built at very large scale in China to retain floodwater [ev_water_yield_luca21_1]. For a downstream user the Chinese finding is the relevant one; for a farmer near the works the Sahelian one is. Neither side compares with and without the works at catchment scale: the Sahelian units are cited statements, the 39% is cited by a review from another study, and in Burkina Faso the number of wells with water year round has not increased significantly since SWC began [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_kabo04_2]. A further Burkina Faso statement, cited from another study with no figures, also sits on the gain side [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_sawa11h1_6].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In the Sahel, stone bunds, zaï and half-moons applied at watershed scale increase ground water level [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_zoug14_1], and in Burkina Faso levels of water in wells have improved, which the source links not to higher rainfall but to SWC measures that control surface runoff and improve infiltration [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_kabo04_1]. On China's Loess Plateau, a large campaign of check-dam construction carried out since the 1970s to retain floodwater and intercept soil sediments reduced streamflow by approximately 39% [ev_water_yield_luca21_1]. In Burkina Faso, cited studies show soil and water conservation techniques improving the availability of ground water in many villages, especially large rock bunds known as digues filtrantes [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_sawa11h1_6].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks what capturing water upstream does to the water that reaches streams and reservoirs below, not whether the farm that captures it has more. The sides now conflict, and what separates them is what is measured and at what scale: the loss is streamflow below a check-dam campaign at very large scale built to retain floodwater [ev_water_yield_luca21_1], while the gains are recharge and water-table statements for small dispersed basins and trenches [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mira19_6, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_locat20_1]. In the Peruvian Andes trenches had little effect on increasing baseflow, with hydrogeological characteristics key to explaining their impact [ev_water_regulation_locat20_1]. None of this is a measured project comparison: the 39% is a secondary citation in a global review, the Peruvian statements are a review's summary, and the barraginha statement is Embrapa's self-assessment of its own technology [ev_water_yield_luca21_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_locat20_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mira19_6].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Upstream capture can both add to and take from downstream water. On China's Loess Plateau, a large campaign of check-dam construction carried out since the 1970s to retain floodwater and intercept soil sediments reduced streamflow by approximately 39% [ev_water_yield_luca21_1]. On the other side, Embrapa says its barraginhas in Brazil help recharge groundwater by raising the water table and revitalise springs and rivers [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mira19_6], and in the Peruvian Andes a few studies have observed catchment-level changes such as reduced quick runoff or increased aquifer recharge, which the source calls plausible but not generalisable [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_locat20_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Both dam figures are measured recharge added by the structure, with no-dam conditions used only as the counterfactual, not an actually measured case; the authors put 'dry' in quotation marks, since mean rainfall was similar in both years and the real difference was rainfall intensity and dry-spell length rather than a named drought [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_dash17_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_dash17_2]. The percolation-tank figures come from one tank at one site; most of the percolated water is drawn back by boreholes close to the tank, so the recharge benefit is local, and the paper itself flags its percolation-efficiency estimate as in the high range of earlier regional estimates [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mass14_1]. The borehole-contribution shares rest on an electrical-conductivity mixing analysis built on stated assumptions about tank-water and aquifer-water conductivity [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mass14_2, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mass14_3]. All five units are irrigated cropping systems in India; the mechanism is not yet shown for rainfed systems.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Check dams and percolation tanks raise catchment water yield by detaining monsoon runoff so it infiltrates to the aquifer rather than running off downstream. In Rajasthan, India, check dams, measured against no-dam conditions (the runoff otherwise flowing on down the ephemeral stream), added recharge of 33 mm over their combined catchment in an average year and 17 mm in a year the authors called 'dry' [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_dash17_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_dash17_2]. In Andhra Pradesh, a small percolation tank — managed aquifer recharge (MAR) by an earth weir across an intermittent stream — sent 57 to 63 percent (average 61 percent) of its stored water to the hard-rock aquifer rather than losing it to evapotranspiration [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mass14_1], and tank percolation supplied 40 percent of the water pumped from nearby irrigation boreholes in both a rainfall-deficit year [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mass14_2] and a normal-rainfall year, when it reached seven additional boreholes [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mass14_3].

justification.mechanism: In mixed crop–livestock settings the evidence is thin and points both ways. On the recharge side, recharge in Ethiopia's Mendae catchment rose from 8 mm before water-harvesting interventions to 107.7 mm after, by water balance (Negusse et al. 2013, cited in a review) [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_gebr18_11], and Embrapa says its barraginhas in Brazil help recharge groundwater by raising the water table and revitalise springs and rivers [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mira19_6]. T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks what capturing water upstream does to the water that reaches streams and reservoirs below, not whether the farm that captures it has more. Studies disagree because the recharge side counts water entering the ground near treated land, while the outflow side counts water leaving the catchment, and the same works can raise the first and lower the second [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_utk22_5, ev_water_yield_gebr18_9]. Scale and intensity also separate them: the outflow losses come from large-scale implementation and basin-wide models, while other studies find limited or no downstream impact on stream flows from small-scale storage, even when implemented widely (Schreider et al., 2002; De Winnaar and Jewitt, 2010; Andersson et al., 2011) [ev_water_yield_dile13_10, ev_water_yield_rock10_1]. The recharge gains have limits in their own sources: without data from untreated sites the Indian project impact is unclear [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_iegind11_3], subsidised tube-well pumping has possibly wiped out any increases in recharge [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_iegind11_4], and in Burkina Faso the number of wells with water year round has not increased significantly [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_kabo04_2]. The Uttarakhand figures are a modelled water budget [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_utk22_5], the outflow findings are all cited second-hand, and most other units are programme reports or cited statements; the digues filtrantes finding is cited from another study, with no figures [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_sawa11h1_6]. That listing is the review's own qualitative evaluation across cited sources, not a measured recharge figure [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_vohl09_3]. That well-level rise is the villagers' own attribution rather than a measurement against a comparable untreated well, and it adds to the recharge side of this row rather than resolving the conflict with the downstream-outflow evidence [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_botreij09_18].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Watershed-scale soil and water conservation is reported to raise groundwater, used here as a component of catchment water yield: stone bunds, zaï and half-moons applied at watershed scale increase ground water level [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_zoug14_1]; in Burkina Faso improved well levels are linked to SWC measures that control surface runoff and improve infiltration [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_kabo04_1]; ISRO survey data record an increase in groundwater recharge in treated areas in India [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_iegind11_3]; piezometers recorded groundwater levels rising in 16 of 21 non-desert districts with an average increase of 1.42 meters [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_verm19_3]; the Uttarakhand water budget shows aquifer recharge up 3.3 percent and water yield from catchment areas up 4.9 percent [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_utk22_5]; and in Ethiopia improvements in the water table made small-scale irrigation possible [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_eth16_7]. In Burkina Faso, cited studies show soil and water conservation techniques improving the availability of ground water in many villages, especially large rock bunds known as digues filtrantes [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_sawa11h1_6]. In Ethiopia's Mendae catchment a water balance gave groundwater recharge of 107.7 mm after water harvesting against 8 mm before (Negusse et al., 2013, cited by Gebremeskel et al.) [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_gebr18_11]. On the other side, the same capture reduces what leaves the catchment: water outflows from treated catchments have been found halved compared with untreated catchments (Garg et al., 2012; Gates et al., 2011, cited by Gebremeskel et al.), reviews cite a decrease in runoff generation harming downstream social–ecological systems (Batchelor et al., 2003; Glendenning and Vervoort, 2011; Garg et al., 2012, cited by Dile et al.), and a global model suggested rainwater harvesting would reduce annual river flows by 18% on average and by up to 80% in a single basin (Wisser et al., 2010, cited by Glendenning et al.) [ev_water_yield_gebr18_9, ev_water_yield_dile13_9, ev_water_yield_glen12_10]. A landscape review of rainwater harvesting across African drylands also lists groundwater recharge and the filling of wells among its benefits [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_vohl09_3]. A CILSS regional synthesis adds a further recharge observation: in Batodi, Niger, the water level in village wells rose by about 14 metres between 1994 and 2004, which the villagers attributed to the runoff-harvesting works [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_botreij09_18].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The same capture of water that recharges groundwater locally also reduces the water flowing downstream, and several studies measure this as a harm to catchment water yield. In India, a water-balance study estimated that increased rainwater harvesting at watershed scale would cut runoff by about 60% while increasing recharge by only 5% [ev_water_yield_glen12_2], and other analyses there found that even a small share of catchment area under rainwater harvesting sharply reduced the mean runoff coefficient, the share of rainfall converted to streamflow [ev_water_yield_glen09_1]. On China's Loess Plateau, decades of check-dam construction are credited with reducing streamflow by approximately 39% [ev_water_yield_luca21_1]. In Ethiopia, modelling under a high sand-dam development strategy and an extreme climate-change scenario found low-flow months rising from 18.2% of the period to 22.7% and 27.3% in two of those months, and the share of river discharge stored in sand dams in the first rainy season rising to 19.9%, compared with 9.3% under the historical reference period [ev_water_yield_lasa13_4, ev_water_yield_lasa13_5]; under a more moderate strategy with 613 sand dams, the same Ethiopian study found no change in low-flow occurrence [ev_water_yield_lasa13_3]. A separate theoretical modelling study concluded that the impact of rainwater harvesting on watershed water levels may be minimal beyond the immediate vicinity of the structure [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_glen12_8]. Whether a project nets out as a local groundwater gain or a downstream water-yield loss depends on the scale of implementation, a few structures versus watershed-wide development, and on where the account is drawn: the same captured water that recharges a well nearby is water that no longer reaches the river. Most of the quantified harm evidence comes from India, China and Ethiopia; this is the distinction, used elsewhere in this tool, between a benefit to the adopting farm and an effect on people downstream.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Check dams, sand dams and runoff-harvesting structures capture surface water that would otherwise run off, so it percolates into the ground and raises local groundwater. In India, floodwater-recession tanks recharged on average 61% of the water budget to percolation, and check dams were found to recharge an additional 33 millimetres of water across their catchment in an average year and 17 millimetres in a dry year [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mass14_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_dash17_1]. Sand dams in Burkina Faso and Kenya are similarly credited with recharging groundwater and supplying wells for domestic use and irrigation [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_foxr03_8, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_biaz12_27], and sand dams more generally can raise local groundwater, though the extent of the effect is often limited in space and time [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ritc21_1].
