T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The class is held at moderate because few of the benefit units say how big the effect is. Most of the pool is practitioner judgements and assertions without drought-loss metrics: an expert account from Brazil, a lender evaluation in China, compiler ratings from Cambodia and Somalia, and a review that counts how often small-reservoir studies cite improved drought resilience; only a Kenyan sand-dam catchment table compares people exposed to droughts against a control catchment, and its values are likely interview-derived [ev_drought_hazard_lasage08_1]. Subsurface dams in Brazil tended to dry out in a rainless year and small ones do not withstand long dry spells, which records no benefit when storage is exhausted rather than damage to the works [ev_drought_hazard_cirilo03_2, ev_drought_hazard_cirilo03_3]. The barraginha statement is Embrapa's self-assessment of its own technology, with no measured drought contrast and no normal-year reference [ev_drought_hazard_mira19_8]. The Burkina Faso analysis marks the limit of storage: a drought year, with a probability of 0.1, cannot be mitigated because there is insufficient water to harvest, and the late severe dry spells need at least three irrigation applications while the reservoir supports only two [ev_drought_hazard_fox05_5, ev_drought_hazard_fox05_6]. The Arvari drought results are model outputs too; the buffer is described for short-term mild drought and as only some buffer over longer runs of dry years, and the same model shows that as harvesting increases, downstream flow decreases [ev_drought_hazard_glen09_2, ev_drought_hazard_glen09_3].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Ponds, cisterns and check dams store runoff for use in dry periods: pond water used as supplemental irrigation reduces crop-loss risk in irregular years in semi-arid Brazil, cisterns in China are reported to be mitigating frequent periods of drought, a review of small reservoirs counts improved drought resilience among their cited benefits, and the compiler of a Cambodian on-farm pond sheet states the pond provides enough water even during drought [ev_drought_hazard_brito07_10, ev_drought_hazard_iegchn07_4, ev_drought_hazard_saru19_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_2844_2017_drought_impacts]. The WOCAT compiler for gabions and rock check dams in Somalia likewise judges drought impacts reduced, citing improved soil moisture retention and water infiltration [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_7778_2026_drought_impacts]. In a Kenyan catchment with sand dams the number of people exposed to droughts fell from 420 to 0 while a control catchment stayed at 600 [ev_drought_hazard_lasage08_1]. In Brazil, Embrapa describes its barraginhas, small semicircular runoff-retention basins dug along runoff paths in pastures and croplands, as storing water in the soil by infiltration and easing the effects of droughts on crops in the lowlands [ev_drought_hazard_mira19_8]. A Burkina Faso risk analysis of a farm reservoir used for supplemental irrigation finds that all of the mild dry spells can be mitigated, which explains the more frequent zero-stress seasons under irrigation than in the control, and that severe dry spells late in the season are partly mitigated, turned into mild ones [ev_drought_hazard_fox05_7, ev_drought_hazard_fox05_6]. In Glendenning's water-balance model of the Arvari catchment in Rajasthan, where community structures store monsoon runoff that recharges the shallow aquifer pumped for irrigation, harvesting decreased the impacts of short-term mild drought, and over runs of consecutive below-average rainfall years the sustainability of groundwater-fed irrigation declined less than without harvesting [ev_drought_hazard_glen09_2, ev_drought_hazard_glen09_3].

Subsurface dams in Brazil tended to dry out in a rainless year and small ones do not withstand long dry spells, which records no benefit when storage is exhausted rather than damage to the works [ev_drought_hazard_cirilo03_2, ev_drought_hazard_cirilo03_3]. The barraginha statement is Embrapa's self-assessment of its own technology, with no measured drought contrast and no normal-year reference [ev_drought_hazard_mira19_8]. The Burkina Faso analysis marks the limit of storage: a drought year, with a probability of 0.1, cannot be mitigated because there is insufficient water to harvest, and the late severe dry spells need at least three irrigation applications while the reservoir supports only two [ev_drought_hazard_fox05_5, ev_drought_hazard_fox05_6]. The Arvari drought results are model outputs too; the buffer is described for short-term mild drought and as only some buffer over longer runs of dry years, and the same model shows that as harvesting increases, downstream flow decreases [ev_drought_hazard_glen09_2, ev_drought_hazard_glen09_3].
justification.mechanism: Ponds, cisterns and check dams store runoff for use in dry periods: pond water used as supplemental irrigation reduces crop-loss risk in irregular years in semi-arid Brazil, cisterns in China are reported to be mitigating frequent periods of drought, a review of small reservoirs counts improved drought resilience among their cited benefits, and the compiler of a Cambodian on-farm pond sheet states the pond provides enough water even during drought [ev_drought_hazard_brito07_10, ev_drought_hazard_iegchn07_4, ev_drought_hazard_saru19_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_2844_2017_drought_impacts]. The WOCAT compiler for gabions and rock check dams in Somalia likewise judges drought impacts reduced, citing improved soil moisture retention and water infiltration [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_7778_2026_drought_impacts]. In a Kenyan catchment with sand dams the number of people exposed to droughts fell from 420 to 0 while a control catchment stayed at 600 [ev_drought_hazard_lasage08_1]. In Brazil, Embrapa describes its barraginhas, small semicircular runoff-retention basins dug along runoff paths in pastures and croplands, as storing water in the soil by infiltration and easing the effects of droughts on crops in the lowlands [ev_drought_hazard_mira19_8]. A Burkina Faso risk analysis of a farm reservoir used for supplemental irrigation finds that all of the mild dry spells can be mitigated, which explains the more frequent zero-stress seasons under irrigation than in the control, and that severe dry spells late in the season are partly mitigated, turned into mild ones [ev_drought_hazard_fox05_7, ev_drought_hazard_fox05_6]. In Glendenning's water-balance model of the Arvari catchment in Rajasthan, where community structures store monsoon runoff that recharges the shallow aquifer pumped for irrigation, harvesting decreased the impacts of short-term mild drought, and over runs of consecutive below-average rainfall years the sustainability of groundwater-fed irrigation declined less than without harvesting [ev_drought_hazard_glen09_2, ev_drought_hazard_glen09_3].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Some structures make flooding worse: in Niger, diversion banquettes visibly increased peak discharges (Heusch) [ev_flood_hazard_heusch95_1], and Ritchie and colleagues pass on a warning that larger sand dams raise the risk of flooding, erosion and seepage [ev_flood_hazard_ritc21_1]. Check dams had minimal effect against extreme floods, especially if ill-designed or not maintained [ev_flood_hazard_luca21_3], and in Morocco flood peaks fell only where floods were not too strong [ev_flood_hazard_roose17_3]. The Tunisian catchment is the main measured result and bundles a grazing closure with the works; most other support is second-hand findings, authors' statements, a user perception survey and practitioner ratings. Much of the benefit falls downstream rather than on the farm that builds the works.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Across sub-practices the evidence points to a moderate reduction in flood hazard. The main measured result is from a semi-arid Tunisian catchment treated with dry-stone contour walls, gully check structures and some bench terraces, alongside a grazing closure of the whole catchment (Bergaoui and Albergel, a before-and-after comparison with no control catchment): flood peaks were strongly clipped and flood rise and base times nearly doubled [ev_flood_hazard_bergaoui00_2], peak discharge of large floods fell to 60% or 87% of its pre-treatment level depending on the reference period [ev_flood_hazard_bergaoui00_3], and the paper's conclusion reports flood volume and peaks falling by about 50% [ev_flood_hazard_bergaoui00_1]. Reviews pass on further results: terraces cut flood peaks on small mountain plots and stone bunds lower peak runoff in Burkina Faso (Roose) [ev_flood_hazard_roose06_1, ev_flood_hazard_roose94_1], check dams cut flooding in Iran and withstood strong floods in Italy (Lucas-Borja and colleagues) [ev_flood_hazard_luca21_1, ev_flood_hazard_luca21_2], and terraces reduced peak flow in the few catchment studies reviewed by Willems and colleagues [ev_flood_hazard_willem21_1]. Authors also state benefits without measuring them: small dams damping flood damage in Morocco (Roose) [ev_flood_hazard_roos10_1], treated ravines and wadi terraces slowing floods in Haiti and Morocco and contour barriers with pits reducing flood risk in the largest storms in Burkina Faso (Roose and co-authors) [ev_flood_hazard_roose17_1, ev_flood_hazard_roose17_2, ev_flood_hazard_roose17_3], hill terraces limiting flood damage in India and spate structures controlling floods in Yemen (World Bank reports) [ev_flood_hazard_utk22_7, ev_flood_hazard_yem12_4], and barraginhas easing floods in Brazil (Embrapa) [ev_flood_hazard_mira19_7]. T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The gains depend on the rainfall year, on where the works are built and on practice choice. In Niger, farm families with soil and water conservation produced an estimated surplus of 70 percent in good rainfall years but a deficit of 28 percent in low-rainfall years [ev_food_security_kabo04_1]; in Malawi's El Nino season, banking lowered the odds of meeting the maize requirement from 0.19 to 0.054 [ev_food_security_boil19_3]. Independent evaluations of Ethiopian programmes found communal, mostly off-farm watershed works did not raise food security, possibly because the programmes were short [ev_food_security_abate21_4, ev_food_security_arega24_1], and compilers record no change for vetiver terraces in Haiti, where land users must wait for degraded soil to recover [ev_food_security_wocat_3223_2017_food_security_selfsufficiency]. Much of the literature is cited second-hand or qualitative, and the Brazilian findings include Embrapa's assessment of its own technology and programme reviews [ev_food_security_mira19_2, ev_food_security_castro22_3]. The class is moderate because the sub-practices differ, from slight for cross-family evidence to strong for in-field practices. A gain in a good season does not by itself show the practice protects food supply through drought. The Anjene account rests on farmer recall and group discussions, and the dietary finding is second-hand with no magnitude [ev_food_security_adgo13_11, ev_food_security_biaz12_26]. That rating is the review's own qualitative evaluation across several cited sources, not a single measured contrast [ev_food_security_vohl09_4]. The same synthesis also records a null result: in Burkina Faso's bad 2007 harvest, households in heavily treated villages still bought cereal at the market, 26 kilograms per person on average against 38 kilograms in lightly treated villages, a gap the authors read as the yield advantage not translating into greater food security that year [ev_food_security_botreij09_21].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Water harvesting and soil and water conservation reduce food insecurity mainly by raising and steadying harvests and by putting stored water on gardens. In the Brazilian semi-arid, subsurface dams gave families more fruit and vegetables and, by most interviewees' account, more food overall, and production cisterns allow daily irrigation of gardens in households that had not grown or eaten vegetables before [ev_food_security_cirilo03_6, ev_food_security_arsky20_6]; in Burkina Faso, runoff cisterns irrigate small gardens and water livestock, improving food security in the lean season [ev_food_security_roose94_1]. In the field, planting basins (zai pits) raised the odds of a Kenyan plot meeting the household maize requirement to 421.75 against 1.67 in the control, and ground cover raised those odds in Malawi's El Nino season [ev_food_security_boil19_2, ev_food_security_boil19_1]. Household food security rises in proportion to the area of a farm improved with bunds, and beneficiaries of Rwanda's terracing project showed drastically improved food consumption scores against a comparison group [ev_food_security_zoug14_1, ev_food_security_rwa18_5]. WOCAT compilers rate food self-sufficiency as improved and the risk of production failure as lowered, and say why: enough stored water to irrigate during drought in Cambodia, better soil moisture in Ethiopia, more cultivable land and crop diversity in Bhutan, more productive fodder and crops in Burkina Faso, and rehabilitated gullies and farmland in Somalia [ev_food_security_wocat_2844_2017_risk_of_production_failure, ev_food_security_wocat_6715_2023_risk_of_production_failure, ev_food_security_wocat_6891_2023_food_security_selfsufficiency, ev_food_security_wocat_6891_2023_risk_of_production_failure, ev_food_security_wocat_1528_2012_food_security_selfsufficiency, ev_food_security_wocat_1528_2012_risk_of_production_failure, ev_food_security_wocat_7778_2026_food_security_selfsufficiency]. In Ethiopia's Anjene catchment, farmers recalled that before terracing the community was highly food insecure and migrated in search of food even in minor droughts, and that terraces improved crop production and reduced seasonal migration [ev_food_security_adgo13_11]. Ethiopian farmers who adopted rainwater-harvesting irrigation properly improved their dietary status (Desta 2004, cited in a review) [ev_food_security_biaz12_26]. A landscape review of in-situ rainwater harvesting across African drylands rates food security — yields in bad years and the bridging of dry spells — as a benefit with a 'Good' evidence basis [ev_food_security_vohl09_4]. A CILSS regional synthesis adds a further perception survey: in 2005-2006 surveys in Niger, 70 percent of people in villages with natural-resource-management investment reported an improvement in food security, against only 1 percent in control villages [ev_food_security_botreij09_20].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The size of the gain is limited because the supporting findings are qualitative, cited second-hand and give no size, while the independent evaluations point the other way. In Ethiopia, an impact evaluation of a bundled watershed project found no significant food-security effect for treated households at any participation level [ev_food_security_abate21_4], and public-works participation in communal soil and water investments did not translate into increased food security, possibly because of the short programme [ev_food_security_arega24_1]; both concern mostly off-farm community works. In Niger, families with soil and water conservation produced a surplus of 70 percent in good rainfall years but a deficit of 28 percent in low-rainfall years [ev_food_security_kabo04_1], so benefits may not hold in the dry years that matter most. That rating is the review's own qualitative evaluation across several cited sources, not a single measured contrast [ev_food_security_vohl09_4]. The same synthesis also records a null result: in Burkina Faso's bad 2007 harvest, households in heavily treated villages still bought cereal at the market, 26 kilograms per person on average against 38 kilograms in lightly treated villages, a gap the authors read as the yield advantage not translating into greater food security that year [ev_food_security_botreij09_21].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Across mixed soil and water conservation and water-harvesting programmes, the reported route to lower food insecurity is higher yields and irrigated gardens. A review tabulates significantly increased food security from check dams and infiltration pits in Malawi [ev_food_security_ngur26_1]; Brazilian studies judge production-cistern irrigation of small beds feasible and important for household food security [ev_food_security_castro22_3]; and higher yields are cited as improving food security in Burkina Faso, especially on farms with soil and water conservation on over half of their plots [ev_food_security_sawa11h1_5]. A landscape review of rainwater harvesting across African drylands also rates food security — yields in bad years and the bridging of dry spells — as a benefit with a 'Good' evidence basis [ev_food_security_vohl09_4]. A CILSS regional synthesis adds a further perception survey: in 2005-2006 surveys in Niger, 70 percent of people in villages with natural-resource-management investment reported an improvement in food security, against only 1 percent in control villages [ev_food_security_botreij09_20].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The same structures can cost yield before they pay off: the same review found soil and stone bunds reducing crop yield by up to 7% in the first few years after construction [ev_crop_yield_adim16_7], and in semi-arid Tanzania, stone bunds were found to reduce maize yield by 13% [ev_crop_yield_adim16_9]. In Ethiopia's high-rainfall Amhara region, a farm survey found no significant yield difference between conserved and non-conserved plots, with the point estimate actually negative, and the authors suggest moisture conservation may contribute to waterlogging, weeds and pests in wetter areas [ev_agricultural_production_value_kass08_2]. Measured harm (maladaptation) — the practice worsening this outcome for some adopters — appears in 13 sources. The Africa-wide maize gain is a model, not a field measurement, and the same authors judge that rainwater harvesting will likely not protect yields against the more frequent lethal high temperatures expected in the Sahel [ev_crop_yield_lebel15_1, ev_crop_yield_lebel15_2]. In an extreme drought the gain disappears: at Lamego, the driest of Thierfelder and colleagues' on-farm sites in central Mozambique, the 2010/2011 season was so heavily affected by drought that no cowpea yield was obtained in any treatment, planting basins with mulch included [ev_crop_yield_thierf15_5].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Soil and water conservation structures raise farm production mainly by conserving moisture and nutrients on the plot over time. In Ethiopia's Blue Nile basin highlands, households that adopted sustainable land and water management technologies early saw 15.2% higher value of production by 2010 [ev_agricultural_production_value_schmidt12_1], and plots that received the investment in the first period saw 20.6% higher production value than matched plots that did not [ev_agricultural_production_value_schmidt12_4]. A review of more than a hundred Ethiopian soil-and-water-conservation studies found stone and soil bunds raising crop yield by up to 10% in Tigray [ev_crop_yield_adim16_8]. A continental model of in situ rainwater harvesting for rainfed maize across Africa finds that, where it steadies yields, the mean potential yield gain is 9 to 39% under the climate of the 1990s, rising to 14–50% by the 2050s depending on the climate model [ev_crop_yield_lebel15_1]. In central Mozambique, Thierfelder and colleagues found planting basins with mulch significantly outyielded the conventional control for cowpea at their driest site [ev_crop_yield_thierf15_4].

justification.conditionality: The same structures can cost yield before they pay off: the same review found soil and stone bunds reducing crop yield by up to 7% in the first few years after construction [ev_crop_yield_adim16_7], and in semi-arid Tanzania, stone bunds were found to reduce maize yield by 13% [ev_crop_yield_adim16_9]. In Ethiopia's high-rainfall Amhara region, a farm survey found no significant yield difference between conserved and non-conserved plots, with the point estimate actually negative, and the authors suggest moisture conservation may contribute to waterlogging, weeds and pests in wetter areas [ev_agricultural_production_value_kass08_2]. Measured harm (maladaptation) — the practice worsening this outcome for some adopters — appears in 13 sources. The Africa-wide maize gain is a model, not a field measurement, and the same authors judge that rainwater harvesting will likely not protect yields against the more frequent lethal high temperatures expected in the Sahel [ev_crop_yield_lebel15_1, ev_crop_yield_lebel15_2]. In an extreme drought the gain disappears: at Lamego, the driest of Thierfelder and colleagues' on-farm sites in central Mozambique, the 2010/2011 season was so heavily affected by drought that no cowpea yield was obtained in any treatment, planting basins with mulch included [ev_crop_yield_thierf15_5].

justification.mechanism: Soil and water conservation structures raise farm production mainly by conserving moisture and nutrients on the plot over time. In Ethiopia's Blue Nile basin highlands, households that adopted sustainable land and water management technologies early saw 15.2% higher value of production by 2010 [ev_agricultural_production_value_schmidt12_1], and plots that received the investment in the first period saw 20.6% higher production value than matched plots that did not [ev_agricultural_production_value_schmidt12_4]. A review of more than a hundred Ethiopian soil-and-water-conservation studies found stone and soil bunds raising crop yield by up to 10% in Tigray [ev_crop_yield_adim16_8]. A continental model of in situ rainwater harvesting for rainfed maize across Africa finds that, where it steadies yields, the mean potential yield gain is 9 to 39% under the climate of the 1990s, rising to 14–50% by the 2050s depending on the climate model [ev_crop_yield_lebel15_1]. In central Mozambique, Thierfelder and colleagues found planting basins with mulch significantly outyielded the conventional control for cowpea at their driest site [ev_crop_yield_thierf15_4].
justification.pool_note: This row draws on 345 evidence unit(s) from 108 source(s); the weighting counts sources, not units, so several findings from one paper do not multiply its say.
justification.statement: water_harvesting_conservation strongly reduces production_gap in BFA, BRA, BTN, CAN, CHN, CMR, COD, DZA, ECU, ERI, ESP, ETH, GHA, HTI, IND, JOR, JPN, KEN, KHM, KOR, MAR, MLI, MOZ, MRT, MWI, NER, NGA, PAK, PER, PSE, RWA, SDN, SOM, TUN, TZA, UGA, USA, ZAF, ZMB, ZWE; measured HARM (maladaptation) in 13 sources — the practice worsened this outcome for some adopters (robust evidence, high agreement → very_high confidence; transfer: in_context).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The class is set by the gains. The fanya juu and soil bund losses and the finding that annual rainfall above 1000 mm affected performance negatively are held out of it, because the synthesis puts that effect down to excessive water availability (water logging) on the furrows of structures [ev_crop_yield_adim16_2, ev_crop_yield_adim16_6]: they are logged as a performance caveat — these structures should not be applied where rainfall is that heavy — rather than as production evidence. The evidence points to three things that separate gains from losses. Practice type: stone bunds, tied ridges and mulching gained, while graded and level fanya juu, soil bunds and grass strips lost yield in the Ethiopian table [ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_2]. Rainfall: the gaining practices were studied at lower average rainfall (695.1 mm for tied ridges, 876.7 mm for mulching) than the losing bunds (1030.2 to 1454.3 mm), and rainfall above 1000 mm reduced performance [ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_6]; practice and rainfall travel together in that table, so the two cannot be fully separated. Time: bunds lose yield in the first few years, while the long-established fanya juu terraces of the Ethiopian with-and-without survey yielded more than un-terraced fields, so fanya juu is not a losing practice everywhere [ev_crop_yield_adim16_7, ev_crop_yield_adgo13_1]. Against those terrace gains, the same paper cites Herweg and Ludi (1999) and Kassie et al. (2008) finding that fanya juu, soil and stone bunds and grass strips did not increase crop yield or biomass in the highlands of Ethiopia and Eritrea [ev_crop_yield_adgo13_12]. For a Task Team Leader the actionable reading is to match the structure to the rainfall regime, favouring in-field moisture capture in drier highlands and avoiding fanya juu and soil bunds where waterlogging is likely, and to budget for an early yield dip. At the dry end, tied ridging gave no advantage in the Kenyan short rains with meteorological droughts, since there was little rain to hold [ev_crop_yield_ndun23_2, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_4, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_5]. On quality, both sides rest mainly on the same Ethiopian synthesis of unweighted means pooled across studies; the Kenyan result is a single-site trial whose lower-variability finding was not tested, the Peruvian figure is cited in a review, and the Ethiopian terrace gains are descriptive statistics from a comparison of terraced and adjacent un-terraced farms, not a controlled trial [ev_crop_yield_adim16_1, ev_yield_stability_ndun23_1, ev_crop_yield_wei16_4, ev_crop_yield_adgo13_2].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In the tropical highlands, soil and water conservation has measured yield gains and measured yield losses, depending on the practice. Gains: an Ethiopian synthesis finds mean grain-yield gains of 322 kg per hectare for stone bunds, 554.3 for tied ridges and 629.2 for mulching, stone and soil bunds raising yields by up to 10% in Tigray, and stone bunds raising soil total nitrogen from 0.16 to 0.20% [ev_crop_yield_adim16_1, ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_4, ev_crop_yield_adim16_8, ev_soil_nitrogen_adim16_1]; in a Kenyan highland trial, tied ridges in long rains with dry spells gave 4.10 against 3.15 t of maize per hectare with manure and fertiliser, and 2.53 against 1.82 t without inputs (not significant), and tended to give less variable yields [ev_crop_yield_ndun23_3, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_1, ev_yield_stability_ndun23_1]; in Peru, 2 to 4-year old bench terraces gave 20% greater yields than adjacent sloping fields [ev_crop_yield_wei16_4]. In the Ethiopian highlands, fields with long-established fanya juu terraces and grass strips yielded 0.95 against 0.49 t of teff, 1.86 against 0.61 t of barley and 1.73 against 0.77 t of maize per hectare on adjacent un-terraced farms, and the terraces improved the water productivity of the three crops by at least 100% [ev_crop_yield_adgo13_1, ev_crop_yield_adgo13_2, ev_crop_yield_adgo13_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_adgo13_7]. Losses: in the same Ethiopian synthesis fanya juu and soil bunds were associated with yield losses of 54 to 193 kg per hectare, bunds cut yields by up to 7% in the first few years, and annual rainfall above 1000 mm affected performance negatively, which the authors suggest may be waterlogging in the furrows of structures [ev_crop_yield_adim16_2, ev_crop_yield_adim16_7, ev_crop_yield_adim16_6].

Practice type: stone bunds, tied ridges and mulching gained, while graded and level fanya juu, soil bunds and grass strips lost yield in the Ethiopian table [ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_2]. Rainfall: the gaining practices were studied at lower average rainfall (695.1 mm for tied ridges, 876.7 mm for mulching) than the losing bunds (1030.2 to 1454.3 mm), and rainfall above 1000 mm reduced performance [ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_6]; practice and rainfall travel together in that table, so the two cannot be fully separated. Time: bunds lose yield in the first few years, while the long-established fanya juu terraces of the Ethiopian with-and-without survey yielded more than un-terraced fields, so fanya juu is not a losing practice everywhere [ev_crop_yield_adim16_7, ev_crop_yield_adgo13_1]. Against those terrace gains, the same paper cites Herweg and Ludi (1999) and Kassie et al. (2008) finding that fanya juu, soil and stone bunds and grass strips did not increase crop yield or biomass in the highlands of Ethiopia and Eritrea [ev_crop_yield_adgo13_12]. For a Task Team Leader the actionable reading is to match the structure to the rainfall regime, favouring in-field moisture capture in drier highlands and avoiding fanya juu and soil bunds where waterlogging is likely, and to budget for an early yield dip. At the dry end, tied ridging gave no advantage in the Kenyan short rains with meteorological droughts, since there was little rain to hold [ev_crop_yield_ndun23_2, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_4, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_5]. On quality, both sides rest mainly on the same Ethiopian synthesis of unweighted means pooled across studies; the Kenyan result is a single-site trial whose lower-variability finding was not tested, the Peruvian figure is cited in a review, and the Ethiopian terrace gains are descriptive statistics from a comparison of terraced and adjacent un-terraced farms, not a controlled trial [ev_crop_yield_adim16_1, ev_yield_stability_ndun23_1, ev_crop_yield_wei16_4, ev_crop_yield_adgo13_2].

justification.mechanism: In the tropical highlands, soil and water conservation has measured yield gains and measured yield losses, depending on the practice. Gains: an Ethiopian synthesis finds mean grain-yield gains of 322 kg per hectare for stone bunds, 554.3 for tied ridges and 629.2 for mulching, stone and soil bunds raising yields by up to 10% in Tigray, and stone bunds raising soil total nitrogen from 0.16 to 0.20% [ev_crop_yield_adim16_1, ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_4, ev_crop_yield_adim16_8, ev_soil_nitrogen_adim16_1]; in a Kenyan highland trial, tied ridges in long rains with dry spells gave 4.10 against 3.15 t of maize per hectare with manure and fertiliser, and 2.53 against 1.82 t without inputs (not significant), and tended to give less variable yields [ev_crop_yield_ndun23_3, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_1, ev_yield_stability_ndun23_1]; in Peru, 2 to 4-year old bench terraces gave 20% greater yields than adjacent sloping fields [ev_crop_yield_wei16_4]. In the Ethiopian highlands, fields with long-established fanya juu terraces and grass strips yielded 0.95 against 0.49 t of teff, 1.86 against 0.61 t of barley and 1.73 against 0.77 t of maize per hectare on adjacent un-terraced farms, and the terraces improved the water productivity of the three crops by at least 100% [ev_crop_yield_adgo13_1, ev_crop_yield_adgo13_2, ev_crop_yield_adgo13_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_adgo13_7]. Losses: in the same Ethiopian synthesis fanya juu and soil bunds were associated with yield losses of 54 to 193 kg per hectare, bunds cut yields by up to 7% in the first few years, and annual rainfall above 1000 mm affected performance negatively, which the authors suggest may be waterlogging in the furrows of structures [ev_crop_yield_adim16_2, ev_crop_yield_adim16_7, ev_crop_yield_adim16_6].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Some evidence finds harm or no effect, and pooling many technologies together can mask which practice is responsible. A meta-analysis attributed most of its negative-yield observations to in-soil water-harvesting technologies specifically [ev_crop_yield_boum16_2], and in Ethiopia soil and stone bunds reduced crop yield by up to 7% in their first few years after construction [ev_crop_yield_adim16_7]. A separate Ethiopian evaluation found no measurable gain in crop productivity or household income from soil and water conservation promoted mainly for off-farm, community resource protection [ev_crop_yield_abate21_1]. At the extreme end of scale, the same global hydrological model that projected a 35% rise in crop production found this would come with an average 18% reduction in river flows, and a reduction of up to 80% in a single river basin, illustrating the trade-off between on-farm production gains and downstream water availability [ev_crop_yield_glen12_9]. Most of the quantified gains are from low-income countries in the Sahel and East Africa (Burkina Faso, Niger, Ethiopia, Mauritania) and lower-middle-income South Asia (India); the harm and no-effect findings are concentrated in Ethiopia. The Africa-wide maize gain is a model, and its authors judge that rainwater harvesting will likely not protect yields against the more frequent lethal high temperatures expected in the semi-arid tropics [ev_crop_yield_lebel15_1, ev_crop_yield_lebel15_2].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Pooled across soil and water conservation technologies, large programme evaluations consistently find higher crop yield and production value where farmers have adopted water harvesting. In India, a watershed project raised average rainfed-crop yield by 24% relative to a control group in one phase and by 26% in the next [ev_crop_yield_iegind11_1], and a separate Indian project achieved a 20.8% increase in rainfed-crop productivity attributable to its interventions [ev_crop_yield_utk22_1]. In Ethiopia, early adopters of sustainable land and water management technologies had a 15.2% higher value of production years later [ev_agricultural_production_value_schmidt12_1], and a national impact evaluation found that soil and water conservation on communal land raised crop yields by 9.1% [ev_crop_yield_eth16_1]. In Mauritania, yields in humid watershed zones rose from 0.5 to more than 1.2 tonnes per hectare [ev_crop_yield_mrt14_2]. In Burkina Faso, zaï pits combined with stone lines are credited with sorghum yield increases of over 100%, and maize yield increases of over 100% when the two measures are combined [ev_crop_yield_ngur26_3], and a regional review found soil and water conservation works raising millet yields by 15% to 50% and sorghum yields by 20% to 85% depending on the region, against a considerable decline in cereal yields in control villages [ev_crop_yield_botreij09_1]. A global hydrological model found that expanding rainwater harvesting could raise crop production by 35% at river-basin scale [ev_crop_yield_glen12_9]. A continental model of in situ rainwater harvesting for rainfed maize across Africa finds that, where it steadies yields, the mean potential yield gain is 9 to 39% under the climate of the 1990s, rising to 14–50% by the 2050s depending on the climate model [ev_crop_yield_lebel15_1].

justification.mechanism: Pooled across soil and water conservation technologies, large programme evaluations consistently find higher crop yield and production value where farmers have adopted water harvesting. In India, a watershed project raised average rainfed-crop yield by 24% relative to a control group in one phase and by 26% in the next [ev_crop_yield_iegind11_1], and a separate Indian project achieved a 20.8% increase in rainfed-crop productivity attributable to its interventions [ev_crop_yield_utk22_1]. In Ethiopia, early adopters of sustainable land and water management technologies had a 15.2% higher value of production years later [ev_agricultural_production_value_schmidt12_1], and a national impact evaluation found that soil and water conservation on communal land raised crop yields by 9.1% [ev_crop_yield_eth16_1]. In Mauritania, yields in humid watershed zones rose from 0.5 to more than 1.2 tonnes per hectare [ev_crop_yield_mrt14_2]. In Burkina Faso, zaï pits combined with stone lines are credited with sorghum yield increases of over 100%, and maize yield increases of over 100% when the two measures are combined [ev_crop_yield_ngur26_3], and a regional review found soil and water conservation works raising millet yields by 15% to 50% and sorghum yields by 20% to 85% depending on the region, against a considerable decline in cereal yields in control villages [ev_crop_yield_botreij09_1]. A global hydrological model found that expanding rainwater harvesting could raise crop production by 35% at river-basin scale [ev_crop_yield_glen12_9]. A continental model of in situ rainwater harvesting for rainfed maize across Africa finds that, where it steadies yields, the mean potential yield gain is 9 to 39% under the climate of the 1990s, rising to 14–50% by the 2050s depending on the climate model [ev_crop_yield_lebel15_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: In-situ structures can also underperform or backfire: at a semi-arid Kenyan site, pitting with fertiliser was the lowest-yielding treatment of all, below even the conventional-tillage control (1.2 versus 1.6 tonnes per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_rock09_9]; and in Zimbabwe, conservation agriculture on its own was found to decrease maize yields with no significant advantage for other crops [ev_crop_yield_mich19_2], and to have no significant impact on any crop in an average-rainfall year [ev_crop_yield_mich19_1]. Measured harm (maladaptation) — the practice worsening this outcome for some adopters — appears in 5 sources. In an extreme drought the gain disappears: at Lamego, the driest of Thierfelder and colleagues' on-farm sites in central Mozambique, the 2010/2011 season was so heavily affected by drought that no cowpea yield was obtained in any treatment, planting basins with mulch included [ev_crop_yield_thierf15_5].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In-situ structures like planting basins and pits raise yields mainly by holding more rainwater where the crop can use it. In Zambia, conservation farming using planting basins plus lime raised yields by 68% against a comparator where timely conventional farming alone achieved 50% [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_1], and a separate Zambian study found conservation farming could raise maize and cotton yields by around 40% through earlier planting and improved soil quality [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_6]. A review of Ethiopian conservation practices found stone bunds adding 321.7 kg per hectare to grain yield on average [ev_crop_yield_adim16_3]. In central Mozambique, Thierfelder and colleagues found planting basins with mulch significantly outyielded the conventional control for cowpea at their driest site [ev_crop_yield_thierf15_4].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Animal production was rated lower on the Niger sheets because treated rangeland must be protected from grazing for the first years while vegetation establishes [ev_livestock_productivity_wocat_1613_2014_animal_production, ev_livestock_productivity_wocat_1614_2014_animal_production]. The Burkina Faso half-moon contrast is against land where direct seeding produced no grain, with compost added to the pits, so it measures bringing degraded land into production rather than an improvement on a cropped field [ev_crop_yield_zour25h1_2]. The FAO manual cites earlier work, the review figures are ranges and single citations rather than pooled estimates, and the WOCAT units are practitioner judgements [ev_crop_yield_fao13c_1, ev_crop_yield_fao13c_2, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_2, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_5]. In Tigray, irrigation from government-supported water-harvesting schemes was found to be risk-increasing on its own, becoming risk-reducing only in combination with improved seeds and fertiliser [ev_yield_stability_kato11_8]. T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Farm ponds that store runoff for supplemental irrigation raise yield especially when paired with fertiliser. In northern Burkina Faso, control grain yield averaged 455 kg per hectare over three years; supplemental irrigation alone raised it to 712 kg per hectare, fertiliser alone to 975 kg per hectare, and the two combined to 1403 kg per hectare — more than three times the farmer's normal yield [ev_crop_yield_foxr03_1]. justification.mechanism: In Ethiopia's Tigray region, a farm survey found stone-bund-conserved plots had a yield premium of 412 Ethiopian Birr per hectare over non-conserved plots [ev_agricultural_production_value_kass08_1]. Nationally, terracing's drought-season effect strengthened with dry-day exposure: yields were 14% lower than matched unterraced plots when dry days were few, but 17% higher when dry days were most frequent [ev_crop_yield_kosm18_5].
justification.pool_note: This row draws on 86 evidence unit(s) from 32 source(s); the weighting counts sources, not units, so several findings from one paper do not multiply its say.
justification.statement: water_harvesting_conservation strongly reduces production_gap in BFA, BTN, CAN, CHN, CMR, COD, DZA, ERI, ESP, ETH, GHA, HTI, IND, KEN, MAR, MLI, MWI, NER, NGA, PER, PSE, RWA, TUN, TZA, UGA; measured HARM (maladaptation) in 6 sources — the practice worsened this outcome for some adopters (robust evidence, high agreement → very_high confidence; transfer: in_context).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The economics do not always work out: a review of Ethiopian conservation practices found negative net present values for graded fanya juu (−148 Ethiopian Birr per hectare) and graded soil bunds (−708 Ethiopian Birr per hectare), which the authors attribute to cost-benefit analyses that do not fully capture on-site and off-site benefits [ev_economic_return_adim16_4]. In Zimbabwe, conservation agriculture was found to generate less revenue than conventional tillage for maize and cowpea over a large part of the rainfall distribution [ev_economic_return_mich19_8]. In Tigray, stone-bund building and maintenance costs were found to be nearly the same as the financial benefits from yield improvement, making the economic case close to break-even [ev_economic_return_nyss07_10]. Measured harm (maladaptation) — the practice worsening this outcome for some adopters — appears in 11 sources. Within this family, micro-catchment, runoff-catchment and terracing systems point positive while cross-family and in-situ readings disagree internally, so the roll-up states conflicting evidence rather than the pooled strong positive.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Water harvesting raises rural household income mainly through higher-value production: in Ghana, net rice profit rose by 16% under soil and water conservation [ev_economic_return_mala24_1]. In Ethiopia's Lake Tana watershed, an IFAD-funded watershed project raised the income of high-participation households by 17.8% over the control group [ev_household_income_abate21_3], though the programme-wide average effect on log income was only 0.044 [ev_household_income_abate21_2].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Against this, the same Ethiopian synthesis found graded fanya juu and graded soil bunds carrying negative net present values of −148 and −708 ETB per hectare [ev_economic_return_adim16_4], and in a Kenyan highland trial net benefits in the drought-affected short rains were higher without tied ridging than with it, except under one soil treatment [ev_economic_return_ndun23_1]. Income and returns are proxies for poverty rather than a poverty measure itself, the Ethiopian net present values are unweighted means from a small set of studies, and the Peruvian per-capita figure is a modelled 'potentially... up to' estimate cited in a review rather than a measured outcome [ev_economic_return_adim16_1, ev_household_income_wei16_1].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: On this AEZ's own evidence, terracing and bunding usually pay in the Ethiopian highlands: teff, barley and maize grown on long-established terraces earned incremental income of US$159, 275 and 141 per hectare per year over un-terraced farms, and terrace investment for barley had an average net present value of US$1542 over 50 years at a 10 percent discount rate, positive across the catchment [ev_economic_return_adgo13_4, ev_economic_return_adgo13_5, ev_economic_return_adgo13_6, ev_economic_return_adgo13_10]. An Ethiopian synthesis gives positive net present values of 3486.2 Birr per hectare for stone bunds, 2794.0 for bench terraces and 5283.4 for level fanya juu [ev_economic_return_adim16_1, ev_economic_return_adim16_2, ev_economic_return_adim16_3]. In Peru, a benefit of 1.96 soles was found for each sol invested in building cochas [ev_economic_return_card22_1], and modelled bench-terrace gains there could raise per capita incomes by up to 15 percent [ev_household_income_wei16_1].

justification.statement: water_harvesting_conservation rural_poverty: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE — material weight on both the benefit and the harm side, so no direction is stated. This is not a null finding: studies found real effects, in opposite directions, and the agreement note lists both sides. Read the conditionality for what separates them (transfer: in_context).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Against this, a Burkina Faso trial found 30-centimetre zaï running at a net loss against its own investment cost [ev_economic_return_zour25h1_4]; a single soil and water conservation measure did not cover its annual costs [ev_economic_return_zoug14_3]; and Brazil's wider production-cistern programme returned a benefit-cost ratio of 0.0858 over its evaluation window, well below one, with the Brazilian income gain turning negative on farms larger than 10 hectares and two subsurface-dam units finding the income effect almost non-existent or limited in a stagnant local economy [ev_economic_return_casag22_9, ev_household_income_casag22_6, ev_household_income_cirilo03_5, ev_household_income_cirilo03_7]. Income and farm returns are proxies for poverty, most units are farm budgets or household surveys rather than poverty measures, and none follows households over time.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In this semi-arid-AEZ evidence, water harvesting and soil and water conservation mostly raise household income and farm returns, mainly through higher yields, garden irrigation and livestock, though not always. In Zimbabwe, first-year planting-basin farmers earned a maize gross margin of 473.36 US dollars per hectare against 70.60 on conventional plots without fertiliser, and the gain held in the fertilised comparison too [ev_economic_return_mazv09_1, ev_economic_return_mazv09_3]. In Burkina Faso, manual zaï and demi-lunes gave a positive net economic benefit, and groundwater rising behind stone bunds let households earn income from vegetables grown near the wells [ev_economic_return_zoug14_1, ev_economic_return_zour25h1_3, ev_household_income_zoug14_1]. A new study of decentralised irrigation, including rainwater-harvesting ponds, finds household income significantly higher among adopters [ev_household_income_silv26_1]. In Brazil, production cisterns and subsurface dams raised family farm income by about 4.6 percent, rising to nearly 11 percent once the top of the income distribution is excluded, with the clearest gains on the smallest farms, and farmers reported better family income and quality of life from a subsurface dam, though it was not their main income source [ev_household_income_casag22_1, ev_household_income_casag22_2, ev_household_income_brito07_7]. Returns to labour for zaï in Burkina Faso exceed the shadow wage [ev_economic_return_kabo04_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The gain is uneven. The same Brazilian cistern programme had a benefit-cost ratio of only 0.0858, raising average yearly income by about R$424.71 against a mean of R$9,328.48 [ev_economic_return_casag22_9], and for farms over 10 hectares the effect was negative [ev_household_income_casag22_6]; outside the Northeast it was not significant [ev_household_income_casag22_4]. In other Brazilian cases subsurface dams brought almost no cash income because little was sold [ev_household_income_cirilo03_5, ev_household_income_cirilo03_7]. In Peru, bench terraces lost money when measured yields and market wages were used, but looked profitable on farmers' own estimates [ev_economic_return_post05_2, ev_economic_return_post05_3, ev_economic_return_post05_4], and a per-person income gain of up to 15% is a model figure [ev_household_income_wei16_1]. Several programmes bundle the structure with grants and training.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In upper-middle-income settings the income gain is small. In Brazil's semi-arid Northeast, a national cistern programme raised farm income by about 4.6% compared with a matched group [ev_household_income_casag22_1], about 11% when the richest 5% of farms are left out [ev_household_income_casag22_2], and more on farms of 0-10 ha [ev_household_income_casag22_5]. Small runoff basins in Brazil raised the income of small family farms by about half a minimum wage a month [ev_household_income_mira19_1], and subsurface dams paid back several times their cost over 10 years [ev_economic_return_cirilo03_10]. In Peru, building cochas (small ponds) returned 1.96 soles per sol invested [ev_economic_return_card22_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The sides differ in season, in what is compared and in how cleanly water capture is isolated. The Kenyan loss is from a short-rains season of meteorological droughts, in a trial that compares tied ridging with and without under the same soil inputs [ev_economic_return_ndun23_1]; it is the cleanest single comparison here. The Zimbabwean gains set a package of basins, manure, fertiliser and residue against conventional practice, so the water-capture effect is mixed with nutrient supply, and the higher-rainfall figure is a sensitivity scenario with assumed yields [ev_economic_return_mazv09_1, ev_economic_return_mazv09_2]. The Indian figure comes from a farmer survey in which few farms had a pond, the pond water was also used for irrigation, and the compared farms differ in other ways [ev_economic_return_pals23_1]. The evidence therefore cannot say whether water capture alone pays in this farming system; the gains belong to packages, and the one isolated test found a loss in a drought season. All of these are farm budgets rather than measures of household poverty, and none follows households over time [ev_economic_return_mazv09_1, ev_economic_return_mazv09_2, ev_economic_return_mazv09_3, ev_economic_return_ndun23_1, ev_economic_return_pals23_1]. Against this, in Tigray stone-bund building costs about as much each year as the financial benefit from the induced yield gain, roughly breaking even [ev_economic_return_nyss07_10]. The Zambian and Ethiopian gains are farm budgets, and the Ethiopian terrace income excludes family labour and is measured on terraces maintained for decades, so it shows what an established, well-maintained system returns rather than the first years after building [ev_economic_return_hagg03_6, ev_economic_return_adgo13_4]. The Kitui income result is likewise a cross-sectional household survey with multi-year recall rather than a randomised comparison; dams were not placed at random, dam households also applied more terracing, bunds and grass lines whose effect cannot be separated, and 'calculated income' is a price-based proxy, not a measured cash amount [ev_household_income_pauw08_1].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In mixed crop–livestock systems, farm budgets show water capture both paying and not paying. In Zimbabwe, planting-basin conservation farming earned a first-year maize gross margin of 473.36 against 70.6 US dollars per hectare for conventional practice without fertiliser and 48.19 with fertiliser, and experienced households could earn US$866.84 per hectare against US$357.16 for a farmer using chemical fertilizer in higher rainfall [ev_economic_return_mazv09_1, ev_economic_return_mazv09_3, ev_economic_return_mazv09_2]. In semi-arid India, net returns rose with livestock and trees to US$ 586 per hectare and to US$ 857 once a farm pond was added [ev_economic_return_pals23_1]. In a Kenyan highland trial, by contrast, net benefits in the short-rains season were higher without tied ridging than with it, except under one soil treatment [ev_economic_return_ndun23_1]. Further farm-budget evidence from mixed crop-livestock systems points the same way. In Zambia, hand-hoe conservation-farming basins gave cotton gross margins 70 percent higher than conventional hand-hoe cultivation and 150 percent higher than conventional ox ploughing, and maize returns to land and peak-season labour 60 to 90 percent higher than hand-hoe tillage [ev_economic_return_hagg03_6, ev_economic_return_hagg03_7, ev_economic_return_hagg03_8]; partial budgets there found a marginal rate of return of 860 percent for switching from hand hoeing to basin digging and 360 percent from ox ploughing to basin digging [ev_economic_return_umar12_2, ev_economic_return_umar12_3]. In the Ethiopian highlands, teff, barley and maize on long-established terraces earned incremental income of US$159, 275 and 141 per hectare per year over un-terraced farms, with an average net present value for barley terracing of US$1542 over 50 years [ev_economic_return_adgo13_4, ev_economic_return_adgo13_5, ev_economic_return_adgo13_6, ev_economic_return_adgo13_10]. In Ethiopia's Tigray, agricultural income from crops and livestock was significantly higher for users than non-users of water-management techniques [ev_household_income_biaz12_18], and Brazilian small family farms saw their monthly income rise once barraginhas filled with water [ev_household_income_mira19_1]. In Kenya's Kitui District, a mixed crop-livestock sand-dam district, calculated household income held up or rose by 27,241 KSh a year for households with a dam against a fall of 38,056 KSh for those without — a difference of 65,297 KSh in a drought year [ev_household_income_pauw08_1].

justification.conditionality: The sides differ in season, in what is compared and in how cleanly water capture is isolated. The Kenyan loss is from a short-rains season of meteorological droughts, in a trial that compares tied ridging with and without under the same soil inputs [ev_economic_return_ndun23_1]; it is the cleanest single comparison here. The Zimbabwean gains set a package of basins, manure, fertiliser and residue against conventional practice, so the water-capture effect is mixed with nutrient supply, and the higher-rainfall figure is a sensitivity scenario with assumed yields [ev_economic_return_mazv09_1, ev_economic_return_mazv09_2]. The Indian figure comes from a farmer survey in which few farms had a pond, the pond water was also used for irrigation, and the compared farms differ in other ways [ev_economic_return_pals23_1]. The evidence therefore cannot say whether water capture alone pays in this farming system; the gains belong to packages, and the one isolated test found a loss in a drought season. All of these are farm budgets rather than measures of household poverty, and none follows households over time [ev_economic_return_mazv09_1, ev_economic_return_mazv09_2, ev_economic_return_mazv09_3, ev_economic_return_ndun23_1, ev_economic_return_pals23_1]. Against this, in Tigray stone-bund building costs about as much each year as the financial benefit from the induced yield gain, roughly breaking even [ev_economic_return_nyss07_10]. The Zambian and Ethiopian gains are farm budgets, and the Ethiopian terrace income excludes family labour and is measured on terraces maintained for decades, so it shows what an established, well-maintained system returns rather than the first years after building [ev_economic_return_hagg03_6, ev_economic_return_adgo13_4]. The Kitui income result is likewise a cross-sectional household survey with multi-year recall rather than a randomised comparison; dams were not placed at random, dam households also applied more terracing, bunds and grass lines whose effect cannot be separated, and 'calculated income' is a price-based proxy, not a measured cash amount [ev_household_income_pauw08_1].

justification.statement: water_harvesting_conservation moderately reduces rural_poverty in BRA, ETH, IND, KEN, ZMB, ZWE; measured HARM (maladaptation) in 1 source — the practice worsened this outcome for some adopters (robust evidence, medium agreement → high confidence; transfer: in_context).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: What separates the sides, where the evidence says it: farm size, since the Brazilian income effect was a gain on small farms but a loss on farms larger than 10 ha [ev_household_income_casag22_5, ev_household_income_casag22_6]; labour costing and the size of the initial investment, since Ethiopian household benefit-cost ratios were 0.42 to 0.78 at market wages and exceeded one only with a shadow wage and a low initial investment [ev_economic_return_schmidt12_6]; and how long benefits are counted, since the Brazilian ratio covers a short window against a long-lived asset and counts income only [ev_economic_return_casag22_9]. For a Task Team Leader, the practical points are targeting smallholders, costing household labour honestly and expecting returns to arrive over years. The largest gains are from bundled programmes with weak attribution, and the Brazilian income effects are for a cistern bundled with a productive grant and training [ev_household_income_casag22_1]; IEG calls the China income estimate not robust and notes the India gains may partly be construction wages, and a Karnataka completion report doubts its own before/after figures [ev_household_income_iegchn07_6, ev_household_income_iegind11_2, ev_household_income_kar20_3]. The losses and nulls come mostly from independent evaluations, though the Ethiopian values may omit off-site benefits [ev_economic_return_adim16_4], and a Kenyan bundle showed no effect on per capita income [ev_household_income_mala24_2]. A review's report of increased incomes from check dams and infiltration pits in Malawi is qualitative and cited second-hand [ev_household_income_ngur26_1]. Income and returns are proxies for poverty. Location and up-front cost add to the separators: the same meta-analysis puts payback at 2 years for the average Asian farmer but more than 15 years for the average African farmer, whose average maize gain is far smaller [ev_economic_return_boum16_7], the Tanzanian profitability holds only where farmers can afford the initial investment [ev_economic_return_biaz12_19], and the Burkina Faso structures paid only with nutrients added [ev_economic_return_biaz12_24]. The payback periods are modelled from average yields, and the Ethiopian and Tanzanian findings are cited second-hand [ev_economic_return_boum16_8, ev_household_income_biaz12_18]. That rating is the review's own qualitative evaluation across several cited sources, not a single measured contrast [ev_household_income_vohl09_5]. A Niger perception survey adds a weak signal on the poverty side itself: villagers perceived poverty to have decreased in 8 of 12 villages with natural-resource-management interventions, but also in 2 of 4 control villages without one [ev_rural_poverty_botreij09_22].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Household income and returns from mixed soil and water conservation and water-harvesting programmes have been found to rise, to stay flat and to fall. Gains run through higher yields, irrigation and diversification: a quasi-experimental study found soil and water conservation raised net rice profit in Ghana by a significant 16 per cent [ev_economic_return_mala24_1]; Brazil's production-cistern programme raised family income by about 4.6%, nearly 11% when the top of the income distribution is excluded, with larger effects on farms of 0 to 10 ha [ev_household_income_casag22_1, ev_household_income_casag22_2, ev_household_income_casag22_5]; a review of 311 Indian watershed case studies found a mean benefit-cost ratio of 2.14 and an internal rate of return of 22 percent [ev_economic_return_josh05_1, ev_economic_return_josh05_2]; Mauritanian dikes returned a financial IRR of 24% [ev_economic_return_mrt14_4]; and programme evaluations report income gains of 54% in Karnataka and 58% on the Loess Plateau over control areas [ev_household_income_iegind11_2, ev_household_income_iegchn07_6]. Losses come from costs exceeding gains: in Burkina Faso the yield increase did not cover the annual costs of single SWC measures [ev_economic_return_zoug14_3]; Ethiopian graded fanya juu and graded soil bunds had net present values of −148 and −708 ETB per hectare [ev_economic_return_adim16_4]; and the Brazilian cistern programme's benefit-cost ratio over its evaluation window was 0.0858 [ev_economic_return_casag22_9]. In Ethiopia, agricultural income from crops and livestock was significantly higher for users than non-users of micro- and macro-catchment techniques (cited in a review) [ev_household_income_biaz12_18], and in Tanzania investment in rainwater harvesting for maize, paddy rice and onion was profitable in the long term as long as farmers could afford the initial investment (Senkondo et al. 2004) [ev_economic_return_biaz12_19]. A meta-analysis valuing average maize gains at world prices puts payback of the water-harvesting investment at 4–5 years at the pooled-average gain, not accounting for capital interest [ev_economic_return_boum16_8]. On the loss side, stone rows and grass strips in Burkina Faso were not cost-effective without added nutrients because of high labour, transport and material costs (Zougmoré et al. 2004) [ev_economic_return_biaz12_24]. A landscape review of rainwater harvesting across African drylands rates household income through enhanced yields as a benefit with a 'Good' evidence basis [ev_household_income_vohl09_5].

justification.statement: water_harvesting_conservation rural_poverty: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE — material weight on both the benefit and the harm side, so no direction is stated. This is not a null finding: studies found real effects, in opposite directions, and the agreement note lists both sides. Read the conditionality for what separates them (transfer: in_context).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The evidence conflicts, and what pulls it apart is how the gain is valued and against what. Crop budgets built on bundled input packages put basins well ahead [ev_economic_return_hagg03_6, ev_economic_return_hagg03_8, ev_economic_return_mazv09_1]; but a Zimbabwe household panel that values predicted yields with inputs held constant finds conservation agriculture generates less revenue than traditional cultivation over a large portion of the rainfall distribution [ev_economic_return_mich19_8]. Other losses are season- or practice-specific: tied ridging in a Kenyan drought season, where net benefits were higher without it, and 30-cm zaï on a Burkina Faso trial, which ran at a loss of −98 624 FCFA per hectare against the experiment's own investment cost [ev_economic_return_ndun23_1, ev_economic_return_zour25h1_4]. Manual zai gives far smaller net benefits than mechanised zai [ev_economic_return_zoug14_1]. The Zimbabwe margins include manure and fertiliser and the high-rainfall figure is a sensitivity scenario [ev_economic_return_mazv09_2]; the Zambian returns are bundled with early planting and purchased inputs, which the authors say dominate the maize results [ev_economic_return_hagg03_8]; and the Zimbabwe panel figure is gross revenue with labour unvalued, so it is neither a profit nor a poverty measure [ev_economic_return_mich19_8]. The newer field trials split the same way, and cost is what separates them: in Nigeria the high production costs of open and tied ridging, with or without mulch, gave net economic losses of about 1, 0.5, 11 and 12%, while mulch on the flat bed paid [ev_economic_return_chir06_10, ev_economic_return_chir06_11]; and in Mozambique basin and conventional returns did not differ significantly at intermediate elevation [ev_economic_return_kida19_3]. The Zambian rates of return come from partial budgets of a single crop, maize. Farm income and returns are proxies for poverty. Both are internal-rate-of-return figures with no significance test and no band rule for strength, read ordinally rather than compared in absolute terms with the other currency figures in this row [ev_economic_return_botreij09_26, ev_economic_return_botreij09_32].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Zai pits, planting pits, contour bunds and planting basins can raise farm income by raising yields. Returns to labour for these practices in Burkina Faso exceed the shadow wage, and bunds show returns above cost at subproject level in Mauritania [ev_economic_return_kabo04_1, ev_economic_return_mrt14_5]. In Zimbabwe, first-year planting-basin farmers earned a maize gross margin of 473.36 USD per hectare against 70.60 on conventional plots in the low-rainfall budget, with 866.84 against 357.16 for experienced farmers in high rainfall [ev_economic_return_mazv09_1, ev_economic_return_mazv09_2]. Zambian crop budgets give hand-hoe conservation-farming basins returns per hectare 70 percent higher than conventional hand hoe cultivation and 150 percent higher than conventional plowing for cotton, and returns to land and peak-season labor 60 to 90 percent higher than hand hoe tillage for maize [ev_economic_return_hagg03_6, ev_economic_return_hagg03_7, ev_economic_return_hagg03_8]. In Zambia, partial budgets found it profitable for a household to switch to conservation agriculture, with a marginal rate of return of 860% from hand hoeing to basin digging and 360% from ploughing to basin digging [ev_economic_return_umar12_2, ev_economic_return_umar12_3]. In Mozambique basins returned $148 per hectare against $104 under conventional tillage, an imputed value of $44 per hectare for a risk-neutral farmer [ev_economic_return_kida19_2, ev_economic_return_kida19_4]. In Ghana tied ridges with grass strips gave a higher net return than flat-land maize in 2010 despite a slightly higher cost [ev_economic_return_dalt14_3], and in Nigeria wood-shavings mulch on a flat bed was expected to increase the financial benefits to farmers by 238% [ev_economic_return_chir06_11]. justification.conditionality: The evidence conflicts, and what pulls it apart is how the gain is valued and against what. Crop budgets built on bundled input packages put basins well ahead [ev_economic_return_hagg03_6, ev_economic_return_hagg03_8, ev_economic_return_mazv09_1]; but a Zimbabwe household panel that values predicted yields with inputs held constant finds conservation agriculture generates less revenue than traditional cultivation over a large portion of the rainfall distribution [ev_economic_return_mich19_8]. Other losses are season- or practice-specific: tied ridging in a Kenyan drought season, where net benefits were higher without it, and 30-cm zaï on a Burkina Faso trial, which ran at a loss of −98 624 FCFA per hectare against the experiment's own investment cost [ev_economic_return_ndun23_1, ev_economic_return_zour25h1_4]. Manual zai gives far smaller net benefits than mechanised zai [ev_economic_return_zoug14_1]. The Zimbabwe margins include manure and fertiliser and the high-rainfall figure is a sensitivity scenario [ev_economic_return_mazv09_2]; the Zambian returns are bundled with early planting and purchased inputs, which the authors say dominate the maize results [ev_economic_return_hagg03_8]; and the Zimbabwe panel figure is gross revenue with labour unvalued, so it is neither a profit nor a poverty measure [ev_economic_return_mich19_8]. The newer field trials split the same way, and cost is what separates them: in Nigeria the high production costs of open and tied ridging, with or without mulch, gave net economic losses of about 1, 0.5, 11 and 12%, while mulch on the flat bed paid [ev_economic_return_chir06_10, ev_economic_return_chir06_11]; and in Mozambique basin and conventional returns did not differ significantly at intermediate elevation [ev_economic_return_kida19_3]. The Zambian rates of return come from partial budgets of a single crop, maize. Farm income and returns are proxies for poverty. Both are internal-rate-of-return figures with no significance test and no band rule for strength, read ordinally rather than compared in absolute terms with the other currency figures in this row [ev_economic_return_botreij09_26, ev_economic_return_botreij09_32].

justification.statement: water_harvesting_conservation rural_poverty: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE — material weight on both the benefit and the harm side, so no direction is stated. This is not a null finding: studies found real effects, in opposite directions, and the agreement note lists both sides. Read the conditionality for what separates them (transfer: in_context).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The gains are per-hectare net incomes from field trials, not measured changes in household income or poverty, which they stand in for. The Kenyan figures come from one trial, and the larger wheat gain also carries a straw mulch [ev_economic_return_wang16_4]. The row rests on three sources, one of them a technology-sheet rating; measured household income for micro-catchments is missing. The half-moon profit comes from a trial on degraded land where the authors count the experiment's own investment, and compost was added to the pits [ev_economic_return_zour25h1_3]. The Vallerani unit is a technology-sheet rating [ev_household_income_wocat_1528_2012_farm_income]. That is an internal-rate-of-return figure with no significance test, read ordinally rather than compared in absolute terms with the other currency figures in this row [ev_economic_return_botreij09_31].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Vallerani tractor-ploughed micro-catchments, half-moons and ridge-furrow systems collect runoff for crops and sown fodder. In a Kenyan field trial, ridge-furrow rain harvesting raised wheat net income by 82% without mulch and 117% with straw mulch over flat planting [ev_economic_return_wang16_3, ev_economic_return_wang16_4]. On crusted degraded soil in Burkina Faso, 1-m half-moons with compost were profitable at 377 275 FCFA per hectare after the investment [ev_economic_return_zour25h1_3]. The Burkina Faso compiler for the Vallerani system links more and better fodder to improved animal health, productivity and market price, and so to higher farm income [ev_household_income_wocat_1528_2012_farm_income]. The same synthesis gives an internal rate of return of 145 percent for demi-lunes on Burkina Faso's Central Plateau [ev_economic_return_botreij09_31].

justification.statement: water_harvesting_conservation moderately reduces rural_poverty in BFA, KEN (medium evidence, high agreement → high confidence; transfer: in_context).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Most literature magnitudes are secondary citations in reviews or vote counts [ev_household_income_saru19_3, ev_household_income_veno12_3]. Sand dams are judged likely not cost-efficient for water supply, Brazilian subsurface dams produced little cash income where electricity, investment capital or an irrigation tradition were missing, and the high Brazilian benefit-cost ratios come from an upper-middle-income context [ev_economic_return_ritc21_1, ev_household_income_cirilo03_7, ev_economic_return_cirilo03_10]. The Kenyan sand-dam income rise compares a small sample of households with a control catchment [ev_household_income_lasage08_1]; the reviewed figures are reported at their upper end, the Indian pond returns come from a cross-sectional survey confounded by farm size and assets [ev_economic_return_silv26_2, ev_economic_return_pals23_1], and the barraginha income finding is Embrapa's self-assessment of its own technology from an informal survey [ev_household_income_mira19_1]. Income and returns are proxies for poverty. The returns hinge on what the water is used for and on inputs: in the Burkina Faso model the yield gain from supplemental irrigation alone does not compensate for the labour and capital invested [ev_economic_return_fox05_2], and in Pakistan pearl millet irrigated from harvested rainwater lost 0.27 US$ per cubic metre in the first year and stayed below break-even by the third [ev_economic_return_waqa25_6]. The Kenyan, Tanzanian and Peruvian returns are second-hand citations, the model profits rely on a high-value tomato crop and vary with the cost put on labour, and the Pakistani figures are projections assuming constant prices and water productivity [ev_economic_return_biaz12_20, ev_economic_return_card22_1, ev_economic_return_fox05_3, ev_economic_return_waqa25_5]. That figure is a calculation from estimated irrigable area rather than a measured income contrast, and is bundled with the well-pumping the recharge supplies [ev_household_income_dash17_3]. In a separate Ethiopian sand-dam catchment, a household survey found no clear difference in economic situation between households with and without dam access, though the authors attribute the weak contrast partly to the small number of dam-linked households surveyed [ev_household_income_lasa13_2]. The Kitui income comparison is a cross-sectional household survey with multi-year recall rather than a randomised comparison; dams were not placed at random, and dam households also applied more terracing, bunds and grass lines whose effect cannot be separated from the dam's own [ev_household_income_pauw08_1].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Small reservoirs, sand dams, farm ponds, runoff cisterns and subsurface dams provide water for dry-season irrigation of vegetables and fruit and for livestock, shifting cropping towards higher-value crops and raising household income [ev_household_income_veno12_2, ev_household_income_ritc21_3]. In Kenya, farmers living near sand dams saw average income rise by 60% as more water in dry periods raised farm yields [ev_household_income_lasage08_1]. In the same Kitui, Kenya sand-dam district, a separate household survey found calculated income held up or rose by 27,241 KSh a year for dam households against a fall of 38,056 KSh for those without — a difference of 65,297 KSh in a drought year [ev_household_income_pauw08_1]. Reviews add that rainwater-harvesting ponds brought statistically significant gains in household income in Burkina Faso, water storage gave Ethiopian smallholders greater income security, harvested water used with precision irrigation in Ethiopia reached a net water value of up to 1.53 USD per cubic metre, and benefit-cost ratios reached up to 3.38 with payback periods of 6.8 to 12 years; Indian farms with a farm pond reported net returns of 857 USD per hectare against 586 without [ev_household_income_silv26_1, ev_household_income_silv26_2, ev_economic_return_silv26_1, ev_economic_return_silv26_2, ev_economic_return_pals23_1]. In Brazil, an Embrapa survey of some communities found small-farm incomes rose by about half a minimum wage per month after the second filling of the barraginhas [ev_household_income_mira19_1]. The Cambodian pond compiler rates farm income up because every crop yielded well once there was enough irrigation water [ev_household_income_wocat_2844_2017_farm_income]. Returns on stored runoff can be high: farm-pond supplemental irrigation of maize in Kenya gave net seasonal revenue of US$ 150 and could raise the annual return by 150% (Ngigi et al. 2005), road-catchment harvesting for paddy in Tanzania returned more than US$ 12 per person-day against US$ 3.7 for rainfed sorghum (Hatibu et al. 2006), and a Peruvian programme building 31 cochas returned 1.96 soles per sol invested (Tafur, cited in a programme review) [ev_economic_return_biaz12_20, ev_economic_return_biaz12_21, ev_economic_return_card22_1]. A Burkina Faso and Kenya model puts net profit from water harvesting with supplemental irrigation, fertiliser and an off-season tomato crop at 151–626 USD per hectare a year in Burkina Faso and 109–477 in Kenya, against at most 15 and 40–130 under current practice [ev_economic_return_fox05_3, ev_economic_return_fox05_4]. In Pakistan, maize irrigated from harvested rainwater earned 0.28 US$ net per cubic metre in the first year, with a cumulative benefit-cost ratio projected at 2.02 by the second year and 3.53 by the third, and fish farming in a farm pond earned US$ 1799 net on average, about US$ 2951 in mini-dams [ev_economic_return_waqa25_5, ev_household_income_waqa25_7]. In Rajasthan, India, modelled recharge from check dams was estimated sufficient to irrigate part of the winter crop area and judged responsible for 16 percent of farm income [ev_household_income_dash17_3].

In the same Kitui, Kenya sand-dam district, a separate household survey found calculated income held up or rose by 27,241 KSh a year for dam households against a fall of 38,056 KSh for those without — a difference of 65,297 KSh in a drought year [ev_household_income_pauw08_1]. Reviews add that rainwater-harvesting ponds brought statistically significant gains in household income in Burkina Faso, water storage gave Ethiopian smallholders greater income security, harvested water used with precision irrigation in Ethiopia reached a net water value of up to 1.53 USD per cubic metre, and benefit-cost ratios reached up to 3.38 with payback periods of 6.8 to 12 years; Indian farms with a farm pond reported net returns of 857 USD per hectare against 586 without [ev_household_income_silv26_1, ev_household_income_silv26_2, ev_economic_return_silv26_1, ev_economic_return_silv26_2, ev_economic_return_pals23_1]. In Brazil, an Embrapa survey of some communities found small-farm incomes rose by about half a minimum wage per month after the second filling of the barraginhas [ev_household_income_mira19_1]. The Cambodian pond compiler rates farm income up because every crop yielded well once there was enough irrigation water [ev_household_income_wocat_2844_2017_farm_income]. Returns on stored runoff can be high: farm-pond supplemental irrigation of maize in Kenya gave net seasonal revenue of US$ 150 and could raise the annual return by 150% (Ngigi et al. 2005), road-catchment harvesting for paddy in Tanzania returned more than US$ 12 per person-day against US$ 3.7 for rainfed sorghum (Hatibu et al. 2006), and a Peruvian programme building 31 cochas returned 1.96 soles per sol invested (Tafur, cited in a programme review) [ev_economic_return_biaz12_20, ev_economic_return_biaz12_21, ev_economic_return_card22_1]. A Burkina Faso and Kenya model puts net profit from water harvesting with supplemental irrigation, fertiliser and an off-season tomato crop at 151–626 USD per hectare a year in Burkina Faso and 109–477 in Kenya, against at most 15 and 40–130 under current practice [ev_economic_return_fox05_3, ev_economic_return_fox05_4]. In Pakistan, maize irrigated from harvested rainwater earned 0.28 US$ net per cubic metre in the first year, with a cumulative benefit-cost ratio projected at 2.02 by the second year and 3.53 by the third, and fish farming in a farm pond earned US$ 1799 net on average, about US$ 2951 in mini-dams [ev_economic_return_waqa25_5, ev_household_income_waqa25_7]. In Rajasthan, India, modelled recharge from check dams was estimated sufficient to irrigate part of the winter crop area and judged responsible for 16 percent of farm income [ev_household_income_dash17_3].

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Soil and water conservation structures cut both runoff and the soil it carries. A review of Ethiopian studies found graded soil bunds reducing surface runoff by 25.2% (from 190.7 to 142.7 mm) and soil loss by 59% (from 43.6 to 17.9 tonnes per hectare) [ev_runoff_reduction_adim16_1, ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_1]; level soil bunds cut runoff by 60.1% and soil loss by 88% (from 17.5 to 2.1 tonnes per hectare) [ev_runoff_reduction_adim16_2, ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_2]; and stone bunds cut runoff by 34.4% [ev_runoff_reduction_adim16_3].
