justification.mechanism: Soil and water conservation structures cut both runoff and the soil it carries. A review of Ethiopian studies found graded soil bunds reducing surface runoff by 25.2% (from 190.7 to 142.7 mm) and soil loss by 59% (from 43.6 to 17.9 tonnes per hectare) [ev_runoff_reduction_adim16_1, ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_1]; level soil bunds cut runoff by 60.1% and soil loss by 88% (from 17.5 to 2.1 tonnes per hectare) [ev_runoff_reduction_adim16_2, ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_2]; and stone bunds cut runoff by 34.4% [ev_runoff_reduction_adim16_3].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Two conditions separate the sides in the sources. Maintenance: the acceleration is tied explicitly to unrepaired breaches in state-built banquettes [ev_erosion_hazard_arab04_2]. Storm size: the tabia hold runoff only up to rains of 50 mm, and in bigger storms the excess overtops them and gullies the whole slope [ev_runoff_reduction_roos10_1]. The actionable reading is to plan and fund upkeep and spillways, not only construction. Elsewhere banquettes simply did not stop gullying: gullied areas on Tunisian banquette land grew by 12% between 1963 and 1973, and over 1947-1968 Algerian banquettes had no influence on the sedimentation rate of the Oued Fodda dam [ev_erosion_hazard_arab04_1, ev_sediment_retention_arab04_1]. Neither side is measured on plots: the protective statement is from an expert manual and the harmful ones are secondary citations within a national evaluation, and the two concern different structures, tabia and banquettes [ev_runoff_reduction_roos10_1, ev_erosion_hazard_arab04_2].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In the Maghreb, contour structures have been reported both to hold runoff and to accelerate erosion. Staggered earth bunds (tabia) in Morocco store the runoff of all rains below 50 mm on the field [ev_runoff_reduction_roos10_1]. In Algeria, a poorly maintained banquette becomes a factor accelerating erosion, because the smallest unrepaired breach triggers a chain reaction through the whole network in torrential and prolonged rains [ev_erosion_hazard_arab04_2].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: On the harm side, channel beds eroded below check dams at 81% of surveyed dams in a Spanish catchment [ev_erosion_hazard_fran21_1]; abandoned runoff structures in Arizona rangeland failed and sped up local gully head retreat [ev_erosion_hazard_stav20_12]; and collapsing stone terraces in Israel's Negev started rill and gully erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_stav20_13]. For big storms the Arizona check dams had no significant effect on runoff volume [ev_runoff_reduction_poly14_2], and the Arizona sediment drop was significant only at a weak test level [ev_sediment_retention_poly14_2]. What separates the two sides is upkeep and storm size: the harm findings come from abandoned or failing structures. Most findings are cited second-hand.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In high-income countries the studies disagree. On the benefit side, a review found bench terracing cut runoff by 9% and sediment yield by 58% [ev_runoff_reduction_meko14_1]; in Arizona, loose-rock check dams cut the number of runoff events from small storms by 60% [ev_runoff_reduction_poly14_1], held back much of the watershed's sediment [ev_sediment_retention_poly14_1] and gave a twofold drop in sediment yield at the outlet [ev_sediment_retention_poly14_2]; a small Belgian pond kept trapping 68% of sediment over 33 years [ev_sediment_retention_meko14_3]; and Spanish terraces reduce runoff when maintained [ev_runoff_reduction_arna15_5].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Nearly all units are programme or lender reports from Ethiopia, India and China, often perception surveys or before/after comparisons; an Uttarakhand water budget showed surface runoff slightly increasing, the Karnataka runoff comparison is against another SWC programme, and IEG doubts the India runoff measurements. Effects mixing runoff and soil-loss metrics are only components of erosion risk. A catchment-restoration meta-analysis in Ethiopia finds minimal effect of catchment treatment on runoff in drought-prone areas with annual rainfall below 500 mm [ev_runoff_reduction_meaza22_3]. The Ethiopian catchment results combine structures with grazing control and vegetation regeneration and are cited in a review, so the share due to the works is not isolated [ev_erosion_hazard_meko14_1]. The 88% and 81% runoff figures are cited second-hand: the first is an upper bound, and the second is a before-and-after result for a catchment-management package rather than the structures alone [ev_runoff_reduction_gebr18_7, ev_runoff_reduction_gebr18_8].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Physical SWC works under public-works and watershed programmes reduce soil loss and downstream runoff, and sediment-control dams with terraces and vegetation trap sediment in the catchment. A meta-analysis of traditional in-situ water harvesting finds soil loss cut by 58.66% and runoff by 53% on average, with soil and stone bunds reducing soil loss by 55.06% and runoff by 49.2% [ev_erosion_hazard_tefe24_1, ev_runoff_reduction_tefe24_1, ev_erosion_hazard_tefe24_4, ev_runoff_reduction_tefe24_5]; in Ethiopian catchments, stone bunds, check dams and vegetation regrowth cut sediment yield from 8.5 to 1.9 t per hectare a year [ev_erosion_hazard_meko14_1, ev_erosion_hazard_meko14_2]. Ethiopian catchment studies cited in a review report physical soil and water conservation decreasing runoff by up to 88% (Taye et al., 2015; Haregeweyn et al., 2015), and integrated catchment management at May Zeg Zeg cutting surface runoff volume by 81% (Nyssen et al., 2010) [ev_runoff_reduction_gebr18_7, ev_runoff_reduction_gebr18_8].

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Check dams and hill reservoirs cut both runoff and the sediment it carries. On China's Loess Plateau, a decades-long check-dam campaign was found to have reduced runoff and sediment by about 15% and 85% respectively, and streamflow by about 39% [ev_runoff_reduction_luca21_2], while separately reducing erosion rates from more than 200 tonnes per hectare per year to 20–25 tonnes per hectare per year [ev_erosion_hazard_luca21_1]. In Tunisia, earth bench-bunds (banquettes) were found to retain 85 mm of runoff, enough to hold back all the rain in a normal year, cutting downstream flows by 17% and hill-reservoir inflows by 13% [ev_runoff_reduction_roose06_4].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The Morocco unit is an evaluator assertion; nothing on water chemistry is measured, and siltation is a component proxy [ev_sediment_retention_iegmar09_3]. The added sediment figures are secondary citations in reviews, in extreme rainfall the sediment accumulated on terraces can reach the channel [ev_sediment_retention_arna15_6], the bench-terrace figure comes from a high-income watershed, and Algerian banquettes had no influence on the sedimentation rate of a downstream dam over 1947-1968 [ev_sediment_retention_meko14_5, ev_sediment_retention_arab04_1]. The Tigray figure is on-field trapping, a component proxy for downstream water quality, part of it soil moved by tillage rather than by water, and the reservoir finding is a second-hand citation without a stated size; both come from the same research team [ev_sediment_retention_gebr05_2, ev_sediment_retention_nyss07_13].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Terracing and retaining walls hold soil on slopes, which an evaluation in Morocco expects to reduce siltation of downstream rivers and dam storage [ev_sediment_retention_iegmar09_3]. Reviews add that fanya juu trapped 64% of sediment (80% with vetiver grass), and bench terracing cut sediment yield by 58% in a small USA watershed [ev_sediment_retention_meko14_6, ev_sediment_retention_meko14_5]. A terracing review finds terraces reasonably effective at reducing sediment transport, though about 20%–30% of sediment may still be delivered [ev_sediment_retention_arna15_6]. On Tigray cropland, Gebremichael and colleagues measured eroded soil accumulating behind stone bunds at 59 t per hectare a year across 202 plots, and a later paper by the same team reports, citing Nigussie et al. (2005), strongly decreased specific sediment yield in reservoirs whose catchments have a high density of stone bunds [ev_sediment_retention_gebr05_2, ev_sediment_retention_nyss07_13].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The benefit can reverse at depth under trees: in the same China meta-analysis, terraces planted with forest showed drier deep soil than sloping land at 140–160 cm and 180–200 cm, which the authors attribute to deep-rooted trees drawing down water that rainfall does not replenish [ev_soil_moisture_chen20_14]. Measured harm, where the practice made water stress worse for some adopters, appears in 1 source. Overall the evidence points to a large reduction in water stress, though the size differs by climate and by type of structure. The Zimbabwe tied-ridge trial covers one drought season and found no difference in the deeper soil layer [ev_soil_moisture_mand21_1].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Terracing raises soil moisture by turning a slope into a flat surface that lets rain infiltrate instead of running off. A meta-analysis of studies across China found terraced land held 12.4% more soil moisture than sloping land on average [ev_soil_moisture_chen20_1], with the benefit varying by climate: 28.6% in semi-humid areas, 15.1% in semi-arid areas, and only 5.4% in humid areas, where soil moisture is less limiting [ev_soil_moisture_chen20_10]. In northern Burkina Faso, water-harvesting reservoirs built for crop irrigation were also found to serve livestock and household needs during periods of domestic water scarcity [ev_water_access_deficit_foxr03_7]. In a Zimbabwean cotton trial in the 2018–2019 drought season, tied contour ridges held significantly more moisture in the top 0–5 and 6–10 cm of soil than conventional tillage, though not at 11–15 cm [ev_soil_moisture_mand21_1].

justification.mechanism: Terracing raises soil moisture by turning a slope into a flat surface that lets rain infiltrate instead of running off. A meta-analysis of studies across China found terraced land held 12.4% more soil moisture than sloping land on average [ev_soil_moisture_chen20_1], with the benefit varying by climate: 28.6% in semi-humid areas, 15.1% in semi-arid areas, and only 5.4% in humid areas, where soil moisture is less limiting [ev_soil_moisture_chen20_10]. In northern Burkina Faso, water-harvesting reservoirs built for crop irrigation were also found to serve livestock and household needs during periods of domestic water scarcity [ev_water_access_deficit_foxr03_7]. In a Zimbabwean cotton trial in the 2018–2019 drought season, tied contour ridges held significantly more moisture in the top 0–5 and 6–10 cm of soil than conventional tillage, though not at 11–15 cm [ev_soil_moisture_mand21_1].

The Ethiopian figure compares long-maintained terraces with un-terraced plots at a single catchment where farmers also apply fertiliser, and the Kenyan result is for tied ridges rather than terraces, so the row rests on few sites and differing practices.

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Supply is bounded by storage: 57% of Kenyan sand dams would hold 4 months of water for their reported beneficiaries [ev_water_access_deficit_neuf17_1]. The Brazilian units are implementer or agency assessments, interviews or census inference from an upper-middle-income context rather than the low-income target [ev_water_access_deficit_castro22_1, ev_water_access_deficit_arsky20_5]. Well-level evidence for semi-arid bunds and zaï now sits in the catchment water yield rows. What upstream capture does to water downstream is a separate question, answered in the catchment water yield rows. The zaï and half-moon results come with compost in the pits, so the moisture gain cannot be credited to the pit alone [ev_soil_water_retention_zour25h1_7, ev_soil_water_retention_sawa11h1_8]. In the Brazilian trial deep ploughing, which is tillage alone and not a capture structure, scored as high as the tied furrows, and the trial ran a single season at a station of the agency that promotes the technology [ev_soil_water_retention_brito07_9].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Storage and recharge structures ease water stress in semi-arid areas: production cisterns in semi-arid Brazil keep livestock watered while clay tanks are dry, an agency review credits consumption and production cisterns with a large drop in rural establishments without any water source, and subsurface dams raise water levels in existing wells used when other sources dry up [ev_water_access_deficit_arsky20_5, ev_water_access_deficit_castro22_1, ev_water_access_deficit_cirilo03_1]. In the field, pits and furrows keep rain in the root zone: in Burkina Faso zaï of 30–40 cm diameter and 1-m half-moons retained moisture for 2-3 weeks through dry spells, and zaï can retain moisture in the soil for seven to ten days after rainfall; in semi-arid Brazil tied furrows kept more soil moisture than the traditional flat system at all crop stages and depths [ev_soil_water_retention_zour25h1_7, ev_soil_water_retention_sawa11h1_8, ev_soil_water_retention_brito07_9].

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Terraces and check dams hold water where it is needed. A global terracing synthesis finds terraced sites more efficient than slopes at reducing runoff and conserving soil water (e.g., soil moisture recharge), with a mean δsm of 1.2 [ev_soil_water_retention_wei16_1]. A terracing review cites Posthumus and Stroosnijder (2010) finding that the soil stays humid for longer on terraces than on sloping fields, and that ponding on very flat terrace beds increases infiltration [ev_soil_moisture_arna15_7], and a check-dam review reports that check dams that store seasonal runoff solve local scarcity in supply [ev_water_access_deficit_luca21_1].

justification.statement: water_harvesting_conservation strongly reduces water_stress in BFA, BRA, CHN, COD, ETH, GHA, IND, KEN, MLI, MWI, NER, NGA, RWA, TZA, UGA; measured HARM (maladaptation) in 1 source — the practice worsened this outcome for some adopters (robust evidence, high agreement → very_high confidence; transfer: in_context).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Tillage alone is not water harvesting: in the Brazilian trial deep ploughing, a tillage practice, scored as high as the tied furrows [ev_soil_water_retention_brito07_9]. The Brazilian trial ran a single season at a station of the agency that promotes the technology [ev_soil_water_retention_brito07_9]. At Melkassa the Ethiopian mulch plots differed from unmulched plots only at maturity, not at planting or flowering [ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_7, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_9, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_11]. The Ethiopian basins did not differ from unmulched plots at planting at Ziway or at any stage at Melkassa [ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_2, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_8, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_10, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_12]. Under meteorological drought and dry spells in Kenya, tied ridging without organic inputs was insufficient in soil moisture conservation since there was little or no rainwater to be held in the basins [ev_soil_water_retention_ndun23_1]. A review found no significant effect of infiltration trenches on soil moisture because only four studies provided sufficient statistical data [ev_soil_water_retention_locat20_1]. The zaï result comes with compost in the pits [ev_soil_water_retention_sawa11h1_8]. The Mauritanian well-level and Andean trench evidence now sits in the in-situ catchment water yield row, which also answers what upstream capture does to water downstream. Those best-practice arms are bundled: planting pits, basins or ripper-with-ridging (the capture element, which is the practice here) come with reduced tillage and mostly with fertiliser, and tillage alone is not water harvesting [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. The trial-level readings are weaker: the authors find no clear tillage effect on rain water productivity in Kenya, no clear effects of tillage in Ethiopia (where the gains that do show come with fertilised treatments), and only a tendency of improvement in semi-arid Tanzania [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_4]. The Burkina Faso trial covers a single season, and every conservation arm also received manure, so its gain belongs to the package rather than to the structures alone [ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_1]. At Houndé, grass strips with zaï (4.84 against 3.10) were not significantly different from the control, and at Péni neither grass strips with zaï (4.51) nor earth bunds with contour ploughing (4.31) differed significantly from the control (3.53), the authors stating that water was not limiting at Péni, which had more rain than Houndé that season [ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_4]. The Sudan comparison ranks treatments without a no-practice value [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. In the Nigerian trial, open and tied ridging without mulch stored only a few per cent more soil water, significant on only one out of the nine measurement dates, and did not consistently raise water use efficiency, so ridging may not be an improvement without a residue mulch [ev_soil_moisture_chir06_7, ev_rain_water_productivity_chir06_8]. The Ethiopian and Iranian soil-moisture figures are cited second-hand. On the sandy field of the same Zimbabwe trial, where little runoff was generated, the ridges made no significant difference to soil moisture after heavy rain or after the dry spell [ev_soil_moisture_mhiz13_3]. That is a meta-analysis finding for terracing structures specifically, not an in-situ-family measurement [ev_soil_moisture_chen20_2]. The Zimbabwe tied-ridge trial covers one drought season and found no difference in the deeper soil layer [ev_soil_moisture_mand21_1].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Pits, basins, bunds and tied ridges catch rain where it falls and hold it in the root zone. A meta-analysis finds infiltration pits have the highest SMD of 114.4% for soil moisture retention, with tied ridging at 48.9% [ev_soil_water_retention_tefe24_2, ev_soil_water_retention_tefe24_5]. In Burkina Faso zaï can retain moisture in the soil for seven to ten days after rainfall [ev_soil_water_retention_sawa11h1_8]; in Brazil tied furrows kept more soil moisture than the traditional flat system at all crop stages and depths [ev_soil_water_retention_brito07_9]; and in Ethiopia hand-dug planting basins held more topsoil water than unmulched plots at Ziway at flowering (27.4 against 25.5) and at maturity (26.5 against 25.9) [ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_4, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_6]. Mulching, the soil-cover form of in-situ water harvesting, improves soil moisture retention with an SMD of 54.0% in the meta-analysis, and maize-stalk mulch in Ethiopia held more topsoil water than unmulched plots at Ziway at each stage measured [ev_soil_water_retention_tefe24_4, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_1, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_3, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_5]. Water productivity, the grain produced per unit of rain, is a route by which capture eases water stress. Grain per unit of rain rises with capture in a set of East and Southern African trials: the best conservation-farming practice per site gave yield increases ranging from 20 to 120% over conventional tillage whilst rain water productivity improved with 10–50% [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. In an on-farm trial at Houndé, Burkina Faso, stone rows with zaï pits, every arm also receiving manure, lifted maize rain water productivity from 3.10 kg per hectare per mm under the farmers' practice of oxen ploughing with NPK and urea to 6.61 [ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_1]. A review reports that contour tied-ridging in eastern Sudan gave the highest water use efficiency of the treatments compared [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. In a Nigerian field trial, tied ridging with wood-shavings mulch stored 8, 26 and 14.4% more soil water than the flat bed in successive seasons, and raised rainfall water use efficiency of sorghum grain from 1.26 to 1.97 kg per hectare per mm [ev_soil_moisture_chir06_7, ev_rain_water_productivity_chir06_9]. Reviews cite tied ridging, open ridging and sub-soiling improving root-zone soil water by 24%, 15% and 3% over traditional tillage in drought-stricken Wollo, Ethiopia (McHugh et al., 2007), tied ridges cutting surface runoff by about 60% and raising rooting-zone soil water by at least 13% in northern Ethiopia (Araya and Stroosnijder, 2010), and 20–25 cm deep contour furrows increasing soil moisture and shrub productivity on rangeland in Iran's Sistan Baluchistan (Jahantigh and Pessarakli, 2009) [ev_soil_moisture_biaz12_6, ev_soil_moisture_dile13_1, ev_soil_moisture_biaz12_8, ev_soil_moisture_stav20_6]. In a Zimbabwean on-farm trial, dead-level contour ridges on silt loam held significantly more soil moisture than an adjacent plot without ridges shortly after a 60 mm rainfall day (14 against 12.1 mm) and after a dry spell lasting 3 weeks (10.4 against 9.2 mm) [ev_soil_moisture_mhiz13_1, ev_soil_moisture_mhiz13_2]. The Chinese terracing meta-analysis confirms soil-water-storage effectiveness across all six terrace types studied [ev_soil_moisture_chen20_2]. In a Zimbabwean cotton trial in the 2018–2019 drought season, tied contour ridges held significantly more moisture in the top 0–5 and 6–10 cm of soil than conventional tillage, though not at 11–15 cm [ev_soil_moisture_mand21_1].

justification.mechanism: Pits, basins, bunds and tied ridges catch rain where it falls and hold it in the root zone. A meta-analysis finds infiltration pits have the highest SMD of 114.4% for soil moisture retention, with tied ridging at 48.9% [ev_soil_water_retention_tefe24_2, ev_soil_water_retention_tefe24_5]. In Burkina Faso zaï can retain moisture in the soil for seven to ten days after rainfall [ev_soil_water_retention_sawa11h1_8]; in Brazil tied furrows kept more soil moisture than the traditional flat system at all crop stages and depths [ev_soil_water_retention_brito07_9]; and in Ethiopia hand-dug planting basins held more topsoil water than unmulched plots at Ziway at flowering (27.4 against 25.5) and at maturity (26.5 against 25.9) [ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_4, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_6]. Mulching, the soil-cover form of in-situ water harvesting, improves soil moisture retention with an SMD of 54.0% in the meta-analysis, and maize-stalk mulch in Ethiopia held more topsoil water than unmulched plots at Ziway at each stage measured [ev_soil_water_retention_tefe24_4, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_1, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_3, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_5]. Water productivity, the grain produced per unit of rain, is a route by which capture eases water stress. Grain per unit of rain rises with capture in a set of East and Southern African trials: the best conservation-farming practice per site gave yield increases ranging from 20 to 120% over conventional tillage whilst rain water productivity improved with 10–50% [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. In an on-farm trial at Houndé, Burkina Faso, stone rows with zaï pits, every arm also receiving manure, lifted maize rain water productivity from 3.10 kg per hectare per mm under the farmers' practice of oxen ploughing with NPK and urea to 6.61 [ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_1]. A review reports that contour tied-ridging in eastern Sudan gave the highest water use efficiency of the treatments compared [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. In a Nigerian field trial, tied ridging with wood-shavings mulch stored 8, 26 and 14.4% more soil water than the flat bed in successive seasons, and raised rainfall water use efficiency of sorghum grain from 1.26 to 1.97 kg per hectare per mm [ev_soil_moisture_chir06_7, ev_rain_water_productivity_chir06_9]. Reviews cite tied ridging, open ridging and sub-soiling improving root-zone soil water by 24%, 15% and 3% over traditional tillage in drought-stricken Wollo, Ethiopia (McHugh et al., 2007), tied ridges cutting surface runoff by about 60% and raising rooting-zone soil water by at least 13% in northern Ethiopia (Araya and Stroosnijder, 2010), and 20–25 cm deep contour furrows increasing soil moisture and shrub productivity on rangeland in Iran's Sistan Baluchistan (Jahantigh and Pessarakli, 2009) [ev_soil_moisture_biaz12_6, ev_soil_moisture_dile13_1, ev_soil_moisture_biaz12_8, ev_soil_moisture_stav20_6]. In a Zimbabwean on-farm trial, dead-level contour ridges on silt loam held significantly more soil moisture than an adjacent plot without ridges shortly after a 60 mm rainfall day (14 against 12.1 mm) and after a dry spell lasting 3 weeks (10.4 against 9.2 mm) [ev_soil_moisture_mhiz13_1, ev_soil_moisture_mhiz13_2]. The Chinese terracing meta-analysis confirms soil-water-storage effectiveness across all six terrace types studied [ev_soil_moisture_chen20_2]. In a Zimbabwean cotton trial in the 2018–2019 drought season, tied contour ridges held significantly more moisture in the top 0–5 and 6–10 cm of soil than conventional tillage, though not at 11–15 cm [ev_soil_moisture_mand21_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Micro-catchments concentrate a small basin's runoff onto a planted pit or furrow. In Ethiopia's eastern drylands, plots with micro-catchments had 31% higher soil moisture in the wet season and 24% higher in the dry season than plots without them [ev_soil_moisture_biaz12_1]. A Chinese meta-analysis found fish-scale pits (a micro-catchment structure) raising soil-water storage by 8.9%, the smallest of six terracing-family structures tested, with level ditches reaching 34.9% [ev_soil_moisture_chen20_7]. In Burkina Faso, a project reported that its micro-basins harvest up to 95% of the rain falling on them, with each micro-basin collecting up to 1,200 litres per rainfall and each hectare collecting an average of 360,000 litres of rain and runoff combined, and that local people report rising well-water levels since the structures were installed [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_1528_2012_harvesting_collection_of_water, ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_1528_2012_water_quantity].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The size of a sand dam limits how many people it can serve: in Kenya, at a consumption rate of 15 litres per person per day, a median-sized dam was found to support between 37 and 84 people for a four-month period, with only 57% of dams holding enough water to supply their reported number of beneficiaries for that long [ev_water_access_deficit_neuf17_1]. In a separate Burkina Faso trial, water-use efficiency showed no difference between irrigated and non-irrigated or fertilised and non-fertilised treatments in a well-distributed rainfall year [ev_rain_water_productivity_foxr03_6].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Farm ponds and sand dams raise water available for both crops and households. In northern Burkina Faso, reservoirs built for crop irrigation were also found to serve livestock and household needs during periods of domestic water scarcity [ev_water_access_deficit_foxr03_7]. In eastern Kenya, rain-and-irrigation water-use efficiency rose from 2.1 to 4.1 kilograms of grain per millimetre per hectare between the lowest and highest supplemental-irrigation treatments [ev_rain_water_productivity_barr05_9], and in Zimbabwe, a modelled rainwater-harvesting system with a rock catchment and infiltration pits found supplemental irrigation alone raising water productivity by 22% on average, from 1.75 to 2.13 kilograms per cubic metre [ev_rain_water_productivity_kahi07_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The Tunisian stone-line units are practitioner judgements, and catchment modelling in Peru found no difference in crop water distribution with partial terracing [ev_water_regulation_willem21_1]. Abandoned or degraded terraces worsen water regulation [ev_water_regulation_willem21_2]. The recharge estimates for terraces and contour ridges now sit in the terracing catchment water yield row. The terracing ratio is an unweighted mean across extracted cases from mixed-income countries [ev_soil_water_retention_wei16_1], and the Chinese finding comes from an independent World Bank evaluation reporting project monitoring with no control [ev_soil_water_retention_iegchn07_2]. That is a compiler judgement for a group spanning earth bunds, stone lines, vegetative strips and fanya juu terraces, direction only [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_3]. The same review cites work finding that the infiltration capacity of the soil is not particularly affected by terracing (Posthumus and Stroosnijder, 2010), so the gain comes from water held longer on the flat bed rather than a change in the soil [ev_soil_moisture_arna15_7]. The Anjene figure compares long-maintained terraces with un-terraced plots at a single catchment where farmers also use fertiliser [ev_rain_water_productivity_adgo13_7]. The Peruvian humidity finding is the farmers' account; the study could not measure it [ev_soil_moisture_post05_8]. The Tigray soil-moisture figure is an earlier study reported within Nyssen et al. [ev_soil_moisture_nyss07_4]. The Canadian comparison is modelled rather than measured and the terrace system was built together with grassed waterways, so the moisture gain cannot be separated from those [ev_soil_moisture_lian19_4].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Terraces and stone lines capture and retain rainwater on slopes, and stone lines contribute to increased infiltration of rainwater into the soil, thereby replenishing water resources [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_6610_2022_water_quantity, ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_6610_2022_water_availability]. Measured soil moisture supports this: a meta-analysis gives terraces an SMD of 40.5% for soil moisture retention [ev_soil_water_retention_tefe24_6], a global terracing synthesis finds terraced sites more efficient than slopes at conserving soil water, with a mean δsm of 1.2 [ev_soil_water_retention_wei16_1], and conversion of slopeland to leveled fields in China increased moisture retention [ev_soil_water_retention_iegchn07_2]. Water productivity, the grain produced per unit of rain, is a route by which capture eases water stress. The FAO compilers rate improving water productivity for the cross-slope barrier group at the middle mark of their scale [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_3]. In Ethiopia's Anjene catchment, terraces improved the water productivity of teff, barley and maize by at least 100% against un-terraced plots [ev_rain_water_productivity_adgo13_7]. A review of farming terraces notes that the soil stays humid for longer on terraces than on sloping fields, and that a very flat terrace bed lets rain pond, reducing runoff and increasing infiltration [ev_soil_moisture_arna15_7]. In Tigray, stone bunds enhance soil moisture storage on both sides of the bund, especially on loamy and sandy soils, with 0.05–0.1 g g−1 more soil moisture at 1–1.5 m depth persisting for at least 2 months after the rainy season (Vancampenhout, 2003, reported by Nyssen et al.) [ev_soil_moisture_nyss07_4]. In Peru, farmers say the soil on bench terraces remains humid twice as long as on sloping fields [ev_soil_moisture_post05_8]. The Chinese terracing meta-analysis adds further terrace types confirmed effective for soil water storage [ev_soil_moisture_chen20_3, ev_soil_moisture_chen20_4, ev_soil_moisture_chen20_5, ev_soil_moisture_chen20_6], and in a Canadian potato belt simulated soil moisture was significantly higher on terraced than non-terraced fields [ev_soil_moisture_lian19_4].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: The class is low and no study puts a size on the drought relief. The same Canadian model also found the opposite in places: a restoration scenario made summer low flows worse in some sub-catchments [ev_wet_eff_goy22_3]. Only the Welsh bog was measured, at a single site and during short dry spells; the rest is modelled. Nothing was tested in a severe drought. justification.mechanism: Rewetting drained peat moderately reduces fire. Drainage dries the peat and makes it burn; raising the water table back up keeps the fuel wet [ev_wet_fire_hazard_ramsar18_1, ev_wgy_ram_14, ev_fire_hazard_page09_3]. Most of the evidence, and all of the sizes, come from tropical peat in Indonesia (with one Malaysian case). After large-scale canal blocking in Riau (Taufik et al.), the frequency of continuous extreme fire-hazard events fell by 40%, but the average area affected was only 5% lower than before rewetting [ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_1, ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_2]. In a matched comparison (Salmayenti et al.), peat restored with dams had significantly fewer fire hotspots in 2019 than similar unrestored peat, 5 against 6 per square km [ev_wet_eff_salm26_1]. A model of Indonesian peatland restoration (Tan et al.) puts the reduction in fire risk at 6%–37% [ev_fire_hazard_tan22_1], and a Malaysian community group that patrols, plants and blocks drains helped cut the extent of forest fires in its area by 98% between 2014 and 2022 [ev_fire_hazard_unepgpa22_3]. Fires are more frequent close to drainage canals, the effect reaching at least 800 m from them [ev_fire_hazard_jauhiainen16_5]. Global syntheses and guidance say the same thing without giving a size: rewetting wetlands reduces risk of peat fires (Griscom et al.), rewetting and restoration are efficient ways to reduce wildfire risk in drained peatlands (UNEP Global Peatlands Assessment), and fire on rewetted organic soils is considered low compared with drained soils (IPCC wetlands supplement) [ev_fire_hazard_griscom17_9, ev_fire_hazard_unepgpa22_1, ev_fire_hazard_ipcc13wl_2].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.mitigation_mechanism: A groundwater model for Central Kalimantan compares relatively intact peat swamp forest with a drained, burnt block of the former Mega Rice Project. In a dry year, the water table fell below the depth at which surface peat can ignite on 15% of the intact peat, against 85% of the drained block [ev_fire_hazard_page09_4].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: The benefit is moderate because it is local and does not hold up at catchment scale or in big floods. No effect was found across a whole 260 km2 UK catchment, drain blocking is notoriously hard to detect at basin scale, and in major floods the whole basin is saturated so wetlands make no difference [ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_catchment_null, ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_basin_null, ev_wetflA_acre_catastrophic_null]. Placement can reverse the effect: a moorland scheme raised downstream risk, restoring the wrong reach raised flooding upstream, and moving a project downstream turned a 14% peak cut into about a 1% increase [ev_wetflA_shut_synchrony_reversal, ev_flood_hazard_gour20_4, ev_flood_hazard_feder22_4]. Rougher floodplains can make local flooding deeper and wider, and rewetting can use up storage that floods would fill [ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up, ev_wetflA_acre_somerset_rewet_cost]. Guidance notes that drained peat is no longer saturated, which itself lowers peaks, so rewetting does not always help [ev_wgy_ram_10]. Most evidence is from the UK and US, much of it modelled, with no measured low- or lower-middle-income result. The benefit arrives downstream, not on the farm.

justification.mechanism: Wetland management moderately reduces flood impacts close to the works. Rewetting and re-roughening land slows storm water, so flood peaks just below the works are lower. On UK peat, peak flows fell 27% where bare peat was re-vegetated, 51% where gullies were also blocked, and 49% at a rewetted gully [ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_O, ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_N, ev_wetflA_gatis_peakflow]. Ditch and drain blocking on Irish and Welsh bogs made stream flow less flashy [ev_flood_hazard_hold04_2, ev_flood_hazard_wils11db_4]. Reconnecting floodplains cut modelled peaks by about 8% to 12% in a base case, and a review puts the average flood-peak cut from river and floodplain measures at 30% [ev_flood_hazard_feder22_2, ev_flood_hazard_bagh25w1_1]. Setting levees back lowered flood levels on large rivers [ev_flood_hazard_knox22_1, ev_flood_hazard_serra22_1]. A Canadian basin model found restored wetland eased the rise in spring flood peaks expected with climate change [ev_wet_eff_goy22_1].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.mitigation_mechanism: Wetland management moderately reduces flood impacts close to the works. Rewetting and re-roughening land slows storm water, so flood peaks just below the works are lower. On UK peat, peak flows fell 27% where bare peat was re-vegetated, 51% where gullies were also blocked, and 49% at a rewetted gully [ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_O, ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_N, ev_wetflA_gatis_peakflow]. Ditch and drain blocking on Irish and Welsh bogs made stream flow less flashy [ev_flood_hazard_hold04_2, ev_flood_hazard_wils11db_4]. Reconnecting floodplains cut modelled peaks by about 8% to 12% in a base case, and a review puts the average flood-peak cut from river and floodplain measures at 30% [ev_flood_hazard_feder22_2, ev_flood_hazard_bagh25w1_1]. Setting levees back lowered flood levels on large rivers [ev_flood_hazard_knox22_1, ev_flood_hazard_serra22_1]. T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: What separates the two sides is scale and position: the reductions are storage and roughness effects on the flood peak passing through or below the wetland [ev_wetflA_acre_wooded_wetland, ev_wet_flood_hazard_ramsar18_2], while the increases arise at catchment scale, where an on-site storage gain need not add up to a downstream benefit [ev_wetflA_acre_synchrony_catchment], and locally, where the roughness that slows the flood raises water level and flooded area on the re-vegetated floodplain itself [ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up]. The influence of drain blocking on flood flows has been notoriously difficult to detect at the basin scale [ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_basin_null]; and during major catastrophic floods the whole basin may be saturated, so the presence or absence of wetlands, or their management, has no effect [ev_wetflA_acre_catastrophic_null]. None of the units is a measurement of a flood outcome in this scope: they are a single review pooling UK, US, Canadian, Irish and Zimbabwean settings and a global policy brief. Any benefit falls downstream or at landscape scale rather than on the farmer's plot, and a farmer whose floodplain is re-vegetated may see deeper, wider flooding locally.

justification.mechanism: Studies disagree on whether wetland management lowers or raises flooding for farmers. On the side of a reduction, wooded wetlands in particular increase flood storage, reduce flood peaks and increase peak travel time [ev_wetflA_acre_wooded_wetland], and a Ramsar briefing note states that wetland protection and restoration buffer communities by reducing wave damage and floods [ev_wet_flood_hazard_ramsar18_2]. On the side of an increase, the same review reports that even where the dominant result is to increase water storage within the wetland, the overall result may still be an increase in flood peaks at the catchment scale [ev_wetflA_acre_synchrony_catchment], and that a change of vegetation from wet meadows to shrubs and trees can double the size and depth of the inundated area for the same size of flood [ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: This benefit does not hold at every severity level: the same review found salt marshes dissipate storm surge less effectively during extreme storms than during moderate ones, man-made levees and dikes behind a marsh can limit its surge-attenuating effect, and one study found neither crop type nor the simple presence of coastal wetlands added much explanatory power once other factors were accounted for. Only 2 of the 8 units measuring a benefit actually state its size, which is why the class is capped at a moderate level even though the direction is consistent. For most farmers this is an off-site benefit: the wetland sits off their land, and the protection shows up downstream or at landscape scale, not on their own plot.

justification.mechanism: Coastal wetlands (salt marshes, mangroves) reduce flood impact mainly by dissipating wave energy and attenuating storm surge before it reaches land: salt-marsh vegetation has been measured giving a significant reduction in wave height compared with unvegetated mudflat, and across a global set of field measurements, coastal habitats reduced wave heights by 35% to 71% on average, with salt marshes alone cutting wave height by about 72%. Croplands within 1 km of mangroves and tidal marshes have also been found to experience less surface-water presence and smaller crop-cover declines than more distant areas.

justification.mechanism: Reconnecting and rewetting floodplains gives storm water somewhere to spread outside the channel. Modelled peak flow fell by up to 37% along a reconnected reach [ev_flood_hazard_feder22_1]; hollow wetlands could store 72% of the runoff from a 2-year storm [ev_wetflA_acre_depression_storage]; and embanking a floodplain raised the modelled downstream peak by 57% [ev_wetflA_acre_cherwell_embankment]. Removing or setting back levees lowered flood levels: by 0.66 m on average along a reach, 50 cm on the Elbe and 0.3 m on the Dutch Rhine [ev_flood_hazard_jacob15_1, ev_flood_hazard_serra22_1, ev_flood_hazard_knox22_4]. A meta-analysis finds that on average wetlands reduce flood frequency and size [ev_flood_hazard_kad16_1]. In a Canadian basin model, restored wetland eased the rise in spring flood peaks [ev_wet_eff_goy22_1].

justification.mechanism: Coastal wetlands reduce cyclone damage, but the benefit is rated low for this practice. Across US coastal counties (Sun et al.), a 1% loss of coastal wetlands is associated with a 0.6% increase in property damage [ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_1]; valued at the margin, the median wetland is worth about $91,000 per km2 per year in storm protection, within a range from less than $800 to $100 million per km2 [ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_4], and for one hurricane the damage linked to earlier wetland loss came to about $430 million [ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_5]. After a cyclone on the Queensland coast (Rowland et al.), croplands within 1 km of mangroves and tidal marshes showed smaller crop cover declines than more distant areas [ev_crop_yield_rowl26w1_2].

justification.mechanism: Drought is a very high threat to restored wetlands because it takes away the water they run on. In a rewetted Indonesian peat restoration area (Hooijer et al.), the peat surface sank sharply during and shortly after the 2019 El Niño drought, at 2.5 to 4 times the rate of the preceding 3.5 years and more than double the 7.5-year mean [ev_climate_shock_hooi24_5]. On a restored floodplain in Belarus, lack of snow cover and severe drought in 2020 meant no spring flooding, and migrating and nesting birds on the restored floodplain meadows declined strongly [ev_wgy_blr_6]. Ramsar technical guidance records, from its authors' knowledge, that a large number of planted areas in degraded tropical peat have been lost to drought, as well as to fire, flooding and out-competition by ferns and sedges [ev_wgy_ram_22].

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: This is one observation in a project terminal evaluation from Belarus, an upper-middle-income temperate setting, and the practice is restoration and maintenance of open floodplain meadows by grazing and mowing, not rewetting of drained land; the indicator is the number of migrating and nesting birds, not a livelihood or a hydrological measure, and the evaluation gives no size for the decline. It also names drought and snowless winters as arriving faster and more severely than the project was designed for. The lesson that transfers is a design one: a floodplain wetland fed by a seasonal flood is exposed whenever drought removes that flood, so its habitat function, and anything that depends on it, should be expected to fail in such years.

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: The Ramsar line is a single expert statement, with no site, frequency, area or measurement, made where the guidance notes there is very little literature on what happens after planting. It does not say whether the flooding came from rivers or from the raised water table of rewetting itself, and it concerns tropical peat-swamp replanting only. The Berbak figure is the only measured loss rate, reported second-hand from van Eijk et al. at a single national-park site [ev_climate_shock_doh18_1]. Together these are a reason to budget for replanting losses and replacement, not a measured rate of loss. The Sumatran case is a single site on a project its authors describe as never fully rewetted; the sentence is cut by a page break, so the number of damaged blockings is not recoverable. What it does show is the mechanism of loss - flood damage to the dams undoing the rewetting in the following dry season - which argues for budgeting dam inspection and repair after each wet season.

justification.mechanism: Flooding can destroy restoration plantings and the structures that keep peat wet. T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: This is a single demonstration site in Indonesian tropical peat, recorded as a case study rather than measured across projects, and the repeat failure after repair is the most transferable part of it. It says nothing about damage to the wetland itself, about coastal or temperate wetland types, or about water-control structures of other designs. Read it as a design and maintenance risk for canal-blocking programmes in deep permeable peat — dam siting relative to the contour, seepage control, and a repair budget that assumes recurrence — rather than as a general sensitivity of wetland management to extreme rainfall. Provenance: humid-tropical, upper-middle-income, with no comparable record from any other peat region.

justification.mechanism: The vulnerable asset is the canal dam that holds the water table up. In December 2005, after an extreme rainfall event, both dams in the Kalampangan Canal were damaged by water seeping underneath and along the sides; they were repaired in March 2006 and were damaged again in August 2006 (ev_climate_shock_ritz13_7). During an extreme rainfall event in August 2007 a further dam was damaged in a flash flood, the canal water level rising by several metres in a short period (ev_climate_shock_ritz13_8). The rainfall is the trigger; the vulnerability is structural, since highly permeable tropical peat lets seepage pass beneath and alongside a dam, and the sunken canals intercept overland and interflow, raising canal discharges when the rain is extreme.

T6E_economic_profile.conditionality: This is a modelled national cost framework for constructed nutrient-retention wetlands, and the recurring item prices forgone agriculture on US cropland, a high-income economy; it cannot be read across to a low- or lower-middle-income landscape, where the opportunity cost of farmland is set by quite different land and tenure arrangements. No currency year is stated in the quoted passage. The monitoring share is a cited summary, not a measurement from these projects, and it is expressed relative to the initial investment, so it scales with however large that establishment cost was. The useful point is structural: where wetlands are restored on farmland, the standing cost is the production forgone, not the upkeep of the works. The Taillardat per-hectare-per-year medians formerly pooled here are total project capital annualised over the restoration event and now sit in establishment cost (the cost-routing rule) [ev_project_cost_cheng20_6].
T6E_economic_profile.effect_mechanism: Two kinds of recurring cost sit in this pool. The first is a land payment in a US national model: where wetlands are restored on farmland, land rental costs cover the opportunity cost of land removed from agricultural production, and for cropland they are, in the mean, more than five times greater than those for pastureland, at US$274 ± 156 per hectare [ev_project_cost_cheng20_6]. Design, construction and maintenance enter the same framework as area-dependent costs annualised over a 50-year management horizon at a real discount rate of 4%, with the rental rates taken from state-level agricultural statistics across the 48 contiguous states. T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The gains are measured against the damaged starting point; compared with intact wetlands, restored sites usually fall short, which is incomplete recovery, not harm [ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_1]. How restoration is done matters: peat sites left to recover on their own are modelled as stagnating or getting worse for decades [ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_6, ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_5]. Harms do occur: rewetting can destroy rare dry habitats that have developed on drained peat [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tann22_3], and a tidal project's most common fish was a non-native predator of the endangered fish it was meant to help [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_2]. Some groups, such as bottom-dwelling invertebrates, showed no change [ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_4, ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_7]. Few results give a size. The Chinese bird count is grey literature from a single site with no comparison, the Indonesian figure is modelled, and almost all measured evidence is from high- and upper-middle-income countries. A review also cites a North American case where restoring individual wetlands did not bring back the Topeka Shiner, a small fish, and the authors argue that species moving between wetlands need restoration across many wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_3].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Wetland management strongly increases biodiversity. Putting water and vegetation back into a drained or damaged wetland restores the conditions wetland species need, and species return from nearby sources. A global meta-analysis found restoring degraded wetlands raised biodiversity by 19%, with clear gains for vertebrates, plants and invertebrates [ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_3]. Reopening tidal flow on coasts produced gains in 57% of monitoring studies [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_1]. Creating wetlands in farmland adds habitat the landscape has lost: in Sweden each new wetland added species to the regional total [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3], and lagoons built on Australian sugarcane farms held at least 36 native fish species [ev_wet_eff_cann22_1]. Rewetting drained German fens is expected to bring back fen plants and animals [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tann22_2], and in Indonesia a model found restoring lost peat swamp forest could remove the extinction risk for its forest birds [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tan22_3]. A Chinese coastal project that turned fish ponds back into a bird roost saw shorebird numbers rise markedly [ev_biodiversity_outcome_rgwo25_6].

The Sumatran plots all lay close to remaining forest, a best case for seed arrival, and the regrowth cannot be credited to rewetting alone [ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3]. The forest-cover statement is an expected benefit, and the bird result is a model that assumes restoration happens at once [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4, ev_biodiversity_outcome_tan22_3]. A meta-analysis of China's coastal wetland restoration found biodiversity 36.8% higher in restored than in degraded wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_1]. Native peat swamp trees regrew on their own in the wettest parts of a Sumatran site [ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3], and a model of Indonesian peatlands found that restoring lost swamp forest could cut the extinction risk of its forest birds from 14% to 0% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tan22_3]. Rewetting a cut-over peatland in Belarus brought reed and sedge back over a large area [ev_wgy_blr_7], and on the Chinese coast a project that turned fish ponds into a bird roost saw shorebird numbers rise markedly [ev_biodiversity_outcome_rgwo25_6].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The class is moderate because few results give a size. Restored peat usually stays below intact peat in moss and specialist cover [ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_1]. Leaving peat to recover on its own is projected to take centuries and can stagnate or get worse [ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_5, ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_6]. Rewetting can harm rare dry habitats that have developed on drained peat, a conflict between climate and nature goals [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tann22_3]. The Belarus project missed its own target [ev_wgy_blr_7]. Most evidence is temperate, boreal and high-income; the tropical evidence is thin, partly an expected benefit and partly modelled.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Raising the water table on drained peat lets peatland plants and animals come back, and actively spreading moss or plants speeds this up. Active restoration with moss transfer brought peat moss and specialist plants close to intact levels within years, while simple rewetting gave slower recovery [ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_7, ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_4]. A review of German fens concludes that rewetting drained fens will increase fen plants and animals, with dry-land species giving way to wetland ones [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tann22_2]. Rewetting a cut-over peatland in Belarus brought reed and sedge back over a large area [ev_wgy_blr_7]. On tropical peat, native swamp trees regrew on their own in the wettest areas [ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3], and an Indonesian model found that restoring lost swamp forest could remove the extinction risk for its forest birds [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tan22_3].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: A restored wetland that falls short of an intact one is a recovery note, not harm, and it is kept apart from the gain above. The slow parts lag: plant assemblages took decades to converge statistically with reference sites and their absolute structural values remained below reference even 100 years after restoration, with biological structure and biogeochemical functioning still lower than reference (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_7, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_1), while inland depressional wetlands fed only by precipitation or groundwater had not recovered to reference conditions decades after restoration (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_8). The global syntheses disagree on whether that shortfall persists, since biodiversity in restored wetlands did not significantly differ from that in natural wetlands (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_2). Not every group responds: macroinvertebrate diversity showed no significant effect (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_4), and a cited North American case found that restoring individual wetlands did not bring back the Topeka Shiner, a small fish; the authors argue species moving between wetlands need restoration across many wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_3]. The project units are weaker than their numbers suggest. The Bulgarian counts are park reports taken within months of the first flooding (ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_2), and the Moldovan result is direction only (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mdicr_2). The Missouri entry is a second-hand table row, direction only (ev_biodiversity_outcome_knox22_1). The Elbe and Cosumnes findings are case studies with a before/after framing and no control site, and the Elbe bird counts are project-success evaluations cited without a named underlying study (ev_biodiversity_outcome_serra22_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_serra22_5). On a different reconnected floodplain, on the Bear River, hydraulic modelling found most of the reconnected area would flood only in a 2-year event and so would not provide the frequent, long-duration inundated habitat that native fish need — a design limitation on that one project, not a finding against reconnection generally [ev_biodiversity_outcome_serra22_4]. The floodplain review is a vote count of authors' own declared success against indicators they chose, not a measured effect against a baseline, and its authors warn that unsuccessful outcomes are likely under-reported (ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_1); it also relays a before-and-after study in which hydrological restoration of inundation levels failed to restore invertebrate food sources for birds, likely because of vague aims and predictions of what the target species required (ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_2). The Sierra Leone claim is an evaluator's assertion about a bundle of grazing by-laws, boundary demarcation and co-management, and it depended on the exit of all Fula settlements and their cattle, a livelihood cost the biodiversity gain does not show (ev_biodiversity_outcome_wcpsl_1). The Lao result rests on project fish-monitoring records inside protected zones (ev_wgy_lao_3). The comparisons against intact reference sites (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_6, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_7, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_8, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_9) are held out of the class for that reason: they measure how far recovery has to go, not what restoration adds over the degraded starting point.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Restoring water to a degraded wetland strongly increases biodiversity. Reinstating hydrology on a degraded wetland puts back standing water and saturated soil, and the gain is measured against that degraded starting point. How degraded that point is comes from a review of agricultural use of wetlands, restating the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment: natural wetlands reclaimed by drainage and land amelioration have lost much of their original character, leading to reduced biodiversity and reduced performance of functions other than crop productivity (ev_biodiversity_outcome_verh09_5). That unit describes what reclaiming an existing wetland cost, not a restoration result; it enters this family row through the existing-wetland home-family route, as a statement of the degraded starting point rather than a measured restoration outcome. Restoring degraded wetlands enhanced biodiversity overall and the diversity of vertebrates, vascular plants and terrestrial and aquatic invertebrates (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_3). The mobile parts of the system return soonest: vertebrate assemblages reached reference structural values within a few years (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_6), and riverine and tidal wetlands kept connected by natural flow variation recovered biogeochemical function and biological structure after 20 and 30 years respectively (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_9). Project cases show the same fast early response. After the first test flooding of the restored Belene Island marshes, park reports cited by the World Bank record fish species rising from 2 to 10 within 2 months and ferruginous duck nesting pairs from 5 to 50 (ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_1); a project-supported inventory found flora and fauna beginning to regenerate after the Lapusna wetland in Moldova was restored (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mdicr_2). Reconnecting floodplains by setting levees back works the same way: a critical review of levee alteration (Knox et al.) reports reduced flood stages and improved biodiversity after a setback on the Missouri River in Iowa (Smith et al.) (ev_biodiversity_outcome_knox22_1) and a setback on the Elbe in Germany was followed by newly established floodplain forest and excavated shallow water bodies, with the documented return of many waterfowl and other bird species and a diversity of habitat types (Serra-Llobet et al.) (ev_biodiversity_outcome_serra22_2). On California's unregulated Cosumnes River, partial levee removal and setback reconnected the river to its floodplain, and the renewed flooding diversified flow and geomorphology, promoted riparian vegetation establishment and supported positive responses from native fish and the aquatic ecosystem (ev_biodiversity_outcome_serra22_5). A review of floodplain wetland restoration studies finds the same direction in how projects report themselves: most published studies deemed their restoration activities successful or partially successful, irrespective of the restoration activity performed (ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_1). The Lao and Sierra Leone units come from protecting existing wetlands rather than restoring them: in Lao PDR, designating fishery conservation zones was followed by an increase in native fish populations and more fish for local consumption (ev_wgy_lao_3), and at Sierra Leone's Mamunta Mayosso sanctuary positive changes in biodiversity conservation are confirmed after cattle settlements were banned (ev_biodiversity_outcome_wcpsl_1).

After the first test flooding of the restored Belene Island marshes, park reports cited by the World Bank record fish species rising from 2 to 10 within 2 months and ferruginous duck nesting pairs from 5 to 50 (ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_1); a project-supported inventory found flora and fauna beginning to regenerate after the Lapusna wetland in Moldova was restored (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mdicr_2). Reconnecting floodplains by setting levees back works the same way: a critical review of levee alteration (Knox et al.) reports reduced flood stages and improved biodiversity after a setback on the Missouri River in Iowa (Smith et al.) (ev_biodiversity_outcome_knox22_1) and a setback on the Elbe in Germany was followed by newly established floodplain forest and excavated shallow water bodies, with the documented return of many waterfowl and other bird species and a diversity of habitat types (Serra-Llobet et al.) (ev_biodiversity_outcome_serra22_2). On California's unregulated Cosumnes River, partial levee removal and setback reconnected the river to its floodplain, and the renewed flooding diversified flow and geomorphology, promoted riparian vegetation establishment and supported positive responses from native fish and the aquatic ecosystem (ev_biodiversity_outcome_serra22_5). A review of floodplain wetland restoration studies finds the same direction in how projects report themselves: most published studies deemed their restoration activities successful or partially successful, irrespective of the restoration activity performed (ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_1). The Lao and Sierra Leone units come from protecting existing wetlands rather than restoring them: in Lao PDR, designating fishery conservation zones was followed by an increase in native fish populations and more fish for local consumption (ev_wgy_lao_3), and at Sierra Leone's Mamunta Mayosso sanctuary positive changes in biodiversity conservation are confirmed after cattle settlements were banned (ev_biodiversity_outcome_wcpsl_1).

Methane is the trade-off: where water stands above the peat surface, methane warming can outweigh the carbon dioxide saved for years [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_4], and restored wetlands can warm the climate for their first years to decades, with the switch to net cooling estimated at 57 to 299 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_4]. Partial rewetting slows but does not stop peat loss [ev_carbon_sequestration_unepgpa22_4]. In a Kalimantan simulation, raising water levels gave only a small, not significant fall in carbon dioxide [ev_carbon_sequestration_page09_2], and planting on rewetted tropical peat has failed: seedlings did no better beside a dammed canal, and aerial seeding survived at about 2% [ev_establishment_survival_page09_6, ev_establishment_survival_pusp21_4]. Most evidence is temperate, boreal and high-income, and the benefit goes to the climate, not to the farmer. T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Wetland management moderately increases carbon storage. Raising the water table on drained peat stops the stored carbon from rotting away, so carbon dioxide losses fall, even though methane rises. Rewetting drained farmland peat in Germany is estimated to save 20 to 35 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per hectare a year [ev_wet_carbon_meye26_1], and each 10 cm the water table is raised cuts net warming by at least 3 tonnes per hectare a year [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_1]. Reviews of Indonesian peat projects report canal blocks raising the water table: by about 60 cm in the dry season 100 m from a block in Riau, by 70 cm within 170 m of a block at Sungai Tohor, and by a metre over 2420 ha where communities built 12 blocks [ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_2, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_4, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_3].

Most other units cover a single gas or carbon pool and cannot set a direction. Methane rises mainly where the water table rises [ev_carbon_sequestration_xu25_7]. Partial rewetting slows peat loss but does not stop it [ev_carbon_sequestration_unepgpa22_4]. Soil carbon fell after restoration in some warm, wet or tidal settings [ev_soil_organic_carbon_xu19_3]. The sources pool many countries and restoration types; read this row alongside the peatland and rewetting rows, which carry net balances.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: The only result here that weighs all gases together found no difference: a global meta-analysis found methane rose by 122.3% after restoration, yet total greenhouse-gas emissions of restored wetlands were no higher than those of disturbed wetlands, because carbon dioxide fell [ev_carbon_sequestration_xu25_3]. IPCC guidance adds that rewetting cuts waterborne carbon losses (a median 36% across collated studies) and that nitrous oxide falls practically to zero when the water table is within 20 cm of the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc13wl_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc13wl_3]. The UN peatland assessment says partly raising water levels gives some climate benefit [ev_carbon_sequestration_unepgpa22_4], and a meta-analysis found soil carbon 13.8% higher in restored than in cultivated wetlands [ev_soil_organic_carbon_xu19_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The size is not stated because almost no unit weighs carbon dioxide against methane: most report a single gas, subsidence or national totals. In a Kalimantan simulation, raising water levels gave only a small, not significant fall in carbon dioxide [ev_carbon_sequestration_page09_2]; laboratory work suggests peat keeps decaying even when waterlogged [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauhiainen16_2]; and methane moved in opposite directions at paired sites [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_4]. The planning model assumes immediate restoration. Revegetation is unreliable: seedlings did no better beside a dammed canal, and aerial seeding survived at about 2% [ev_establishment_survival_page09_6, ev_establishment_survival_pusp21_4]. A measured net balance from a rewetted site in this income group would strengthen the row. The South Sumatra tree figures count carbon in the trees only, not the peat below, and come from a single project; the Indonesian water-table results are cited second-hand in a review [ev_wet_carbon_budi20_1, ev_wet_carbon_budi20_2, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_2].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In upper-middle-income peatlands, mostly Indonesia and Malaysia, the evidence points to a carbon benefit of unstated size: rewetting slows subsidence and the peat decay behind it, and carbon dioxide from peat is lowest when the water table is near the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauhiainen16_1]. Canal blocking in Kalimantan raised the dry-season water table [ev_water_table_depth_page09_1]. A planning model for Indonesian peatlands counts large avoided emissions from restoration, mostly from preventing peat decay and fire [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan22_2], and a synthesis judges rewetting a better climate option than keeping peat drained [ev_carbon_sequestration_lup23_1]. On burned peat in South Sumatra, planted native trees took up 11.3 tonnes of CO2 per hectare a year (Shorea balangeran) and 12.4 tonnes (Dyera polyphylla) in their wood [ev_wet_carbon_budi20_1, ev_wet_carbon_budi20_2]. Reviews of Indonesian peat projects report canal blocks raising the water table: by about 60 cm in the dry season 100 m from a block in Riau, by 70 cm within 170 m of a block at Sungai Tohor, and by a metre over 2420 ha where communities built 12 blocks [ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_2, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_4, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_3].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: This class is built from a very small, specific evidence base, just two sources, both studying existing or converted coastal wetlands rather than restoration projects measured directly, so the strong_positive rating does not mean every restoration project will show this scale of gain. Other meta-analyses of the same coastal systems find a much more mixed picture: a global meta-analysis found no significant difference in carbon-dioxide or nitrous-oxide flux between restored and natural salt marshes, though restored marshes had significantly lower methane flux than natural ones [ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_11, ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_12]; the same study found restored and natural marshes accumulated soil carbon at statistically indistinguishable rates, even though restored marshes' total carbon stocks still lagged behind natural marshes [ev_soil_organic_carbon_liu24_10]; and a separate meta-analysis found restored coastal wetlands showed no significant improvement in soil organic carbon compared with degraded wetlands, while restored inland wetlands did show a significant gain [ev_soil_organic_carbon_wu25w1_5]. A global meta-analysis of restored wetlands found soil organic carbon was significantly lower than in cultivated and natural wetlands specifically where restoration used a plantation approach, where the wetland had tidal hydrology after restoration, or in wetter, warmer or lower-latitude sites [ev_soil_organic_carbon_xu19_5]. Establishment itself is also a gamble: across a large pooled dataset the mean survival rate of coastal wetland plantings was only 53%, with 17% of observations seeing more than 95% of transplants survive and 23% seeing less than 5% survive [ev_establishment_survival_liu24_1, ev_establishment_survival_liu24_2]. The underlying studies are concentrated in China, North America and other high-income or upper-middle-income settings; applying this class to low- and middle-income rural coastal contexts is a transfer outside where the evidence was measured.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Coastal wetlands (mangroves and salt marshes) are strong natural carbon sinks because they take up far more carbon dioxide than the methane they emit. A comparison of wetland types found mangroves and salt marshes were the only two that remained net carbon sinks, because of the limited methane generated in coastal wetlands compared with the scale of carbon-dioxide uptake [ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_5]. A global meta-analysis of natural coastal wetlands found that converting them to other land uses increased their greenhouse-gas warming potential by 7.8 times for constructed wetlands, 22.3 times for cropland and 29.5 times for aquaculture ponds on average, implying a correspondingly large potential benefit from protecting or restoring the wetland instead of converting it [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan20_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The methane cost of putting water onto land sits in the same sources. Methane emission from vegetated areas rose significantly when flooding reached zones that previously had no standing water, although average emission from pulsed sites stayed below that of permanently flooded sites [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_8], and the created shallow lakes caused methane emissions to the atmosphere even as they offered a net flux reduction [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_9]. The nitrous oxide benefit reaches only as far as the water does: in the upland plots, fluxes did not differ between flooded and dry periods [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_10]. Because the register has no variable for an individual gas, the carbon dioxide and nitrous-oxide gains and the methane rise from the same experiment enter the pool with opposite signs, which makes the evidence look more divided than it is: both sources report a net gain with a methane penalty inside it. The row rests on a pair of pumped experimental basins in temperate Ohio and a review of boreal and northern European peat-extraction after-use. No unit states a net balance over any horizon, none measures how the balance changes as the created wetland matures, and none is from a low- or lower-middle-income setting [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mits05_6, ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_8].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Creating a wetland builds a new carbon store from scratch. In created riverine basins in Ohio, organic matter in surface soils increased by approximately 1% per 3-year period over the decade after construction [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mits05_6], and nitrous oxide fluxes from marsh and edge plots were lower when those plots were inundated than when the same plots were exposed to air [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_9]. Shallow lakes created on former peat-extraction sites had the potential to reduce net greenhouse-gas flux through carbon sequestration [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_8].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The class is moderate because few results give a size. What the peat was drained for matters: rewetting farmed and tropical peat cools quickly, but on forestry-drained peat methane can cancel all the cooling for decades [ev_wgy_ram_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_5]. Water standing above the surface makes methane warming outweigh the carbon saved [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_4]. Partial rewetting slows but does not stop peat loss [ev_carbon_sequestration_unepgpa22_4]. In a Kalimantan simulation, raising water levels gave only a small, not significant fall in carbon dioxide [ev_carbon_sequestration_page09_2], and revegetation on tropical peat has failed: seedlings did no better beside a dammed canal, and aerial seeding survived at about 2% [ev_establishment_survival_page09_6, ev_establishment_survival_pusp21_4]. Much of the evidence is modelled or guidance, mostly from temperate and high-income peat. The South Sumatra tree figures count carbon in the trees only, not the peat below, and come from a single project; the Indonesian water-table results are cited second-hand in a review [ev_wet_carbon_budi20_1, ev_wet_carbon_budi20_2, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_2].
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Rewetting peat moderately increases carbon storage. Raising the water table on drained peat stops the stored carbon from rotting away. Over a hundred-year view, rewetting gives net carbon dioxide removal in most peat soils, raises methane, and cuts nitrous oxide and waterborne carbon losses [ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_1]; IPCC guidance puts the median cut in waterborne carbon at 36% and says nitrous oxide falls practically to zero once the water table is within 20 cm of the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc13wl_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc13wl_3]. Each 10 cm the water table is raised cuts net warming by at least 3 tonnes per hectare a year [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_1]. A German scenario of wet farming on fen peat cut emissions in a single state from 5.5 to 1.2 to 3.1 million tonnes a year [ev_carbon_sequestration_tann22_1], and Ramsar guidance holds that, after an early methane peak, rewetting is far better for the climate than staying drained [ev_wgy_ram_1, ev_wgy_ram_3]. Ditch blocking on UK bogs and canal blocking in Kalimantan raised the water table [ev_water_table_depth_hold04_1, ev_water_table_depth_page09_1]. On burned peat in South Sumatra, planted native trees took up 11.3 tonnes of CO2 per hectare a year (Shorea balangeran) and 12.4 tonnes (Dyera polyphylla) in their wood [ev_wet_carbon_budi20_1, ev_wet_carbon_budi20_2]. Reviews of Indonesian peat projects report canal blocks raising the water table: by about 60 cm in the dry season 100 m from a block in Riau, by 70 cm within 170 m of a block at Sungai Tohor, and by a metre over 2420 ha where communities built 12 blocks [ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_2, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_4, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_3].

justification.mechanism: Rewetting peat moderately increases carbon storage. Raising the water table on drained peat stops the stored carbon from rotting away. Over a hundred-year view, rewetting gives net carbon dioxide removal in most peat soils, raises methane, and cuts nitrous oxide and waterborne carbon losses [ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_1]; IPCC guidance puts the median cut in waterborne carbon at 36% and says nitrous oxide falls practically to zero once the water table is within 20 cm of the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc13wl_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc13wl_3]. Each 10 cm the water table is raised cuts net warming by at least 3 tonnes per hectare a year [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_1]. A German scenario of wet farming on fen peat cut emissions in a single state from 5.5 to 1.2 to 3.1 million tonnes a year [ev_carbon_sequestration_tann22_1], and Ramsar guidance holds that, after an early methane peak, rewetting is far better for the climate than staying drained [ev_wgy_ram_1, ev_wgy_ram_3]. Ditch blocking on UK bogs and canal blocking in Kalimantan raised the water table [ev_water_table_depth_hold04_1, ev_water_table_depth_page09_1]. On burned peat in South Sumatra, planted native trees took up 11.3 tonnes of CO2 per hectare a year (Shorea balangeran) and 12.4 tonnes (Dyera polyphylla) in their wood [ev_wet_carbon_budi20_1, ev_wet_carbon_budi20_2]. Reviews of Indonesian peat projects report canal blocks raising the water table: by about 60 cm in the dry season 100 m from a block in Riau, by 70 cm within 170 m of a block at Sungai Tohor, and by a metre over 2420 ha where communities built 12 blocks [ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_2, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_4, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_3].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The size is not stated and methane is the trade-off. Restored freshwater marshes gain soil carbon at the cost of significant methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_hemes18_4], and restored wetlands can warm the climate for their first years to decades, with the switch to net cooling estimated at 57 to 299 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_4]. Converting a natural riverside wetland to pasture lowered its warming effect in a meta-analysis, a reminder that keeping land wet has a methane cost [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan20_3]. Most evidence is from the United States and other high-income settings, and the benefit goes to the climate, not to the farmer.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Rewetting degraded wetlands cuts greenhouse-gas emissions because carbon dioxide uptake more than offsets the methane and nitrous oxide [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_3]; emissions are lowest when the water table sits near the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_4]. Measurements on restored wetlands on drained Californian peat showed a net greenhouse-gas benefit in some cases [ev_carbon_sequestration_hemes18_5]. A global meta-analysis found methane rose by 122.3% after restoration, yet total emissions were no higher than in disturbed wetlands [ev_carbon_sequestration_xu25_3]. Restored forested wetlands on former US farmland were modelled to store 15.8 to 92.4 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per hectare every five years [ev_carbon_sequestration_jenk10_1].
