T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The gain is local: the groundwater rise fell to 50% within about 9 m of the ditch, and effects beyond the wetland could not be judged [ev_wetflA_bring_gw_decay, ev_wetflA_bring_outside_inconclusive]. Average flows from the same UK bog fell after blocking, mainly because less time was spent at peak flow [ev_water_yield_wils11db_3], and in the Canadian model a restoration scenario made low flows worse in some sub-catchments [ev_wet_eff_goy22_3]. All evidence is from high-income temperate or boreal settings, partly modelled, and none measures water reaching farmers downstream.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: The evidence on whether wetland work gives a catchment more water is conflicting, because the two kinds of practice point different ways. Blocking ditches in drained peat raises the water table close to the ditch: across boreal and temperate wetlands (Bring et al.), restoration raised groundwater by 22 cm near the work, about as much as drainage had lowered it [ev_wetflA_bring_gw_rise, ev_wetflA_bring_conclusion]. After drains were blocked on a UK upland bog (Wilson et al.), stream flows stayed higher and fell away more slowly [ev_water_yield_wils11db_2], and in a Canadian basin model (Goyette et al.) adding wetland area gradually offset the fall in low flows expected under climate change [ev_wet_eff_goy22_2]. The restoration and rewetting family's own row points the other way, to less water overall: wetlands tend to evaporate more and reduce total runoff even as they support dry-season flow.

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The size of the reduction is not stated. Most of the evidence is about what existing wetlands do compared with other land, not about the effect of restoring them [ev_water_yield_bull03_5, ev_water_yield_kad16_1]. On groundwater the review finds about as many wetlands recharging less than surrounding land as more, with floodplains on sandy soils in India and West Africa recharging when flooded [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_bull03_10, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_bull03_11]. The groundwater rise from ditch blocking is local and effects beyond the wetland could not be judged [ev_wetflA_bring_gw_decay, ev_wetflA_bring_outside_inconclusive], and in the Canadian model a restoration scenario made low flows worse in some sub-catchments [ev_wet_eff_goy22_3]. Evidence is mainly from North America and Europe, with a few African and Indian cases in the global review. For a downstream water user, a restored wetland may mean steadier but slightly smaller flows.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Wetlands slightly reduce the total water leaving a catchment, even though they can support flow in dry periods: the trade-off is less water overall in exchange for steadier flows. A meta-analysis of wetland flow regulation (Kadykalo et al.) finds that, on average, wetlands reduce the frequency and size of floods and augment low flows, but also reduce streamflow and runoff [ev_water_yield_kad16_1]. A global review of existing wetlands (Bullock et al.) finds strong evidence that wetlands evaporate more water than forests, grassland or arable land: two thirds of studies (48 of 74) conclude they increase annual evaporation or reduce annual river flow, and two thirds (47 of 71) that they reduce river flow in dry periods, while in 20% of cases they increase dry-season river flow [ev_water_yield_bull03_5, ev_water_yield_bull03_8, ev_water_yield_bull03_9]. Restoration itself can raise the water held near the site: ditch blocking raised groundwater by 22 cm near the work across boreal and temperate wetlands [ev_wetflA_bring_gw_rise], and in a Canadian basin model adding wetland area gradually offset the fall in low flows expected under climate change [ev_wet_eff_goy22_2].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The class is moderate because the benefit is local. No effect was found across a whole 260 km2 UK catchment, and in major floods the whole basin is saturated so wetlands make no difference [ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_catchment_null, ev_wetflA_acre_catastrophic_null]. Placement can reverse the effect: a moorland scheme raised downstream risk, and moving one project downstream turned a 14% peak cut into about a 1% increase [ev_wetflA_shut_synchrony_reversal, ev_flood_hazard_feder22_4]. A rougher floodplain can make local flooding deeper and wider, and rewetting can use up storage that floods would fill [ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up, ev_wetflA_acre_somerset_rewet_cost]. The 30% figure covers a bundle of measures, not wetlands alone [ev_flood_hazard_bagh25w1_1]. Most evidence is from the UK and US, much of it modelled, and the benefit arrives downstream, not on the farm.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Wetland management moderately reduces flood risk. Rewetting and re-roughening land slows storm water, so flood peaks near the works are lower. On UK peat, peak flows fell 27% where bare peat was re-vegetated, 51% where gullies were also blocked, and 49% at a rewetted gully [ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_O, ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_N, ev_wetflA_gatis_peakflow]. Ditch and drain blocking on Irish and Welsh bogs made stream flow less flashy [ev_flood_hazard_hold04_2, ev_flood_hazard_wils11db_4]. Reconnecting floodplains cut modelled peaks by about 8% to 12% in a base case, and a review puts the average peak cut from river and floodplain measures at 30% [ev_flood_hazard_feder22_2, ev_flood_hazard_bagh25w1_1]. justification.mechanism: Wetland management moderately reduces flood risk. Rewetting and re-roughening land slows storm water, so flood peaks near the works are lower. On UK peat, peak flows fell 27% where bare peat was re-vegetated, 51% where gullies were also blocked, and 49% at a rewetted gully [ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_O, ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_N, ev_wetflA_gatis_peakflow]. Ditch and drain blocking on Irish and Welsh bogs made stream flow less flashy [ev_flood_hazard_hold04_2, ev_flood_hazard_wils11db_4]. Reconnecting floodplains cut modelled peaks by about 8% to 12% in a base case, and a review puts the average peak cut from river and floodplain measures at 30% [ev_flood_hazard_feder22_2, ev_flood_hazard_bagh25w1_1]. In a Canadian basin model restored wetland eased the expected rise in spring flood peaks [ev_wet_eff_goy22_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: What separates the two sides is scale and position: the reductions are storage and roughness effects on the flood peak passing through or below the wetland [ev_wetflA_acre_wooded_wetland, ev_wet_flood_hazard_ramsar18_2], while the increases arise at catchment scale, where an on-site storage gain need not add up to a downstream benefit [ev_wetflA_acre_synchrony_catchment], and locally, where the roughness that slows the flood raises water level and flooded area on the re-vegetated floodplain itself [ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up]. The influence of drain blocking on flood flows has been notoriously difficult to detect at the basin scale [ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_basin_null]; and during major catastrophic floods the whole basin may be saturated, so the presence or absence of wetlands, or their management, has no effect [ev_wetflA_acre_catastrophic_null]. None of the units is a measurement of a flood outcome in this scope: they are a single review pooling UK, US, Canadian, Irish and Zimbabwean settings and a global policy brief. Siting matters as much as the practice: whether a wetland intervention lowers flood hazard depends on where it sits in the catchment and how large the flood is.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Studies disagree on whether wetland management lowers or raises flood hazard. On the side of a reduction, wooded wetlands in particular increase flood storage, reduce flood peaks and increase peak travel time [ev_wetflA_acre_wooded_wetland], and a Ramsar briefing note states that wetland protection and restoration buffer communities by reducing wave damage and floods [ev_wet_flood_hazard_ramsar18_2]. On the side of an increase, the same review reports that even where the dominant result is to increase water storage within the wetland, the overall result may still be an increase in flood peaks at the catchment scale [ev_wetflA_acre_synchrony_catchment], and that a change of vegetation from wet meadows to shrubs and trees can double the size and depth of the inundated area for the same size of flood [ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The benefit is not uniform across storm severity: the same review found salt marshes attenuate storm surge less effectively during extreme storms than during moderate ones, and man-made levees or dikes behind a marsh can limit its surge-attenuating effect. Only 2 of the 8 units measuring a benefit state its size, which is why the class is capped at a moderate level even though the direction is consistent.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Coastal wetlands reduce flood hazard mainly by dissipating wave energy and attenuating storm surge before it reaches land: salt-marsh vegetation has been measured giving significantly greater wave attenuation than unvegetated intertidal mudflat, and across a global set of field measurements, coastal habitats reduced wave heights by 35% to 71% on average, with salt marshes alone cutting wave height by about 72%. A sizeable proportion of salt-marsh and mangrove restoration projects report improved protection from storm events as an outcome.

justification.mechanism: Reconnecting and rewetting floodplains gives storm water somewhere to spread. Modelled peak flow fell by up to 37% along a reconnected reach [ev_flood_hazard_feder22_1]; hollow wetlands could store 72% of the runoff from a 2-year storm [ev_wetflA_acre_depression_storage]; and setting levees back lowered flood levels, by 50 cm on the Elbe [ev_flood_hazard_serra22_1]. A meta-analysis finds that on average wetlands reduce flood frequency and size [ev_flood_hazard_kad16_1]. In a Canadian basin model restored wetland eased the expected rise in spring flood peaks [ev_wet_eff_goy22_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: What separates the sides is what the land was used for. Losses come where cropland on drained peat or lakebed is rewetted; gains come where seasonal floods return to grazing land [ev_agricultural_production_value_rgwo25_2, ev_livestock_productivity_loth04_1]. The loss can be local rather than national: Finland expects only a minor national effect [ev_wgy_qa_5]. Several measured studies found no change: a matched Uganda evaluation found no significant yield change, and most Sumatran smallholders with a canal block noticed no impact, though about 10% reported lower yields [ev_crop_yield_fp034e_5, ev_crop_yield_ward20_1]. Much of the loss side is European expert statement; the Cameroon gain is a project's own grey-literature account with no comparison area.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Wetland management has been found both to cut and to raise farm production. Where floods return to grazing land, livestock gain: after pilot flood releases in Cameroon the breeding rate of cows rose from 16% to 50% [ev_livestock_productivity_loth04_1], and reopening a creek in Ghana enhanced cattle farming [ev_livestock_productivity_ghppar_2]. Where farmed land is rewetted, crop output falls: rewetted peat becomes unsuitable for crops such as potatoes and carrots [ev_wgy_qa_6, ev_wgy_ram_17]; wet-farming crops are mostly not food [ev_wet_cropyield_temm26_5]; and rewetting arable fen in England caused a large loss of arable food production, partly offset by more grazing [ev_agricultural_production_value_rgwo25_2]. Near Poyang Lake, tenant farmers' crops are damaged by protected birds with no compensation [ev_wgy_poy_2].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: What separates the sides is who bears the cost and how it is replaced. Losses come where farmland or wetland access is taken away and compensation is small or absent [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_2, ev_wgy_poy_1]; gains come from wages, compensation, new livelihoods and niche products [ev_household_income_bbr_3, ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_4, ev_wet_econret_neud26_2]. Several gains go to society, not households, and are held out of the class: a restored fen at Wicken Fen has a benefit-cost ratio of 4.4 against 1.3 for farming, and restored US wetlands repay public costs within a year, but both count climate and other public benefits [ev_economic_return_rgwo25_1, ev_economic_return_jenk10_4]. The Cameroon and Chinese ecotourism gains are project accounts in grey literature [ev_economic_return_loth04_5, ev_economic_return_rgwo25_7]. The South Sumatra comparison is second-hand and gives no figure [ev_wet_econret_budi20_2]. A European review comparing restoration costs with values for wetland services taken from other studies puts the benefit to society at more than 4,000 euros per hectare a year, against a restoration cost of about 227 euros per hectare a year [ev_economic_return_strz25_4]; this is a return to society, not to households, so it is held out of the rating.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Household income has been found both to rise and to fall with wetland management. It falls where farmland is taken out of use: at Poyang Lake, households that returned farmland to the lake saw income fall [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_2, ev_wgy_poy_1]; a Uganda project evaluation found lower total income among project households [ev_household_income_fp034e_2]; German farms rewetting grassland lost on average 35% of gross margin [ev_wet_hhinc_meye26_1]; in the US, carbon and hunting markets pay landowners only about 18% of farming returns [ev_economic_return_jenk10_5]; and in Indonesia existing livelihoods will no longer be feasible on rewetted peat [ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_5]. It rises through payments, wages and products that sell: compensation transfers at Poyang, restoration jobs in South Africa, and high-value products such as thatching reed [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_4, ev_household_income_bbr_3, ev_wet_econret_neud26_2]. German fen wet pastures with hardy breeds were profitable in all scenarios [ev_economic_return_tann22_4]. In Cameroon, restored floods nearly doubled household fish catches and added an estimated 4,360 euros per square kilometre a year [ev_fish_catch_loth04_2, ev_economic_return_loth04_5]. In South Sumatra, a cited study found native peat-swamp trees (Shorea balangeran and Dyera polyphylla) worth more than the current practice of burning to plant sonor rice [ev_wet_econret_budi20_2].

justification.mechanism: Household income has been found both to rise and to fall with wetland management. It falls where farmland is taken out of use: at Poyang Lake, households that returned farmland to the lake saw income fall [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_2, ev_wgy_poy_1]; a Uganda project evaluation found lower total income among project households [ev_household_income_fp034e_2]; German farms rewetting grassland lost on average 35% of gross margin [ev_wet_hhinc_meye26_1]; in the US, carbon and hunting markets pay landowners only about 18% of farming returns [ev_economic_return_jenk10_5]; and in Indonesia existing livelihoods will no longer be feasible on rewetted peat [ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_5]. It rises through payments, wages and products that sell: compensation transfers at Poyang, restoration jobs in South Africa, and high-value products such as thatching reed [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_4, ev_household_income_bbr_3, ev_wet_econret_neud26_2]. German fen wet pastures with hardy breeds were profitable in all scenarios [ev_economic_return_tann22_4]. In Cameroon, restored floods nearly doubled household fish catches and added an estimated 4,360 euros per square kilometre a year [ev_fish_catch_loth04_2, ev_economic_return_loth04_5]. In South Sumatra, a cited study found native peat-swamp trees (Shorea balangeran and Dyera polyphylla) worth more than the current practice of burning to plant sonor rice [ev_wet_econret_budi20_2].

justification.statement: wetland_management rural_poverty: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE — material weight on both the benefit and the harm side, so no direction is stated. This is not a null finding: studies found real effects, in opposite directions, and the agreement note lists both sides. Read the conditionality for what separates them (transfer: adjacent).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The direction is a slight gain carried by modelled returns to a wet crop, and the loss for oil-palm households is kept as harm to those adopters, not averaged away. What separates them is the starting point: a household that can grow and sell sago or another wet crop gains a modest return, while a household giving up drained oil palm loses income relative to what it had. Neither review measures a household or attaches a magnitude to the loss, the sago returns are cited from other studies with no inflation adjustment, and the oil-palm finding comes from a bundled rewetting and revegetation programme. Both sources describe Indonesian and Malaysian upper-middle-income settings, so a low- or lower-middle-income humid-tropics investment has no directly applicable evidence here, and compensation or a payment is likely to be needed where drained plantation crops are retired.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: All the units here concern wet use of tropical peat and come from reviews citing other work. On the gain side, sago, a crop that grows on shallow peat without drainage, is cited at an internal rate of return of 12.9–19%, rising to 17.4–19.2% once environmental benefits are counted [ev_economic_return_tan21_9], and the same review concludes from NPV, IRR and BCR that paludiculture may generate a small margin of economic benefit, while adding in the same sentence that its benefits relative to conventional drainage-based crops are still too low and that not all costs and externalities are documented [ev_economic_return_tan21_10]. On the loss side, communities that have relied on oil palm cultivation will find it challenging to participate in peatland restoration, since rewetting may entail lower productivity and financial return for their crops [ev_household_income_mish21_5].

justification.statement: wetland_management rural_poverty: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE — material weight on both the benefit and the harm side, so no direction is stated. This is not a null finding: studies found real effects, in opposite directions, and the agreement note lists both sides. Read the conditionality for what separates them (transfer: adjacent).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The class is moderate, and its strength comes from the coastal units: it concerns shoreline protection and coastal stabilization against a degraded marsh or coast, not soil loss from fields. The 0.61 effect size is on a scale the source does not define (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_3); the Chinese figure is a pooled response ratio across restoration types that include building dikes as well as planting (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_1). The peatland evidence is a single runoff-volume unit, not an erosion measurement: at a blanket-peat restoration, the share of storm rainfall becoming storm discharge did not change at either restored site relative to the bare control (ev_wetflA_shut_runoffcoef_null), the paper concluding that restoration shifted the timing and peak of delivery rather than the volume - a null that says the peatland evidence here does not speak to erosion. The Manalana gully result is a programme narrative without a measurement, and it concerns gullies cutting through the wetland itself rather than soil loss from surrounding fields (ev_erosion_hazard_bbr_1). Sediment that a wetland traps from water flowing through it is a water-quality service, not prevention of landscape erosion, and those units vote in the water-quality row, not here. Nothing in the pool measures soil loss on farmland, and apart from the South African case all of it comes from high- and upper-middle-income coastal and upland settings.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Vegetation and wetland structures hold soil and sediment in place, and the result is clearest for coastal marsh. Against a degraded shore, salt-marsh planting enhances shoreline protection, which the meta-analysis measures as vertical accretion, elevation change, sediment deposition and shoreline change rates (effect size 0.61) (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_3). A meta-analysis of China's coastal wetland restoration (Liu et al.) found coastal stabilization - indicators such as vertical accretion rate - significantly improved in restored against degraded wetlands, by 19.7 % (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_1). In the restoration sub-practice, South Africa's Manalana wetland is the only case: rehabilitation structures halted the advance of erosion gullies that would otherwise have continued throughout the wetland and degraded the entire area (ev_erosion_hazard_bbr_1).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Much of the pool is not a restoration result at all: the paired-study evidence measures what EXISTING marsh does against bare mudflat (ev_erosion_hazard_shep11_3, ev_erosion_hazard_shep11_4), which is an argument for protecting marsh that is already there rather than a measured gain from creating or replanting it, and a sizeable minority of those paired studies did not report a positive effect. The vegetation-removal experiment and its meta-analysis are the same kind of evidence - what existing marsh loses when its plants go, not what restoration adds - and vegetation had no effect on vertical erosion of the marsh surface (ev_erosion_hazard_sill19w1_3); their outcome is erosion of the marsh edge itself. The restored-versus-degraded pooled values are effect sizes and shares of studies whose scale the sources do not define (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_3), which is why direction is firmer than magnitude here; the Chinese stabilization figure pools restoration types that include building dikes as well as planting (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_1). This is shoreline and tidal-flat erosion only - it carries nothing about soil loss from cropland or rangeland - and the field sites are coasts in the United States, United Kingdom, China and the Netherlands, with the authors noting that matched restored and degraded pairs are few.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Marsh vegetation attenuates waves and currents as water passes through the canopy, so suspended sediment settles, the bed accretes and surface elevation is maintained while lateral erosion of the shoreline is reduced. That mechanism is measured from both ends: inside existing marsh against adjacent unvegetated mudflat, where most paired studies reported increased accretion or surface elevation or reduced erosion and the pooled effect on shoreline stabilisation was positive (ev_erosion_hazard_shep11_3, ev_erosion_hazard_shep11_4); and in planted marsh, which improved shoreline protection against degraded wetland (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_3). A meta-analysis of China's coastal wetland restoration (Liu et al.) found coastal stabilization - indicators such as vertical accretion rate - significantly improved in restored against degraded wetlands, by 19.7 % (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_1). A field experiment on a wave-stressed shoreline tests the mechanism from the loss side: lateral erosion where aboveground and belowground vegetation was removed (114.19 cm) was significantly higher than in vegetated controls (76.76 cm), whereas removing only the aboveground vegetation made no difference (ev_erosion_hazard_sill19w1_1, ev_erosion_hazard_sill19w1_2); across 15 previous comparisons of marsh-edge erosion between vegetated and vegetation-reduced conditions, the mean effect size of 1.22 shows a generally positive effect of vegetation on the reduction of marsh-edge erosion (ev_erosion_hazard_sill19w1_4).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The no-relationship class rests on that null alone, and it is about water volume, not soil. The unit behind this row is a runoff-coefficient null (ev_wetflA_shut_runoffcoef_null), and the paper's own conclusion is that restoration altered the timing and peak of storm delivery while leaving the volume of runoff produced unchanged. It is therefore evidence that re-vegetation and gully blocking did not reduce how much water ran off, and it should not be read as evidence that they fail to reduce erosion - no sediment or soil-loss measurement is present in this pool, which is why the cell states no relationship rather than a reduction, and the row stands as an evidence gap. The observation comes from an upland English blanket-peat site in a high-income temperate setting, with no tropical peat and no farmland, so this row marks an evidence gap rather than a finding of no effect.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Re-vegetating bare blanket peat, alone or together with gully blocking by stone and timber dams, is the peatland practice behind this row. On the only quantity measured here - the share of storm rainfall leaving as storm discharge - restoration changed nothing at either restored site relative to the bare, unrestored control (ev_wetflA_shut_runoffcoef_null).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The class is slight and carries no strength: neither unit measures soil loss. The Manalana result is a programme narrative from a sustainable-development case study, with no measurement of gully extent or sediment, and it concerns gullies cutting through the wetland itself rather than erosion on the farmland around it (ev_erosion_hazard_bbr_1). The meta-analysis compares existing wetlands with drained or absent ones, mostly in North America and Europe, and reports runoff and streamflow, not erosion; less runoff is a route to less erosion, not a measure of it (ev_runoff_reduction_kad16_1). A measured erosion or sediment-yield finding after a wetland is rehabilitated would let this row say how much.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Wetlands hold water and slow it, which keeps it from cutting into the land. At the Manalana wetland in South Africa's Sand River catchment, rehabilitation structures halted actively advancing erosion gullies that would otherwise have continued through the wetland and degraded the entire area (ev_erosion_hazard_bbr_1). A weighted meta-analysis of the flow-regulation services of wetlands (Kadykalo et al.) adds the water side: on average wetlands decrease runoff and streamflow (ev_runoff_reduction_kad16_1).

A weighted meta-analysis of the flow-regulation services of wetlands (Kadykalo et al.) adds the water side: on average wetlands decrease runoff and streamflow (ev_runoff_reduction_kad16_1).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The strong class rests on both units agreeing, not on depth of evidence, and each has limits. The Moldovan figure is a project completion report's own estimate from inlet and outlet sampling over part of a year, scaled by an assumed flow, with no pre-restoration or unrestored reference [ev_nutrient_removal_mdicr_1]. The Chinese figure is a pooled response ratio for a broad water-purification category across coastal restoration types, from planting mangroves to breaking dikes, not a measured nutrient load [ev_nutrient_removal_liu24_1]. Neither concerns a wetland restored on former cropland, which is where phosphorus release is reported elsewhere in the wetland evidence, and both settings - a river-fed Ramsar wetland and the Chinese coast - are upper-middle-income, so the transfer to a low-income farmed catchment is untested.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Water slowed and spread through a rehabilitated wetland drops sediment and gives plants and soil time to take up and transform nutrients. On Moldova's rehabilitated Lapusna wetland, estimated annual nutrient retention is about 17 tons N and 3.0 tons P, assuming an average annual flow through of 10,600,000m3 [ev_nutrient_removal_mdicr_1]. On the Chinese coast, a meta-analysis of coastal wetland restoration (Liu et al.) found water purification and waste treatment indicators significantly improved against degraded wetlands, by 69.3 % [ev_nutrient_removal_liu24_1].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Phosphorus is where this fails. By the 10th year total phosphorus showed little retention and even export, falling by only 2% in the naturally colonising basin and rising by 14% in the planted one, after a consistent pattern of retention over the first 8 years [ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_3, ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_4]: the created wetland had become a net phosphorus exporter in its tenth year. Sediment and total phosphorus retention were diminishing after 10 years of river flow [ev_sediment_retention_mits05_5], so the particulate fraction of the service decays as the basin fills while the dissolved-nutrient service persists. Both studies sit in temperate, high-income rainfed cropland, Ohio and Sweden, and both concern created wetlands fed by river or catchment water rather than restored ones; the Ohio basins were continuously pumped, which is not how a wetland in a farmed catchment is fed. Nothing was measured in a tropical or lower-income rainfed system.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In rainfed cropping catchments a wetland works as an interception point for the nutrients leaving the fields. In the 10th year after construction, average nitrate removal by the created riverine basins was 42%, the highest of the decade [ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_1], and soluble reactive phosphorus retention continued to be significant at around 70%, 63% in the planted basin and 73% in the naturally colonising one, with no significant difference between them [ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_2]. In Swedish farmland, nutrient retention and diversity proved compatible aims, since biodiversity was neither locally nor regionally harmed by high nitrate levels [ev_nutrient_removal_thie09_6].

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The class is strong but rests on a single source: the Chinese meta-analysis, whose figure is a pooled response ratio for a broad water-purification category across restoration types from planting mangroves to breaking dikes, not a measured nitrogen or phosphorus load [ev_nutrient_removal_liu24_1]. The salt-marsh sediment result compares planted marsh with adjacent natural wetland, so it says a planted marsh may trap sediment at least as well as an intact one, hedged by its authors, not what planting changed against the pre-restoration shore, and it does not set the class [ev_sediment_retention_liu24_15]. Everything here is from the Chinese coast and high-income planted marsh; nothing comes from a low- or lower-middle-income farmed catchment. A second independent source measuring a nutrient or contaminant outcome below a restored coastal wetland would firm this up.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: A restored coastal wetland slows tidal flow and waves, so suspended particles and the nutrients and contaminants bound to them drop out of the water column and are held in the marsh. T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Creating a wetland on nutrient-enriched farmland can reverse the sign. Negative phosphorus removal - the wetland exporting phosphorus rather than retaining it - was reported in a minority of the reviewed wetlands, and most of those had been created on former cropland or cattle pasture, where soil rich in phosphorus from its cropping history can release after construction (ev_nutrient_removal_land16_6); the rest were new wetlands released from initially phosphorus-rich sediments. That is the setting a rural scan targets, so legacy soil phosphorus belongs in the design brief. At site level a created basin exported total phosphorus in its tenth year while its twin barely retained any, after years of consistent retention (ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_4, ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_3), and sediment and total-phosphorus retention were diminishing after a decade of river flow (ev_sediment_retention_mits05_5) - the sediment and phosphorus services age out while the nitrogen service holds. A substantial minority of individual wetlands showed no demonstrable nitrogen removal (ev_nutrient_removal_land16_8), and net annual release of nitrogen, though rare, has been observed (ev_nutrient_removal_land16_9). The quantified ceiling claims are modelled, not measured, and every unit is high-income temperate - inflows in the review included treated wastewater and urban runoff as well as agricultural runoff, so the pooled efficiency is not a farmland-only number.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: A created wetland works as a reactor placed in the flow path: residence time rises, nitrogen is removed by plant uptake and denitrification and phosphorus settles with sediment, so a share of the incoming load leaves the water. Across created and restored freshwater wetlands that is a measured net removal of total nitrogen and total phosphorus, both as mass rates and as a share of the incoming load (ev_nutrient_removal_land16_1, ev_nutrient_removal_land16_2, ev_nutrient_removal_land16_3, ev_nutrient_removal_land16_4, ev_nutrient_removal_land16_5), and nitrate and soluble-reactive-phosphorus retention persisted into the tenth year of a created riverine pair (ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_1, ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_2, ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_3). Where new wetlands are put matters more than how many: modelled placement in the highest nitrogen-surplus areas removes far more nitrogen than placement on non-agricultural land, at a higher cost because it takes cropland out of production (ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_4, ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_2, ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_3), and the gain flattens as restoration spreads beyond the hotspots (ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_5). Created wetlands can be designed to hold nutrients and carry species diversity at the same time rather than trading them off (ev_nutrient_removal_thie09_6).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The gain is measured against the degraded starting point, and against that baseline restored extraction sites leak less (ev_nutrient_removal_rasa23_5). Measured against their intact natural counterparts the same restored sites leaked more nutrients and carbon, associated with greater water-table variation (ev_nutrient_removal_rasa23_4); that is incomplete recovery towards an intact peatland, not harm, and the two comparisons must not be netted. The real reversals are in the Ramsar report's cited synthesis. In some cases restoration causes a temporarily increased flush of nutrients into downstream water courses, though the release decreases in the longer term (ev_wgy_ram_8); and on nutrient-rich, formerly fertilised agricultural fens, rewetting may even increase the nutrient problem by mobilising hitherto bound phosphorus and nitrogen, internal eutrophication (ev_wgy_ram_9). Agricultural peat is exactly the land a rural scan would target, so a downstream nutrient pulse in the early years, and a sustained phosphorus problem on fertilised fens, should be planned for rather than assumed away. The measured case in this pool found no significant water-quality improvement and no significant reduction in aqueous carbon losses after rewetting an eroding upland blanket peat, with dissolved organic carbon rising non-significantly afterwards (ev_wetflA_gatis_waterquality_null); the quantity measured there is dissolved organic carbon routed to the nearest water-quality outcome, not nutrients, and water colour did change. Everything here is boreal or temperate peat in high-income countries or unspecified settings; nothing covers tropical peat or a farmed low- or lower-middle-income catchment, and the Ramsar statements give direction without magnitude or site.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Rewetting a cut-over peat site - raising the water table, filling or blocking ditches, mulching and transferring a moss layer - stabilises the water table and keeps the exposed peat saturated, so less nutrient and carbon load is flushed from the surface. Against the realistic do-nothing counterfactual of an abandoned extraction site, the loads leaving restored sites were lower (ev_nutrient_removal_rasa23_5). The Ramsar technical report, citing the literature, generalises this: disturbed peatlands release substantial quantities of humic acids, nitrogen, sulphur, heavy metals and suspended solids, whereas drain-blocking generally leads to a substantial reduction in their outflow (ev_wgy_ram_6, ev_wgy_ram_7).

T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: The recovery is partial. The near-ditch groundwater evidence, with its small footprint and inconclusive effects outside the wetland soil, now sits in the catchment water yield rows. The English rise is in the mean rather than the typical state: median water-table conditions remained similar at all distances after restoration, so the significant mean rise is driven by the wet tail [ev_wetflA_gatis_watertable]. The Neman model is a scenario estimate, and its basin total corresponds to 0.14–0.7% of the total annual Neman River discharge into the Baltic Sea - water held in the peat, not delivered to users [ev_water_regulation_sta22_1]. Every unit is temperate or boreal, from the UK, Ireland, Fennoscandia, Canada and the Neman basin, and none measures water available to a farming system.
T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: In the high-income boreo-temperate evidence, rewetting measurably puts water back where the drain took it from. On an eroding English upland peatland, peat barriers across gullies raised mean water tables significantly at all distance classes, in the peat pans from 0.003 m below ground level to 0.064 m above it and in the vegetated haggs from 0.188 to 0.175 m below ground within 0.5 m of the pan edge [ev_wetflA_gatis_watertable]. On cutaway peat, the water-table level was successfully recovered by active restoration through ditch blocking and dam construction [ev_water_regulation_rasa23_6]. A basin-scale model of rewetting drained peat in the Neman basin (Stachowicz et al.) puts the extra water retained at 69 to 344 m3·ha−1, or 23.6–118 M m3 across the basin [ev_water_regulation_sta22_1].

data limitations, an adjusted approach was adopted in which the target 
areas for afforestation were identified by integrating non-forested

EV_evidence_register.quote:
The best CEM techniques were diﬀerent for both sites. In Mbeere
South, tied ridging was the best followed by mulching practice while in
Meru South mulching was the best. The tied ridges in the semi-arid site
were hardly destroyed during the cropping season leading to increased
water content in the soil proﬁle and good crop performance while in the
sub-humid site the ridges were repaired often. On clay soils (in Meru
South), ridge tillage can induce water logging, and later on followed by
mass movement/soil erosion (FAO, 1993). Mulching retained more soil
water content in Meru South since the region received more rainfall
compared with Mbeere South. In addition, soils in Meru South are ﬁne
textured, clay while Mbeere South the soils are coarser. Reduced soil
water retention is observed in coarse textured (Mbeere South) than in
ﬁne-textured soils

EV_evidence_register.quote: Suitability Trapezoidal bunds can be used for growing crops, trees and grass. Their most common application is for crop production under the following site conditions: Rainfall: 250 mm - 500 mm; arid to semi-arid areas. Soils: agricultural soils with good constructional properties i.e. significant (non-cracking) clay content. Slopes: from 0.25% - 1.5%, but most suitable below 0.5%.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: Slopes

relationship.direction: Keep 0.25–1.5% guidance for crop-producing trapezoidal bunds, preferably below 0.5%, with even ground inside. Above 1.5% is technically feasible but needs prohibitively large earthworks.

source_profile.construction_above_1_5_pct: Technically feasible; prohibitively large quantities of earthwork.
source_profile.soil: Agricultural soil with significant non-cracking clay suitable for bund construction.

EV_evidence_register.quote: A trapezoidal bund consists of a base bund, connected to two side bunds at an angle of about 135° and a distance between the tips of 10 – 100 m. Overflow is discharged around the tips of the side bunds. The wings of the side bunds are pref- erably reinforced with stones. Often they are constructed using machinery. Enclosed areas can reach 1 ha in size (C:A 15:1 – 100:1). The technology is suitable for areas with 200 – 400 mm of annual rainfall.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: annual rainfall

source_table.practice: Cultivated above-ground earthen reservoirs and tanks

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Cultivated reservoirs / tanks are above ground earthen water retention struc-
tures. Tanks are constructed on gentile slopes (1 – 10%) by excavating soil and/or 
building bunds (reservoirs). In this system collected water is either directed from the 
tank to lower fields or into a below ground tank or shallow well for irrigation (C:A ratio 
10:1 – 100:1). When the water of the reservoir is used, the reservoir itself is cropped 
on soil residual moisture. This system is suitable for areas with 150 – 600 mm annual 
rainfall.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: slopes

relationship.direction: Keep the 1–10% construction range for cultivated above-ground tanks, paired with 150–600 mm annual rainfall. The drained reservoir bed can be cultivated on residual moisture. Other excavated ponds have separate guidance.

source_profile.cultivation: After stored water is used, residual moisture supports cropping of the tank bed.
source_profile.storage: Above-ground earthen water retention by excavation and/or bund construction.

EV_evidence_register.quote: Cultivated reservoirs / tanks are above ground earthen water retention struc- tures. Tanks are constructed on gentile slopes (1 – 10%) by excavating soil and/or building bunds (reservoirs). In this system collected water is either directed from the tank to lower fields or into a below ground tank or shallow well for irrigation (C:A ratio 10:1 – 100:1). When the water of the reservoir is used, the reservoir itself is cropped on soil residual moisture. This system is suitable for areas with 150 – 600 mm annual rainfall.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: annual rainfall

EV_evidence_register.quote: Small earth and stone dams: Rainwater storage systems such as small dams in Ethiopia and Tanzania (known as ndivas), are communally constructed around foot- slopes of hills or along irrigation canals to store the runoff from ephemeral or per- ennial rivers. The reservoirs have neither plastered walls nor covered surfaces. The water is mostly used communally for livestock consumption, and for supplementary irrigation. Ndivas are suitable suitable for areas with 300 – 600 mm of rainfall.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: rainfall

relationship.direction: small earth/stone storage dams suit semi-arid rainfall

source_table.practice: Negarim tree microcatchments

EV_evidence_register.quote: Negarim are small diamond-shaped runoff basins, surrounded by low earth bunds. Runoff infiltrates at the lowest apex, where the trees are planted. Reported sizes of negarim are 100-250 m² in Israel and up to 400 m² in India. As 15-90% of rainfall may be harvested as runoff and used for the tree crop, the catchment to cropping area ratio ranges between 3:1 and 10:1; in flatter catchments and drier areas this may be up to 25:1. They are applied on sloping land (1-20%), however are com- monly found on slopes of 1-5% in areas of 150-500 mm/y of rainfall.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: slopes

relationship.direction: WOCAT describes application on 1–20% slopes, commonly 1–5% in areas receiving 150–500 mm/year. Common use supplies no optimum score.

EV_evidence_register.quote: Meskat is rectangular shaped runoff basin. It consists of a catchment area called meskat of about 500 m² in size, and a cropping area called mankaa of about 250 m² (C:A ratio of 2:1). The entire system is surrounded by an approximately 20 cm high bund, and provided with spillways to allow runoff to flow into the mankaa. A meskat can have more than one mankaa arranged in series (see figure below). Surplus runoff spills over one mankaa to the other. Meskats are suitable on slopes of 2-15% and for areas with an annual rainfall of 200 – 400 mm.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: slopes

EV_evidence_register.quote: Triangular / V-shaped bunds: Very similar to negarim, these earthen bunds of about 0.5 m in height enclose a pit in the apex, where the water is stored until it infiltrates into the soil. The structures are about 1 – 7 m wide and they are usually aligned in staggered rows. The tips of the basins need to be on the contour. The C:A ratio is about 5:1. They are widely used for tree establishment: for almonds, apricots, peaches, pistachio, olives or pomegranate trees, and for fodder bushes. Generally they are applied on slopes up to 20% in areas with more than 300 mm annual rainfall.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: slopes

relationship.direction: V-shaped bunds are applied up to moderately steep slopes

EV_evidence_register.quote: Semi-circular bunds are usually made of earth or stone and have commonly a diam- eter of 2-8 m (up to 12 m). The bund tips are set on the contour line, facing upslope. Bunds are 30-50 cm high. They are built in a staggered sequence over a plot; that is the second line catches runoff that flows between the structures in the line above; and so on. The C:A ratio ranges between 1:1 and 3:1. In dry conditions, the bunds are bigger. In wetter conditions, more bunds of smaller radius are constructed per hec- tare. They are applied on slopes up to 15%, however earthen bunds are rarely used on slopes steeper than 5%, receiving more than 300 mm/y of rainfall.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: slopes

relationship.direction: applied up to the upper value, but earthen bunds are rarely used above the lower value

EV_evidence_register.quote: Eyebrow terraces: Microbasins which supply single trees or bushes with runoff on hillsides are sometimes termed eyebrow terraces. They are also known as ‘platform terraces’ as their cultivated area is kept level. The catchment size is 5 – 50 m² and the cultivated area 1 – 5 m². This technology can be applied on slopes of up to 50%; the steeper the gradient, the more the bunds have to be reinforced by stone (where available).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: slopes

relationship.direction: eyebrow terraces reach steep hillsides; the steeper, the more the bunds need stone reinforcement

EV_evidence_register.quote: Cultivated strips: On gentle slopes alternating cropping strips along the contour are built: the upper one is used as a catchment and the lower one is cropped. The width of the cropped strip ranges from 1 – 3 m. The C:A ratio is usually 1:1 but can reach 1:5 depending on rainfall and the crop. Often on the sides and the lower end of the cropped area soil bunds are constructed to impede runoff from the cropped area. Cultivated strips are used on flat land or on gentle slopes of up to 4% with at least 1 m deep soils and that receive rainfall of more than 200 mm/y.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: slopes

relationship.direction: runoff/cultivated strips only on flat or gently sloping land

EV_evidence_register.lineage_of: Epaphra 2001; Gerhardt and Nemarundwe 2006; Franzel et al. 2002a; Nyeko et al. 2004
EV_evidence_register.quote: In studies conducted by Epaphra (2001) in Tanzania and Gerhardt and Nemarundwe (2006) in Zimbabwe, it was noted that over 60% of women in Tanzania are responsible for managing tree species planted on farms while over 80% in Zimbabwe are responsible for watering young seedlings. This trend is conﬁrmed by Franzel et al. (2002a) in a study undertaken in Embu, Kenya to determine early stages of adoption of calliandra fodder in the central highlands of Kenya. It was found that although 91% of households using calliandra fodder were male headed, in 89% of these households females were responsible for manag- ing calliandra. A similar scenario was observed in Uganda by Nyeko et al. (2004) whereby in over 80% of households with calliandra, women were involved in management.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: women's share of on-farm tree labour

relationship.direction_cue: over 60% of women in Tanzania are responsible for managing tree species planted on farms
relationship.outcome_raw: labour burden falls on women: over 60% of women in Tanzania manage planted farm trees, over 80% in Zimbabwe water young seedlings, and in 89% of (91% male-headed) calliandra households in Embu Kenya females manage the calliandra

EV_evidence_register.quote: An economic study undertaken in several sites in Kenya and Uganda showed that beginning in the second year after planting 500 calliandra shrubs, a farmer’s net income increases by about US$ 101–122 a year by substituting dairy meal with calliandra. On the other hand, if a farmer uses calliandra fodder shrubs as a supplement for dairy meal, the farmer’s income increases by about US$ 62–115 a year. This is about 5–10% of the total income from the farm.

EV_evidence_register.quote: This review shows that agroforestry systems in East Africa stock an average of 24.2 ± 2.8 Mg C ha−1 in biomass and 98.8 ± 12.2 Mg C ha−1 in the soil (Fig. 3). The combined estimate of carbon in biomass and the soil is larger than what was estimated to be the potential carbon storage (29–53 Mg C ha−1) of agrosilvicultural systems in the humid tropics of Africa (Albrecht and Kandji, 2003), but lower than systems with high stem density, large mean tree size, and longer maximum ages i.e. over 60 years reported in Southeast Asia (Roshetko et al., 2007). The difference with earlier estimates is mostly in the soil part where several method­ ological issues need to be considered (Hairiah et al., 2020), such as variation in the soil depth included and changes in soil bulk density that influence which soil is included in a fixed-depth sample (Schrumpf et al., 2011). The amount varies depending on agroforestry practice, ranging from 26.7 ± 7.0 Mg C ha−1 in improved fallows to 153±23 Mg C ha−1 in homegardens.

QUEUE/SOURCE CAVEAT: the regional sentence names 'Asia' twice with opposite signs — an apparent typo in the published text (the 48%-decrease region is almost certainly Africa per the later regional breakdown 33%/48%/33%). Not resolvable from the text, so no regional unit emitted from this sentence. VOTE-COUNT review: percentages are shares of STUDIES reporting a direction, not effect magnitudes, so metric = narrative. PICOS: 58 of the 74 reviewed studies are agroforestry studies and 53 of those are trees INTRODUCED TO THE FARM (typically alley cropping); only 12 studies concern off-farm natural forest patches. The pooled vote-counts are therefore dominated by, but not exclusive to, agroforestry — read as agroforestry-weighted, not agroforestry-pure.

EV_evidence_register.quote: The overall trend across the studies shows that in the majority of cases (52%) there was a net positive (47%) or neutral (5%) effect of tree presence on food yields or food yield proxies. However, when the results are disaggregated by region, there is a degree of variability (Fig. 5). For example, in the Americas and Asia, tree presence was more likely to enhance food yields with positive effects of trees on yields reported in 58% and 54% of studies for these regions respectively; while in Asia the opposite is the case, with the majority of studies (48%) reporting decreased food yields as a result of tree presence (Fig. 5).

Como pontos relevantes, foram identificados:  valorização da terra (conservação do solo); diversificação agríco- la; melhoria na qualidade do solo (fertilidade do solo);  aumento da renda familiar e melhoria na qualidade de vida da família (impacto social e econômico). As produtividades alcançadas (Tabela 6.5) demonstram que a barra- gem subterrânea constitui-se em uma alternativa tecnológica que pro- porciona garantia ao agricultor de obter sua safra, desde que se tenha o mínimo de chuva necessário (Tabela 6.6) para atender às necessida- des das culturas exploradas. (English: the subsurface dam is not the main source of income of the family in the area studied; due to climatic adversities, nothing was harvested from the subsurface dam in the 2005/2006 agricultural year (Table 6.5); outsourcing of labour, because the children, on reaching a certain age, went to study in the city. As relevant points the following were identified: valuation of the land (soil conservation); agricultural diversification; improvement of soil quality (soil fertility); increase in family income and improvement in the family's quality of life (social and economic impact). The yields achieved (Table 6.5) show that the subsurface dam is a technological alternative that gives the farmer a guarantee of obtaining a harvest, provided the minimum rainfall needed (Table 6.6) to meet the needs of the crops grown occurs.)

EV_evidence_register.quote: tre estas tecnologias, o uso da irrigação de salvação tem reduzido os riscos da exploração agrícola em anos cuja precipitação pluviométrica é irregular, proporcionando até duas colheitas em anos considerados normais de chuvas. Segundo Porto et al. (1983), no Semi-Árido brasi- leiro, três em cada dez anos são considerados normais com relação à quantidade e à distribuição das chuvas. Define-se a irrigação de salvação como a lâmina de água aplicada à cul- tura nos veranicos que comumente ocorrem durante o período chuvoso na região Nordeste, de forma a não permitir que a cultura sofra estresse hídrico e, em alguns casos, morra. No Semi-Árido brasileiro, após as pri- meiras chuvas, é comum ocorrerem períodos de 20 a 30 dias sem novas chuvas, comprometendo seriamente a germinação e outras fases de de- senvolvimento das culturas. (English: [Am]ong these technologies, supplemental (salvation) irrigation has reduced the risks of farming in years with irregular rainfall, allowing up to two harvests in years considered normal. According to Porto et al. (1983), in the Brazilian semi-arid three in every ten years are considered normal in rainfall quantity and distribution. Salvation irrigation is defined as the depth of water applied to the crop during the dry spells (veranicos) that commonly occur during the rainy season in the Northeast, so as not to let the crop suffer water stress and, in some cases, die. In the Brazilian semi-arid, after the first rains, periods of 20 to 30 days without new rain are common, seriously compromising germination and other crop development phases.)

relationship.outcome_raw: runoff-harvesting pond (barreiro) water applied as supplemental irrigation during in-season dry spells reduces crop-loss risk

EV_evidence_register.quote: Los estudios que han analizado cómo las zanjas de infiltración evolucionan en el tiempo muestran impactos a corto plazo: a medida que las zanjas de infiltración se llenan gradualmente de sedimentos, su rendimiento disminuye. Por ejemplo, en un estudio en Etiopia18, las zanjas fueron efectivas para reducir la escorrentía y la erosión solo durante dos o tres años. Otro estudio en México mostró que 16 de 24 zanjas se llenaron al 50% de su volumen después de menos de cuatro años y que todas las zanjas establecidas se llenarían por completo después de once años19. (English: Studies that analysed how infiltration trenches evolve over time show short-term impacts: as infiltration trenches gradually fill with sediment, their performance declines. For example, in a study in Ethiopia, trenches were effective at reducing runoff and erosion for only two or three years. Another study in Mexico showed that 16 of 24 trenches filled to 50% of their volume after less than four years and that all established trenches would fill completely after eleven years.)
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: colmatación / mantenimiento de zanjas

(English: As to use, the dams were divided into two classes: 94 active dams: those used by the community at least once after construction; 57 inactive dams: never used by the community after construction. EV_evidence_register.quote: Problemas construtivos - Os principais problemas cons- trutivos detectados em algumas das barragens subterrâneas foram: • Erro de locação: local impróprio por apresentar bacia de contribuição pequena, e assim baixa capacidade de retenção de água; • Escavação insuficiente, sem alcançar a rocha no fundo da aluvião; • Problema com a lona na hora de sua colocação, sem alcançar o leito rochoso, permitindo fuga por baixo; • Solos com baixo nível de infiltração; • Poço com baixa permeabilidade, dificultando a entra- da de água; • Barragens construídas em solos salinizáveis. Esses problemas ocorreram em diferentes locais, em decorrência quase sempre da falta de acompanhamento técnico adequado. (English: Construction problems - The main construction problems detected in some of the subsurface dams were: siting error (improper site with a small contributing basin and so low water-retention capacity); insufficient excavation not reaching bedrock; problems with the plastic sheet during placement, not reaching bedrock and allowing leakage underneath; soils with low infiltration; well with low permeability hindering water entry; dams built in salinisable soils. These problems occurred in different places, almost always as a result of lack of adequate technical follow-up.)

EV_evidence_register.attribution: Horvath et al. 2017 — threshold calibrated against NWI wetlands in Iowa and Georgia
EV_evidence_register.justification_quote:
The CTI is calculated as [100 × ln (α/tan (β))] where 
100 is used to convert the value to an integer, α = ((flow accumulation +1) × pixel area 
(m2)), and β = slope (radians) (Beven and Kirkby, 1979).
EV_evidence_register.observed_dataset: CTI derived from USGS National Elevation Dataset (about 30 m)
EV_evidence_register.quote:
By setting a threshold, we reduced both over and under 
prediction of locations where potential topographic conditions could support wetlands. 
Preliminary results from our comparison between CTI and the NWI data from Iowa and 
Georgia suggested that a CTI threshold of at least 550 would include all wetland types and 
much of the variation of CTI within each wetland type (Fig. 1).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: Compound Topographic Index (CTI, = TWI scaled to integer) threshold for potential wetland area

relationship.direction: cells at or above the CTI threshold are treated as topographically suitable — they carry the potential to accumulate water and support wetlands; below it potential falls to the low class unless soils are poorly drained (combined with soil drainage in the potential-wetland-area index)
relationship.unit: CTI (topographic wetness index scaled to an integer, see justification_quote)

EV_evidence_register.selection_justification:
In general, lower slope areas with sufficient overland runoff will collect water resulting in 
conditions with a greater potential to support wetlands.

EV_evidence_register.quote:
From the drainage classifications, poorly and very poorly drained soils are the 
most frequent, longest, and most deeply saturated or inundated of the soil drainage classes 
and thus should be considered an indicator of potential to support perennial types of 
wetlands.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: SSURGO/STATSGO2 drainage class (poorly + very poorly drained, PVP)

relationship.direction: poorly and very poorly drained soils (longest, deepest saturation/inundation) indicate potential to support perennial wetlands; better-drained classes do not

EV_evidence_register.attribution: Horvath et al. 2017; PVP grid cross-checked against hydric-soil grid
EV_evidence_register.quote:
Therefore, we selected cells 
having a PVP of 80% as a break point for further analyses. As a secondary evaluation, we 
compared our PVP soil drainage grid to a soil grid having ≥50% hydric conditions. The two 
were in agreement 85% of the time, suggesting that our greater than 80% PVP soil grid 
adequately represented both the saturation and inundation duration necessary to support 
perennial wetlands. Grid cells with less than 80% PVP soils would likely include somewhat 
poorly drained conditions, resulting in moderate saturation and inundation durations that 
would more successfully support non-perennial types of wetlands, particularly when located 
in lower topographic positions (Tiner, 1999).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: percent poorly + very poorly drained soil per cell (PVP) break point

relationship.direction: at or above the PVP break point the soil represents the saturation and inundation duration needed for perennial wetlands; below it soils are more likely somewhat poorly drained and suit non-perennial wetland types, particularly in lower topographic positions — not an absolute exclusion
relationship.unit: percent of soil map unit poorly or very poorly drained (PVP)

EV_evidence_register.attribution: Horvath et al. 2017 (EPA EnviroAtlas PWA layer)
EV_evidence_register.quote:
After defining the initial CTI threshold and the appropriate break points for PVP 
percentages, we combined the CTI and PVP layers into a single index layer of categorical 
classes of PWA: 1) high (CTI values ≥ 550 combined with 80–100% PVP of the summed 
soil components), 2) moderate (CTI values ≥ 550 combined with 1–79% PVP), 3) low (80–
100% PVP with CTI values ≤ 550), and 4) none (0% PVP or CTI values < 550 and < 80% 
PVP).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: Potential Wetland Area (PWA) classes combining PVP soils and CTI

relationship.direction: joint soil-drainage × topographic-wetness classification of potential wetland area; poorly drained soil can compensate for low CTI (low class) and vice versa (moderate class)

EV_evidence_register.justification_quote:
Wetland restoration is more likely on certain landscapes (e.g., agriculture) than others 
due to the lack of substantive infrastructure and the potential for the restoration of hydrology;
EV_evidence_register.quote:
To create the PRW-Ag layer, we combined the PWA classes with LULC classes from the 
2006 NLCD. LULC classes that were unlikely to be selected for wetland restoration, such as 
developed lands or large water bodies, were excluded from the selection. While wetland 
restoration can occur and provide benefits within other land use classes, such as open or low 
intensity development sites, these developed classes are also more likely to contain 
unsuitable land cover such as impervious surfaces and may also be more likely to be 
commercially valuable for other uses. In such cases, buffers may be a more suitable 
alternative to offset impacts to streams. It was assumed that natural land covers, such as 
forest, grassland, and existing wetlands, would not require extensive restoration. We, 
therefore, focused on agricultural land (pasture/hay [land cover code = 81] and cultivated 
crops [land cover code = 82]) in combination with the PWA classes.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: NLCD 2006 land cover filter for potentially restorable wetlands on agricultural land (PRW-Ag)

relationship.direction: agricultural land (pasture/hay and cultivated crops) is the restorable target; developed land and large water bodies are excluded (impervious, commercially valuable, hydrology not restorable); natural covers are not targeted because they would not need extensive restoration — not because they are unsuitable

EV_evidence_register.attribution: Uuemaa et al. 2018 — GIS-MCA criterion (equal-weight linear sum of four criteria)
EV_evidence_register.justification_quote:
topography, since a wetland area needs to be generally ﬂat,
but natural landforms, such as swales and gullies, can facilitate wetland construction [8];
EV_evidence_register.quote:
Slope was the simplest derivative, since low slope angles are more suitable
for wetlands than steeper slopes. However, in New Zealand, wetlands can also occur on steeper
slopes. Therefore, in the current study, we deﬁned the maximum suitable slope for wetland as 3◦.
Smaller slopes were assigned a higher suitability for wetland development.

relationship.direction: suitability declines with slope; above the maximum the cell is not suitable for wetland creation/restoration (authors note the cap is a local design choice — wetlands can occur on steeper slopes in New Zealand)

EV_evidence_register.attribution: Uuemaa et al. 2018 — GIS-MCA criterion
EV_evidence_register.quote:
Higher TWI values indicate higher soil moisture content and
also a higher suitability for wetland. TWI has been used effectively to predict soil moisture and has
also been tested for identifying wetlands by several authors [23,40]. However, TWI alone did not
provide sufﬁcient results. Therefore, we used TWI only as one parameter. TWI was calculated using
SAGA GIS [41]. Values of TWI were divided into deciles and assigned values from 0 to 1 to create
a suitability map.

relationship.direction: monotonic increasing — higher TWI, higher wetland suitability; used only as one criterion because TWI alone was insufficient

EV_evidence_register.attribution: Uuemaa et al. 2018 — in-stream wetland design only (off-stream options not considered)
EV_evidence_register.justification_quote:
Therefore, the potential wetland sites in our analysis occurred along the streams or drainage
ditches, and there is a higher probability for suitable wetland sites to exist along the higher-order
streams.
EV_evidence_register.observed_dataset: virtual stream network from LiDAR DEM flow accumulation
EV_evidence_register.quote:
We created distance maps with a maximum distance of 125 m from the streams, and converted them
into suitability maps with each pixel having values from 0 to 1. The closer a site is to a higher-order
stream, the higher its suitability as a wetland site. In addition, the suitable area around higher-order
streams was wider than around the lower-order streams.

relationship.direction: suitability decreases with distance from the (virtual) stream network and is zero beyond the maximum distance; closer to higher-order streams is better and the suitable band is wider along higher-order streams

EV_evidence_register.quote: In Burkina Faso, the widespread adoption of Zai pits, often combined with stone lines, represents the most ideal bottom-up adaptation success [1]. Driven by farmer-led inno- vation and later supported by NGOs, this practice bundle addresses multiple constraints simultaneously. The Zai pits concentrate scarce rainfall and organic amendments, directly enhancing soil moisture and fertility [133], while the stone lines reduce erosion and further improve infiltration upstream [1]. This is evidenced by yield increases of over 100% for sorghum [45] and over 100% for maize when combined [44].

context.note: CAUTION — this is NOT restoration evidence: the wetlands are already drained and cultivated, and the figure is the income households DERIVE from farming the converted wetland, i.e. the opportunity cost that rewetting would take away, not a benefit of wetland management. Tagged comparator=existing_wetland so it stays out of the NbS roll-up. MONQI farm monitoring of 27 in-depth households per site (96 survey respondents in Rugeramigozi, 157 in Cyabayaga), six interview rounds over seasons A, B and C, 2007; gross margin = gross income minus variable costs; hillside gross margin for comparison was 681 US$ in Cyabayaga and 275 in Rugeramigozi. Artefact of record is the author's Wageningen PhD thesis; page numbers are the THESIS PDF pages, not the Ecological Economics article's. Operational finding: the cooperatives charged with maintaining the shared drainage and irrigation channels were a source of conflict and were poorly managed, and farmers had little influence over their own organisations. Relevant to M2b stream B for any wetland scheme that depends on collective water management.
context.practice_as_described: wetlands 'officially reclaimed for agricultural purposes' (Cyabayaga reclaimed for rice in 1978, Rugeramigozi in 1999-2000) with central drainage and irrigation channels; farmers grouped into cooperatives growing one approved crop — rice monocropping in Cyabayaga, maize and sorghum rotated with legumes, vegetables in the dry season — with inorganic fertilisers and pesticides
context.region: Cyabayaga and Rugeramigozi wetlands, Rwanda

EV_evidence_register.quote:
KIIs and FGDs frequently cited land scarcity, 
population pressure, and limited availability of viable livelihood alternatives outside the programme 
as constraints on households’ ability to move away from wetland-based activities. KIIs in the south-
western region also raised a concern about project boundaries. Respondents noted that wetland 
restrictions were implemented in some project districts while similar wetland uses continued in 
neighbouring districts, creating pressure on households in project areas and the risk that wetland use 
would be displaced across district boundaries rather than reduced overall.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: land scarcity and cross-district displacement of wetland use

context.note: independent IEG field assessment: protected-area restrictions imposed with almost no consultation or compensation.
context.practice_as_described: Ramsar protected-area designation of coastal lagoons with demarcation and local by-laws
context.region: coastal lagoon Ramsar sites

EV_evidence_register.quote:
these Ramsar areas District Assemblies, in close consultation with traditional clan and 
community leaders, have passed local by-laws regulating use o f  these areas. Even so, 
many communities complained that the Ramsar areas were imposed upon them with 
almost no consultation or compensation.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: Ramsar areas imposed without consultation or compensation

context.note: IEG: staff cut from 51 to 25 after the project; old vehicles, no boats.
context.practice_as_described: Wildlife Division management of protected coastal lagoon Ramsar sites
context.region: Keta Lagoon Complex

EV_evidence_register.quote:
The WLD i s  under-equipped and under-funded for the task, again reflecting low 
government ownership. Thus, for example, the most important wetland area, the Keta 
Lagoon Complex covering 101,023 ha located in the delta o f  the River Volta, has only 2 
officers and 4 field staff to manage the area.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: wetland agency under-staffed and under-funded

context.note: IEG: community poverty forces reliance on harvesting wetland resources; Box 3 also records micro-credit at 50 per cent per 3 months as the main constraint for a mangrove group.
context.practice_as_described: co-management of protected coastal lagoons with small NGO projects (mangrove regeneration, drainage improvement, apiary)
context.region: coastal lagoon Ramsar sites

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Overall success in co-management, however, is constrained by the monetary 
poverty o f  many communities - their low levels o f  education preclude self-help and 
forces a heavy reliance on harvesting local resources.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: poverty constrains wetland co-management

context.note: self-evaluation; management effectiveness tracked staffing density and completed demarcation/by-laws.
context.practice_as_described: protected-area conservation management of wetland sanctuaries (demarcation, by-laws, community action plans, field staff)
context.region: Mamunta Mayosso Wetland Sanctuary vs Sierra Leone River Estuary

EV_evidence_register.quote:
MMWS has achieved higher scores than SLRE. Most activities were spearheaded at 
MMWS, such as the management and community action planning, the formation of CSMC, and 
some basic infrastructures. The higher scoring at Mamunta Mayosso site is mainly a result of 
the boundary demarcation with beacons and trees, still missing at SLRE, the advanced stage of

number of field staff in relation to PA size: 140 ha/staff as compared to 3,000 ha/staff at SLRE.

context.note: independent IEG review: farmer transition enterprises around the restored wetlands were subsidised; viability without subsidy unknown; no financial analysis of livelihood effects was presented.
context.practice_as_described: restoration of 4,035 ha of former Danube floodplain marshes (Belene Island, Persina Nature Park; Kalimok-Brushlen) by building infrastructure to regulate water flows and allow controlled flooding of former marshes, with protected-area management plans and Natura 2000 designation
context.region: Danube floodplain, Persina Nature Park (Belene Island) and Kalimok-Brushlen

EV_evidence_register.quote:
However, there remains a risk that environmentally -friendly rural 
enterprises may not be viable without continued subsidies

context.note: self-evaluation: weak inter-agency coordination let a commune re-drain the adjacent polder, cutting water to the restored wetland; corrective hydro-works needed.
context.practice_as_described: Lapusna wetland (Ramsar site, Lapusna-Prut confluence near Sarata-Razesi): 'ecological reconstruction of the forest on 26 ha, using tall saplings', zone delineation, two concrete bridges with outflow systems, ten wooden bridges; after adjacent polder drainage cut inflow, hydro-technical works redirected part of the Lapusna River flow through the wetland by an underground pipe and consolidated the dam
context.region: Lapusna wetland, Prut basin, Hincesti/Leova

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Wetland rehabilitation was affected by resource-use conflicts due to stricter enforcement of 
access restriction by Government as a result of the emergence of a common border with the EU 
and weak administrative coordination. Conflicts over access to wetlands delayed reforestation; 
community activities to rehabilitate drainage works in the adjacent agricultural land limited water 
flow to the wetlands; and the local environmental authority erred in providing permits for these 
works. The Project responded adequately to the water flow issue by funding corrective works.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: adjacent drainage works cut water to restored wetland

context.note: project-end social survey (2008 vs 2003): wetland resource use fell under access restrictions enforced by border guards and the forest agency; frustration with restrictions.
context.practice_as_described: Lapusna wetland (Ramsar site, Lapusna-Prut confluence near Sarata-Razesi): 'ecological reconstruction of the forest on 26 ha, using tall saplings', zone delineation, two concrete bridges with outflow systems, ten wooden bridges; after adjacent polder drainage cut inflow, hydro-technical works redirected part of the Lapusna River flow through the wetland by an underground pipe and consolidated the dam

EV_evidence_register.raw_name: access restrictions cut wetland resource use

context.bundle_components: peatland rewetting; sedge-mire mowing and shrub removal; floodplain meadow grazing; protected-area management; forest biotope protection
context.note: Terminal evaluation (document review, key-informant interviews, remote/online plus site visits). NO MECHANISM vs NO EFFECT: the evaluation states in the same paragraph that project design included no activities or expected results to benefit vulnerable groups (operational unit ev_wgy_blr_op1). Belarus is upper-middle income; the programme was state-run on state-owned land, so there was no farmer opportunity cost to compensate. Second instance of the pattern in which a rewetting programme delivers hectares and carbon with no identifiable household benefit.
context.practice_as_described: UNDP-GEF project 'Conservation-oriented management of forests and wetlands': rewetting of disturbed peatlands (cascade dams blocking drains), hydrological regulation and mowing/shrub removal on open sedge mires, floodplain meadow restoration by grazing and mowing, protected-area management plans, and transfer of rare forest biotopes into protection, across nine pilot sites

EV_evidence_register.quote:
The 
evaluation team found no evidence that the project's activities had a direct impact on improving the 
situation of ordinary people in Belarus, including vulnerable groups.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: no evidence of direct benefit to ordinary people / vulnerable groups

relationship.direction_cue: found no evidence that the project's activities had a direct impact
relationship.outcome_raw: direct improvement in the situation of ordinary people, including vulnerable groups, from the programme; the evaluators found NO EVIDENCE of a direct household effect. Read with ev_wgy_blr_op1: the design contained NO household mechanism, so this records an absence of benefit where none was designed, not a tested null of a livelihood intervention

context.region: Turov and Pogost floodplain meadows, Pripyat river

relationship.direction_cue: resulted in a strong decline in the number of migrating and nesting birds

context.note: Target (700 ha) about 60% achieved: sedge seed was practically absent in donor bogs for three years, so most of the area was left to natural succession, with reed and cattail colonising first. The vegetation is a habitat-structure outcome, not a species count.
context.practice_as_described: rewetting of 950 ha of the Dokudovskoe cultivated/cut-over peat bog, soil preparation, planting of marsh plants and a little sedge seed on 70 ha; elsewhere natural colonisation
context.region: Dokudovskoe mire, Lida district, Grodno region

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Sedge communities on the peatland Dokudovskoe (1,200 ha) occupy no more 
than 20 ha 
End of Project Target  
Sedge communities on peatland Dokudovskoe occupy at least 700 ha 
End of Project Status 
By 2020, pilot activities on creation of sedge communities underway on 950 
hectares of cultivated peat bog. Dokudovskoe  peatland rewetted (950 ha). 
Activities for accelerated restoration of open sedge marshes were planned 
for an area of about 700 ha in 2021, using machinery for soil preparation, 
collection and sowing of seeds of marsh plants. However, for three years in 
the natural bogs of Sporoske and Zvanets sedge seeds were practically absent 
for unknown reasons. Therefore, marsh plants were planted and a small 
amount of sedge seeds were used on an area of 70 ha.  
On the rest of the area prepared for planting of marsh plants seeds, 
restoration took place naturally. In this regard, reed and cattail were the first 
to appear on these areas, which in the process of development will be 
replaced by sedge communities  
Mapping of vegetation in the Dokudovskoe  peatland conducted in July-
August 2021; 2021-2022 monitoring activities determined the area of 
reinstated bog plant communities: Phragmites-sedge communities (Carex 
acuta, C. rostrata, C. pseudocyperus, Phragmites australis) on peatland 
Dokudovskoe occupy at least 398 ha (botanical report).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: Dokudovskoe: sedge communities after rewetting vs baseline

relationship.outcome_raw: area of reinstated Phragmites-sedge fen plant communities on the rewetted Dokudovskoe cut-over peatland, end of project against baseline, from vegetation mapping

At the more arid locations of Laikipia and Machakos, each site
recorded complete crop failures in two out of three and four
experimental seasons, respectively. At Laikipia, only long rains
2001 resulted in yields after 400 mm seasonal rainfall. Average
seasonal yields ranged from 2.1 t ha1 for conventional tillage with
fertilizer to 3.7 t ha1 for ripper with fertilizer. At the Machakos
location, two seasons out of four resulted in yields less than
0.3 t ha1. Seasonal yields at the Machakos site varied from a
minimum of 0 kg ha1 harvested maize grains due to meteor-
ological drought
