EV_evidence_register.quote:
Air temperature was lowered by up to 6°C at midday under compared to outside the canopy 
of F. albida (Figure 4.3c). Temperature reached 36oC and was highly variable in the open field, 
while it reached a maximum of 29oC and fluctuated less under the canopy. Temperature 
exceeded 28oC, for about six hours day-1 (i.e., from 10:00-16:00 GMT) in the open fields and 
for less than two hours (i.e., from 12:300-14:300 GMT) for under the canopy. For close to three 
hours around midday (i.e. from 10:40-13:30 GMT), temperature was significantly cooler under 
tree crowns than in open fields (P<0.001).

relationship.outcome_raw: maize rain water productivity, EB + CP + OM + NPK + Urea vs control, Péni (letters a vs ab: not significantly different)

context.note: Makoka Research Station, southern Malawi; randomised block design, 3 replicates, 11.5 x 11.0 m plots, established 1995/96; neutron-probe soil water to 150 cm, 1997/98-1999/00. Comparators: SM = sole maize, no fertiliser or GLM; MP = maize + pigeonpea, no fertiliser or GLM. Authors: rainfall exceeded potential evaporation during the cropping season in all years. Season 1997/98. process: WUE = total above-ground biomass of the whole system (trees + crops) / seasonal water use, water use estimated from rainfall + change in 0-150 cm soil water (runoff and drainage assumed negligible). NOT grain yield per water: biomass includes gliricidia. Authors' own caveat (p13-14): soil evaporation and water-table abstraction not quantified; accounting for them might raise sole-crop WUE and lower sole-gliricidia WUE - the contrast is likely overstated. Treatment P value for WUE <0.001 in every season (Table 1).
context.practice_as_described: Gliricidia sepium trees planted in alternate furrows between maize ridges (0.5 m within, 1.5 m between rows), pruned to 30 cm above ground 2-4 weeks before crop planting and again when maize reached ca. 60 cm (and whenever shading maize); prunings incorporated into the ridges / top-dressed as green leaf manure (GLM); no inorganic fertiliser; trees left unpruned after maize harvest
context.region: Makoka Research Station, southern Malawi

a new term, “propagule limitation” to describe situa-

in natural availability due to removal of mangroves by

of mangrove propagules to a restoration site.

reported_values.frequency: days flooded per month at lower end of elevation band

context.review_needed: Does the local directional guidance apply to this rehabilitation site and datum? Approval must not create global cutoffs.
context.vertical_reference: local mean sea level; not an interchangeable global DEM datum

EV_evidence_register.quote: Relationship between site elevation (cm above mean sea level) and flooding frequency (days per month) for each month of the year. Green colour coding shows elevations that are optimal for planting, and red indicates areas where careful site assessment is needed before deciding to plant. The brighter the red, the greater the need for site assessment. Elevations above 200 cm (2 m) and below mean sea level may be unsuitable for planting mangroves. Flooding frequency (days flooded per month) is based on tidal records from Ganh Hao tide station for the period 2010 to 2013. Note that the flooding frequency refers to the lower end (marked) of each elevation range, and the number of days flooded decreases with increasing elevation within each elevation band.

EV_evidence_register.quote: According to the extracted soil data layers based on ecological needs of wild pistachio and combining all data layers for this species, the best suitable conditions areas were determined. The results of integration of all produced maps showed that in terms of EC and organic matters 890.36 ha (100 %) of the total plantable area has the suitable conditions for P. atlantica reforestation and afforestation activities. For other characteristics such as pH, texture, depth, slope, aspect and elevation, the best suitable areas were defined as follow, 864.35 ha (97.7 %), 806.42 ha (90.79 %), 145.3 ha (16.31 %), 818.78 (91.96 %), 257.79 (32.8 %), 285.67 (32.8 %), of the total plantable areas, respectively. Finally, after combining all the data layers, 353.44 ha (36.69 %) of the plantable areas had the best conditions for P. atlantica plantation activities (Figs. 13-17).

EV_evidence_register.quote: Where natural regeneration is an option to restore a degraded mangrove area, and availability of propagules and seeds is ensured, restoration planning should first examine and validate the potential existence of primary stresses such as blocked tidal inundation that might prevent nat- ural succession from occurring, and remove those stressors to enhance natural recovery. This can be achieved through hydrological restoration, that is re-modification and re-establishment of original conditions of the ecosystem including tidal regimes (Turner and Lewis 1996; Kamali and Hashim 2011). Where signs of natural recov- ery are not observed within 6 to 12 months after adjustments of the physical conditions, consid- eration for undertaking actual mangrove refor- estation either through direct planting of propagules collected from the forest or nursery- raised seedlings should be considered and evalu- ated (see also Chapter 6).

EV_evidence_register.attribution: Gardiner 2021 narrative review

context.note: Mechanism: wind loading on stems/roots exceeds the critical wind speed for overturning or breakage (Equations 1-4). Thresholds synthesised from Oliver and Mayhead 1974, Gardiner 1995, Valta et al. 2019. Acclimation: trees in windier climates are more stable.
context.practice_as_described: planted and managed (production) forests - stands established and managed by thinning, felling and ground preparation
context.region: global, emphasis on planted and managed forests in Europe, Japan, New Zealand

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Together, these data suggest that 
damage starts to occur in forests when canopy top hourly 
wind speeds exceed approximately 8.5 m s−1 and gust speeds 
outside the forest exceed 25–30 m s−1. It is not possible to 
give definitive global values because there will be differences 
due to site and forest conditions, and, because of acclimation 
to the wind environment, trees growing in windier climates 
will be generally more stable than those growing in less 
windy environments (Nicoll et al. 2008). The other impor­
tant point to note is that the level of damage increases almost 
exponentially with an increase in the gust wind speed, so the 
difference in levels of damage for two almost identical storms 
may be quite large.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: wind damage onset and near-exponential rise with gust speed

relationship.direction_cue:
the level of damage increases almost 
exponentially
relationship.outcome_raw: wind damage to forest stands as a function of gust speed - onset threshold and near-exponential rise above it

roughness will have a higher wind speed at canopy top 
compared to a shorter younger stand, and the taller stand 
will be generally more likely to fail, even if the CWS values at 
canopy top calculated in Equations (1) to (4) do not vary 
much.

EV_evidence_register.attribution: Gardiner 2021 narrative review

context.note: Mechanism: remaining trees are not acclimated to the new wind conditions created by the canopy change. Management (thinning regime, edge design, felling sequence) modulates the asset's wind risk - an M2b Stream-A modifier.
context.practice_as_described: planted and managed (production) forests - stands established and managed by thinning, felling and ground preparation; thinning, gap creation in harvesting, clear-cutting of upwind stands
context.region: global, emphasis on planted and managed forests in Europe, Japan, New Zealand

EV_evidence_register.quote:
One of the most important factors changing the level of 
risk to forests and stands is any new gap or edge created 
in the stand (Quine et al. 1995; Gardiner et al. 1997). 
This is because the remaining trees will not be accli­
mated to the new wind conditions created by a change 
in canopy structure and will be particularly vulnerable 
(Gardiner et al. 2016). Such changes can be created by 
management interventions, such as thinning (Mitchell 
2013; Wallentin and Nilsson 2014), gap creation during 
harvesting operations (Stacey et al. 1994), edges pro­
duced by clear cutting of upwind stands (Rowan et al. 
2003) (see Figure 2), or the construction of a road or 
other infrastructure (Quine et al. 2020). It is a particular 
problem when the protection of taller trees is removed 
in a thinning from above because the remaining smaller 
trees have a sudden large increase in exposure (Duperat 
et al. 2020).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: new gaps/edges from thinning or felling raise wind vulnerability

relationship.outcome_raw: wind vulnerability of trees left after a new gap or edge (thinning, harvesting gaps, clear-cut upwind edges, roads)

context.note: Narrative review of African wetland hydro-ecology and herbivore use (multi-country, LIC/LMIC-dominated, no single country/income tag). Supporting evidence p2: during drought years low-quality swamp forage acts as a buffer resource preventing mass starvation; swamp habitat was heavily used in the drought of 1969 (Western 1973). Mechanism: flood-recharged soil moisture and deep-rooted perennial grasses reaching the water table.
context.practice_as_described: no intervention: seasonal use of EXISTING African wetlands (dambos, pans, riverine grasslands, floodplains, swamps, deltas) by wild and domestic herbivores; loss studied where dams or rice schemes removed flooding
context.region: sub-Saharan Africa (Okavango, Logone/Waza, Inner Niger Delta, Usangu, Zambezi, dambos of central and southern Africa)

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Plant zonation on
ﬂood frequency and duration gradients occurs in
predictable sequences across Africa and this variation
combined with increasing retention of soil moisture
for plant growth over the dry season with increasing
ﬂooding provides critical resource heterogeneity for
herbivores. Consequently, wetlands are essential dry-
season habitats for wild and domestic herbivore
populations across Africa, often providing key re-
sources that buffer herbivore population numbers in
the face of severe dry seasons and droughts.

Initial soil C sequestration rates under agroforestry could reach
some very high values, for example, reaching sequestration rates of
up to 8 t C ha1 y1 (Fig. 4A) at a few sites, but other young sites
reported very low sequestration rates of less than 1 t C ha1 y1. All
sites less than 10 years old reported sequestration rates between
about 0.5 and 2 t C ha1 y1, and none of the compiled studies
reported C losses (Fig. 4A). Our only observation from an old site
(50 years) also showed a small ongoing sequestration rate. Overall,
soil C stocks in agroforestry appear to increase at a diminishing rate
for up to 25 years before settling on a new steady state (Fig. 4B).
This can be explained through litter input from trees leading to an
early C sequestration in surface litter, resulting in some of the very
high reported initial sequestration rates. Surface litter is likely to
reached steady values after a few years with little or no further C
accumulation. Soil humus fractions could build up over the longer
term, but at slower rates. The result suggests that although some
very high initial soil C sequestration rates could be possible in some
systems, they could not be sustained over more than a few years
(Fig. 4).

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Net soil CH4 emissions were
reduced (i.e. more CH4 oxidation) when agriculture was shifted to
improved fallow, slash-and-burn systems and tree plantations on
arable land, but increased with a change to shaded perennial-crop
systems (Table 5).
Any reduced net CH4 emissions in agroforestry (i.e. greater
uptake) compared with agriculture (as seen for improved fallow,
slash-and-burn systems, and tree plantations on arable land) was
probably mainly related to greater soil pore space in soils under
agroforestry compared with agricultural ﬁelds, as reﬂected in
reduced soil bulk density under agroforestry (Table 5). Since
diffusion of CH4 into the soil has been proposed as the primary
constraint on CH4 oxidation rates (Dobbie and Smith, 1996; Ball
et al., 1997; Priemé et al., 1997; Christiansen and Gundersen, 2011),
the larger soil pore space under agroforestry may be the primary
reason for enhanced CH4 oxidation rates.
It has also been observed that CH4 uptake rates of soils can be
reduced by application of ammonium-N fertilizer because it has
been shown at the enzymatic level that NH4
+ can strongly inhibit
CH4 oxidation rates (Steudler et al., 1989; King, 1997; Topp and
Pattey, 1997; Le Mer and Roger, 2001; Dutaur and Verchot, 2007).
CH4 oxidation rates under agricultural ﬁelds may thus be further
reduced by exposure to often excessive N fertilizer applications.
The difference in CH4 oxidation was relatively small in shaded
perennial crop systems (Table 5), and the growth of N-ﬁxing trees
in these systems (Makumba et al., 2006; Akinnifesi et al., 2007,
2010) may provide N at levels where it can inhibit CH4 oxidation in
the soil.

relationship.outcome_raw: net soil CH4 emission higher (less CH4 oxidation) after a shift from agriculture to shaded perennial-crop systems; N from N-fixing shade trees may inhibit CH4 oxidation

context.note: 22 plots (5 x 20 m) in 6 villages on Viti Levu, Vanua Levu and Taveuni within 40 km of the cyclone track, surveyed 2017 and 2019 (132 stems, 27 species). Cyclone Winston (20 Feb 2016) was the first cyclone in recorded history to make landfall in Fiji as a 'Category-5 storm' (p4) and the strongest on record in the South Pacific. Damage partly from farmers' recall immediately after the cyclone. Family: multistrata village agroforests (homegarden-like); the paper also covers fallow and forest patches within the agroforest. Mechanism: wind loading - defoliation, branch and crown snapping; damage severity rose with stem diameter (p5-6).
context.practice_as_described: active subsistence agroforests of coastal Fijian villages - shifting mosaics of planted (crop) areas, recent fallows and forested areas in which culturally or ecologically important trees are retained when land is cleared, pruned or pollarded, and productive trees are purposely planted
context.region: Viti Levu, Vanua Levu and Taveuni, Fiji

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Across all sites and plots, 58.2% of tree stems suf-
fered some type of damage, either defoliation, branch 
or crown snapping, or uprooting. Specifically, of 
these tree stems that were damaged, 50% of stems 
experienced defoliation, 29.9% had branch snap-
ping, 27.6% had crown snapping, and 1.5% (2 trees) 
were uprooted (Fig. 1.). The proportion of trees that 
survived for the different damage types were as fol-
lows: no damage (0.96), defoliation (1.00), branch 
snapping (0.82), and crown snapping (0.73) (Fig. 2). 
There were no significant differences in survival 
across damage types (Table 2). Although nearly 45% 
of stems sustained damage of branch snapping or 
greater severity, stem mortality over three years was 
relatively low (12.2%).

context.practice_as_described: cacao agroforestry (cacao with shade trees and by-crops - bananas, fruit and timber trees) under organic and conventional management, compared with cacao monoculture, first five years after establishment (Alto Beni, Bolivia; Armengot et al. 2016 as summarised by the review)
context.region: Sara Ana, Alto Beni, La Paz, Bolivia

EV_evidence_register.quote:
The studies set out in the previous paragraph corroborate the one 
conducted by Armengot et al. (2016) in Sara Ana (390 m a.s.l.), Alto 
Beni, in the department of La Paz, Bolivia on a hypothesis that lower 
return on labor is expected in CSAF and organic systems due to higher 
work demand. The study aimed to determine the mean difference be­
tween the productivity and the return on labor (return per working day) 
of 4 different cacao production systems: CSAF and monoculture under 
organic and conventional management, respectively. In this trial, cacao 
and by-crop yields, costs, revenues, and labor were registered during the 
first 5 years after establishment. Results showed that cacao yields were, 
on average, 41% higher in monocultures, but the revenues derived from 
CSAF by-crops economically overcompensated for this difference. 
Nonetheless, the return on labor across the years was roughly twice as 
high in CSAF systems (organic) compared to monocultures (conven­
tional). Whereas similar cacao yields and return on labor were found in 
conventional and organically managed CSAF systems. Overall, in this 
study, results showed that cacao-CSAF systems and/or practices have a 
higher return on labor.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: cacao yield AF vs monoculture

relationship.outcome_raw: cacao yield in agroforestry vs monoculture, first years after establishment: higher in monocultures (shade and by-crop competition in the agroforestry systems)

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Rahman et al. (2017) assessed the socioeconomic potential of CSAF 
systems and the barriers to their expansion, as a land-use alternative to 
swidden cultivation in the Gunung Salak valley, Bogor District, West 
Java, Indonesia. Data were collected through semi-structured ques­
tionnaire interviews (20 CSAF and 20 swidden farmers) and 2 FGD 
sessions. Data analysis was performed by computing the net present 
value (NPV), the benefit-cost ratio (B/C), and the payback period (PBP). 
The comparison results showed that the investigated CSAF systems had 
higher NPV and benefit-cost ratio (B/C) than the swidden cultivation 
systems. In addition, results showed that CSAF products (fruit, vegeta­
bles, etc.) have high monetary value and help strengthen social cohesion 
when shared with neighbors.

context.note: Household survey (154 randomly sampled households, 4 villages in the buffer zone of Amani Nature Reserve, East Usambara, Tanzania, 2001) plus PRA; farms classified improved vs traditional by observation (Table 3). Not randomised: improved farms are larger, mostly in the highlands, keep more dairy cattle and have more off-farm income; net income regression shows land size, tenure, cash crops, dairy and off-farm income as drivers (Table 5). USD at TZS 876.4 (Nov 2001). Gross income; improved households also bear higher costs. Net operating profit differs far more (Table 6) because living expenses are subtracted - not used.
context.practice_as_described: 'improved agroforestry systems': land use well planned, multipurpose trees (many nitrogen-fixing) planted as windbreaks, shelterbelts or around fields, intercropped with annual crops or in alley farming, densely cultivated annual and perennial crops enriched with well-managed cash crops (cardamom, black pepper, cinnamon, cloves), manure used where cattle are kept; compared with traditional slash-and-burn / short-fallow cultivation with few trees
context.region: East Usambara Mountains, Tanga region

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Cash crop revenues, especially from cardamom culti-
vation and total income, were significantly higher when
improved cultivation methods were used rather than
traditional methods, but the household overhead costs
(food, rent, taxes, other costs) were also higher with
improved systems. Farmers practicing improved agro-
forestry seemed to invest more in their land; expensive
cash crop seedlings and more working days were used;
labor was occasionally hired. Improved farms also had
more cattle than those using traditional ways of culti-
vation.
The households obtained twice as much annual
gross income with improved agroforestry systems than
by using traditional practices. This gross income, con-
verted to per-capita income, becomes US$ 157 vs US$
74 for improved and traditional systems, respectively
(US$ 1 = TZS 876.4, November 2001).

context.note: Meta-analysis (mixed linear models on yield difference D and response ratio RR) of 94 peer-reviewed publications from West, East and southern Africa; comparator unfertilised maize (continuous maize without legumes). RR/D computed excluding fallows amended with fertiliser. Q-Q plots suggest asymmetry and publication bias. Herbaceous green-manure legumes and natural fallows are in the same paper but are not tree-based practices and are not emitted. Mechanism (p2): woody legume fallows harness biological nitrogen fixation during the fallow period. Pairs from 48 publications (391 pairs, improved fallows the majority). Range = 95% CI of the mean RR; banded on its midpoint.
context.practice_as_described: non-coppicing woody legumes (Cajanus, Sesbania, Tephrosia) grown as 1-3-year rotational 'improved fallows' then cleared, maize cropped for one to three seasons after the fallow, or planted as relay intercrops within weeks of maize and left as short fallows after harvest
context.region: sub-Saharan Africa (West, East and southern)

EV_evidence_register.justification_quote:
Both
woody and herbaceous legume fallows are based on
the principle of harnessing biological nitrogen fixa-
tion (Cherr et al. 2006; Giller et al. 1997; Sanchez
1999) by the legumes during the fallow period.
EV_evidence_register.quote:
When comparing relay intercropping with rotation-
al fallows of non-coppicing species, 48 publications
with a total of 391 pairs of observations were used.
Improved fallows constituted 70.6% of the cases and
relay intercrops the remaining 29.4%. Although the
95% confidence intervals overlapped response was
higher in rotational fallows than in relay intercrops.
The 95% confidence interval for RR was 1.27–1.43
in rotational fallows, where as in relay intercrops it
was 1.11–1.30.

EV_evidence_register.justification_quote:
Within
the remaining recently lost mangrove areas, we sought
to understand those factors most likely to influence
restoration success. These include: the tidal range; recent
sea level rise; projected future sea level rise; recent change
in sediments; time since loss; average size of loss patches;
and the proximity of loss areas to remaining mangroves. An
advisory team was convened to review these variables and,
using Delphi methods, an averaged restoration potential
score (from 1 to 100) was calculated for each of the more
than 6000 mangrove units under assessment.
EV_evidence_register.quote:
As a starting point for mangrove restoration, it is prudent
to consider putting them in places where they have been
recently lost, provided the driver of loss can be prevented
from recurring and the local conditions remain suitable.
Such areas are most likely to have local conditions of soil,
tides and elevation appropriate for restoration, while their
proximity to remaining mangroves can greatly facilitate
natural regeneration processes.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: proximity to remaining mangroves

how to restore mangroves are also locally informed. This
includes local ecological and physical conditions, of course,

EV_evidence_register.quote:
On every coastline waves and currents create change, sometimes bringing
sediments to the coast, but sometimes causing erosion and the loss of
land. Where mangroves occur they generally reduce erosion and enhance
sedimentation. The mangrove vegetation reduces wave energy and slows
the flow of water over the soil surface, reducing the water’s capacity to
dislodge sediments and carry them out of the mangrove area.  At the same
time the slower water flows can allow already suspended sediments to
settle out from the water, resulting in increased deposition of sediment.

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Carbon. Vast quantities of carbon
are tied up both in the living trees
of the mangrove forests and in their
rich soils. Unlike many other tropical
forests, they sequester carbon and
store it away in the soils where it can
remain for millennia, as the saline,
waterlogged conditions prevent the
breakdown of organic material by fungi
or bacteria. Mangroves are thus often
seen as critical for long-term storage
and sequestration of carbon – removing
carbon dioxide from the atmosphere
and storing it in their biomass and soil.

Water purification. Mangroves,
and associated biota such as algae,
bacteria, and filter-feeding animals,
play an important role in removing
excess nutrients from the water. Some
of these are bound into the soils;
others may be broken down and, in
the case of nitrogenous waste, may
be released into the water as inert
nitrogen. Mangroves can also help
to trap sediment passing through
their complex aerial root structure.
Such services are not limitless, and
excessive nutrients can remain and
threaten marine life, but in many
cases the role in removing toxins and
nutrients is highly important.

context.note: Comparator = the authors' control, traditional bush fallow with 3-year cropping in a 6-year cycle (50% farming intensity). Other arms in the same model: no-till with herbicide, and 3-year cropping in a 12-year cycle bush fallow. Simulation: SCUAF (simplified USLE) erosion over a 20-year horizon for a sandy Oxic Paleustalf, 7% slope, seeded with IITA Ibadan plot erosion rates (Kang and Ghuman 1989; Sabel-Koschella et al. 1984); maize yield from Lal (1981) yield-cumulative-soil-loss function. Mechanism: hedgerows lower erosion through a tree proportionality factor in SCUAF (degree to which erosion is controlled by the tree component); lower cumulative soil loss sustains maize yield; pruning raises labour. PVINR = present value of incremental net returns over 20 years vs the 6-year-cycle bush fallow control, 1988 naira (US$1 = N5.00), farmer receives no salvage value (p = 0). Ordinal use only; no currency normalisation. Reversal kept: at a high discount rate the 2 m alley is less profitable than the erosive control (PVINR printed negative, text layer garbled). Authors attribute alley cropping's loss of rank to its establishment cost: up to two years before the shrubs give any benefit (p363).

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Reconstruction refers to restoring native plant communities on
land recently in other resource uses, such as crop production or
pasture. Active approaches could include ameliorating the soil to
increase organic matter content, decreasing bulk density, or reduc-
ing the weed seedbank; outplanting seedlings; or direct seeding.
Passive approaches rely on recolonization of open land by natural
dispersal means, but success can be limited by proximity to appro-
priate source plants and composition of initial seral species
(Benjamin et al., 2005). A combination of approaches may be useful
as well—actively seeding or planting seedlings of keystone species
at wide spacing and subsequently relying on passive dispersal to
ﬁll remaining niches with other desired species (e.g., Scowcroft
and Yeh, 2013).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: Proximity to appropriate source plants and composition of initial seral species

relationship.direction_cue:
success can be limited by proximity to appro-
priate source plants
relationship.note: Availability of appropriate source plants within effective natural dispersal reach supports passive recolonization; qualitative regeneration capacity, not an increasing response to distance. No executable curve.

context.note: Lincoln silvopasture experiment, Canterbury Plains (660 mm rain, about 60% of potential ET; summer drought common). Silvopasture and open pasture are two ADJACENT experiments analysed in separate ANOVAs, so silvopasture-vs-open contrasts are not formally tested (quasi-experimental). Neutron-probe soil moisture to 2 m, 1991-1996, growing seasons 2 to 6 after planting. Drainage inferred from daily rainfall exceeding 90% of the current soil moisture deficit (p4); small macropore or lateral flows not detectable. The open lucerne pasture also showed no drainage, so the contrast is clearest against ryegrass/clover open pasture. A trees-only plot drained once, in September 1993 (p7).

DROUGHT INTENSITY (p7) = how far that year's rainfall fell below the site's long-term (at least 30-year) mean annual rainfall, in percent. Table 1 (pp3-7, caption 'Characterization of silvopastoral system (SPS) sites in an environmental gradient in Argentina') gives ONE value per site, the shortfall of the dry year recorded there (21-55%; e.g. Chaco 1 27%, Santiago del Estero 37%, La Rioja 46%). context.note: Acronyms: AF = agroforestry, here the 25-year-old walnut alley-cropping system (pea sown in the alleys between hybrid walnut tree lines); AC = agricultural control = the same crop in full sun with no trees, in the northern part of the same parcel (the baseline); EXC = rain-excluded plots (mobile rainout shelters removed 135 mm of rain, April to end of May = the imposed spring drought); CTL = rainfed plots with normal rainfall; PARinc = cumulated incident photosynthetically active radiation over the crop cycle (MJ/m2): AC received 1,112 MJ/m2, AF quadrats 19% (south of trees) to 35% (north) less; > 920 = lighter shade, < 920 = heavier shade. Result (p7, Fig. 6 grain yield): under normal rainfall trees cut pea yield by 25-77% vs AC; under drought by only 1-47%. Absolute grain yields are shown only in Fig. 6 (not in the text layer). context.note: BASELINE (the 'control', pp359-360 and Fig. 3): traditional shifting cultivation / bush fallow with 3 years of maize cropping in a 6-year cycle (50% farming intensity: half the land cropped, half resting in bush). PVINR = present value of incremental net returns = sum over a 20-year planning horizon of (net return per ha of the new system - net return per ha of the baseline), discounted at 10% (World Bank opportunity cost of capital for Nigeria), in 1988 naira (US$1 = N5.00); scenario one = low population density, no yield penalty on fallow land; p = 0 = farmer receives none of the change in land (salvage) value. So N1755 per ha is how much MORE the 4 m alley system earns than the 6-year-cycle bush fallow over 20 years in present value; the baseline's own absolute net return is not reported. Fig. 3 (p360), caption 'Per hectare present value (discount rate = 10%) of incremental net returns of four alternative land use systems as compared to a 3-year cropping in a 6-year cycle bush fallow system in south-western Nigeria. No yield penalties are imposed, reflecting the case of low population density'. Other arms vs the same baseline: 3-year cropping in a 12-year cycle bush fallow N2547 (most profitable when land is abundant), no-till with herbicide N1712, 2 m alley cropping N1373. Labour costs would need to fall by at least 10% for the 4 m alley system to match the 12-year fallow (p360). Under high population density (Fig. 4, fallow yields penalised) the 4 m alley system ranks first (N7377, unit ehui90_9). Simulation: SCUAF (Soil Changes Under AgroForestry, a simplified USLE erosion model) for a sandy Oxic Paleustalf on a 7% slope near Ibadan, seeded with IITA plot erosion rates; maize yield from Lal (1981) yield-cumulative-soil-loss function. Ordinal use only; no currency normalisation.

AWCI = available water capacity index = (soil moisture - permanent wilting point) / (field capacity - permanent wilting point): 0 = wilting point, 1 = field capacity; 0.5 is the authors' coffee water-stress reference. Table 5 (p130), caption 'Number of days with available water capacity index (AWCI) of three soil layers of soils managed under shaded and unshaded, between February 2009 until June 2010'; layers I = 0-20 cm, II = 20-40 cm, III = 40-160 cm. ALL THREE LAYERS were drier under shade: layer I mean AWCI unshaded 0.24 vs shaded 0.16 (ratio 1.55), days below wilting point 110 vs 145, days above 0.5: 110 vs 41; layer II 0.39 vs 0.19 (ratio 2.11), days below wilting point 28 vs 128, days above 0.5: 179 vs 61; layer III 0.97 vs 0.78 (ratio 1.25), days below wilting point 0 vs 0, days above 0.5: 501 vs 427, days at or above field capacity 225 vs 126. This unit encodes layer II, the layer with the largest gap and where most coffee roots sit (p13); layers I and III point the same way and are summarised by unit decarvalho21_5 ('Soil moisture of shaded area was lower than unshaded area for all depths'). Practice: Coffea arabica on one smallholder farm in Araponga, Minas Gerais, with Erythrina verna shade trees planted between the rows; baseline = the same coffee in full sun on the same slope position and management. Paired comparison on ONE farm, one shaded and one unshaded 10 x 10 m area, one sensor set per area, Aug 2009 - Jun 2010; no replication and no significance test (case study). Mechanism (p13): less rain reaches the soil under the canopy (interception) and drier surface soil pushes coffee roots deeper into layer II.

context.note: Field inventory of 19 homegardens (two 249 m2 circular subplots each; trees >5 cm diameter at breast height (DBH) measured, biomass from the general Brown 1997 allometric equation, roots taken as 25% of above-ground biomass, carbon = 0.5 x biomass). Mean above-ground carbon 35.3 Mg C/ha (coefficient of variation 60%), mean total carbon 107 Mg C/ha incl. soil carbon 0-30 cm (p3, Table 1: 'Carbon stocks by main pools for 19 homegarden systems in Indonesia'). The Imperata/cassava comparator values are NOT measured in this study: they come from ASB inventories (Hairiah 1997; Palm et al. 1999) with a similar method but soil sampled 0-15 cm; only above-ground carbon is compared, so the soil difference does not enter this unit. Space-for-time land-use comparison, no randomisation, no statistical test reported. Figure 2 (p6): 'Comparison of above-ground carbon stocks for various land-use systems in Lampung, Indonesia' - bars for mature agroforests, secondary forests, young (rubber) agroforests, Imperata, cassava and homegardens; the bar values are image-only. Absolute difference in the same sentence: about 34.7 Mg C/ha more than Imperata-cassava. Left out: the young rubber agroforest comparison (another agroforestry system, not a counterfactual land use) and the mature agroforest / secondary forest comparisons (homegardens lower by 66 and 51 Mg C/ha; those are older reference systems, not a counterfactual for planting). Authors write 'significantly more' but report no test, so significance is not_reported. Mechanism (p6): Imperata and cassava keep low woody biomass because of periodic fires or annual harvest, while homegarden trees accumulate woody biomass. Stock after 13 years, not an annual rate; homegardens still young and accumulating (p6).
context.practice_as_described: Smallholder homegardens (HGS = homegarden systems) on the 0.25 ha home lots of transmigrant households in Pakuan Ratu district, Lampung: species-rich tree-based systems around the house mixing trees for fruit, vegetables, spice, oil, medicine and other non-wood products and services (NWPS) with timber trees (e.g. sengon Paraserianthes falcataria, teak), perennial understorey plants and annual crops (cassava, maize, rice, vegetables); average age 13 years (12-17), established either straight after secondary-forest removal or after intensive sugarcane/seasonal-crop cultivation; understorey management ranges from intensive cassava cropping to natural regeneration, pasture or bare soil. Gardens with half or more annual crops or one market tree crop, or a quarter or more rice paddy/fishpond, were excluded. BASELINE (comparator): Imperata cylindrica (alang-alang) grassland and cassava fields in the same area - low-biomass land kept low by periodic fires and annual harvest - as measured by the Alternatives to Slash-and-Burn (ASB) project.
context.region: Pakuan Ratu district, Lampung province, Sumatra (ASB benchmark area; transmigration settlement)

data indicate that homegardens had approximately 34.7 Mg

relationship.outcome_raw: above-ground carbon stock (Mg C per ha) of established homegardens vs Imperata grassland / cassava fields in the same district (space-for-time; homegarden higher by an absolute amount stated beside the multiplier)

EV_evidence_register.attribution: [dropped 2026-11-06 by Pete; reason:other; note:T3/T6 backlog round-2 decision B8 (2026-11-06, docs/decisions/t3t6_round2_2026-11-06.html): projected time-averaged carbon from the same plots as the measured comparison (roshetko02_1 kept)]

context.note: Field inventory of 19 homegardens (two 249 m2 circular subplots each; trees >5 cm diameter at breast height (DBH) measured, biomass from the general Brown 1997 allometric equation, roots taken as 25% of above-ground biomass, carbon = 0.5 x biomass). Mean above-ground carbon 35.3 Mg C/ha (coefficient of variation 60%), mean total carbon 107 Mg C/ha incl. soil carbon 0-30 cm (p3, Table 1: 'Carbon stocks by main pools for 19 homegarden systems in Indonesia'). The Imperata/cassava comparator values are NOT measured in this study: they come from ASB inventories (Hairiah 1997; Palm et al. 1999) with a similar method but soil sampled 0-15 cm; only above-ground carbon is compared, so the soil difference does not enter this unit. Space-for-time land-use comparison, no randomisation, no statistical test reported. Table 5 (p7): 'Projection of time-averaged above-ground carbon stock of Lampung homegardens, assuming current species component and projected linear growth for three rotation classes for various rotation ages' - this unit is Example 1 (long-lived NWPS species 60-year rotation, medium-lived NWPS 30 years, timber 15 years). Projection, not measurement: linear growth from current stocks; Imperata-cassava time-averaged stock (about 2.2 Mg C/ha, p6) is from Palm et al. 1999. Sensitivity rows left out of this unit but stated on p7-p8: rotations cut by one-third / one-half give 38.8 / 30.2 Mg C/ha (16.6 / 12.7 times the comparator, Table 5 Examples 2-3); a high-stock, long-rotation subset gives 122.5 / 104.4 Mg C/ha (Table 6 Examples 4-5). Direction holds under every assumption. Same source and comparison as ev_carbon_sequestration_roshetko02_1 (measured stock) - do not count as independent.
context.practice_as_described: Smallholder homegardens (HGS = homegarden systems) on the 0.25 ha home lots of transmigrant households in Pakuan Ratu district, Lampung: species-rich tree-based systems around the house mixing trees for fruit, vegetables, spice, oil, medicine and other non-wood products and services (NWPS) with timber trees (e.g. sengon Paraserianthes falcataria, teak), perennial understorey plants and annual crops (cassava, maize, rice, vegetables); average age 13 years (12-17), established either straight after secondary-forest removal or after intensive sugarcane/seasonal-crop cultivation; understorey management ranges from intensive cassava cropping to natural regeneration, pasture or bare soil. Gardens with half or more annual crops or one market tree crop, or a quarter or more rice paddy/fishpond, were excluded. BASELINE (comparator): Imperata cylindrica (alang-alang) grassland and cassava fields in the same area - low-biomass land kept low by periodic fires and annual harvest - as measured by the Alternatives to Slash-and-Burn (ASB) project.
context.region: Pakuan Ratu district, Lampung province, Sumatra (ASB benchmark area; transmigration settlement)

Considering these
species classes and rotation lengths, the time-averaged above-
ground C stock for Lampung homegardens is estimated to be
56.5 Mg C ha"1 (see Example 1 in Table 5). This is 54.3 Mg ha"1
more (24.7 times greater) than the time-averaged C stock
reported for Imperata-cassava systems (Palm et ah, 1999).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: time-averaged above-ground carbon stock (projected), homegarden vs Imperata-cassava

context.note: Asset side (crop-specific): rambutan and sengon (Paraserianthes falcataria) together are 21% of all trees (living and dead) in the 19 homegardens; 25% of the rambutan were dead, 33% of all dead trees. The authors attribute the deaths to drought sensitivity but name no drought event, so severity is unspecified; kept narrative: the share is printed only as the number words 'Twenty-five percent', which the number-provenance gate does not read, and the quote gives no comparison with other species' mortality. Site rainfall 2200-2500 mm with 1-4 months under 50 mm (p2). Sengon's 'inconsistent performance' in the following sentence is not tied to a hazard and is left out. Species-selection lesson, routed out of practice cells by claim_scope.
context.practice_as_described: Rambutan (Nephelium lappaceum) fruit trees planted by farmers in their homegardens - chosen from experience on other sites in Lampung and Java or government promotion - which the authors judge poorly adapted to the site. Baseline: none (a mortality share within the surveyed trees).
context.region: Pakuan Ratu district, Lampung province, Sumatra

However, both species appear to be poorly
adapted to Pakuan Ratu. Twenty-five percent of the rambutan
surveyed were dead, a result of their sensitivity to drought; this is
33% of the total dead trees surveyed.

relationship.direction_cue: were dead, a result of their sensitivity to drought
relationship.outcome_raw: share of surveyed rambutan trees found dead in the homegardens, attributed by the authors to drought sensitivity (no event named, no undamaged comparator species rate given)

context.note: Narrative review (no systematic search, no pooled statistics) of 1990s silvopastoral research; the effect is reported second-hand from the cited primary study (claim_basis=cited_secondary). Cited primary: Wick, Tiessen & Menezes 2000, Plant and Soil 222:59-70 ('Land quality changes following the conversion of the natural vegetation into silvo-pastoral systems in semi-arid NE Brazil'). Retained trees in pasture rather than planted silvopasture. The 'long-term' study duration is not given in the review. P = phosphorus, K = potassium, C = carbon.
context.practice_as_described: Silvopastoral system: two native trees (Ziziphus joazeiro and Spondias tuberosa) left standing in pastures after the natural vegetation was converted to pasture, compared with the same pastures away from the trees (baseline = open pasture without trees). The review describes the mechanism as litterfall and fine-root sloughing adding soil organic matter, nitrogen fixation, and animal droppings adding nutrients.
context.region: semi-arid north-eastern Brazil

EV_evidence_register.lineage_of: Wick B., Tiessen H. and Menezes R.S.C. 2000. Plant and Soil 222: 59-70
EV_evidence_register.quote:
It is now well recognized that trees can enrich soil
conditions in agroforestry systems through various
biological processes and mechanisms including in-
crease in soil organic matter content from ﬁne root
sloughing and litterfall, increased soil N through N2
ﬁxation Nair et al. 1999; Nygren et al. 2000,
changes in soil chemical, physical, and biological
properties by meso and micro fauna around roots, and
enhancement of the total nutrient pool by faunal
droppings Belsky et al. 1993; Tornquist et al. 1999;
Wedderburn and Carter 1999. In a long-term study
in semiarid northeastern Brazil, the presence of two
native tree species, Ziziphus joazeiro and Spondias
tuberosa, in pastures of varied conditions were shown
to signiﬁcantly increase available P and total C, and
increase exchangeable K by 50% Wick et al. 2000.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: total soil C under native pasture trees vs open pasture

relationship.direction_cue: signiﬁcantly increase available P and total C
relationship.outcome_raw: total soil carbon higher in pasture under the native trees than in pasture without them (the review gives no carbon value; available phosphorus also higher and exchangeable potassium higher, not encoded - no project variable for P or K)

context.note: Narrative review (no systematic search, no pooled statistics) of 1990s silvopastoral research; the effect is reported second-hand from the cited primary study (claim_basis=cited_secondary). Cited primary: Jayasundara, Dennett & Sangakkara 1997, Tropical Grasslands 31:529-537. The outcome is grass NITROGEN yield (kg N harvested in the grass), not grass dry-matter biomass: it is encoded under forage_productivity as the nearest variable and should be read as forage nitrogen output. The review gives no absolute N yields or significance test. Farming system assumed (fodder grass with tree legumes) - the review does not state it.
context.practice_as_described: Mixed pasture of the nitrogen-fixing fodder tree Leucaena leucocephala (leucaena) with the grass Setaria sphacelata; baseline = Setaria grass grown as a monoculture without trees. Mechanism given in the quote: fixed nitrogen transferred from the tree to the companion grass.
context.region: Sri Lanka

EV_evidence_register.lineage_of: Jayasundara H.P.S., Dennett M.D. and Sangakkara U.R. 1997. Tropical Grasslands 31: 529-537
EV_evidence_register.quote:
In some cases, N2 ﬁxing trees planted in silvopas-
toral systems can transfer N to companion grasses.
For example, in mixed pastures of leucaena and Se-
taria sphacelata, transfer of N from the tree compo-
nent to grass has been reported from Sri Lanka:
Setaria derived 21% of its N from leucaena compan-
ion trees and, in comparison with a grass monocul-
ture, Setaria had a 16% higher N yield Jayasundara
et al., 1997.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: companion-grass N yield, leucaena + Setaria vs Setaria monoculture

relationship.outcome_raw: nitrogen yield of the companion grass (Setaria) grown with leucaena 16% higher than in grass monoculture; 21% of the grass nitrogen came from the trees

context.note: Narrative review (no systematic search, no pooled statistics) of 1990s silvopastoral research; the effect is reported second-hand from the cited primary study (claim_basis=cited_secondary). Cited primary: Abdulrazak, Muinga, Thorpe & Orskov 1996, Animal Science 63:381-388. A feeding trial of cut tree fodder (cut-and-carry), not a grazing trial; the trees' place on the farm is not described. 'Increase in live weight' is the review's wording - the primary likely reports live-weight GAIN; check the primary before using the size. No absolute weights given in the review.
context.practice_as_described: Cut forage of the fodder trees Gliricidia sepium (gliricidia) and Leucaena leucocephala (leucaena) fed as an incremental supplement to steers (Bos taurus x Bos indicus) offered Napier grass (Pennisetum purpureum). Baseline as reported by the review: steers given Napier grass without the tree-legume supplement (the review implies but does not spell out the unsupplemented control). Mechanism (review p2): tree legume forage supplies protein to low-protein diets.
context.region: lowland (coastal) Kenya

EV_evidence_register.lineage_of: Abdulrazak S.A., Muinga R.W., Thorpe W. and Orskov E.R. 1996. Animal Science 63: 381-388
EV_evidence_register.quote:
In lowland Kenya, Abdulrazak
et al. 1996 observed linear live weight gains in
steers given incremental supplements of gliricidia and
leucaena forage with Napier grass. In that study,
feeding the legume as 27% of total dry matter resulted
in a 57% increase in live weight.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: steer live weight with gliricidia/leucaena forage supplement vs Napier grass alone

relationship.outcome_raw: steer live weight 57% higher when the tree-legume forage made up 27% of total dry matter intake, compared with steers on Napier grass (the review reports linear gains with incremental supplementation)

context.note: Narrative review (no systematic search, no pooled statistics) of 1990s silvopastoral research; the effect is reported second-hand from the cited primary study (claim_basis=cited_secondary). Cited primary: Harvey 2000, Ecological Applications 10(1):155-173 ('Windbreaks enhance seed dispersal into agricultural landscapes in Monteverde, Costa Rica'). Seed rain is a proxy for woody-plant biodiversity (dispersal), not a census of established species. Family set to linear_boundary because the FAM registry places windbreaks there, although they sit in pastures. Costa Rica is high income in the project lookup.
context.practice_as_described: Windbreaks (lines of trees) planted in cattle pastures; baseline = open pasture without trees. Mechanism stated in the quote: animals that visit the trees carry and deposit tree seeds, so more tree species can persist and re-establish in the pasture landscape.
context.region: Monteverde, Costa Rica

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Animals transport and deposit tree seeds, allowing
such species to persist in the landscape and poten-
tially re-establish their population. Harvey 2000
points out that windbreaks can have a signiﬁcant im-
pact on tree species diversity in pastures. She
observed total annual seed rain density and total an-
nual species richness to be signiﬁcantly greater in
windbreaks compared to open pastures in Costa Rica.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: seed rain density and richness, pasture windbreaks vs open pasture

relationship.direction_cue:
signiﬁcantly greater in
windbreaks compared to open pastures
relationship.outcome_raw: total annual seed-rain density and total annual seed-rain species richness significantly greater in windbreaks than in open pasture (no values in the review)

context.note: Narrative review (no systematic search, no pooled statistics) of 1990s silvopastoral research; the effect is reported second-hand from the cited primary study (claim_basis=cited_secondary). The review says research has 'shown repeatedly' that fodder banks raise animal production but gives no values and cites only Argel, Lascano & Ramirez 1998 (ACIAR Proceedings 86:319-323, Leucaena in Latin American farming systems) for the establishment delay. Timescale is our reading of 'lengthy establishment period', not stated in years.
context.practice_as_described: Grazed fodder bank: a stand of fodder trees or shrubs (tree legumes such as leucaena) established on part of the pasture and grazed by cattle; pasture must be taken out of use while the trees establish. Baseline = the extensive grass pasture without a fodder bank. Mechanism: the bank adds protein-rich browse to the cattle diet (review p2-3).
context.region: Central America / Latin America (not specified)

EV_evidence_register.lineage_of: Argel P.J., Lascano C.E. and Ramirez L. 1998. ACIAR Proceedings No. 86: 319-323
EV_evidence_register.quote:
For instance, re-
search has shown repeatedly that integration of a
grazed fodder bank can bring about positive increases
in animal production. However, lengthy establish-
ment period and the sacriﬁce of pasture area delay
positive results and therefore hinder adoption Argel
et al., 1998.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: animal production with a grazed (tree) fodder bank

relationship.outcome_raw: animal production increases when a grazed fodder bank is integrated into the pasture system; the gain is delayed by the long establishment period and the pasture area given up while trees establish

context.note: Follow-up survey of 101 cattle farmers (66 RISEMP participants, 35 non-participants), Dec 2008-Feb 2009, logistic regression of adoption on treatment group, farm capital and information sources. The source_id says Nicaragua but the study site is Esparza, Costa Rica (high income in the project lookup). Hedged ('may reduce') and cited to the first author's own dissertation (Garbach 2012), no values. Farmer interviews on p9 echo it: 'my pasture grass suffers' (#22), 'Trees compete with grasses' (#74). Kept as a harm/trade-off finding. Same page notes forage banks attract rats and snakes (some farmers abandoned them) - no project variable for pest/wildlife conflict, not encoded.
context.practice_as_described: RISEMP (Regional Integrated Silvopastoral Approaches to Ecosystem Management Project, 2002-2008, GEF / World Bank) silvopastoral conservation practices in Esparza, Costa Rica: reintroducing trees and shrubs into permanent cattle pastures. 'Multistrata (complex) live fences' = linear plantings of large trees along pasture edges left unpruned to a full canopy (>4 m tall); 'simple live fences' = small trees along pasture edges pruned every 6-8 months; also pasture trees at low (<30/ha) or high (>30/ha) density and fodder banks of leguminous shrubs (Leucaena). Treatments: PES (payment for ecosystem services) payments only, technical assistance (extension) only, or both; baseline = farmers not in the programme. This unit: multistrata live fences vs pasture edges with simple pruned fences / no large trees (the baseline is implied, not stated). Mechanism in the quote: tree canopy shades out the grass.
context.region: Esparza, Pacific coast of Costa Rica (seasonally dry, 1500-2000 mm rain)

the largest comparative weight (5), followed by the physical
parameters (3) and the ecological contexts (1). The explicative fac-

privilege to the agricultural areas (5) and population density (3).

context.note: Meta-analysis of 84 articles / 1741 paired observations (terraced vs sloping control, same site conditions, at least one growing season; p2). Unweighted analysis of a response ratio with bootstrapped confidence intervals (MetaWin 2.0, categorical random-effects model); the paper writes the effect size as r = 1 - Xt/Xs but reports positive values as soil-moisture GAINS on terraces, so the reported percentages are read as terraced-over-sloping increases. Studies mostly from the Loess Plateau and the Yunnan dry-hot valleys (Fig. 1 map). Mechanism (p5-6): terracing turns the slope surface into a horizontal plane, cuts the flow lines and lets rainfall infiltrate in place instead of running off. The abstract states 12.9% overall; the results section (p2) and conclusion (p7) state 12.4% - the results figure is used. Overall pooled effect, all structures, land uses, climates and depths. Absolute soil-moisture amounts are not reported for the pooled effect. Family set to cross_family because the pool mixes terraces with level ditches (in-situ trenches) and fish-scale pits (micro-catchment half-moons).
context.practice_as_described: Terracing in China: reshaping hillside fields into terraces that lower the slope gradient and shorten slope length so rainfall is intercepted and infiltrates on the spot. The meta-analysis pools six terracing structures: level (bench) terraces, reverse-slope terraces (platform tilted into the hill), slope-separated terraces (one-third of the slope levelled into a platform that receives runoff from the remaining sloping section), sloped terraces, level ditches (contour trenches cut across the slope that trap runoff) and fish-scale pits (half-moon / semicircular pits). BASELINE (comparator): soil moisture in the corresponding non-terraced sloping land with the same ecosystem type, dominant plant species and soil type.
context.region: China (national meta-analysis; mostly Loess Plateau and southwest dry-hot valleys)

context.note: On-farm, non-randomised paired comparison in one watershed, 1995-96 season, 8 m2 quadrats; one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Bonferroni tests at 5%, plus regressions of yield differences on tillage and weeding differences to control for farmer management. The 1995-96 season had good rainfall (1004 mm vs a 848 mm average, p3) - a normal-to-good year, not a hazard. Yields of terraced zones were also adjusted for 5% and 15% of land lost to the terrace structures (p3). IMPORTANT: the Loss Zone did not out-yield the Control, so the whole-plot effect of terracing is smaller than the Accum Zone contrast. Mechanism (p2, p5): terraces stop soil loss so topsoil, nutrients and water-holding capacity accumulate above the structure. Table 1 ('Mean wheat grain and straw yield in soil accumulation zone (T1), soil loss zone (T2) and control zone (T3), 100 kg/ha'); the table cells are garbled in the scanned text layer, so the multiplier from the text is used. Accum Zone significantly higher than Control at 5% (Bonferroni) with no, 5% and 15% land-loss adjustment. Accum Zone only - the Loss Zone did not differ from the Control (ev_crop_yield_gebr99_2). Left out: wheat straw (also about twice; a fodder by-product).
context.practice_as_described: Stone terraces (stone bunds built along the contour that develop into terraces) at least 3 years old on farmers' wheat and fava bean (broad bean) plots, slope 20-30%, highland central Tigray (above 2500 m), managed by the farmers. Each terraced plot was sampled in two zones: the Soil Accumulation Zone (Accum Zone, just above a terrace, where eroded soil collects) and the Soil Loss Zone (just below the next terrace up). BASELINE (comparator): non-conserved plots without terraces in the same watershed (Control zone), same soil and geology; 70 terraced and 70 non-conserved plots split equally between the two crops.

context.note: Yields: farm records 1992-2011 (observed, not modelled). Years classed by the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) of the growing season: 5 dry, 12 normal, 3 wet (p6, Fig. 4). context.practice_as_described: Rangeland rehabilitation with Vallerani mechanised micro-catchment water harvesting (MWH): a tractor-pulled plough cuts intermittent contour bunds (pits about 3 m long, 2 m apart, 0.3-0.5 m deep with subsoiling to 0.7 m) that collect runoff and sediment from 10-17 m uncultivated interspace strips upslope; native saltbush (Atriplex halimus) seedlings were planted in the bunds in 2014 and grazing was excluded. Baseline: the untreated interspace (the runoff-contributing strip upslope of each bund), sampled within 2 m of the shrub - not land outside the scheme. The authors could not separate the effect of the water harvesting from that of the planted shrubs.

context.note: Household questionnaire, July-September 2018 (dry season, low fire year), 181 households; 19.9% of respondents (about 36 households) already had a canal block on their farm (p6, section 'Previous canal block experience'). The quoted shares are of those respondents. The paragraph continues onto page 7: 'No respondents reported positive impacts on yield or farm access' (the sentence breaks across the page, so it is recorded here, not quoted). Mechanism: the block raises the canal and peat water level; one respondent with a block said 'now in dry season it is very dry and wet season it floods' (p6), and the discussion (p9-10) notes the uncertain effect of raised water tables on oil palm yields. Direction coded negative because the only yield changes reported were losses, but most respondents with a block (the 61.3% share) noticed no impact of any kind - a weak, minority harm signal from recall, not a measured yield loss. Self-report, no significance test, small subsample. Farm-access difficulty (12.9%) has no VONT variable and is not encoded. The perceived impacts of HYPOTHETICAL 40-cm and gated blocks (Fig. 4, Fig. 5: harvest, farm access, fire risk) are perceptions of a scenario, not observed change, and give no units.
context.practice_as_described: Canal blocking to rewet drained tropical peatland on smallholder farms (main income oil palm; also areca nut and coconut) in three villages of Jambi province, Sumatra. Dams are built across the drainage canals so that water stops draining from the peat and the water table rises: '40-cm blocks' (the dam keeps the canal water level at most 40 cm below the surface and lets the rest drain away), 'full blocks' (no water drains past the dam) and 'blocks with gates' (farmers can manage the water level and still pass by boat). The blocks reported here were built 2000-2018 (median 2016), mostly by the government, to rewet the farms or to prevent fire, improve irrigation or prevent flooding. No livelihood package was applied alongside (the authors note livelihood projects and revegetation were only small trials in the area). BASELINE (comparator): the same farmers' conditions before the block was built, as recalled by the respondent (before-after recall; no measured control plot).
context.region: Jambi province, Sumatra (three villages on drained peat)

relationship.outcome_raw: self-reported change in crop yield (mainly oil palm) on smallholder farms that already had a canal block, versus before the block: most respondents with a block noticed no impact at all, a minority reported lower crop yields, and none reported higher yields

context.note: Table 4.12 'Overall comparisons of tree survival in micro basin trench and control' (p72, thesis p60): Log Rank (Mantel-Cox), Breslow and Tarone-Ware tests per species and pooled, all P > 0.2 (pooled Log Rank P = 0.642). Thesis p73 (p61): 'the micro catchments did not significantly influence survival of either of the tree species'. Descriptive survival (Figures 4.6-4.8, pp69-71): Cordia africana survived better in the control than in either micro-catchment (six months: control 82%, micro basin and trench 64%); Grevillea robusta survived best in the micro basin by 18 months; mango best in the micro basin at 36 months - no consistent ordering. Small trial (at least three seedlings per treatment per farmer, 29 farmers). Mechanism intended: the basin / trench holds runoff at the seedling to extend soil moisture into the dry season; the author attributes the null to severe dry-season moisture scarcity that the structures could not bridge (farmers could not water: taps far from homes), plus insect/termite attack and free-grazing livestock browsing (pp73-75). Most deaths occurred 6-12 months after planting (onset of the dry season). Ordinary dry season, no named drought: no hazard_type. Design recorded as rct (on-farm replicated controlled trial; farmers volunteered, treatments not stated as randomised). Species pooled for the overall test, so claim_scope stays practice_technology.

Seedlings of Cordia africana, Grevillea robusta and mango (Mangifera indica) planted in the main rainy season (June-September) and followed for 36 months (June 2013 - June 2016) on 29 farms (replicates). BASELINE (comparator): the ordinary planting hole dug to each farmer's own specification (control), same farm, same species.

Authors' rationale (p4): tenure insecurity is long-term risk that undermines investments with a long gestation period. Re-reviewed full PDF pp1-14 on 2026-11-04 under v1.9.4. Source performs its own vote-count synthesis; primary_measured identifies that original aggregate analysis, not new household observations. Count this review once; its constituent studies are not independent replication of this review. Partial agroforestry sample and expanded agroforestry plus non-agroforestry conservation sample must remain distinct. Source p5 says 22 partial studies and nine remaining within 32; Table 2 footnote says 23. This internal denominator inconsistency is retained, not repaired. Reported vote percentages are neither adoption effect sizes nor calibration thresholds. No pooled marginal probability or common significance cut-off is available. Purposive selection, publication/significance bias, equal study weights and absent quality adjustment limit transfer (pp11-12). Table 2 p6 reports 11 included, six significant positive, one negative, four insignificant; Table 3 p7 reports 18 included, 12 positive, one negative, five insignificant. switch to sivlopasture. If they perceive that the proﬁts of silvopasture would be un-

gered species or taxes, they are less likely to come forward to invest in
silvopasture. A stable policy environment would further sivlopasture adoption.

ceives that uncertain government regulations on private land may be the greatest
threat for silvopasture adoption (factor priority score 0.578).

context.note: Review's OWN pooled estimate (random-effects meta-analysis of Hedges' g; outcomes transformed so a positive g is the desirable direction, i.e. g > 0 for fire = fewer fires, p22). Table 6 'Meta-analysis findings by intervention group' (p31); columns Intervention, Outcome, g, 95% CI, N (effect estimates), I2, tau2. Left out of this lane: 'Natural land cover' and 'Income' rows (single estimates, N = 1: Beresford et al. 2013 and McNally et al. 2011 -> cited originals, not units); 'Vegetation cover' row (NDVI/EVI vegetation index = proxy, no VONT id; ontology hold); land-tenure, public-audit and early-warning rows (not NbS). Included PA studies are mostly Latin America (Brazil, Colombia, Costa Rica, Mexico, Peru) plus Indonesia, Madagascar, Tanzania and multi-LMIC panels; income_group set to upper_middle (the dominant group), not upgraded. Review reports funnel-plot asymmetry consistent with small-study / publication bias (p28) and rates most included studies high risk of bias. The 4 estimates are Carmenta et al. 2016, Nelson & Chomitz 2011, Nolte 2014 (protected areas) and Tabor et al. 2017 (PES/REDD+), p26. Caveat stated by the review (p26): Carmenta et al. 2016 found the fire reduction inside the forest occurred alongside an INCREASE in fire in the densely populated 10 km buffer zone (leakage; not in the pooled estimate). Figure 15 gives the near-identical intervention-pooled value (g = 0.31; 0.22, 0.40; p22).
context.practice_as_described: Protected areas (PAs): legal designation and management of existing natural forest and other natural land as protected areas, pooled by the review with a small number of payments-for-ecosystem-services (PES) / REDD+ evaluations (the review groups 'protected areas (including PES)', p26). No planting or restoration: the practice is keeping existing forest standing. BASELINE (comparator): comparable unprotected land with no intervention ('No intervention' in Table 4, pp23-25), mostly via matched controlled before-after / difference-in-differences quasi-experimental designs. Mechanism (review, p22/p26): protection restricts the clearing and burning that ignite forest fires, so fire occurrence inside the protected forest falls.

context.note: Regional synthesis of the 'Etude Sahel' (CILSS/USAID-funded study of 20+ years of natural-resource-management investment in Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger and Senegal); the figures come from the national study teams' reports, which this report summarises, so units are coded cited_secondary with the national report named. p19 text; Table 1 (p20, 'Augmentation des rendements du mil et du Sorgho dans trois régions du Niger', source Etude Sahel Niger) gives the before/after means, e.g. millet Tahoua 285 -> 405 kg/ha (absolute values, p20). Region-level range, structure types pooled.
context.practice_as_described: Soil and water conservation works ('aménagements de CES' - conservation des eaux et des sols) on degraded rainfed cereal land: runoff-harvesting structures - zaï (planting pits, 'tassa' in Hausa), demi-lunes (crescent-shaped micro-catchments), cordons pierreux (contour stone bunds), digues filtrantes (permeable rock dams) - which, per the report (p19), break the surface crust and slow runoff so rain infiltrates and more water is stored for crops, while fines and nutrients are trapped in the pits; farmers add organic manure (fumure organique) to treated fields alongside the structures (p19, p44). Niger study villages (Tahoua, Maradi, Tillabéri): mainly zaï and demi-lunes on rehabilitated plateau/crusted land (p19). BASELINE: yields before the works and control villages without works (whose yields fell).

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Au Niger, l’augmentation des rendements grâce aux aménagements CES est évalué selon les 
régions à 15 à 50 % pour le mil et à 20 à 85 % pour le sorgho. En revanche dans les villages 
témoins on assiste plutôt une baisse considérable des rendements des céréales. Selon les localités, 
cette diminution est de 25% à 60 % pour le mil et 40% à 70 % pour le sorgho. (English: In Niger, the increase in yields thanks to SWC works is estimated, depending on the region, at 15 to 50% for millet and 20 to 85% for sorghum. By contrast, in the control villages there is rather a considerable fall in cereal yields. Depending on the locality, this decrease is 25% to 60% for millet and 40% to 70% for sorghum.)
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: millet grain yield on fields with soil and water conservation works vs before the works, across Niger regions (range 15 to 50%); control villages without works saw millet yields fall 25% to 60%

context.note: Regional synthesis of the 'Etude Sahel' (CILSS/USAID-funded study of 20+ years of natural-resource-management investment in Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger and Senegal); the figures come from the national study teams' reports, which this report summarises, so units are coded cited_secondary with the national report named. p20. 2007 season described by the authors as typical of bad Sahel seasons: late rains, mid-season flooding, abrupt end of rains at grain filling, dry spells of 14-23 days. Central Plateau (Plateau Mossi) of Burkina Faso: stone bunds, zaï, demi-lunes and combinations, with organic manure; <5% improved varieties. EV_evidence_register.quote:
Des poches de sécheresse de 14 à 23 jours ont été observées dans cette région. C’est dans 
ces conditions  climatiques défavorables, que les technologies de collecte des eaux de 
ruissellement  ont montré tout leur intérêt grâce à leur capacité à réduire le stress climatique, et en 
garantissant une bonne production malgré tout.  En effet, pendant que les rendements sur les 
champs non-aménagés étaient de  400 à 500 kg/ha, les champs aménagés en CES quant à eux 
avaient des rendements de 800 à 1100 kg/ha, soit du simple au double. D’une manière générale, 
les aménagements ont permis un accroissement moyen des rendements de 30% à 100% suivant les 
techniques utilisées, malgré le faible taux (<5%) d’utilisation de variétés améliorées dans cette 
région. (English: Dry spells of 14 to 23 days were observed in this region. It is in these unfavourable climatic conditions that runoff-harvesting technologies showed their full value through their capacity to reduce climatic stress, guaranteeing good production in spite of everything. While yields on untreated fields were 400 to 500 kg/ha, fields treated with SWC had yields of 800 to 1100 kg/ha, i.e. double. EV_evidence_register.quote:
Au Niger et comme le montre le tableau 10, les  taux de rentabilité interne des investissements 
dans les techniques de GRN varient de 31% à 82%. Pour le zaï deux cas ont été distingués. Dans 
le premier cas l’agriculteur réhabilite des terres dégradées qui lui appartiennent et dans le 
deuxième cas il achète de la terre dégradée afin de la réhabiliter. Cela augmente ses 
investissements et diminue le taux de rentabilité interne de 82% à 39%.  Néanmoins, même 
l’investissement dans l’achat de terres dégradées est vite rentabilisé. (English: In Niger, as Table 10 shows, the internal rates of return on investments in NRM techniques range from 31% to 82%. For zaï two cases were distinguished. In the first the farmer rehabilitates degraded land he owns and in the second he buys degraded land in order to rehabilitate it. This increases his investment and lowers the internal rate of return from 82% to 39%. Nevertheless, even the investment in buying degraded land pays off quickly.)
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: internal rate of return of zaï on degraded land the farmer already owns (82%); falls to 39% when the farmer buys degraded land to rehabilitate

relationship.direction_cue: diminue le taux de rentabilité interne de 82% à 39%
relationship.outcome_raw: internal rate of return of zaï on degraded land the farmer already owns (82%); falls to 39% when the farmer buys degraded land to rehabilitate

EV_evidence_register.lineage_of: Etude Sahel Niger (2006) national study report
EV_evidence_register.quote:
Pour la protection de la régénération naturelle,  le taux de rentabilité interne est de 31%. Il est 
estimé que l’investissement initial inclut le temps pour s’occuper des jeunes pousses estimé à 24 
hommes/jours équivalents (hj) de travail par hectare. Le coût moyen de la main d’œuvre salariée 
dans les villages d’étude a été de 1 000 FCFA par hj, soit un investissement initial de 24 000 
FCFA seulement pour débuter la protection de la régénération naturelle. Le calcul des bénéfices 
est nettement plus compliqué. Ce calcul est basé sur une estimation de la  production de bois sur 
une période de 20 ans, sur une augmentation du rendement de mil et  de la production de tiges de 
5% pendant les 4 premières années. D’autres bénéfices, comme la valeur fourragère des feuilles et 
des gousses et l’impact sur la fertilité des sols (fixation de l’azote par certaines espèces et la 
restitution de matière organique aux champs) n’ont pas été inclus dans les calculs. (English: For the protection of natural regeneration, the internal rate of return is 31%. The initial investment is estimated to include the time spent tending the young shoots, estimated at 24 person-days equivalent (pd) of work per hectare. The average cost of hired labour in the study villages was 1,000 FCFA per pd, i.e. an initial investment of only 24,000 FCFA to start protecting natural regeneration. The calculation of benefits is much more complicated. It is based on an estimate of wood production over 20 years, and on a 5% increase in millet yield and stalk production during the first 4 years. Other benefits, such as the fodder value of leaves and pods and the impact on soil fertility (nitrogen fixation by some species and return of organic matter to the fields) were not included in the calculations.)
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: internal rate of return of protecting natural regeneration on farmland (31%), benefits = wood over the horizon plus a small millet grain and stalk gain in the first years; fodder and fertility benefits excluded

relationship.direction_cue: le taux de rentabilité interne est de 31%
relationship.outcome_raw: internal rate of return of protecting natural regeneration on farmland (31%), benefits = wood over the horizon plus a small millet grain and stalk gain in the first years; fodder and fertility benefits excluded

context.practice_as_described: Soil and water conservation works ('aménagements de CES' - conservation des eaux et des sols) on degraded rainfed cereal land: runoff-harvesting structures - zaï (planting pits, 'tassa' in Hausa), demi-lunes (crescent-shaped micro-catchments), cordons pierreux (contour stone bunds), digues filtrantes (permeable rock dams) - which, per the report (p19), break the surface crust and slow runoff so rain infiltrates and more water is stored for crops, while fines and nutrients are trapped in the pits; farmers add organic manure (fumure organique) to treated fields alongside the structures (p19, p44). L’augmentation du nombre d’arbres dans les champs de culture s’est traduite dans beaucoup de

model_use_provenance.quote:
Considering the factors that influence wetland development, the availability of data, and the evalu­
ation of the importance of each factor, 30 indicators were selected, including 10 hydrological fac­
tors, five soil factors, five vegetation factors, and six terrain factors. Details such as units, resolution, 
and data sources are presented in Table 1. All factors were ultimately resampled to 500 m using 
ArcGIS10.6 with Albers projection.

Mean decrease accuracy (MDA) was used to analyze the contribution of each variable to the 
potential wetland distribution. The larger the MDA value is, the more important the variable in 
predicting the result.

The simulation of potential wetland distribution can indicate latent areas for wetland restoration. 
However, wetland loss in China is greatly influenced by human activities, especially encroachment 
of agriculture and expansion of built-up land (Mao et al. 2018a). Overlaying the results of this study 
with those of the China_LUCC for 2020 showed that 8795.5 km2 of potential wetlands in China 
were anthropogenically occupied and unsuitable for wetland restoration. The second national wet­
land resources survey also shows that infrastructure occupation has become one of the five major 
threat factors affecting the change in wetlands in China, and it has permanent effects. Therefore, 
when considering wetland restoration, the first step is to mask off the existing built-up land area 
from the results.

context.note: Regional potential-occurrence model used upstream of restoration targeting; former-wetland history, implementation success, legal availability and global transfer are not demonstrated.
context.practice_as_described: Restoration targeting overlays potential marsh/wetland distribution with current cover. This unit describes an upstream input in that workflow, not observed restoration success.
context.region: China nationwide model, resampled to 500 m

reported_values.importance_source: Figure 8, PDF page 16; visually verified. Percentage points of relative MDA importance, not runtime weights.

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Figure 9a shows the spatial distribution of potential suitable areas for wetland restoration, with 
the results of this study indicating potential wetlands and remote sensing results indicating crop­
land, grassland, or woodland. Potential wetlands accounted for the largest proportion in grasslands 
at 49.8%, with wetlands mainly distributed in the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau, followed by croplands at 
15.4%, with wetlands mainly in Sanjiang and Songnen plains of Heilongjiang Province. The optimal 
land cover types for wetland restoration in different geographical subdivisions varied significantly, 
with NEC accounting for the most at 34.4% and mainly dominated by woodland and cropland, fol­
lowed by QTP and MXP at 32.1% and 19.7%, respectively, and mainly dominated by grassland 
(Figure 9b). Because there were more areas suitable for forest swamping in the northeastern forest 
area, the areas for wetland restoration were in forested areas. However, because woodlands are also 
ecological types with important ecological functions, the balance between restoration of woodlands 
and wetlands needs to be explored.

Mechanism: more and larger (remnant forest) trees hold more woody biomass carbon per hectare. context.note: Morphological trench descriptions, p3 (Resultados e Discussao; trench positions in methods p2); confirmed in Conclusion 1 (p5): sediment carried by erosion from upslope areas was retained by the riparian vegetation. Mechanism (p1-2 introduction; p5): runoff carrying sediment from the cotton field enters the forest, where vegetation and litter slow it and the sediment settles at the forest entrance. Table 1 (p3) soil physical/chemical comparisons (cultivated vs forest soil) were not extracted as effects: they compare land uses, not retention. No nitrate or water-quality measurement was made; soil P under the forest was 2.3 times that of the cultivated soil but not significantly different (p5), so no nutrient_removal unit was emitted.
context.practice_as_described: An EXISTING (preserved) native riparian forest (mata ciliar) at the foot of a slope cropped with cotton under conventional tillage, Panama municipality, Goias, Brazil (Cerrado, dystrophic Red Latosol / Typic Haplustox). A 204 m downslope transect ran from mid-slope in the cotton field (160 m) to the end of the riparian forest (44 m) at the river bank; four soil trenches were opened inside the forest at 4, 14, 24 and 34 m from its edge. BASELINE (comparator): no without-forest control - retention is inferred from where sediment layers stop within the forest (trenches deeper inside the forest show an unburied A horizon). The forest is retained native vegetation, not planted or regenerated.
