context.note: Figure 3 'Biomass yield of millet (Pennisetum glaucum) crop grown alone or in association with Guiera senegalensis (n = 3 per treatment)... treatments are significantly different (P < 0.05)' (p7). Abstract (p1) states the same result as 'over 900% greater'. Severity: authors' words 'severe in-season drought that was imposed' (p7) and 'severe drought stress' (p1). strength_class from BANDS fold_change (the staging gate requires it): this multiplier is the ratio between two arms of one randomized trial, i.e. a response ratio; the crop-only baseline is described only as crop failure (no number). JUDGEMENT CALL: the Pete 2026-10-20 rule (fold-change without baseline = direction only) was framed on a soil-carbon stock; flagged for a human. Panicle result ('over seven times') is in the same quote. Baseline wording (p7, preceding sentence): millet without shrubs resulted in crop failure with virtually no panicle production and very low biomass. Experiment: randomized complete block split-plot (p3). No normal-year (non-drought) comparison in this study; the authors cite Dossa et al. 2012 for higher yields near shrubs in low-rainfall years.
context.practice_as_described: Native woody shrub Guiera senegalensis grown in pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum) fields - an optimised shrub-intercropping system at Keur Matar, Senegal (long-term trial since 2003): shrub density raised to 1500-1833 shrubs/ha by planting, shrubs coppiced annually and the cut biomass incorporated into the soil instead of being burned (p3). Zero-fertilizer plots only. BASELINE (comparator): crop-only subplots where shrubs and their major roots were removed in 2003. This dry-season experiment used drip irrigation until early flowering, then withheld water for 41 days to impose an in-season drought (p4, p6). Mechanism tested: hydraulic redistribution (HR) - shrub roots lift water from moist deep soil and release it into dry surface soil at night, where millet roots take it up (deuterium tracer applied to 1 m deep shrub roots appeared in millet stems within 12-96 h).
context.severity_cue: severe in-season drought that was imposed

context.note: Fig. 2a 'Mean ± standard error of the a cacao and b plantain ... yields in the four production systems' (p5). Contrast estimate AF vs mono -52.3 ± 5.3 (P < 0.001), in the quote. Authors' caveat in the same paragraph (p4): the AF-vs-mono gap was mainly driven by the conventional monoculture - organic monoculture yielded 48% less than conventional monoculture, while organic and conventional agroforestry yielded similarly (P = 0.16); the agroforestry arm also got half the fertiliser dose. 2014 was a regional low-yield year ('unfavorable weather conditions', p4) - not named as a drought, so no hazard tag (#38). context.practice_as_described: Cacao agroforestry (AF) in a long-term randomised field trial at Sara Ana, Alto Beni, Bolivia: cacao (625 trees/ha) planted under shade trees - mainly Inga and Erythrina, plus timber, fruit and palm trees, 304 shade trees/ha - with plantain as a by-crop, replaced by banana in the agroforestry plots from 2012 (p3). BASELINE (comparator): full-sun cacao monoculture (cacao + plantain until end-2011, then cacao alone). Both arms were run under organic and under conventional management (agroforestry conventional 'Afc', agroforestry organic 'Afo', monoculture conventional 'Mc', monoculture organic 'Mo'); the AF-vs-mono contrast pools the two managements. Mechanism (authors, p4): lower light incidence and lower tree vigour under shade reduce cacao yield.

context.note: Table 1 'Seasonal rainfall, above-ground biomass and grain yield for maize grown under 0, 25 and 50% artificial shade (Cg 0%, Cg 25% and Cg 50%) or in the CTd agroforestry system' (p4). Mechanism (authors, p9): understorey maize flowered 5 days later in the wet season but 15-24 days later in seasons when flowering came after available soil moisture was depleted, 'resulting in crop failure'; because artificial shade of similar intensity delayed flowering by at most 5 days, the delay and yield loss are attributed to below-ground competition for water with the trees, which outweighed the benefit of cooler temperatures. BASELINE (comparator): Cg 0% = unshaded sole maize at the same density. The trial also had sole maize under 25% and 50% artificial shade nets (Cg 25%, Cg 50%); these nets mimic shade and are NOT the practice, so they are not used as a comparator or treatment here (catalogue #38c).

context.note: Results 3.2 and Figure 1 'Seasonal mean diurnal timecourses of meristem temperature ... in the CTd agroforestry system' (p4); the text layer prints the degree sign as '8C'. The cooling weakened in later seasons (L95, S95/96) as the trees grew taller and lower branches were pruned, letting air flow under the canopy (p4, p7) - a weakening service, not a harm. Supra-optimal meristem temperatures (above 34 C) occurred in L95 and especially S95/96 (p4), but the cooling is a seasonal-mean shade effect, not mitigation of a named heat event, so no hazard_type (catalogue #38b). Despite the cooling, yield fell under the trees (ev_crop_yield_lott09_1 to _4): below-ground competition outweighed the microclimate benefit (abstract, p1).

context.note: Section 4.3.1 Water accessibility (report p24 = PDF p31). Mechanism: sand behind the dam stores water and protects it from evaporation (p6). Twelve of 137 households said their source now holds water for a shorter period, mostly where the dam broke or water use rose sharply (p31) - kept as context. Design: cross-sectional household survey with five-year recall, with-dam vs without-dam groups; dams not randomly placed; the authors check that rainfall does not explain the group differences (Table 4.1, p29) but households with dams also apply more terracing, bunds and grass lines (p30-31) and the effect of those cannot be separated (p31, p53).
context.practice_as_described: Sand dams: small concrete (mortar and rock) walls 1-4 m high built by communities with the NGO SASOL across ephemeral (seasonal) riverbeds; sand accumulates behind the wall and stores rainy-season runoff as shallow groundwater in the sand, which protects it from evaporation and prolongs the period water can be abstracted from scoop holes (p6, p9). BASELINE (comparator): survey households without a dam (no dam built, or a dam that broke), and each household's own situation before dam construction / five years earlier (recall survey of 98 households with and 39 without dams, 2006; p6).
context.region: Kitui District, eastern Kenya

context.note: p5, with Figure 2 (p4) 'Relationship between peat carbon dioxide (CO2) loss and peat water table level' pooling field fluxes and modelled annual emissions from several studies. Evidence is the water-table gradient across undrained and drained sites, not a before/after rewetting measurement; in deeply drained peat the CO2 data scatter widely and models disagree on the response (p5). No net CO2e balance for rewetted tropical peat is given in the review.
context.practice_as_described: Review of greenhouse-gas dynamics in natural, degraded (drained, deforested, burned) and restored tropical peatlands. Hydrological restoration (rewetting) = blocking drainage canals with dams to bring the water table (WT) closer to the peat surface (p4-p5); vegetation restoration = re-establishing (ideally woody) cover. BASELINE (comparator): drained / degraded peat with a deep water table; the review stresses that in situ data on restored tropical sites are limited (p1).
context.region: lowland ombrotrophic peat swamps of south-east Asia (Borneo, Sumatra, Peninsular Malaysia)

EV_evidence_register.quote:
In both undrained and abandoned drained peatlands 
where the WT can rise up to the peat surface during 
periods when precipitation exceeds water runoff 
capacity, the lowest CO2 flux rate occurs when the 
WT is close to the peat surface (Figure 2; Jauhiainen 
et al. 2005, 2008, 2012a; Hirano et al. 2009, 2014; 
Sundari et al. 2012). This can be explained by the 
reduced oxic space in the uppermost peat, which 
results in reduced rates of aerobic decomposition and 
the consequent CO2 emissions.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: peat CO2 emission from decomposition as the water table approaches the peat surface

relationship.direction_cue:
the lowest CO2 flux rate occurs when the 
WT is close to the peat surface
relationship.outcome_raw: CO2 flux from peat decomposition is lowest when the water table is close to the peat surface, in both undrained and abandoned drained peat, because the oxic layer shrinks and aerobic decomposition slows - the basis for rewetting to cut CO2 loss

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Undrained peat swamp 
forest is at very low risk of fire, even during extreme 
drought conditions (Page et al. 2002), since the WT 
is close to the forest floor and the entire peat column, 
together with the living forest biomass, is almost 
permanently moist. Logged-over forest is at greater 
risk of ignition due to an altered microclimate that 
promotes drying of the peat surface and aboveground 
fuels (Siegert et al. 2001). Peatlands where the WT is 
maintained at an artificially low level by drainage, i.e. 
in or adjacent to agricultural land, is at greatest risk

relationship.direction_cue: agricultural land, is at greatest risk
relationship.outcome_raw: undrained peat swamp forest is at very low fire risk even in extreme drought because the water table is near the forest floor and the peat stays moist; logged-over forest is at greater risk and drained peat (low water table) is at the greatest risk of combustion

context.note: Abstract of the thesis article (p21). Table 5 (Cuadro 5, p30) 'Carbon stored (Mg ha-1) in the aboveground biomass of the shade-canopy plants in different coffee-plantation types': total C1 7.8 c, C2 18.9 b, C3 27.4 ab, C4 35.3 a (F 9.63, P 0.0003; LSD Fisher p<0.05) - every shaded type stores significantly more than full sun. Woody plants: C2 10.2, C3 21.9, C4 29.3 Mg C/ha. Reversal inside the total: the COFFEE plants themselves hold less carbon under shade (C1 7.8 a vs C2 4.6, C3 3.4, C4 3.8 b, P 0.0206). Mechanism: the added shade trees (service, timber, fruit) store carbon in standing woody biomass (abstract p21; results p29). #39 caveat: timber extraction was nil (p37), so the timber-tree stock is standing; firewood is cut on 63% of farms (p30) and musaceae stems are harvested and regrow, so their 1.9 Mg C/ha (7%) is cycling rather than durable storage. Stock, not a rate; aboveground only (no soil or belowground carbon); allometric equations, carbon fraction 0.47 (p25). No N2O / fertiliser emissions accounted, so not a net balance. Artefact = Pinoargote Chang 2014 CATIE MSc thesis, same study as Pinoargote et al. 2016 Forests, Trees and Livelihoods (accepted as artefact of record, Pete 2026-11-06 E1).
context.practice_as_described: Four coffee (Coffea arabica) plantation types on smallholder farms, typed a priori by the botanical make-up of the shade canopy: C1 = coffee in full sun (no shade canopy); C2 = coffee with bananas/plantains (musaceae) and service shade trees (some nitrogen-fixing legumes, mainly Inga spp.); C3 = coffee with service trees and timber trees (Cordia alliodora, Cedrela odorata); C4 = coffee with service trees, timber trees, fruit trees (Citrus, mango, avocado) and musaceae. 27 farms (26.2 ha) in El Cua, El Tuma-La Dalia, Jinotega and Rancho Grande, north-central Nicaragua (4 C1, 8 C2, 8 C3, 7 C4); mean plantation age 8 years, mean shade 44%; conventional management in all types (fungicides, soil and foliar fertiliser, insecticides or berry-borer traps, shade-tree regulation, coffee pruning, chemical and manual weeding) (pp23-24). THIS UNIT: C4 (coffee under service, timber and fruit trees plus musaceae). BASELINE (comparator): C1, coffee grown in full sun without a shade canopy, on neighbouring smallholder farms (space-for-time, cross-sectional).
context.region: north-central Nicaragua (El Cua, El Tuma-La Dalia, Jinotega, Rancho Grande; 509-1199 m a.s.l.)

context.note: Abstract statement (p39 printed, PDF p1); results text p43 says the same without the significance wording. Species-specific: the paper finds the opposite sign with calliandra (ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_2). Leucaena alley crop exceeded calliandra alley crop by 1.2 Mg per ha per season (p44-45) and 2.6 Mg grain per ha per yr annualised (p46, Figure 2). Maize grain yield results reported for SR 1994 to LR 1996 (four seasons); LR 1993 showed no treatment differences, SR 1993 was a crop failure from insufficient rainfall and LR 1994 was disturbed by chafer grubs (p43). Treatment means are shown only in Figure 1 (p44, 'Mean maize grain yield (1994-96 seasons) of the various treatments'), an image with no text layer: values not read. Means separated by Tukey at P < 0.05 (p42). Mechanism (Discussion p47): prunings supply nitrogen to the maize; hedges compete below ground (light competition minimal at 50 cm hedge height); calliandra's dense superficial roots compete harder than leucaena's deep tap root. | Hedgerow species: Leucaena leucocephala. Counted as practice evidence for T3/T6 (Pete 2026-11-07, F3: species specificity matters for T4).
context.practice_as_described: Alley cropping (hedgerow intercropping) of maize between planted hedgerows of leucaena (Leucaena leucocephala), hedges lopped each season and the leafy prunings incorporated into the alley soil, no nitrogen fertiliser (Trt 2). BASELINE: maize monoculture with no trees, both unfertilised (Trt 10) and with 50 kg N/ha fertiliser (Trt 9). Randomised complete block trial, 4 replicates, 9 m x 10 m plots, on-station at the Kenya Agricultural Research Institute (KARI) Regional Research Centre, Embu, central highlands of Kenya (1480 m; 1200-1500 mm rain in two seasons, long rains LR and short rains SR). Hedgerows of calliandra (Calliandra calothyrsus) or leucaena (Leucaena leucocephala) planted April 1992, 4.5 m between hedgerows and 0.5 m within rows, six maize rows (75 cm x 25 cm) per alley; hedges lopped to 50 cm before each maize planting, leafy prunings (about 2 Mg dry matter per ha per season, about 60 kg N) spread and hoe-incorporated, woody stems removed for firewood; root pruning by 1 m trench each season; every plot got basal phosphorus (50 kg P/ha/yr as triple super phosphate). Ten treatments (Trt): 1/2 = calliandra/leucaena alley cropping, prunings incorporated, no fertiliser; 3/4 = calliandra/leucaena alley cropping, prunings removed (carried to Trt 5/6); 5/6 = maize monocrop receiving calliandra/leucaena prunings from outside (biomass transfer), no fertiliser; 7/8 = as 5/6 plus 25 kg N/ha fertiliser; 9 = maize monocrop with 50 kg N/ha (calcium ammonium nitrate, the recommended rate); 10 = maize monocrop, no fertiliser (complete control). Treatments applied from LR 1993 (pp40-42).
context.region: Embu, Eastern Province, central highlands of Kenya (south-eastern slopes of Mt Kenya)

context.practice_as_described: Zai (also tassa, towalen): planting pits 20-40 cm wide and 10-20 cm deep dug with a pick every 80-120 cm in staggered rows on crusted, degraded land at the start of the dry season, the earth thrown downslope as a crescent; the untilled surface (5-10 times the pit area) is the runoff catchment; one or two handfuls of dried manure powder (1-3 t/ha), manure, compost or ash with straw are buried in each pit before the rains, attracting termites; sorghum or millet sown in the pits (PDF p504). context.practice_as_described: Masonry and gabion check dams (seuils imperméables en gabions ou en maçonnerie de gros blocs avec mortier): eleven impermeable sills built across medium ravines of a 49 ha catchment where water was critical at the end of the dry season, sometimes with stilling basins or wells, to trap organic-rich sediment, infiltrate runoff and store water for irrigation and livestock; the trapped "fonds frais" are then cropped intensively (banana, malanga, yam, fruit trees, sugar cane, vegetables) with manure and residues (pp568-569). context.hazard_magnitude: 100-year flood flow, as recorded in 1993; approximately 40 million acre-feet in excess of bank-full discharge over the 80-day flood at St. Louis
context.note: Commentary (Restoration Ecology 3(1):4-17), not a hydrological study. The 13-million-acre figure is a storage-volume calculation (p10: 111 million acre-feet passed St. Louis in 80 days; bank-full discharge 450,000 cfs; excess approximately 40 million acre-feet; 'Distributed at a three-foot depth (the approximate depth of a deep marsh), these waters would have covereda little more than 13 million acres'). No flood routing, no peak/stage modelling, no siting: the authors say 'Hydrologically, of course, this argument is incomplete. The key to the effectiveness of an additional 13 million acres of flood storage is in its location' (p11) and 'Generating the figure of 13 million acres involved some facile number crunching ... The hard work - producing the hydrologic assessments and computer analyses - remains to be done' (p12). Treat as a volume-capacity estimate (STAGE/VOLUME, not PEAK). Severity cue from p5: 'Such a land area, it appears, could have easily contained most of the floodwaters that devastated the valley in 1993.' Magnitude from p10 and p13 ('If the 100-year flood flow, as recorded in 1993, were to be treated'). claim_basis=modelled per lane brief; strength left unspecified (no reduction metric).
context.practice_as_described: Wetland restoration: 'strategically placing at least 13 million acres of wetlands on hydric soils in the basin' (abstract), i.e. restoring riverine and palustrine wetlands on drained hydric soils (former beaver ponds and wetlands) by 'low-scale engineering techniques' so that they 'intercept and hold precipitation where it falls and store floodwaters where they occur' (abstract; p10). Mechanism: storage of excess flood volume at about a three-foot depth (deep marsh). BASELINE (comparator): the present drained and levee-confined basin (wetland area reduced from about 45 to under 20 million acres since 1780).
context.region: Upper Mississippi and Missouri River basins above St. Louis / Thebes, Illinois (USA)

context.note: Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment 110:132-142. OCR'd scan; body pages are two-column and interleaved in the text layer, so all quotes come from the single-column abstract (cached PDF p2; p1 is a repository cover page). Trapping efficiency = deposited / incoming sediment, measured with erosion pins and outflow samplers. Per p8 (interleaved, not quotable) the 54-85% was measured in 1993 only (first year after landscape redesign, 15 major erosion events; total trapping up to 15.3 t/ha/yr); after dredging in early 1994 sedimentation became too small to measure because on-site mulch-tillage erosion control became effective, and the authors estimate long-term trapping at about 50-80% (p8, p11). Sediment trapping (54-85%) exceeded nutrient trapping (35-70%) because delivered sediment was enriched in fines (p8; the line is interleaved with Fig. 4 labels, not quotable). Pond volume is 30-260 m3 per ha of watershed.
context.practice_as_described: Small dry detention ponds at field borders: where runoff concentrates in slope depressions and overtops the downslope field border, the border was raised by earth embankments (1.25-1.66 m high at the pour point) to create a detention pond holding water only during storms, drained by a perforated standpipe into an underground tile outlet with an orifice plate; outflow routed through a grassed waterway or pipes to the toe slope (p2 abstract; p4-5). Fields upslope farmed under integrated farming with mulch tillage and mustard cover crops (potato - winter wheat - maize - winter wheat rotation) (p3). BASELINE (comparator): sediment entering the pond from the upslope field (inflow vs delivered sediment), i.e. without the pond the incoming sediment would leave the field.
context.region: Scheyern Experimental Farm, Tertiary hills about 40 km north of Munich, Bavaria, Germany (4 watersheds 1.6-7.8 ha; 834 mm/yr)

context.practice_as_described: Farmer-managed natural regeneration (FMNR; French 'régénération naturelle assistée', RNA): farmers protect and manage the natural regrowth (shoots) produced by living tree and shrub stumps in their cropped fields - select the shoots to keep, cut the others, prune the kept stems every year and harvest branches for fodder, wood and organic matter (section 'Le principe et fondement de la RNA'); occasionally enriched by direct seeding of useful species. Not planted trees. Maradi and Zinder regions, Niger: parklands of 20 to 80 trees/ha, often dominated by Faidherbia albida (Zinder). BASELINE: control fields without trees ('champs témoins sans arbres') in the same regions.

context.note: Damage-cost-avoided household survey after super cyclone Sidr (15 Nov 2007; p1 'super cyclone Sidr', p3 'Category IV', 'wind speed up to 240 km/h and produced 6 m of tidal waves'). 300 household heads, 100 per site, 5 villages x 20 households per site; recall survey in Dec 2015, eight years after the event (p12: 'completely based on the memory of the respondents'). Kruskal-Wallis test across all THREE sites (Table 3, p8); no pairwise site-A vs site-B test, so significance left not_reported. Mangrove presence varies at site level only (one site per arm), so unreplicated=true. Confounds named by the authors: site-B about 5 km closer to the cyclone path (Table 1: 30 vs 25 km; p11), sites only 'anecdotally similar' in exposure; authors: 'this study is not enough to conclude with a value' (p12). Currency TK (1 US$ = TK 68 in 2007, Table 3 footnote). farming_system left blank: paddy with shrimp/aquaculture mixed culture, most respondents' primary occupation non-farm (Table 2). Mechanism stated by the authors: mangroves attenuate wind and storm surge (p3, p8, p10). Table 3 TML: site-A TK 69,726, site-B TK 133,537, site-C TK 156,589 (H 69.22, p<0.01). Discussion p10 states the same difference as 'mean avoided damage ... TK 63,811 compared to site-B' (not emitted separately as avoided_damage_value: same data, would double-count in the wind_cyclone cell). Abstract restates as US$ 1025 per household, 'about half'.
context.practice_as_described: No intervention: the EXISTING Sundarbans mangrove forest (natural reserve forest, Ramsar/World Heritage site). Site-A = Jiudhara union, Morrelganj, Bagerhat: 'a location in the shadow of mangrove and within a polder' (polder-35/2, embankment 4-5 m). BASELINE = site-B, Bara Bighai union, Patuakhali Sadar: 'a location not in the shadow of mangrove, but within a polder' (polder-43/2, same embankment height). Site-C (no mangrove, no polder) is a grey-infrastructure arm and is NOT the counterfactual used here. 'Polder' = an embanked low-lying area protected by an earthen dyke. 'Shadow of mangrove' = sheltered by the forest from the cyclone's seaward side (p5, Table 1).
context.region: southwest coastal Bangladesh (Bagerhat and Patuakhali districts), Sundarbans fringe

at site-B was almost double compared to site-A, whereas site-C had the largest amount of

EV_evidence_register.quote:
3. Excessive level of shade - Previously, the concept of shade for frost 
protection assumed that the coffee plants needed a complete, permanent 
cover from the shade trees. Under such circumstances, excess shade caused 
coffee production losses comparable to those caused by frosts [Carvalho 
et al., 1961; Franco, 1963]. In southern Brazil floral bud differentiation 
occurs during the winter. If there is not enough light at the canopy level, 
there will generally be more vegetative bud differentiation at the expense 
of flower bud differentiation, thus decreasing coffee production [Cannel, 
1975].

excess shade caused 
coffee production losses
relationship.outcome_raw: coffee production losses under excessive (complete, permanent) shade, compared by the authors with frost losses; mechanism: too little light at the canopy shifts winter bud differentiation from flower to vegetative buds

SRC.study_country is blank for this source; IDN is stated on p2. DiD restoration effect for dams in 2019: -1.1 km-2 (p < 0.05) (p5). Subgroups of the same data (not separate units, #61): significant only where >=4 dams (-1.7 km-2), 1-year-old dams -2.2 km-2 (p = 0.002), 2-year-old dams not significant, insignificant in most land covers except NVO (-5.3 km-2), stronger in the south (p5); effect only within the 0.25 km2 cells around dams, none in larger cells (p5). Dams plus wells reduced 2019 hotspots by 22% across 3,920 km2 and account for 38% of the 2015-2019 reduction (p7, p9) - combined figure kept here, not emitted. Cropland: restored areas still showed a (smaller) reduction while unrestored cropland rose (p8). Authors suggest dams are less effective in strong El Nino years (p8, speculative - not encoded).

We estimated blue carbon sequestration by calculating how 
much mangrove restoration reduced CO2 concentrations in the 
atmosphere.  We used measurements reported in Cameron 
et al. (2019) of GHG emissions of t 17 ± 5.6 tCO2e per year 
from partially inundated aquaculture ponds in Indonesia with 
no mangrove coverage. Then, we added a 15 ± 5 tCO2e per 
year biomass sequestration rate from mangrove restoration 
(average 35 years) as estimated by Cameron et al. (2018). 
Finally, we added the soil carbon burial estimated in 6.5 ± 2.1 
tCO2e per year by Alongi (2014) to come up with a total blue 
carbon reduction per year per hectare of 38.5 ± 12.7 tCO2e.

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Beijing Forestry University partnered with Mangrove Foundation and Dongtai 
Coastal Economic Development District to restore 50 ha of aquaculture fishing 
pond into a high tide roosting site, under the mechanism of eco-compensation. 
The main objectives were to restore muddy tidal areas, sand beach and shallow 
water with water levels controlled by a sluice gate. Monitoring facilities, nature 
education information and a visitor centre were also developed as part of the 
restoration project to realise its ecosystem services. These include research, 
education, and ecotourism. During the preparation of Tiaozini and Yancheng’s 
nomination for World Heritage in 2018, the local government established a 
wetland park in the reclaimed area, restoring a high tide roosting site. 
While the cost to fishery companies was estimated at around $100,000 per 
year, the ecotourism and biodiversity benefits have been significant. Shorebird 
populations have increased markedly, from around 70,000 shorebirds in 
2020 to 350,000 birds in 2024.

context.note: Discussion p8, drawing on Results p5-7. Columns read: Ecozone · Continent · Forest type · Mean · Median · SD · CI (95%) · No. of chronosequences and/or permanent plots. Unit is BIOMASS (dry matter), not carbon: carbon ≈ 0.47 x biomass (paper p4; IPCC carbon fraction) - not converted here. YS rate = AGB predicted at 20 yr divided by 20 (assumes linear growth, p4-5). LINEAGE: this source is the primary for the tropical/subtropical rows of IPCC 2019 Refinement Vol 4 Ch4 Table 4.9 (identical values); the IPCC rows are NOT emitted separately. Partial data overlap with Cook-Patton 2020 (compilations share ForC/Poorter 2016 plots; Cook-Patton p5 says some of its input data were used to update these IPCC rates) - flagged for Pete, not collapsed. Old-growth (OG) rows not emitted: no intervention (existing-forest sink, not a restoration effect).
context.practice_as_described: Natural regeneration: younger secondary forest (stand age 20 years or less since the last anthropogenic disturbance or abandonment) regrowing naturally, without planting; chronosequence plots. BASELINE: none - an absolute rate (mean net change in above-ground live tree biomass per hectare per year, dry matter), not a with/without contrast.
context.region: Tropical rainforest, Africa (FAO global ecological zone x continent; pantropical plot-data synthesis, 42 countries)

EV_evidence_register.quote:
If the priority is maximizing per-hectare carbon removals from 
2025 to 2050, existing secondary forests generally outperform new 
regeneration (Fig. 2c). The optimal 25-year window for each grid 
cell (19–43 years on average) could remove 20.7 ± 13.1 MgC ha−1 on 
average, compared with 18.8 ± 12.4 MgC ha−1 over the first 25 years 
of new regeneration.

context.note: Model: random forest on 109,708 field estimates (5-year age classes) x 66 covariates, Chapman-Richards curves per ~1-km cell, stand age 1-100 yr; validation RMSE 0.62 Mg C ha-1 yr-1, R2 0.41, worst in 5-10 yr classes (RMSE 1.93, p4). Above-ground live carbon only. p4; on average +10% versus new regeneration (in the quote), up to 820% in some cells; the Discussion (p4) says "up to 8-fold by 2050". Existing-forest study: comparator_policy routes it to protection_cbfm, kept out of the NbS roll-up. No lineage collapse: Cook-Patton 2020 makes no protection claim. Carbon-market eligibility barrier for this practice is unit ev_finance_credit_access_robinson25_4.

BASELINE in the paper: new natural regeneration over its first 25 years (18.8 ± 12.4 MgC/ha); recorded as an absolute value because the true counterfactual of protection (clearance) is not modelled.

context.note: p5. Operational barrier: carbon-market methodologies do not credit protection or improved management of very young secondary forests; reforestation projects need land cleared for at least 10 years and forest-protection projects need forests at least 10 years old (in the quote). Second-hand: the authors cite Brancalion et al. 2024 (ref 29, "A call to develop carbon credits for second-growth forests", Nat. Ecol. Evol. 8:179-180). Global statement; not tied to a country.
context.practice_as_described: Protecting very young (under 10 years) secondary forests, or managing them, as a carbon-financed climate mitigation action.

EV_evidence_register.quote:
However, there are limited mechanisms to protect young second-
ary forests. No carbon market methodologies currently credit protect-
ing or improving management in very young secondary forests29. Rules 
require at least 10 years of cleared land prior to reforestation projects, 
while forest protection projects require forests to be at least 10 years 
old. Improved forest management projects only apply in places with 
logging operations, covering a fraction of secondary forests29.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: limited mechanisms (carbon-market methodologies) to protect young secondary forests

context.note: Multilevel meta-analysis, 734 effect sizes from 59 studies for the restored-vs-unrestored comparison (p4); 83 studies overall. PICOS caveat: terrestrial restoration in general, not forest-only - 59% of effect sizes from woody and 41% from non-woody ecosystems; past land use semi-natural, agriculture, forestry, mining, urban (p4, p3). Tagged cross_family because natural and assisted restoration are pooled. Moderators from the same dataset (not separate units, #61): restored-site biodiversity rose about 0.6% per year with restoration age relative to unrestored (LnRR 0.006 per yr, p5); restoration of former agricultural and semi-natural land gave larger gains than forestry, mining or urban land (Figure 5a, p8); site size had no effect (p5). context.hazard_magnitude: expected annual values integrated over nine return periods (2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, and 1,000 y) of storm surge plus waves, tropical cyclones included (p8)
context.note: Global model (PNAS 2026; restoration explicitly modelled): van Zelst XBeach wave-attenuation lookup + EuroTop dike overtopping on 495,361 shore-normal transects, GLOFRIS coastal flood risk at ~1 km, GTSR surge enriched with IBTrACS cyclones (p8). ONE DATASET, ONE UNIT (#61): the same runs give expected annual damage (EAD) to built-up assets reduced by US$800 million/yr = 2.3% of damage on mangrove coastlines (same quote); future 2080 reductions 3.8% (EAD) and 5.4% (EAAP) of total impacts (p2); West Africa has the largest relative reduction, 11% of EAD and 18% of EAAP, Southeast Asia the largest absolute (p2). People-affected chosen because T3 is risk to livelihoods. Strength slight (3% < 10% band) - the global share is diluted by coastlines with no restoration potential; residual risk 'remains high' (p2). Authors' caveats (p6-7): assumes functional dikes everywhere mangroves are restored (many restoration sites lack dikes, so benefit may be over- or under-stated); restored stands assumed to keep pace with sea level; cyclone damage to mangroves NOT modelled; wave attenuation nonlinear in forest width, so small patches add little. Benefit applies once restored stands are established (timescale not stated, left blank). Income context: global mixed; country list not given for the global figure.

BASELINE: the same dikes (FLOPROS protection standards) with present mangrove widths (Global Mangrove Watch 2010) and no restoration; benefit = difference between the two flood-risk runs (p2, p8).

In the semi-arid tropics and arid environments, RWH has already played an important role
in stabilizing crop yields by mitigating the negative impacts of high evapotranspiration.

deficits between the 1990s and the 2050s should not always be interpreted as potentially
benefiting from climate change. This is particularly true in the Sahel, where an increased
frequency of lethal high temperature events could have devastating effects on food production
(Battisti and Naylor 2009).

context.note: NATURAL stands (no planting) - asset evidence for the hazard->mangrove link only. Single-species system (A. marina var. australasica). 8 sites, 7-month monitoring + decadal radioisotope sedimentation rates. Chronic fine-mud accretion up to 23 mm/yr did NOT harm the stand - plants were healthier there (coded 'none' = no damage, conservatively, rather than 'negative'). Counter-signal in the same data: unit 2 (higher seedling/pneumatophore death at the top site). HIC temperate edge-of-range system - low transferability.
context.practice_as_described: No restoration: naturally expanding Avicennia marina var. australasica stands (mangrove cover up 50% or more 1955-2000 as catchment urbanisation raised sediment input).
context.region: Mangemangeroa and Waikopua estuaries, Whitford embayment, Auckland, North Island, New Zealand

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Our study was conducted at an estuary that is experi-
encing high rates of sedimentation (as high as 23 mm
yr–1) with associated increases in mangrove plants over
large areas of the estuary. We recorded clear differ-
ences in both plant and benthic communities along a
gradient of decreasing sedimentation. Mangrove plant
architecture and health were linked to high mud con-
tent of the sediment and elevated sedimentation pat-
terns. Mangrove plants at the landward sites, charac-
terised by a high percentage of mud and relatively high
TP, TN and organic content, were taller, had higher
numbers of pneumatophores and had the highest num-
bers of new seedlings over the monitoring period. Fur-
ther, Fv/Fm indicated that mangrove plants were less
stressed at these upper estuarine sites.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: mangrove plant architecture and health vs sedimentation

relationship.direction_cue:
were taller, had higher
numbers of pneumatophores and had the highest num-
bers of new seedlings
relationship.outcome_raw: mangrove architecture and health along a gradient of sedimentation up to 23 mm/yr: plants at the high-sedimentation, muddy landward sites were taller, had more pneumatophores and new seedlings, and lower photosynthetic stress

context.note: Asset threat at the ESTABLISHMENT stage: wave/current reworking of a muddy substrate (erosion pins: <1 cm SW vs 17 cm NE over Sept 2014-Mar 2015) prevents seedling establishment. Natural recruitment, not planting, but the mechanism is what planting on an exposed eroding mudflat faces. hazard_type wave_exposure = 'planting on exposed, eroding shores' (the quote names waves and currents). Two-site contrast, no statistics -> unreplicated.
context.practice_as_described: Mangrove fringe of Cu Lao Dung: after conversion to shrimp ponds and sugar-cane fields triggered wave erosion, 'more mangroves were planted in the 1980s to protect the shoreline'; the pioneer Sonneratia caseolaris 'was planted at the shore' and other species colonised naturally (p3). Stand = planted + naturally expanded fringe.
context.region: Cu Lao Dung island fringe, Song Hau (Bassac) River mouth, Mekong Delta, Viet Nam

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Field measurements along Cu Lao Dung 
show that a dense mangrove forest mostly 
formed of saplings has encroached upon 
the tidal flats in the southwest area, while 
large mature trees with few seedlings char-
acterize the northeast fringe (Figure 3).
We ascribe this difference to bottom 
characteristics, with sandy sediments in 
the southwest providing a relatively stable 
substrate for mangrove expansion, while 
waves and currents erode the soft, muddy 
bottom of the northeast fringe, thus pre-
venting establishment. This observa-
tion was corroborated by placement of 
erosion pins that showed erosion of less 
than 1 cm between September 2014 and 
March 2015 in the southwest area and 
17 cm in the northeast.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: erosion of soft muddy bottom preventing establishment

relationship.outcome_raw: waves and currents eroding the soft muddy bottom prevent mangrove seedling establishment (northeast fringe: mature trees, few seedlings) vs dense sapling encroachment on the stable sandy southwest fringe; erosion pins

EV_evidence_register.attribution: Balke et al. 2011, 2013

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Avicennia alba and Sonneratia alba seed-
lings (the latter grow in the Mekong Delta 
fringe) are sensitive to erosion during 
early establishment; they can only estab-
lish if the bottom substrate is stable. 
Balke et al. (2013) indicate that as little 
as 1–3 cm of vertical erosion can result 
in seedling failure. In addition, if a storm 
that produces strong currents hits the 
mangroves, the seedlings dislodge (Balke 
et al., 2011).

relationship.outcome_raw: seedlings of the pioneer species A. alba and S. alba fail with as little as 1–3 cm of vertical erosion and are dislodged by storm currents

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Through detailed observations of a fringe 
mangrove forest in Vietnam, we were able 
to identify a series of feedbacks between 
hydrodynamics, sediment transport, and 
mangrove trees (Figure  8). These feed-
backs affect the large-scale evolution of 
the entire mangrove fringe. As a result, 
we find that mangroves do engineer the 
landscape, favoring sediment deposition 
and dissipating waves and preferentially 
colonizing sandy substrates.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: sediment deposition / wave dissipation by the fringe forest

relationship.outcome_raw: fringe mangroves favour sediment deposition (trap sediment) and dissipate waves, engineering the landscape

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Significant increase in total number of pneumatophores in subplots from P- 6 to P-13
(table 4) was associated with the increase of large S. alba tree density. Therefore the decrease of the
number and average above-ground length of pneumatophores at the inner plots where density of large
S. alba trees was similar to that of P-13 attributed to burying of pneumatophores. Usually S' alba has
ability to form the new cable root with pneumatophores from higher level in case of sediments bury
old ones (fomlinson, 1989). But newly established pneumatophores and cable root were not found
with dead individuals at inner plots. Judging from these observation, decline of S. alba is attributed to
inhibition of normal respiration with burying of pneumatophores.

context.note: Replicated mesocosm experiment (12 replicates per species x treatment; randomisation not stated -> quasi_experimental). TARGET CELL: modest burial at the rate typical of the pioneer zone (cumulative 3 cm in 3 weeks) did little damage at the seedling stage; only the smallest-seeded species lost seedlings (separate species unit 2). Authors note (p11) the accretion dose could not be raised and that complete burial is often deadly (cited) - a dose limit, so 'none' holds only at this burial depth.
context.practice_as_described: Mesocosm seedling establishment: ripe propagules sown 2.5 cm into pots of silty estuary sediment (S. apetala: germinated seeds planted), tidal inundation 5 h/day; bed-level treatments weeks 2-4: erosion (2 cm removed/week, cumulative 6 cm), control, accretion (1 cm added/week, cumulative 3 cm); 34 days; 12 replicates per species x treatment. Authors frame results for mangrove restoration planting (p12).
context.region: outdoor mesocosm, south China (Pearl River Estuary silty sediment; propagules from Guangzhou Nansha, Hainan Dong Zhai Gang and a third site)

context.note_append, relationship.outcome_raw: p.72: the 'opposite' is explained in the next sentence: Abdulai (2018) found shade trees 'led to soil water competition with the coffee trees during severe drought, resulting in enhanced coffee mortality'. That is a drought harm.
